Some activated macrophages may fuse, forming multinucleated giant cells. Collections of activated macrophages, often with T lymphocytes are seen in granulomatous inflammation. Sometimes it is associated with central caseating necrosis.

Granulomas may be formed in response to various stimuli:

• Immune granulomas - due to T-cell mediated response; macrophages activate T cells to produce cytokines, such as IL-2 and IFN-γ

• Foreign body granulomas - due to inert foreign bodies in the absence of a T-cell mediated response

questions.question: Epithelioid granulomas are not seen in which of the following diseases?
questions.explanation:
Kikuchi's lymphadenitis is associated with histiocytic necrotizing lymphadenitis. It does not show epithelioid granulomatous lesions.

Common conditions characterized by epithelioid granuloma formation:

• Tuberculosis

• Sarcoidosis (non-caseating granuloma)

• Brucellosis

• Cat scratch disease (stellate shaped or round granuloma)

• Syphilis (gumma )

• Lymphogranuloma inguinale

• Leprosy

• Inflammatory bowel disease

• Toxoplasmosis

questions.question: A pathologist observes the given findings during the examination of a lymph node sample. Which of the following is the least likely cause?
questions.explanation:
The given histopathological image of a lymph node shows a non-caseating granuloma. Tuberculosis is least likely as it is commonly associated with caseating granulomas.

Non-caseating granulomas can be seen in the following conditions:

• Leprosy

• Cat-scratch disease

• Sarcoidosis

• Berylliosis

• Crohn's disease

• Hypersenitive pneumonitis

• Foreign body granuloma

• Q fever

• Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's).

• Hodgkin's lymphoma

questions.question: Which of the following structures lack labile cells?
questions.explanation:
The liver contains stable cells, not labile cells.

Based on the regenerative capacity of cells, tissues are classified into 3 types:

• Labile tissues

• Stable tissues

• Permanent tissues

Labile cells refer to continuously proliferating cells that are lost and replaced by the maturation of stem cells and the proliferation of these mature cells. Tissues containing these cells can readily regenerate after an injury as long as the pool of stem cells is preserved.

Some examples of labile cells include:

• Hematopoietic cells in the bone marrow

• Majority of surface epithelia -

• Stratified squamous epithelia of the skin, oral cavity, vagina, and cervix

• Cuboidal epithelia of the ducts draining exocrine organs (salivary glands, biliary tract)

• Columnar epithelium of the GIT, uterus, and fallopian tubes

• Transitional epithelium of the urinary tract

questions.question: Which of the following tissues does not consist of stable cells?
questions.explanation:
Cardiac muscle does not contain stable cells. It contains permanent cells which are terminally differentiated and non-proliferative.

Based on the regenerative capacity of cells, tissues are classified into 3 types:

• Labile tissues

• Stable tissues

• Permanent tissues

Stable cells are quiescent (in the G0 stage of the cell cycle) and have only minimal proliferative activity in their normal state. However, they can divide in response to injury or loss of tissue mass.

They include the following:

• Parenchyma of solid tissues (liver, kidney, and pancreas)

• Endothelial cells

• Fibroblasts

• Smooth muscle cells

questions.question: Which of the following does not contain permanent cells?
questions.explanation:
Smooth muscle does not contain permanent cells. It consists of stable cells that are capable of dividing in response to injury or loss of tissue mass.

Based on the regenerative capacity of cells, tissues are classified into 3 types:

• Labile tissues

• Stable tissues

• Permanent tissues

Permanent cells are those which are considered to be terminally differentiated and non-proliferative in postnatal life. In permanent tissues, the repair is typically dominated by scar formation. These cells include:

• Neurons

• Cardiac muscle

• Skeletal muscle - contains satellite cells attached to the endomysial sheath which have some regenerative capacity

questions.question: Oval cells are seen in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Oval cells refer to stem cells in the liver. They are located in the canals of Hering.

Regeneration of the liver occurs by two major mechanisms:

• Proliferation of remaining hepatocytes - occurs following partial hepatectomy (resection of up to 90% of the liver can be corrected by this mechanism)

• Repopulation from progenitor cells (oval cells) - occurs following chronic liver injury or inflammation

questions.question: Which of the following is a false statement regarding TGF-β?
options: It increases the synthesis of collagen
It increases the degradation of the extracellular matrix
It is involved in the development of fibrosis in solid organs
questions.answer: B. It increases the degradation of the extracellular matrix
questions.explanation:
TGF-β (transforming growth factor-β) decreases the degradation of the extracellular matrix by inhibiting metalloproteinases.

It is produced by most cells in granulation tissue, including alternatively activated macrophages.

The functions of TGF-β include:

• Stimulates fibroblast migration and proliferation

• Increases synthesis of collagen and fibronectin (connective tissue proteins)

• Decreased degradation of ECM by inhibiting metalloproteinases

• Involved in scar formation after injury

• Development of fibrosis in lung, liver, and kidneys following chronic inflammation

• Anti-inflammatory action by inhibiting lymphocyte proliferation and activity

questions.question: All of the following delay healing except:
questions.explanation:
Glucocorticoid excess results in delayed healing, not glucocorticoid deficiency.

Various factors affect wound healing including mechanical factors (pressure and torsion and site of injury) and location and extent of the injury.

Vitamin C helps in the activation of prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases which help in the hydroxylation of procollagen. As inadequately hydroxylated procollagen is vulnerable to enzymatic degradation, vitamin C plays an essential role in wound healing.

questions.question: In healing by primary intention, by when do macrophages replace neutrophils at the site of injury?
questions.explanation:
By day 3 of healing by primary intention, macrophages replace the neutrophils at the site of injury.

The sequence of events in wound healing is as follows:

Time after injury
Events

Within 24 hours

Neutrophils:

• Migrate from the incision margin towards the fibrin clot

• Release proteolytic enzymes that begin to clear the debris

Basal cells:

• Located at the cut edge of the epidermis

• Show increased mitotic activity

24 to 48 hours

Epithelial cells:

• Migrate and proliferate from the wound edges towards the center

• Deposit basement membrane components

• Form a continuous epithelial layer that closes the wound

Day 3

• Macrophages become predominant, with very few neutrophils

• Granulation tissue progressively invades the incision space

• Collagen fibers at the incision margins

• Increased thickness of the epithelial layer through continued epithelial proliferation

Day 5

• Neovascularization reaches its peak as granulation tissue fills the incisional space

• As new vessels are leaky, new granulation tissue is often edematous

2nd week

• Continued collagen accumulation

• Fibroblast proliferation.

End of the 1st month

• Scar contains cellular connective tissue

• Largely devoid of inflammatory cells

• Covered by an essentially normal epidermis

questions.question: A 38-year-old man underwent excision of a lipoma. The swelling had been excised with a clear linear incision and was sutured cleanly. In this wound, when would you expect peak neovascularization?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario of a clean surgical incision that is sutured is an example of healing by primary intention. In this type of healing, neovascularization reaches its peak by day 5, as granulation tissue fills the incisional space.

These new vessels are leaky, allowing the passage of plasma proteins and fluid into the extravascular space. Hence, new granulation tissue is often edematous.

questions.question: A patient presented with an abscess on his back. Septic precautions were taken and the abscess was drained. On follow up, a healthy scar was visible. What is the type of collagen seen in the provisional matrix in this type of healing?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is an example of wound healing by secondary intention. The initial provisional matrix in this type of healing is composed of type III collagen, fibrin, and plasma fibronectin.

It is later replaced by a matrix composed primarily of type I collagen.

This type of healing occurs when cell or tissue loss is more extensive, such as in large wounds, abscesses, ulceration, and ischemic necrosis in parenchymal organs. The repair process involves a combination of regeneration and scarring.

questions.question: The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair may give rise to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen during repair leads to the formation of hypertrophic scar. When this scar tissue grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound, it is known as a keloid.

Collagen plays a role in the normal adherence of tissue edges at the site of injury. Contraction in the size of a wound is an important part of the normal healing process. An exaggeration of this process gives rise to contractures. They are particularly prone to develop on the palms, soles, anterior thorax and are commonly seen after serious burns.

Inadequate formation of granulation tissue or formation of a scar leads to wound dehiscence and ulceration.

The following image shows a hypertrophic scar.

questions.question: A 24-year-old man comes with the following findings. He says that he cut himself while shaving 3 months back. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The history of a shaving cut and the image showing a large area of scar tissue are suggestive of a keloid.

A keloid refers to excess accumulation of collagen at the scar site with growth of the scar tissue beyond the boundaries of the original wound. It does not regress.

Option A: Exuberant granulation or proud flesh refers to the protrusion of excessive amounts of granulation tissue above the level of the surrounding skin. This blocks re-epithelialization.

Option B: The accumulation of excessive amounts of collagen may give rise to a raised scar known as a hypertrophic scar. However, it remains within the boundaries of the original scar.

Option D: Pyogenic granuloma is a benign, vascular tumor.

questions.question: A patient presented to the OPD with the following finding on her finger. She says that she cut her finger while chopping vegetables 2 weeks ago. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and clinical findings are suggestive of exuberant granulation.

It is a deviation in wound healing where excessive amounts of granulation tissue protrude above the level of the surrounding skin and blocks re-epithelialization. It is also known as proud flesh.

questions.question: In postoperative patients, what is the strength of the incision site in comparison with normal skin following suture removal at the end of 1 week?
questions.explanation:
When sutures are removed, usually at 1 week, the wound strength is approximately 10% of that of normal skin.

This increases rapidly over the next 4 weeks. Wound strength reaches approximately 70 to 80% of normal by 3 months. Beyond this, there is not much improvement.

questions.question:
A patient presented with the following finding. Which of the following can cause this condition?

1. Elevated vascular hydrostatic pressure
2. Reduced vascular hydrostatic pressure
3. Elevated plasma osmotic pressure
4. Reduced plasma osmotic pressure
questions.explanation:
The finding seen in the given image is pitting edema. Edema can be caused by elevated hydrostatic pressure and reduced colloid osmotic pressure.

Under normal circumstances, there is little net movement of fluid out of vessels due to the balance of:

• Vascular hydrostatic pressure which has the tendency to push water and salts out of capillaries into the interstitial space

• Plasma osmotic pressure or colloid oncotic pressure which has a tendency to pull water and salts back into vessels.

The pressure dynamics seen inside a capillary is given below.

At arterial end
At venous end

• Capillary hydrostatic pressure = 30-35 mmHg

• Capillary hydrostatic pressure = 15-20 mmHg

• Osmotic Pressure = 25 mmHg

• Osmotic Pressure = 25 mmHg

• Hydrostatic Pressure > Osmotic Pressure → Fluid moves out of the capillary

• Hydrostatic Pressure < Osmotic Pressure → Fluid moves into the capillary

Many pathologic disorders are associated with an increase in capillary hydrostatic pressure or a decrease in plasma osmotic pressure, which lead to edema.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about transudate?
options: It is a non-inflammatory edema or effusion
It is a protein-poor and cell-poor fluid
It has a specific gravity of less than 1.012
It is caused by increased vascular permeability
questions.answer: D. It is caused by increased vascular permeability
questions.explanation:
Transudate results from increased fluid pressures or diminished oncotic forces in the plasma and is not due to increased vascular permeability.

There are 2 types of extravascular fluid - transudate and exudate

Transudate
Exudate

Non-inflammatory edema
Inflammatory edema

Ultrafiltrate of plasma
Increased vascular permeability caused by inflammatory mediators

Low protein content (<3g/dl), mainly albumin
High (>3g/dl) protein content

No tendency to coagulate
Coagulates readily due to high content of fibrinogen

Low specific gravity (<1.012)
High specific gravity (>1.018)

Low LDH levels
High LDH levels

Low cell count (< 500-1000/ µL)
High cell count

Eg. Edema in congestive cardiac failure
Eg. Pus

These differences are depicted in the image below.

questions.question: In which of the following conditions does edema result from decreased colloidal osmotic pressure?
questions.explanation:
In nephrotic syndrome, edema occurs due to massive proteinuria that leads to a decrease in plasma colloid osmotic pressure.

The common causes of reduced plasma osmotic pressure are conditions that cause inadequate synthesis or increased loss of albumin (mainly) and other plasma proteins from circulation. These conditions include:

• Protein-losing glomerulopathies (nephrotic syndrome)

• Liver cirrhosis (ascites)

• Malnutrition

• Protein-losing gastroenteropathy

Edema can also occur due to increased hydrostatic pressure as a result of impaired venous return. This is seen in conditions like:

• Congestive heart failure

• Deep venous thrombosis

• Renal artery stenosis

questions.question: Which of the following is not true?
options: Periorbital edema is seen in severe renal disease
Pitting edema occurs due to edema in subcutaneous tissues
Exudative effusions are typically protein-rich and cloudy
Chylous peritoneal effusion is an example of an exudate
questions.answer: D. Chylous peritoneal effusion is an example of an exudate
questions.explanation:
Chylous peritoneal effusion caused by the lymphatic blockage is an example of a transudate.

Transudative effusions are typically protein-poor, translucent, and straw-colored. However, there may be certain exceptions like chylous peritoneal effusions which may be milky due to the presence of lipids absorbed from the gut.

Exudative effusions are protein-rich and often cloudy due to the presence of WBCs.

Subcutaneous edema has the following features:

• Dependent edema - dependent areas (towards gravity) have high hydrostatic pressures i.e., in the legs when standing and the sacrum when recumbent

• Pitting edema - finger pressure over markedly edematous subcutaneous tissue displaces the interstitial fluid and leaves a depression.

Edema resulting from renal dysfunction often appears initially in parts of the body containing loose connective tissue, such as the eyelids. Thus, periorbital edema is a characteristic finding in severe renal disease.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false?
options: Arteriolar dilation is seen in hyperemia.
questions.answer: D. Congestion is seen in inflammation
questions.explanation:
Hyperemia is seen in inflammation, not congestion.

The differences between hyperemia and congestion are summarised below:

Hyperemia
Congestion

Active process due to arteriolar dilation
Passive process due to impaired venous outflow

Edema is absent
Edema is present

Red color of the tissues
Blue-red color of the tissue (due to deoxyhemoglobin)

Seen in inflammation
Seen in right heart failure and portal venous obstruction in cirrhosis

questions.question: An 82-year-old man presents to the ER with fever and tachycardia since last night. On examination, he is drowsy, his BP is 92/54 mmHg and his temperature is 103 °F. His wife tells you he had been diagnosed with a urinary tract infection 5 days ago for which he had been prescribed antibiotics. He is a known case of colon cancer and also has a history of myocardial infarction 6 months ago. What type of shock is he likely suffering from?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of septic shock as a result of gram-negative sepsis originating from a urinary tract infection.

Gram-negative organisms contain lipopolysaccharide in the outer membrane, which triggers the release of cytokines, such as tumor necrosis factor (TNF). These cytokines cause a cascade of events culminating in increased capillary permeability and redistribution of circulatory volume into the interstitium. It is also known as warm shock, due to fever and increased perfusion.

Other types of shock are:

• Anaphylactic shock - sudden circulatory collapse due to type I hypersensitivity reaction

• Cardiogenic shock - ventricular failure, often following myocardial infarction; is a form of cold shock

• Hypovolemic shock - due to blood or fluid loss

questions.question: What is the first step of hemostasis?
options: Binding of platelets to exposed vWF
questions.explanation:
The first step of hemostasis is arteriolar vasoconstriction.

The normal process of hemostasis is as follows:

1. Arteriolar vasoconstriction - After vascular injury, local neurohumoral factors induce transient vasoconstriction.

2. Primary hemostasis - The various steps involved in this process are:

• Platelets bind via glycoprotein Ib (GpIb) receptors to von Willebrand factor (vWF) on exposed extracellular matrix (ECM)

• Activation of platelets which undergo a change in shape and release their granules

• Released adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and thromboxane A2 (TxA2) induce additional platelet aggregation through platelet GpIIb-IIIa receptor binding to fibrinogen

• Formation of the primary platelet plug

3. Secondary hemostasis - Local activation of the coagulation cascade involving tissue factor and platelet phospholipids results in fibrin polymerization, cementing the platelets into a definitive secondary hemostatic plug.

4. Clot stabilization and resorption - Counter-regulatory mechanisms, mediated by tissue plasminogen activator (tPA, a fibrinolytic product) and thrombomodulin, confine the hemostatic process to the site of injury.

questions.question: Which of the following coagulation factors is bound and activated by tissue factor?
questions.explanation:
The tissue factor binds and activates factor VII.

Tissue factor is produced by the subendothelial cells in the vessel wall such as vascular smooth muscle cells and fibroblasts. It is a membrane-bound procoagulant glycoprotein.

Secondary hemostasis involves a sequence of events, which results in the polymerization of fibrin. This is achieved by cross-linking fibrin monomers into insoluble strands that serve to stabilize the loose platelet clot formed in primary hemostasis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not found in α-granules of platelets?
questions.explanation:
Serotonin is present in the dense or delta(δ) granules of the platelets, not alpha(α) granules.

Platelets are disc-shaped, anucleate cell fragments that are released from the megakaryocytes in the bone marrow into the bloodstream. The functions of these platelets depend on their glycoprotein receptors, contractile cytoskeleton, and cytoplasmic granules.

There are two types of cytoplasmic granules present in platelets:

• Alpha granules

• Dense or delta granules

α-granules contain:

• Adhesion molecule P-selectin on their membranes

• Proteins involved in coagulation like -

• Fibrinogen

• Coagulation factor V

• vWF

• Protein factors involved in wound healing like -

• Fibronectin

• Platelet factor 4 (a heparin-binding chemokine)

• Platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF)

• Transforming growth factor β (TGF β)

 δ-granules contain:

• Adenosine diphosphate (ADP) and adenosine triphosphate (ATP)

• Ionized calcium

• Serotonin

• Epinephrine

questions.question: A patient with prolonged bleeding is found to have vitamin K deficiency. The function of which of the following clotting factors would be unaffected in this condition?
questions.explanation:
A deficiency of vitamin K does not alter the function of factor V.

Vitamin K is required as a cofactor for the γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX, and X. Calcium binds to γ-­carboxylated glutamic acid residues that are present in these factors during clotting.

This action of vitamin K is antagonized by drugs such as warfarin, which is widely used as an anticoagulant.

questions.question: The function of which of the following factors is not screened by the partial thromboplastin time assay?
questions.explanation:
The partial thromboplastin time (PTT) assay screens the function of the proteins in the intrinsic pathway. As factor VII is only a part of the extrinsic pathway, it cannot be assessed by this test.

The factors assessed by the PTT assay are XII, XI, IX, VIII, X, V, and II and fibrinogen.

In this assay, clotting of plasma is initiated by the addition of negatively charged particles (e.g., ground glass) that activate factor XII (Hageman factor) together with phospholipids and calcium, and the time to fibrin clot formation is recorded.

questions.question: What is the function of thrombomodulin?
questions.explanation:
Thrombomodulin is an anticoagulant.

It is produced by all endothelial cells except those in cerebral microcirculation. It binds to thrombin on the endothelial cell surface. When bound in this complex, thrombin loses its ability to activate coagulation factors and platelets, and instead cleaves and activates protein C. Activated protein C/protein S complex is a potent inhibitor of coagulation factors Va and VIIIa. This action results in an anticoagulant effect.

The effect of recombinant thrombomodulin administration in sepsis-induced coagulopathy and DIC is being studied currently.

Other important anticoagulant substances are:

• Antithrombin III - It inhibits the activity of thrombin and other factors like XIIa, XIa, Xa, and IXa. It is activated by binding to heparin-like molecules.

• Proteins C and S - These proteins are vitamin K–dependent proteins that inactivate factors Va and VIIIa.

• Endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2) and nitric oxide (NO) - These are potent vasodilators and inhibitors of platelet aggregation.

• Tissue factor pathway inhibitor - This is derived from the endothelium and inhibits tissue factor VIIa and Xa molecules.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of Virchow's triad?
questions.explanation:
Hyperviscosity is not part of Virchow’s triad. However, hyperviscosity states as in polycythemia vera may, in turn, cause small vessel stasis that may cause thrombosis.

Virchow's triad in thrombosis:

1. Injury to endothelial cells can alter local blood flow and affect coagulability.

2. Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), in turn, can cause endothelial injury.

3. Hypercoagulability of blood

These factors may promote thrombosis independently or in combination.

questions.question: In which of the following structures are lines of Zahn seen?
questions.explanation:
Thrombi often have grossly and microscopically apparent laminations called lines of Zahn. These are formed by pale platelet and fibrin deposits alternating with darker red cell-rich layers.

They signify that a thrombus has formed in flowing blood. Their presence can therefore distinguish antemortem clots from the nonlaminated postmortem clots.

The below histopathological image of a thrombus shows these alternating bands called lines of Zahn.

questions.question: Which of the following do chicken fat clots refer to?
questions.explanation:
Chicken fat clots refer to post-mortem clots i.e., clots that are formed after death.

Postmortem clots are gelatinous and have a dark red (currant jelly) dependent portion where red cells have settled by gravity and a yellow (chicken fat) upper portion due to coagulation of plasma.

Antemortem clots can be differentiated from postmortem clots by:

• Presence of lines of Zahn

• Attachment to the underlying vessel wall

questions.question: Saddle embolus is seen in which of the following vessels?
questions.explanation:
An embolus in the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery is referred to as a saddle embolus.

Pulmonary emboli (PE) originate from deep venous thromboses and are the most common form of thromboembolic disease. In more than 95% of cases, PE originates from leg deep vein thrombi (DVTs).

Fragmented thrombi from DVTs are carried through progressively larger veins and the right side of the heart, before slamming into the pulmonary arterial vasculature. Depending on the size of the embolus, it can have 3 fates:

• It can occlude the main pulmonary artery

• It can straddle the pulmonary artery bifurcation (saddle embolus)

• It can pass out into the smaller, branching arteries

The CT image given below shows a saddle embolus lodged in the main pulmonary artery extending into both its limbs as indicated by the red arrows.

questions.question: Following autopsy, an H&E stained specimen of the lung was obtained which is given below. What could be the likely cause of death?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the presence of laminated swirls of squamous cells in the pulmonary arteriole which is characteristically seen in amniotic fluid embolism(AFE).

AFE is a life-threatening obstetric emergency characterized by sudden cardiorespiratory collapse and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). The underlying cause is the infusion of amniotic fluid or fetal tissue into the maternal circulation via a tear in the placental membranes or rupture of uterine veins.

Findings at autopsy include:

• Presence in the maternal pulmonary micro-vasculature of-

• Squamous cells shed from fetal skin

• Lanugo hair

• Fat from vernix caseosa

• Mucin derived from the fetal respiratory or gastrointestinal tract

• Marked pulmonary edema

• Diffuse alveolar damage

• Presence of fibrin thrombi in many vascular beds due to DIC

questions.question: Which of the following is not seen in patients with DIC?
questions.explanation:
Increased prothrombin time (PT) is a feature of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).

Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) is an acute, subacute, or chronic thrombohemorrhagic disorder occurring as a secondary complication in a variety of diseases.

It is characterized by the activation of the coagulation sequence, which leads to the formation of microthrombi throughout the microcirculation of the body. As a consequence of the thrombotic diathesis, there is a consumption of platelets, fibrin, and coagulation factors and, secondarily, activation of fibrinolytic mechanisms.

Laboratory investigations in DIC reveal the following:

• Thrombocytopenia

• Prolonged prothrombin time (PT)/thrombin time (TT)

• Decreased fibrinogen level

• Elevated levels of fibrin-split products (D-dimers)

questions.question: Red infarcts do not occur in which of the following organs?
questions.explanation:
White infarcts occur in the spleen, not red infarcts.

Red infarcts occur in the following conditions:

• Venous occlusions (e.g., testicular torsion)

• Loose, spongy tissues (e.g., lung), where blood can collect in the infarcted zone

• Tissues with dual circulations (e.g., lung and small intestine), which allows blood to flow from an unobstructed parallel supply into a necrotic zone

• Tissues previously congested by sluggish venous outflow

• When flow is re-established at a site of previous arterial occlusion and necrosis (e.g., following angioplasty of an arterial obstruction)

 The below image shows a hemorrhagic, roughly wedge-shaped pulmonary red infarct.

White infarcts occur with arterial occlusions in solid organs with end-arterial circulation (e.g., heart, spleen, and kidney), and where tissue density limits the seepage of blood from adjoining capillary beds into the necrotic area.

The below image shows a sharply demarcated white infarct in the spleen.

Septic infarctions occur when infected cardiac valve vegetations embolize or when microbes seed necrotic tissue. In these cases, the infarct is converted into an abscess, with a correspondingly greater inflammatory response.

questions.question: A bridge construction worker presents with generalized bone pain. He is found to have ischemic necrosis of bilateral femoral heads, left tibia, and right humerus. Caisson disease is suspected. What is this condition related to?
questions.explanation:
Caisson disease is a chronic form of decompression sickness which occurs when individuals experience a sudden decrease in atmospheric pressure.

It is named after the pressurized vessels that are used in bridge construction as workers in these vessels are known to suffer from both acute and chronic forms of decompression sickness.

When air is breathed at high pressure, increased amounts of gas, particularly nitrogen, are dissolved in the blood and tissues. If there is a sudden fall in pressure, the nitrogen comes out of the solution in the tissues and the blood and forms gas emboli. In Caisson disease, the persistence of gas emboli in the skeletal system leads to the development of multiple foci of ischemic necrosis. The more common sites are the femoral heads, tibia, and humeri.

questions.question: Chest X-ray of a 60-year-old woman with dyspnoea at rest revealed right-sided pleural effusion. A pleural fluid analysis was done. Which of the following findings would rule out a transudative cause?
questions.explanation:
High plasma protein content in the pleural fluid would rule out a transudative cause. In a transudative effusion, the fluid has low protein content, little or no cellular material, and low specific gravity.

It is essentially an ultrafiltrate of the blood plasma. It is produced as a result of osmotic or hydrostatic imbalance across the vessel wall. There is no increase in vascular permeability.

The table below gives the differences between transudative and exudative effusion.

Features
Transudate
Exudate

Process
Passive (increased pressure)
Active (inflammation)

Vascular permeability
Normal
Increased

Plasma protein leak
Absent
Present

Protein content of fluid

Low S.G<1.012

Low protein

High S.G>1.020

High protein

Fibrin
Absent
Present

Inflammatory cells
Absent
Present

questions.question: Which of the following are caused by single-gene mutations?
questions.explanation:
Mendelian disorders are caused by single-gene mutations.

A mutation is defined as a permanent change in the genetic material that can result in altered protein function and phenotypic changes.

Mutations that affect germ cells are transmitted to the progeny and can give rise to inherited diseases.

Human genetic disorders can be broadly classified into three categories:

1. Single-gene mutations - these diseases usually follow the classic Mendelian pattern of inheritance.

2. Chromosomal disorders - These arise from the structural or numerical alteration in the autosomes and sex chromosomes. Like a monogenic disease, they are uncommon but associated with high penetrance.

3. Complex multigenic disorders - They are more common and are caused by interactions between multiple variant forms of genes and environmental factors. Such variations in genes are common within the population and are also called polymorphisms.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases is associated with non-sense mutation?
questions.explanation:
A non-sense mutation is seen in β0 thalassemia.

A point mutation is a change in which a single base is substituted with a different base. The point mutations within the coding sequences of the DNA are of two types:

1. Missense mutations: These involve alteration of a single base in a triplet of bases. It leads to the replacement of one amino acid by another in the gene product. These mutations alter the meaning of the sequence of the encoded protein. Based on the substituted amino acid coded, the missense mutations are again of two types:

• Conservative missense mutation: The substituted amino acid is biochemically similar to the original. It typically causes little change in the function of the protein.

• Non-conservative missense mutation: This type of mutation replaces the normal amino acid with a biochemically different one.

2. Nonsense mutations: It is a point mutation in a sequence of DNA that results in a premature stop codon.

For example, a point mutation affecting the codon for glutamine (CAG) creates a stop codon (UAG) if U is substituted for C. This change leads to premature termination of β-globin gene translation, and the short peptide that is produced is rapidly degraded. The resulting deficiency of β-globin chains can give rise to a severe form of anemia called β0 thalassemia.

Option B: α-thalassemias are caused by inherited deletions that result in the reduced or absent synthesis of α-globin chains.

Option C: Sickle-cell anemia is an example of non-conservative missense mutation. It occurs due to the replacement of the 6th glutamic acid by valine in the beta-globin gene on chromosome 11.

Option D: Hereditary spherocytosis (HS) is an inherited disorder caused by intrinsic defects in the red cell membrane skeleton that render red cells spheroid less deformable and vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction.

questions.question:
Which of the following traits are examples of co-dominance inheritance?

1. ABO blood group

2. Hair colour

3. Height

4. Skin color

5. HLA
questions.explanation:
ABO blood group and HLA are both examples of codominant inheritance.

In a codominant phenotype, alleles of a gene pair in a heterozygote are fully expressed. Thereby resulting in an offspring with a phenotype that is neither dominant nor recessive and both the alleles of a gene pair contributes to the phenotype.

Mendelian traits are usually described as dominant or recessive:

• A dominant allele produces a dominant phenotype in individuals who have one copy of the allele, which can come from just one parent.

• A recessive allele produces a recessive phenotype, in individuals who have two copies of the allele, one from each parent.

The illustration below shows the codominant inheritance pattern of the blood group.

Hair colour, height, and skin color are polygenic traits.

questions.question: What is the term for the phenomenon where a single mutant gene leads to many end-effects?
questions.explanation:
Pleiotropism is characterized by a single mutant gene, which may lead to many end effects.

For example, in sickle-cell anemia, the point mutation in the gene not only predisposes the red blood cells to hemolysis but can also block the vessels. This leads to splenic fibrosis, organ infarcts, and bone changes. The numerous differing end-organ derangements are all related to the primary defect in hemoglobin synthesis.

Option B: In variable expressivity, a trait is seen in all individuals carrying the mutant gene but is expressed differently among them.

Option C: Polymorphisms are caused by interactions between multiple variant forms of genes and environmental factors.

Option D: Genetic heterogeneity refers to mutations at several genetic loci that may produce the same trait. An example of this is profound childhood deafness - an apparently homogeneous clinical entity that results from many different types of autosomal recessive mutations.

questions.question: Which of the following is autosomal dominant?
questions.explanation:
Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant disorder.

It is caused by a mutation of the fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR-3) gene.

The primary defect is abnormal chondrocyte proliferation at the growth plate that causes development of short and thick bones.

Clinical features:

• Short limbs

• Normal trunk

• Large head

• Saddle nose

• Exaggerated lumbar lordosis

• Severe spinal deformity may lead to cord compression

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman presents with sudden onset chorea and behavioral changes. Genetic investigation reveals CAG repeats. What is the mode of inheritance of this disease?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Huntington's disease. It is an autosomal-dominant inherited disorder.

Huntington disease (HD) also known as Huntington chorea is associated with CAG repeats and anticipation. It has an adult-onset and cell loss within a specific subset of neurons in the basal ganglia and cortex is seen. The characteristic features of HD include involuntary movements, dementia, and behavioral changes.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man is being evaluated for weakness and atrophy of distal limb musculature. Physical examination showing characteristic facies is given below. What is the mode of inheritance of this disease?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and image showing the characteristic hatchet facies are suggestive of myotonic dystrophy (dystonia myotrophica). It is an autosomal dominant genetic disorder affecting muscle function.

There are mainly two types:

• DM1 - In this type, the affected gene is DMPK, which codes for myotonic dystrophy protein kinase, a protein expressed predominantly in skeletal muscle. The gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 19.

• DM2 - It is caused by a defect of the CNBP gene on chromosome 3.

questions.question: After evaluation, a patient with the given finding is diagnosed with Bourneville disease. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
questions.explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)/ Bourneville disease is an autosomal-dominant genetic disorder.

TSC affects the differentiation, proliferation, and migration of cells early in development. This results in a variety of hamartomatous lesions that may affect virtually every organ system of the body. Two distinct genetic loci have been identified which are on chromosome 9 (TSC1) and on chromosome 16 (TSC2).

The most common cutaneous manifestation of TSC is hypomelanotic macules (ash-leaf macules) and is observed in most children with tuberous sclerosis. It presents at birth or appears within the first few years of life and may fade or disappear in adulthood.

The following image shows an ash-leaf macule.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases have autosomal recessive inheritance?
questions.explanation: Albinism is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern.

questions.question: A 55-year-old man presents with a dark tan despite avoiding sun exposure. He was recently diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. Physical examination reveals hepatomegaly. His liver microscopy on Prussian blue staining is given below. What is the mode of inheritance of his disease?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of hereditary hemochromatosis. It is an autosomal recessive genetic disorder that involves the HFE gene.

Hemochromatosis is characterized by excessive iron accumulation that results in tissue damage. It consists of a triad of:

• Micronodular cirrhosis

• Bronzing of the skin

• Diabetes mellitus

Diagnosis is by elevated levels of serum ferritin, serum iron, transferrin saturation, and confirmation by a gene assay.

Note: Autosomal recessive disorders include almost all inborn errors of metabolism.

questions.question: Which of the following patients has a disease showing the given mode of inheritance?
options: A 16-year-old boy with hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon
A 15-year-old boy with ataxia, cardiomegaly, scoliosis, and pes cavus
A 1-year-old boy with micro-thrombocytopenia, eczema and recurrent infections
questions.answer: B. A 15-year-old boy with ataxia, cardiomegaly, scoliosis, and pes cavus
questions.explanation:
The given pedigree chart is pointing towards an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance. A boy with cardiomegaly, scoliosis, and pes cavus is suggestive of Friedreich’s ataxia. This is an autosomal recessive inherited disease, resulting from a mutation of a gene locus on chromosome 9.

The condition causes nervous system damage and movement problems. It usually begins in childhood and leads to impaired muscle coordination (ataxia) that worsens over time. Scoliosis, cardiomegaly, and foot problems may also develop.

Option A: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout the colon are suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis(FAP) which is an autosomal-dominant inherited disorder.

Option C: Vitamin D–resistant rickets is an X-linked dominant inherited disorder.

Option D: A child with a triad of micro-thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infections points towards Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome. It is an X-linked recessive inherited disorder.

questions.question: A newborn on routine head-to-toe examination was found to have ambiguous genitalia. Further investigations confirmed a deficiency of the 21-hydroxylase enzyme. What is the mode of inheritance of the given condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of congenital adrenal hyperplasia. It includes a group of autosomal recessive disorders, each of which involves a deficiency of an enzyme involved in the synthesis of cortisol, aldosterone, or both.

The most common form is known to occur due to the deficiency of 21-hydroxylase, resulting from mutations or deletion of CYP21A.

questions.question: A baby is brought to the OPD with a history of vomiting and poor feeding. Examination reveals a musty odor in the baby's sweat and urine. Guthrie's test is found to be positive. Which of the following is false about this condition?
options: The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive
It is due to mutations in the PKU gene
It is an inborn error of amino acid metabolism
questions.answer: B. It is due to mutations in the PKU gene
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of phenylketonuria (PKU). It is caused by mutations in the PAH gene which encodes for phenylalanine hydroxylase.

Phenylketonuria is the most common inborn error of amino acid metabolism. It is less commonly known as phenylalanine hydroxylase (PAH) deficiency. The mode of inheritance is autosomal recessive.

questions.question: A 28-year old man presents to the clinic with complaints of lower back pain and passing dark red-colored urine. He was diagnosed with malaria and is on antimalarials for the past 3 days. The peripheral smear of the patient is shown below. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency. It is the most common enzyme deficiency in humans, inherited as an X-linked recessive disorder. The gene that codes for G6PD is located in the distal long arm of the X chromosome at the Xq28 locus.

The inheritance pattern is similar to that of hemophilia and color blindness, where males usually manifest the abnormality and females are carriers. Females may be symptomatic if they are homozygous or if inactivation of their normal X chromosome occurs.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy is brought to the pediatrician with delayed developmental milestones. On examination, multiple lip lacerations and the given nail findings are noted. Laboratory reports reveal hyperuricemia. What is the mode of inheritance in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Lesch–Nyhan syndrome. It is an X-linked recessive inherited disorder characterized by the deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyl transferase (HGPRT).

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome and its variants are caused by mutations in the HPRT gene on the X chromosome.

The disorder is associated with 3 major clinical elements:

• Overproduction of uric acid (hyperuricemia)

• Neurologic disability - intellectual disability and delayed milestones

• Behavioral problems - self-mutilation (excessive biting of lips and nails)

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl with the given physical findings develops mitral regurgitation due to mitral valve prolapse. Eye examination reveals bilateral dislocation of the lens. This condition most commonly results from an inherited defect in which of the following proteins?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Marfan's syndrome. It is due to the inherited defect of the protein fibrillin 1.

Fibrillin is a major building block of microfibrils. This constitutes the structural components of the suspensory ligament of the ocular lens and serves as substrates for elastin in the aorta and other connective tissues.

It occurs in two homologous forms:

• Fibrillin-1: encoded by FBN1, mapped on chromosomes 15q21.1. Mutations cause Marfan's syndrome.

• Fibrillin-2: encoded by FBN2, mapped on chromosomes 5q23.31. Mutations cause congenital contractural arachnodactyly.

questions.question: The most striking abnormalities of the Marfan syndrome are seen in which of the following systems?
questions.explanation:
Skeletal abnormalities are the most striking feature of Marfan syndrome.

Skeletal abnormalities include:

• Unusually tall, with exceptionally long extremities and long, tapering fingers and toes

• The joint ligaments in the hands and feet are lax, suggesting that the patient is double-jointed. Typically, the thumb can be hyper-extended back to the wrist

• The head is commonly dolichocephalic (long-headed) with bossing of the frontal eminences and prominent supraorbital ridges

Spinal deformities include:

• Kyphosis

• Scoliosis

• Rotation/slipping of the dorsal or lumbar vertebrae

• Pectus excavatum (deeply depressed sternum)

• Pigeon-breast deformity

Ocular changes include bilateral subluxation or dislocation (outward and upward) of the lens, referred to as ectopia lentis.

Cardiovascular lesions are the most life-threatening features of this disorder. The two most common lesions are:

• Mitral valve prolapse

• Dilation of the ascending aorta due to cystic medionecrosis

The images given below show features seen in patients with Marfan's syndrome.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of death in Marfan syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Cardiovascular lesions, like rupture of aortic dissections, are the most life-threatening features of the Marfan syndrome.

The weakening of the media predisposes the aorta to an intimal tear. It may initiate an intramural hematoma that cleaves the layers of the media to produce aortic dissection.

After causing the cleavage of the aortic layers for a considerable length, sometimes extending to the root of the aorta or down to the iliac arteries, the hemorrhage often ruptures through the aortic wall.

Although mitral valve lesions are more frequent, they are clinically less important than aortic lesions. Loss of connective tissue support in the mitral valve leaflets makes them soft and billowy, creating a so-called floppy valve.

Valvular lesions, along with the lengthening of the chordae tendineae, frequently give rise to mitral regurgitation. Similar changes may affect the tricuspid and, rarely, the aortic valves.

questions.question:
Which of the following mode of inheritances is seen in Ehler–Danlos syndrome?

1. Autosomal dominant

2. Autosomal recessive

3. Mitochondrial

4. X-linked dominant

5. Genomic imprinting
questions.explanation:
The mode of inheritance of Ehler–Danlos syndrome (EDS) encompasses two Mendelian patterns, namely:

• Autosomal dominant

• Autosomal recessive

The biosynthesis of collagen can be disturbed by genetic errors that may affect any one of the numerous structural collagen genes or enzymes necessary for posttranscriptional modifications of collagen. Such molecular heterogeneity results in the expression of EDS as a clinically variable disorder, with varied patterns of inheritance.

questions.question: A 20-year-old woman presents with back pain and weakness. On examination, she is found to have lax skin. X-ray findings are shown below. Lab reports show a deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of the kyphoscoliotic form of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS). This was previously known as Type VI EDS.

The kyphoscoliotic form of EDS is caused by the deficient activity of the enzyme procollagen-lysine, 2-oxoglutarate 5-dioxygenase 1 (PLOD1, or lysyl hydroxylase 1).

It is a generalized connective tissue disorder characterized by:

• Friable hyperextensible skin

• Thin scars

• Easy bruising

• Generalized joint laxity

• Severe muscular hypotonia at birth

• Progressive scoliosis may be present at birth or may develop within the first year of life

questions.question: What type of collagen is involved in the classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Classic Ehlers-Danlos syndromes (EDS) type involves type V collagen (defects in genes COL5A1 and COL5A2).

Types I and II of EDS are termed as classic forms. Type I is severe, while type II is milder.

It has an autosomal-dominant type of inheritance. Clinically, this type is characterized by skin and joint hypermobility, atrophic scars, and easy bruising.

questions.question: The dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is classified as:
questions.explanation: Dermatosparaxis type of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (EDS) is type VIIc.

questions.question: Which of the following pair is incorrectly matched?
questions.answer: C. Spinal muscular atrophy - Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: Spinal muscular atrophy has an autosomal recessive inheritance, not autosomal dominant.

questions.question: A 1-month-old infant diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency presented with failure to thrive, recurrent emesis, and hepatosplenomegaly. Bilateral adrenal calcification was noted radiologically. Which of the following enzyme is deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Wolman disease. It is due to a deficiency of the lysosomal acid lipase enzyme. It is an autosomal recessive disease.

It leads to the accumulation of cholesterol esters and triglycerides. It presents in the first few weeks of life with:

• Failure to thrive

• Vomiting

• Abdominal distention

• Steatorrhea

• Hepatosplenomegaly

• Hyperlipidemia

• Extensive bilateral calcifications of the adrenal glands

No specific therapy is available and death usually occurs within 6 months of life.

questions.question: Which of these is not a form of sphingolipidoses?
questions.explanation:
Hurler disease is a mucopolysaccharidosis.

Sphingolipidoses are a group of lysosomal storage disorders characterized by the accumulation of sphingolipids. It includes:

• Niemann–Pick disease

• Fabry disease

• Krabbe disease

• Gaucher disease

• Tay–Sachs disease

• Metachromatic leukodystrophy

questions.question: What is the most common lysosomal storage disorder?
questions.explanation:
Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder.

It is an autosomal recessive disorder resulting from mutations in the gene encoding glucocerebrosidase.

questions.question: An 8-month-old child presents with mental retardation, blindness, and muscle weakness. On evaluation, deficiency of hexosaminidase α-subunit is found. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and hexosaminidase α-subunit deficiency are seen in Tay–Sachs disease.

Sphingolipidoses with their deficient enzyme:

1. GM1 Gangliosidoses - GM1 Ganglioside β- galactosidase deficiency

• Type 1- infantile, generalizsed

• Type 2- juvenile

2. GM2 Gangliosidosis:

• Tay–Sachs disease - Hexosaminidase α-subunit

• Sandhoff disease - Hexosaminidase β-subunit

• GM2 Gangliosidosis variant AB - Ganglioside activator protein

Note: Tay–Sachs disease is the most common form of GM2 gangliosidosis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about Tay–Sachs Disease?
options: Affected infants are normal at birth
Neurons in the CNS, ANS, and retina are affected
Accumulations stain positive for oil red O and Sudan black B
Whorled configurations within mitochondria are seen
questions.answer: D. Whorled configurations within mitochondria are seen
questions.explanation:
In Tay–Sachs disease, an electron microscope shows whorled configurations within lysosomes composed of onion-skin layers of membranes.

Affected infants appear normal at birth but begin to manifest signs and symptoms at about 6 months of age. The involvement of neurons in the central and autonomic nervous systems and retina dominates the clinical picture.

There is a severe motor and mental deterioration, beginning with motor incoordination and mental obtundation. This leads to muscular flaccidity, blindness, and increasing dementia. Over the span of 1 or 2 years, a completely vegetative state is reached, followed by death at age 2 to 3 years

On histologic examination, the neurons are ballooned with cytoplasmic vacuoles, each representing a markedly distended lysosome filled with gangliosides.

A cherry-red spot appears in the macula, representing the accentuation of the normal color of the macular choroid. This is in contrast with the pallor produced by the swollen ganglion cells in the remainder of the retina. This finding is characteristic of Tay-Sachs disease and other storage disorders affecting the neurons.

The image given below shows a cherry-red spot on retina.

questions.question: Patients with metachromatic leukodystrophy will have which of the following enzyme deficiency?
questions.explanation:
Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive condition caused by the deficiency of arylsulfatase A.

The deficiency of this enzyme leads to the accumulation of cerebroside sulfate. These sulfatides can contribute to white matter injury, demyelination, and gliosis.

Macrophages with vacuolated cytoplasm are scattered throughout the white matter. They contain metachromatic material, which can be detected in the urine and peripheral nerves when stained with toluidine blue.

questions.question: Which of the following enzyme is deficient in patients with Krabbe disease?
questions.explanation:
Krabbe disease is due to the deficiency of galactosylceramidase.

The onset of symptoms is between 3 and 6 months of age, dominated by motor signs such as stiffness and weakness. They often don't survive beyond the age of 2 years. The brain shows loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes with a similar process affecting the peripheral nerves.

The aggregation of engorged macrophages called globoid cells in the brain parenchyma and around blood vessels is the characteristic and diagnostic feature of Krabbe disease.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following diseases will have ceramide trihexoside accumulation?
questions.explanation:
Ceramide trihexoside (also known as globotriaosylceramide) is accumulated in Fabry disease.

The enzyme defect seen in this disease is α-galactosidase A.

Clinical features:

• Painful acroparaesthesia

• Hypohidrosis

• Abdominal cramping

• Diarrhea

• Small petechiae around the umbilicus

• Lenticular opacities

• Corneal dystrophy

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about Niemann–Pick disease?
options: Inherited deficiency of aryl sulfatase is present
questions.answer: A. Inherited deficiency of aryl sulfatase is present
questions.explanation:
Niemann–Pick disease types A and B are two related disorders that are characterized by lysosomal accumulation of sphingomyelin due to an inherited deficiency of sphingomyelinase.

The disease is typically inherited as an autosomal recessive condition on chromosome 11.

Type A is a severe infantile form with extensive neurologic involvement, marked visceral accumulations of sphingomyelin, progressive wasting, and early death within the first 3 years of life.

Type B disease patients have organomegaly, but generally no central nervous system involvement. They usually survive into adulthood.

questions.question: Given below is an electron microscopy picture of lysosomes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Electron microscopy showing zebra bodies is suggestive of Niemann–Pick disease.

Zebra bodies are engorged secondary lysosomes that contain membranous cytoplasmic bodies resembling concentric lamellated myelin figures. Similar zebra bodies can also be seen in mucopolysaccharidoses.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding I-cell disease?
options: It is characterised by defective phosphorylating enzymes
It is a glycogen storage disorder
It is associated with gingival hyperplasia
High levels of hydrolytic enzymes in plasma are seen
questions.answer: B. It is a glycogen storage disorder
questions.explanation:
Inclusion-cell (I-cell) disease, also referred to as mucolipidosis II, is a part of the lysosomal storage disease family.

It is characterized by the deficiency of phosphorylating enzymes essential for the formation of the mannose-6-phosphate recognition marker.

Acid hydrolases lacking the recognition marker cannot be targeted to the lysosomes but are secreted extracellularly.

It is characterized by:

• Coarse facial features

• Gingival hyperplasia

• Clouded corneas

• Restricted joint movements

• Claw hand deformities

• Kyphoscoliosis

• High plasma levels of lysosomal enzymes

questions.question: Which of the following is false about mucopolysaccharidosis?
options: Hunter syndrome is due to a deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase
Hurler syndrome is due to a deficiency of α-L-iduronidase
They are inherited as autosomal recessive traits, except Hunter syndrome
Hunter syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant disease
questions.answer: D. Hunter syndrome is inherited as an autosomal dominant disease
questions.explanation:
All the mucopolysaccharidoses are inherited as autosomal-recessive traits except Hunter syndrome. It is inherited as an X-linked recessive disease.

The mucopolysaccharidoses (MPSs) are a group of closely related syndromes that result from genetically determined deficiencies of enzymes involved in the degradation of mucopolysaccharides (glycosaminoglycans).

Mucopolysaccharides are abundant in the ground substance of connective tissues. In the absence of enzymes involved in their degradation, they accumulate within lysosomes in various tissues and organs of the body. Two among these are:

• Hurler syndrome - deficiency of α-L-iduronidase

• Hunter syndrome - deficiency of iduronate 2-sulphatase

questions.question: Which glycogen storage disorder is a lysosomal storage disease?
questions.explanation:
Glycogen storage disorder type II, also called Pompe disease, is the only glycogen storage disease with a defect in lysosomal metabolism.

It is an autosomal-recessive metabolic disorder. It is caused by the accumulation of glycogen in the lysosome due to deficiency of the lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase enzyme.

questions.question: A 4-year-old boy presented with severe pain in his left leg which worsened over the last few months. On examination, hepatosplenomegaly and developmental delays were noticed. Labs revealed the following findings on light and oil immersion respectively of the bone marrow aspiration. Which of the following is deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and bone marrow aspiration images showing necrotic bone with lack of osteocytes in the lacunae (Image A) and Gaucher cells (Image B)are suggestive of Gaucher's disease. This condition has a deficiency of glucocerebrosidase.

Gaucher cells are plump macrophages that characteristically have a crumpled tissue paper appearance (Image B) of the cytoplasm. It is due to the accumulation of glucocerebrosides.

They can be seen in Virchow–Robin spaces (perivascular fluid-filled cavities that surround perforating arteries and veins in the brain parenchyma) in patients with cerebral involvement.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about Gaucher’s disease?
options: Type 1 has splenic and skeletal involvement
Type 1 has no detectable enzyme activity
questions.answer: C. Type 1 has no detectable enzyme activity
questions.explanation:
In type 1, enzyme activity is reduced but detectable.

Gaucher disease is of two types:

Type 1: Chronic non-neuropathic form

Type 2: Acute neuronopathic form

Most common
Less common

Spleen and skeletal system are mainly involved
Hepatosplenomegaly is seen

Spares the central nervous system

The central nervous system is involved

Enzyme activity is reduced but detectable
No detectable enzyme activity

Principally in Jews of European stock

Has no predilection for Jews

Longevity is shortened

 Death at an early age

questions.question: A 1-year-old child presents with growth retardation and abdominal distension. On examination, the child has characteristic doll-like facies with thin extremities. Blood investigations reveal hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia. USG abdomen shows hepatomegaly and renomegaly. What deficiency causes the given clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Gierke disease. It is due to the deficiency of glucose 6 phosphatase enzyme.

The condition usually manifests as:

• Failure to thrive

• Stunted growth

• Hepatomegaly

• Renomegaly

Hypoglycemia is due to the failure of glucose mobilization which often leads to convulsions. Lactic acidosis, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia result from deranged glucose metabolism. Many patients also develop gout, skin xanthomas, and bleeding tendency (due to platelet dysfunction).

With treatment, most patients survive and develop late complications (e.g., hepatic adenomas).

questions.question: Which enzyme is deficient in McArdle’s syndrome?
questions.explanation:
McArdle’s syndrome is caused due to the deficiency of muscle phosphorylase.

In the skeletal muscles, as opposed to the liver, glycogen is used predominantly as a source of energy during physical activity. If enzymes hydrolyzing glucose are deficient, there will be an accumulation of glycogen in the muscles. This will cause muscle weakness due to impaired energy production.

Enzyme deficiencies leading to muscle glycogen storage include:

• McArdle disease/type V glycogenosis - deficiency of muscle phosphorylase

• Type VII glycogen storage disease - deficiency of muscle phosphofructokinase

Typically, individuals with myopathic forms present with muscle cramps after exercise. This is because lactate levels in the blood fail to rise after exercise due to a block in glycolysis.

chapters.chapter: Chromosomal Disorders And Other Genetic Disorders

questions.question: At what stage of mitosis is standard karyotyping performed?
questions.explanation:
Standard karyotyping refers to an arrangement of chromosomes from a cell that is undergoing mitosis at metaphase.

At other mitotic stages, the chromosomes are not sufficiently condensed or are too dispersed to allow for the counting and comparison of pairs under the microscope. In a metaphase spread, the individual chromosomes take the form of two chromatids connected to the centromere.

A variety of staining methods are available to identify the individual chromosomes on the basis of a distinctive and reliable pattern of alternating light and dark bands. The most common method used involves a Giemsa stain and is hence called G-banding. Standard G-banding can detect approximately 400 to 800 bands per haploid set.

The image below shows G-banding (karyogram of human male using Giemsa staining):

questions.question: In cytogenetic terminology, how are the following marked structures designated?
questions.explanation:
The short arm of a chromosome (marked as 1) is designated p (for petite), and the long arm (marked as 2) is referred to as q (the next alphabet).

In a banded karyotype, each arm of the chromosome is divided into two or more regions bordered by prominent bands. The regions are numbered (e.g., 1, 2, 3) from the centromere outward. Each region is further subdivided into bands and sub-bands, and these are ordered numerically as well.

questions.question: What aberration occurs when a break occurs at both ends of a chromosome with the fusion of the damaged ends?
questions.explanation:
A ring chromosome is an aberrant chromosome whose broken ends fuse together to form a ring.

Ring chromosomes behave abnormally in meiosis or mitosis and usually result in serious consequences. In rare cases, the telomeres at the ends of a chromosome fuse without any loss of genetic material, which results in a normal phenotype. A ring chromosome is denoted by the symbol r in human genetics.

The following image shows a representative karyotype from a well-differentiated transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder. The chromosome indicated by 'r' represents a ring chromosome. Also evident are monosomy 9, 18, and X and trisomy 7.

Option A: In a translocation, a segment of one chromosome is transferred to another.

Option C: Inversion refers to a rearrangement that involves two breaks within a single chromosome, with reincorporation of the inverted, intervening segment.

Option D: Isochromosome formation results when one arm of a chromosome is lost and the remaining arm is duplicated. It results in a chromosome consisting of two short arms only or of two long arms.

questions.question: Which of the following is not associated with the change in genetic material?
questions.explanation:
Inversion involves only a rearrangement of the genetic material. There is no change in the genetic material.

It occurs as a result of two breaks within a single chromosome. The intervening segment between the breaks gets inverted and reincorporated. It is of two types:

• Paracentric - inversion involving only one arm of the chromosome

• Pericentric - inversion involving opposite sides of the centromere

Inversions are often fully compatible with normal development.

Transversions are mutations where a purine base pair is replaced by a pyrimidine or vice versa.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about Down's syndrome?
options: Leukemia is the major cause of death in early childhood
It is the most common chromosomal disorder
Robertsonian translocations of chromosome 21 are less common
These children are prone to develop autoimmune diseases
questions.answer: A. Leukemia is the major cause of death in early childhood
questions.explanation:
In Down's syndrome, the major cause of death in infancy and early childhood is cardiac disease, not leukemia.

Down's syndrome is the most common chromosomal disorder and is a major cause of mental retardation. Maternal age is a strong risk factor. This condition can occur by the following mechanisms:

• Majority of cases - meiotic nondisjunction of chromosome 21 in the ovum

• Rarely - Robertsonian translocation of the long arm of chromosome 21 to another acrocentric chromosome (e.g., 22 or 14)

The clinical features of Down's syndrome include:

• Mental retardation

• Facial dysmorphism - flat facial profile, oblique palpebral fissures, and epicanthic folds

• Congenital heart disease - endocardial cushion defects (ASD, VSD, AV valve malformations)

• Atresias of the esophagus and small bowel

• Neuropathologic changes characteristic of Alzheimer's disease - in patients > 40 years

• Increased risk of developing acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7)

• Predisposition to autoimmune diseases and serious lung infections

questions.question: A 1-year-old child was brought by the mother with complaints of delay in reaching motor milestones. Examination revealed oblique palpebral fissures, epicanthal folds, and the following finding. Auscultation revealed a pan-systolic murmur in the left sternal border. This child is at risk of developing which of the following?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing a single palmar crease (simian crease) are suggestive of Down's syndrome. It is associated with an increased risk of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AML-M7) in affected children < 2 years old.

Children with trisomy 21 have a 10 to 20-fold increased risk of developing acute leukemia.

• In children < 2 years of age - acute megakaryoblastic leukemia(AML-M7) is the most common

• In children > 3 years of age - acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is the most predominant

questions.question: A 7-month-old infant is being evaluated for failure to thrive. Examination reveals low-set ears, a short neck, and the following findings. Auscultation reveals a holosystolic murmur over the pulmonic area. Which of the following statements about this condition is false?
options: Karyotype of this child is 47, XY + 18
It may be associated with horseshoe kidney
There is increased risk of leukemia
questions.answer: D. There is increased risk of leukemia
questions.explanation:
The images show the index finger overlapping other fingers and rocker bottom feet. This along with the clinical features is suggestive of Edward's syndrome. Leukemia is not a feature of this condition.

It is due to the inheritance of a complete extra copy of chromosome 18 as a result of meiotic nondisjunction (47, XY+18). The incidence is 1 in 8000 births.

The clinical features of Edward's syndrome include:

• Low-set ears

• Short neck

• Overlapping fingers

• Congenital heart defects

• Renal malformations

• Limited hip abduction

• Rocker-bottom feet

• Prominent occiput

• Mental retardation

• Micrognathia

Note: Although, rocker bottom feet are seen in both Edward's syndrome and Patau's syndrome, overlapping of fingers is characteristic of Edward's syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is not seen in children with Patau syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Low set ears are a feature of Patau syndrome, not high set ears.

Patau syndrome occurs due to trisomy 13 and is characterized by:

• Microphthalmia

• Polydactyly

• Microcephaly and mental retardation

• Cleft lip and palate

• Cardiac defects

• Umbilical hernia

• Renal defects

• Rocker-bottom feet (commonly seen in Edwards syndrome also)

questions.question: What hypothesis states that one X chromosome, maternal or paternal, is randomly inactivated during development?
questions.explanation:
Lyon's hypothesis states the idea of the inactivation of the X chromosome.

It states the following:

• Only one of the X chromosomes is genetically active

• The other X undergoes heteropyknosis and is rendered inactive (known as Barr body)

• Inactivation of either the maternal or paternal X occurs at random among all the cells of the blastocyst on or about day 5.5 of embryonic life

• Inactivation of the same X chromosome persists in all the cells derived from each precursor cell.

The molecular basis of X inactivation involves the XIST gene.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man was referred for infertility evaluation. On examination, he was tall with a lack of body hair. Gynecomastia and micropenis were also noted. Karyotyping analysis revealed an XXY karyotype. Which of the following statements is not true about the condition?
options: Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced
questions.answer: A. Levels of follicle-stimulating hormone are reduced
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Klinefelter's syndrome. In this condition, the follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) levels are elevated.

The clinical features include:

• Eunuchoid body habitus - elongated body and long legs (increased length between the soles and the pubic bone)

• Absence of secondary sexual characteristics - lack of body and facial hair, deep voice

• Small atrophic testes

• Micropenis

• Gynecomastia

• Lower IQ, but no mental retardation

The following hormonal variations are seen in these patients:

• Elevated FSH

• Elevated estradiol

• Low testosterone

• Insulin resistance - increased incidence of type 2 diabetes

Patients with Klinefelter syndrome are at a higher risk for:

• Male breast cancer (20x more common than in normal males)

• Extragonadal germ cell tumors

• Autoimmune diseases - systemic lupus erythematosus

questions.question: A 16-year-old girl is referred for evaluation of primary amenorrhea and short stature. Examination shows a webbed neck, widely spaced nipples, and absent secondary sexual characteristics. USG abdomen shows a small uterus and streak ovaries. What is the most common karyotypic abnormality seen in individuals with this condition?
options: Isochromosome of the long arm of X chromosome
Deletion of portions of long arm of X chromosome
Deletion of ends of long and short arm of X chromosome
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is highly suggestive of Turner's syndrome. In this condition, the most common karyotypic abnormality seen is a missing entire X chromosome, seen in more than half the cases.

Less commonly, structural abnormalities of the X chromosome and mosaicism can also occur. The common feature of the structural abnormalities is to produce partial monosomy of the X chromosome.

In order of frequency, the structural abnormalities of the X chromosome include the following:

• An isochromosome of the long arm, 46,X,i(X)(q10), resulting in the loss of the short arm

• Deletion of portions of both long and short arms, resulting in the formation of a ring chromosome - 46, X,r(X)

• Deletion of portions of the short or long arm - 46X,del(Xq) or 46X,del(Xp).

The mosaic patients have a 45,XO cell population along with one or more karyotypically normal or abnormal cell types.

Few patients with this condition also have Y-chromosome sequences, either as a complete Y chromosome or as fragments of Y chromosomes translocated on other chromosomes. These patients are at a higher risk for the development of a gonadal tumor (gonadoblastoma).

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not caused by trinucleotide-repeat mutations involving non-coding regions?
questions.explanation:
Huntington's disease is due to CAG (trinucleotide) repeat mutation in the coding region of the gene, not the non-coding region.

Expansion of trinucleotide repeats is an important genetic cause of human disease, particularly neurodegenerative disorders. The causative mutations are associated with the expansion of a stretch of trinucleotides that usually share the nucleotides G and C. In all cases, the DNA is unstable, and an expansion of the repeats above a certain threshold impairs gene function.

Expansions affecting noncoding regions will cause a loss of function mutation. They include:

• Fragile X syndrome

• Myotonic dystrophy

• Friedreich ataxia

Expansions affecting coding regions cause a gain of function mutation. They include:

• Spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy disease)

• Huntington disease

• Dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy (Haw–River syndrome)

• Spinocerebellar ataxia types 1, 2, 3, 6, 7

questions.question: 70 CGG premutations in the FMR1 gene are characteristic of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
CGG premutations in the FMR1 gene are characteristic of fragile X ataxia. It is also known as fragile X tremor and fragile X-associated primary ovarian failure.

Normally, the FMR1 gene is methylated and silenced, and the number of CGG repeats remains < 55.

However, abnormalities in this gene lead to the accumulation of CGG-containing FMR1 mRNAs, which are toxic to the cell. Depending on the type of mutation, there are 2 distinct syndromes:

• Fragile X ataxia syndrome (FXTAS): 55-200 repeats (premutation) which causes gain of function

• Fragile X syndrome (FXs): 200- 4000 repeats (full mutation) leading to loss of function

More than half the individuals with FXTAS develop a progressive neurodegenerative syndrome starting in their 6th decade. It is characterized by intention tremors and cerebellar ataxia and may progress to Parkinsonism.

Option B: Prader-Willi syndrome is associated with deletion of paternal chromosome 15q12 and the silencing of the maternal allele.

Option D: Friedreich ataxia is due to GAA repeat sequences in the noncoding regions.

questions.question: What is the mode of inheritance of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
Leber hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON) is an example of mitochondrial inheritance. It is inherited along the maternal line, as shown in image 4.

In diseases following the mitochondrial pattern of inheritance, all children of an affected mother and normal father develop the disease. However, children born to an affected father and a normal mother do not inherit the disease. Hence, only the daughters of the affected mother will transmit the disease.

This is because this condition is due to a mutation in the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), which is derived from the maternal mitochondria. The ovum contains several mitochondria, while the spermatozoa have very few mitochondria if present. Hence, the mitochondrial DNA of the zygote is entirely derived from the ovum.

LHON is a neurodegenerative disease that manifests as progressive bilateral loss of central vision. Visual impairment starts between ages 15 and 35, leading eventually to blindness. Other features include cardiac conduction defects and minor neurologic manifestations.

questions.question: A young male patient as shown below presents with complaints of infertility. On examination, he lacked pubic and facial hair. The genital examination was consistent for a micropenis. Further investigations reveal elevated LH and FSH levels. What is the most common cardiac lesion associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture most likely suggests Klinefelter's syndrome. The most common cardiac lesion in this condition is mitral valve prolapse which is seen in nearly half the adults.

Systemic manifestations associated with Klinefelter's syndrome:

• Gynecomastia

• Type 2 diabetes and metabolic syndrome

• Mitral valve prolapse

• Osteoporosis and fractures

• Male infertility

• Higher risk for breast cancer, extragonadal germ-cell tumors

• Systemic lupus erythematosus

questions.question:
A 5-year-old girl is brought for evaluation of intellectual disability. She also has difficulty in walking and balancing, and her speech is delayed for her age. The parents also say that she frequently has sudden bouts of laughter. She is a known case of seizure disorder since the age of 3. This condition is associated with which of the following chromosomal abnormalities?

1. Deletion of paternal gene on chromosome 15
