2. Deletion of maternal gene on chromosome 15

3. Uniparental disomy of paternal chromosome 15

4. Uniparental disomy of maternal chromosome 15
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Angelman syndrome. It can occur due to one of the following genetic abnormalities:

• Deletion (most common) - band q12 on the long arm of maternal chromosome 15

• Paternal uniparental disomy - inheritance of both chromosomes of a pair from the paternal pair of chromosomes

• Defective imprinting - defect in the resetting/maintaining of imprints during gametogenesis or after fertilization

Prader-Willi syndrome
 AngelMan syndrome

Deletion

(most common)

Paternal chromosome 15

Maternal chromosome 15

Uniparental disomy

(less common)

Maternal disomy (duplication)
Paternal disomy (duplication)

Clinical features

Elevated ghrelin levels - hyperphagia

Truncal obesity

Severe hypotonia

Short stature

Small hands and feet with hypotonia

Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism

Cognitive impairment

Short stature

Severe mental retardation with lack of speech

Stiff arm movements

Spastic, uncoordinated walk (ataxia)

Seizures

Inappropriate outbursts of laughter (happy puppets)

Chromosome 15 diseases (mnemonic - MAP):

• M: Marfan syndrome

• A: Angelman syndrome

• P: Prader Willi syndrome

The following images show children suffering from Prader-Willi syndrome.

The following image shows a child suffering from Angelman syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a hallmark of malignancy?
questions.explanation:
Cancer cells are insensitive to growth-inhibitory signals.

All cancer cells are known to show around 8 fundamental physiological changes in the cell, which are considered as the hallmarks of cancer. These changes include the following:

1. Self-sufficiency in growth signals - once activated, tumors can proliferate without external stimuli

2. Insensitivity to growth-inhibitory signals - tumors do not respond to inhibitors of cell growth. This is attributed to the inactivation of the tumor-suppressor genes in cancer cells

3. Altered cellular metabolism - tumor cells switch to aerobic glycolysis, called the Warburg effect

4. Evasion of apoptosis

5. Limitless replicative potential

6. Sustained angiogenesis

7. Ability to invade and metastasis

8. Ability to evade the host immune response

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the Warburg effect?
options: Cancer cells are characterized by high levels of glucose uptake
Cancer cells convert glucose to lactic acid even in the presence of ample oxygen
Conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the HMP pathway
Aerobic glycolysis provides cancer cells with metabolic intermediates
questions.answer: C. Conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the HMP pathway
questions.explanation:
Increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid is done via the glycolytic pathway (not HMP).

Even in the presence of ample oxygen, cancer cells demonstrate a distinctive form of cellular metabolism. This is characterized by high levels of glucose uptake and increased conversion of glucose to lactic acid via the glycolytic pathway. This phenomenon is called the Warburg effect.

Aerobic glycolysis provides rapidly dividing tumor cells with metabolic intermediates that are required for the synthesis of cellular components, whereas mitochondrial oxidative phosphor­ylation does not.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about adenomas?
options: They can be of non-glandular origin
questions.answer: B. Pleomorphic adenoma is an example
questions.explanation:
Pleomorphic adenoma is an example of a mixed tumor consisting of epithelial and myoepithelial cells with or without stromal components.

Adenomas are benign epithelial tumors. They can arise from:

• Glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example, follicular adenomas of the thyroid, which arise from the thyroid gland and forms glandular structures

• Glandular cells but form non-glandular structures - for example, heterogeneous mass of adrenal cortical cells growing as a solid sheet

• Non-glandular cells and form glandular structures - for example, benign epithelial neoplasm that arises from renal tubular cells growing in the form of numerous tightly clustered small glands

questions.question: Which of the following is a disorganized but benign mass composed of cells indigenous to the involved site?
questions.explanation:
Hamartomas are disorganized but benign, masses composed of cells indigenous to the involved site.

Examples of hamartoma include:

• Mammary hamartoma

• Pulmonary chondromatous hamartoma

• Splenic hamartoma

• Neurocristic hamartoma

• Fibrous hamartoma of infancy

Option A: Choristomas are heterotopic rests of cells.

Option D: Teratomas arise from totipotent germ cells. They contain recognizable mature or immature cells or tissues belonging to more than one germ cell layer, and sometimes all three germ layers.

Option C: Papillomas are benign epithelial neoplasms. They are characterized by microscopically or macroscopically visible finger-like or warty projections from epithelial surfaces.

questions.question: While examining an excision biopsy sample, the pathologist notices anaplastic cells. Which of the following tumors will show this characteristic finding?
questions.explanation:
Anaplasia or lack of differentiation is a characteristic feature of malignant neoplasm like sarcoma.

Differentiation refers to the extent to which neoplastic parenchymal cells resemble the corresponding normal parenchymal cells, both morphologically and functionally.

The image below shows a hepatocellular carcinoma characterized by large anaplastic carcinoma cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, large hyperchromatic nuclei, and prominent nucleoli. The normal trabecular structure of the liver is distorted.

questions.question: What is the normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio?
questions.explanation:
The normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio is 1:4 to 1:6.

Normal nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio implies that the volume occupied by the cytoplasm is 4 to 6 times greater than the volume occupied by the nucleus.

Abnormal nuclear morphologies that are seen in malignant cells:

• Nuclei disproportionately large for the cell

• Nuclear shape is variable and often irregular

• Chromatin

• Coarsely clumped

• Hyperchromatic

• Nucleoli are abnormally large

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman is diagnosed with metastatic breast cancer. Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in the microscopic examination of the resected tumor?
questions.explanation:
Loss of polarity is a microscopic finding in malignant neoplasm, like metastatic breast cancer.

In malignancy, the orientation of cells is markedly disturbed, and polarity is lost. Sheets or large masses of tumor cells grow in an anarchic, disorganized fashion.

Morphological changes in cancer cells:

• Anaplasia

• Pleomorphism

• Nuclear changes

• Nuclei disproportionately large for the cell

• Nuclear shape is variable and often irregular

• Chromatin - coarsely clumped and hyperchromatic

• Nucleoli are abnormally large

• Atypical mitosis

• Loss of polarity

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of post-coital bleeding. On per speculum examination, a friable mass is seen and a punch biopsy is done. The presence of which of the following features in microscopic examination of biopsy specimen differentiates invasive carcinoma from carcinoma in situ?
questions.explanation:
Once the tumor cells breach the basement membrane, the tumor is said to be invasive.

Progression of cancer occurs in the following stages: dysplasia→carcinoma in situ→invasive carcinoma

In situ carcinoma is when dysplastic changes are marked and involve the full thickness of the epithelium, but the lesion does not penetrate the basement membrane. It is a pre-invasive neoplasm.

The tumor is said to be invasive when the basement membrane is breached by the tumor cells.

questions.question:
Choose the correct statement(s):

Assertion (A): All tumors with invasive properties metastasize.

Reason (R): The invasive property of the tumor permits them to penetrate into the blood vessels or lymphatics, thus allowing them to spread to distant sites.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true; R is false
A is false; R is true
questions.answer: D. A is false; R is true
questions.explanation:
All tumors with invasive property (malignant tumors) may not necessarily metastasize.

Examples of tumors with invasive properties but do not metastasize are:

• Gliomas

• Basal cell carcinomas of the skin

Both of these cancers invade early in their course, but rarely metastasize. Thus, it is evident then that the properties of invasion and metastasis are separable.

questions.question: A 40-year-old patient is diagnosed with a breast lump. On clinical examination, nodes are not palpable. Mammography is suggestive of a malignant tumor. Which of the following nodes is often biopsied to assess the presence of metastasis microscopically?
options: Largest lymph node in the region of the primary tumor
Smallest lymph node in the region of the primary tumor
First lymph node that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor
Last lymph node that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor
questions.answer: C. First lymph node that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor
questions.explanation:
The sentinel lymph node, which is the first node in a regional lymphatic basin that receives lymph flow from the primary tumor, is often used to assess the presence or absence of metastatic lesions in the lymph nodes microscopically.

Sentinel node mapping can be done by the injection of radiolabeled tracers or colored dyes. Examination of frozen sections of the sentinel lymph node is often performed during surgery. It can guide the surgeon to the appropriate therapy.

Sentinel node examination has also been used for detecting the spread of:

• Melanomas

• Colon cancers

questions.question: Which of the following is not an angiogenesis promoter in tumor cells?
questions.explanation:
Thrombospondin is an anti-angiogenic factor.

Angiogenic and antiangiogenic factors are produced by tumor and stromal cells and are essential for the vascularization of tumors.

Angiogenic activators include:

• Angiogenin

• Interleukin-8

• Growth factors:

• Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)

• Basic fibroblast growth factor (bFGF)

• Transforming growth factor (TGF)-α and β

• Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-α

• Platelet-derived endothelial growth factor

• Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor

• Placental growth factor

• Hepatocyte growth factor

• Epidermal growth factor

Anti-angiogenic factors include:

• Angiostatin

• Endostatin

• Interferon

• Platelet factor 4

• Thrombospondin

• Prolactin 16 KD fragment

• Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-1, 2, and 3

questions.question: Which of the following malignancies is least likely to occur in those with only alcohol abuse and without any additional risk factors?
questions.explanation:
Alcohol abuse alone increases the risk of carcinomas of the oropharynx (excluding lip), larynx, and esophagus.

Alcohol and tobacco together synergistically increase the risk of cancers in the upper airway and digestive tract.

questions.question: A textile factory worker who is repeatedly exposed to benzene is at increased risk of developing which of the following tumors?
questions.explanation:
Repeated exposure to benzene is associated with increased risk of acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

Malignancies associated with repeated exposure to benzene:

• Acute myeloid leukemia (AML)

• Acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL).

• Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

• Multiple myeloma.

Note: While studies have shown that benzene has a propensity to cause bladder carcinoma , it is most commonly associated with AMLs.

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient employed in plastic industry for 30 years is diagnosed with a tumor in the liver. On resection, the gross specimen shows greyish white lesions with multiple reddish-brown hemorrhagic foci and several blood-filled spaces shown by arrows in the image given below. Which of the following is not a risk factor for the development of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and findings of the gross specimen are suggestive of angiosarcoma of the liver and beryllium is not a risk factor for the development of this tumor.

Angiosarcoma of the liver is associated with exposure to:

• Vinyl chloride

• Androgenic steroids

• Arsenic

• Thorotrast

Histological specimen of angiosarcoma of the liver is given below.

questions.question: A 50-year-old patient is diagnosed with lung carcinoma. Which of the following is implicated in the causation of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Radon is implicated in the causation of lung carcinoma.

Carcinogens implicated in lung carcinoma are:

• Asbestos

• Arsenic

• Beryllium

• Chromium

• Nickel

• Radon.

questions.question: A 50-year-old patient who is a known case of cholangiocarcinoma presents with intermittent fever and jaundice. Which of the following organisms is commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Opisthorchis viverrini (liver fluke) is implicated in the pathogenesis of cholangiocarcinoma.

Apart from Opisthorchis viverrini, Clonorchis sinensis is also known to cause cholangiocarcinoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is the least radiosensitive cell in blood?
questions.explanation:
The least radiosensitive cell in the blood is the platelet.

The most radiosensitive cell in the blood is the lymphocyte.

The most radiosensitive phase of the cell cycle is G2M.

The least radiosensitive is the S phase.

chapters.chapter: Molecular Basis Of Cancer And Tumor Immunity

questions.question: Which of the following is overexpressed in patients diagnosed with glioma?
questions.explanation:
Gliomas show overexpression of PDGF-β and TGF-α.

Isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type glioblastomas are associated with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) amplification and homozygous CDKN2A deletion.

questions.question: Which of the following is associated with loss of function mutation in RET proto-oncogene?
questions.explanation:
Loss of function mutation in RET proto-oncogene is associated with Hirschsprung's disease.

Hirschsprung's disease is caused by mutations in other genes encoding proteins involved in enteric neurodevelopment. These include:

• RET ligand glial-derived neurotrophic factor

• Endothelin

• Endothelin receptor

Note: Medullary thyroid carcinoma and multiple endocrine neoplasias, types 2A and 2B are usually due to gain of function mutations in RET proto-oncogene.

questions.question: Which of the following tumors is associated with mutation of the ALK receptor?
questions.explanation:
Anaplastic lymphoma kinase (ALK) is a membrane-bound receptor tyrosine kinase. When aberrantly expressed, it is associated with neuroblastoma pathogenesis. It serves as a therapeutic target.

Neuroblastoma is one of the most common solid cancers among children.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a painless loss of vision. Fundus examination reveals the lesion shown in the image. Which of the following GTP-binding proteins show point mutations in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and fundus examination are suggestive of uveal melanoma which is associated with a point mutation of GNAQ protein or GNA11 genes.

Uveal melanomas (UM) originate from melanocytes in the interior wall of the eye. This includes the iris, ciliary body, and the choroid with marked differences in light exposure (from dark anterior to illuminated posterior).

GNAS mutation causes pituitary adenoma and other endocrine tumors.

The 3 RAS genes in humans (H-RAS, K-RAS, and N-RAS) are the most common oncogenes in human cancer. They code for a family of proteins called GTP-binding (G) proteins, which are involved in transmitting signals within cells (cellular signal transduction). When RAS is 'switched on' by incoming signals, it subsequently switches on other proteins, which ultimately results in cell growth, differentiation, and survival.

Mutations in RAS genes can lead to the production of permanently activated RAS proteins. As a result, this can cause unintended and overactive signaling inside the cell, even in the absence of incoming signals. Because these signals result in cell growth and division, overactive RAS signaling can ultimately lead to cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following are coded by the MYC genes?
questions.explanation:
MYC oncogene codes for nuclear regulatory proteins. It is the most commonly involved transcription factor in tumors.

The MYC proto-oncogene MYC activates the expression of many genes that are involved in cell growth. It upregulates the expression of telomerase and reprograms somatic cells into pluripotent stem cells.

questions.question: Which of the following is associated with the translocation of cyclin D1?
questions.explanation:
Translocation of cyclin D1 is seen in mantle cell lymphoma.

Mantle cell lymphoma is an uncommon lymphoid neoplasm that is characterized by overexpression of cyclin D1. It is a type of non Hodgkins lymphoma that involves (11;14) translocation i.e. between IgH locus on chromosome 14 and the cyclin D1 locus on chromosome 11.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about Knudson's two-hit hypothesis theory on retinoblastoma?
options: Familial type is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
It involves both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q14
In sporadic cases, both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast
In familial cases, children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene and the other copy is normal
questions.answer: A. Familial type is inherited as an autosomal recessive trait
questions.explanation:
Retinoblastoma is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait.

Knudson's hypothesis, also known as the two-hit hypothesis or multiple-hit hypothesis states that cancer is the result of accumulated mutations in a cell's DNA. Two mutations (hits), involving both alleles of RB at chromosome locus 13q14, are required to produce retinoblastoma.

In familial cases, children inherit one defective copy of the RB gene in the germline (the first hit), and the other copy is normal. Retinoblastoma develops when the normal RB allele is mutated in retinoblasts as a result of a spontaneous somatic mutation (the second hit). Most individuals inheriting a germline defect in one RB allele develop unilateral or bilateral retinoblastoma as it is an autosomal dominant disease.

Sporadic cases are comparitively rare. In sporadic cases, both normal RB alleles must undergo somatic mutation in the same retinoblast (two hits).

The image given below shows the Knudson's two-hit hypothesis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about p53?
options: P53 inactivation causes cell cycle arrest at G2-M
Cancers demonstrate biallelic loss of function mutations in TP53
p53 can be inactivated by E6 protein of HPV
questions.answer: B. P53 inactivation causes cell cycle arrest at G2-M
questions.explanation:
P53 is the tumor suppressor gene and activation (not inactivation) causes cell cycle arrest at the G1-S and G2-M phase of the cell cycle.

P53 regulates:

• Cell cycle progression

• DNA repair

• Cellular senescence

• Apoptosis

It is activated by:

• Anoxia

• Inappropriate signaling by mutated oncoproteins

• DNA damage

It is the most frequently mutated gene in cancers. It upregulates the expression of proteins such as the cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor p21, thereby causing cell-cycle arrest at the G1-S. It also transactivates and transrepresses target gene to induce G2/M arrest. Mutation in the p53 gene causes resistance in tumors to radiation and chemotherapy.

The E6 protein of human papillomavirus (HPV) binds to and helps in the degradation of p53 and stimulates the expression of telomerase reverse transcriptase (TERT), which is the catalytic subunit of telomerase, thereby helping in the longevity of the cells. E6 from high-risk HPV types has a higher affinity for p53 than E6 from low-risk types.

Li-Fraumeni syndrome is an autosomal dominant disorder due to a defect in the tumor suppressor gene P53 located on chromosome 17.

questions.question: Which of the following is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia?
questions.explanation:
p63 is essential for the differentiation of stratified squamous epithelia.

p53 is ubiquitously expressed, while p63 and p73 show more tissue specificity.

p73 has strong pro-apoptotic effects after DNA damage induced by chemotherapeutic agents.

questions.question: A 22-year-old man was found to have multiple GI polyps. He was operated on for thyroid cancer 2 years back. His family history is significant for breast cancer in his mother and endometrial cancer in his aunt. Germline loss-of-function mutations of which gene is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Cowden syndrome. This condition is caused due to germline loss of function mutation in PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homolog) gene.

PTEN is a membrane-associated phosphatase encoded by a gene on chromosome 10q23 that is mutated.

Cowden syndrome is characterized by skin appendage tumors and an increased incidence of epithelial cancers, particularly of the breast, endometrium, and thyroid.

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presented with hearing loss and tinnitus. MRI was done and showed the presence of bilateral acoustic schwannomas. Which protein involved in cytoskeletal stability is mutated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and MRI findings are suggestive of neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF-2). Merlin protein is mutated in NF-2, sporadic schwannomas, and meningiomas.

Cells lacking Merlin do not establish stable cell-to-cell junctions. They are insensitive to normal growth arrest signals generated by cell-to-cell contact.

questions.question: Germline loss-of-function mutation of which gene causes Gorlin syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Germline loss-of-function mutations of the PTCH1 gene cause Gorlin syndrome.

Gorlin syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. Clinical features include:

• Multiple basal cell carcinomas

• Highly characteristic facies - large forehead

• Bifid or misshapen ribs

• Vertebral and other skeletal anomalies

• Pits of the skin of the palms and soles

• Dysgenesis of the corpus callosum

• Calcification of the falx cerebri - at an earlier age than is seen in non‐affected individuals

• Macrocephaly

Acquired biallelic loss-of-function mutations of PTCH1 cause sporadic basal cell carcinomas and medulloblastoma.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man patient presents with anemia and abdominal pain. On examination, he has pigmented macules over the palms, soles, and oral mucosa. Further investigations reveal loss-of-function mutations of the STK11 gene. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of Peutz–Jeghers syndrome.

Loss-of-function mutations of STK11 cause the Peutz–Jeghers syndrome. The STK22 gene, also known as LKB1, encodes a serine/threonine kinase that is an important regulator of cellular metabolism.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder. It is associated with arborizing polyps of the gastrointestinal tract (small intestine > colon > stomach). It increases the risk of multiple epithelial cancers, particularly of colon, breast, lung, pancreas, and thyroid.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman presents with complaints of a palpable mass in both breasts. Histopathology examination shows the following finding. Immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor positivity. Which protein that maintains cell adhesion, and thereby inhibits cell motility, is mutated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of lobular carcinoma of the breast which involves mutated E-cadherin protein. In this condition, the histopathological examination shows infiltrating small monomorphic discohesive tumor cells arranged in an Indian-file or single-file pattern.

The image below shows the single file pattern seen in lobular carcinoma of the breast.

Reduced cell surface expression of E-cadherin is seen in carcinomas of:

• Breast

• Esophagus

• Colon

• Ovary

• Prostate

E-cadherin is a cell-surface protein that maintains intercellular adhesiveness. Loss of E-cadherin causes disaggregation of cells, which can then invade locally or metastasize.

Germline loss-of-function mutations of the E-cadherin gene lead to familial gastric carcinoma. Sporadic gastric carcinomas are also associated with the loss of E-cadherin expression.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the BRCA genes?
options: BRCA1 is located on the long arm of chromosome 17
BRCA 2 mutation is associated with male breast carcinoma
questions.answer: B. BRCA1 mutation causes well-differentiated cancer
questions.explanation: BRCA2 (not BRCA 1) mutation causes well-differentiated cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding apoptosis?
options: p53 induces apoptosis in cells with DNA damage
Extrinsic apoptotic pathway is more frequently disabled in cancer cells
Chemoradiation induces apoptosis in cancer cells
BCL2 is over-expressed in follicular lymphomas
questions.answer: B. Extrinsic apoptotic pathway is more frequently disabled in cancer cells
questions.explanation:
The intrinsic apoptotic pathway is most frequently disabled in cancer cells to evade cell death.

p53 is an important pro-apoptotic protein that induces apoptosis in cells that are unable to repair DNA damage.

Chemotherapy and radiation therapy kills cancer cells mainly by inducing apoptosis via the intrinsic pathway.

In greater than 85% of follicular B-cell lymphomas, the anti-apoptotic gene BCL2 is overexpressed due to a (14;18) translocation.

questions.question:
Which of the following genes promote epithelial-mesenchymal transition in epithelial tumors?

1. MYC

2. SNAIL

3. TWIST

4. BRCA1

5. RET
questions.explanation:
SNAIL and TWIST, which encode transcription factors, promote epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).

In EMT, carcinoma cells downregulate certain epithelial markers (e.g., E-cadherin) and upregulate certain mesenchymal markers (e.g. vimentin and smooth muscle actin). This favors the development of a promigratory phenotype that is essential for metastasis. EMT has been documented mainly in breast carcinoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase?
questions.explanation:
ABL is a non-receptor tyrosine kinase.

Tyrosine kinases may be receptors and non-receptors.

Nonreceptor tyrosine kinases normally localize to the cytoplasm or the nucleus. These are:

• ABL - translocation causes CML and point mutation causes ALL

• JAK mutation - seen in polycythemia vera, essential thrombocythemia, and myelofibrosis as well as other myeloproliferative disorders

Receptor tyrosine kinases:

• VEGFR

• PDGFR

• EGFR

In chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and some acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL), the ABL gene is translocated from its normal abode on chromosome 9 to chromosome 22 where it fuses with the BCR gene forming the Philadelphia chromosome. The resultant chimeric gene encodes a constitutively active, oncogenic BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase.

questions.question: Mutation in which of the following oncogenes can serve as a tumor antigen?
questions.explanation:
RAS is an oncogene that undergoes mutation and serves as a tumor antigen.

Tumor cells express antigenic molecules on their surface that elicit an immune response. These are called tumor antigens. Some tumor cells evade immune response which results in growth of the tumor.

questions.question: Which of the following mechanisms does not lead to immune evasion by the tumor cells?
options: Inhibition of PD-1 receptor on T-cells
questions.answer: A. Inhibition of PD-1 receptor on T-cells
questions.explanation:
Inhibition of PD-1 receptor (programmed death -1 receptor) on T cells causes activation of immunity against the tumor cells, not evasion.

PD-1 receptors present on T cells inhibit T-cell activation. This allows tumors to evade the host immunity by the upregulation of the expression of factors like PD-L1 and PD-L2, which act on PD-1 receptors.

questions.question: An 8-year-old girl is referred with recurrent blistering rashes over the face and upper limbs which worsened following exposure to sunlight. There is a history of similar skin lesions in her family and 2 of her uncles were diagnosed with skin cancers at young ages. Examination reveals the presence of multiple lentigos and xerosis. What is the likely pathological mechanism of this condition?
questions.answer: B. Defective DNA nucleotide excision repair
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of xeroderma pigmentosum. It is caused by a defect in the DNA nucleotide excision repair pathway resulting in inability to repair pyrimidine dimers.

Clinical features of xeroderma pigmentosum:

• Actinic keratosis

• Hyperkeratotic lesions

• Multiple lentigos

• Xerosis

• Corneal scarring

The image of a child with xeroderma pigmentosum is given below.

questions.question: Which of the following disorders is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism?
questions.explanation:
Fanconi syndrome is not associated with defective homologous recombination DNA repair mechanism. It is a rare disorder of kidney tubule function.

Diseases with defects in DNA repair by homologous recombination:

• Bloom syndrome and ataxia–telangiectasia triggered by DNA-damaging agents such as ionizing radiation

• Fanconi anemia is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in multiple genes responsible for coding for proteins that participate in DNA repair pathways and are triggered by DNA-crosslinking agents like chemotherapeutic drugs.

• Familial breast cancer is due to inherited gene defects in BRCA1 and BRCA 2 genes

questions.question: A 30-year-old patient presents with right iliac fossa pain. Imaging shows the presence of an ileocaecal mass. Biopsy of the mass shows a starry sky pattern. What is the translocation involved in this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and biopsy findings are suggestive of Burkitt lymphoma and the translocation involved is t(8;14).

Burkitt lymphoma, also known as small non-cleaved-cell lymphoma, is a highly aggressive B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma. It is characterized by the translocation and deregulation of the c-myc gene on chromosome 8.

The classic t(8;14)(q24;q32) reciprocal translocation results in the transposition of the c-myc proto-oncogene on chromosome 8 with one of the immunoglobulin heavy chain (IGH) genes on chromosome 14. This results in activation of the c-myc gene and is considered responsible for tumor proliferation.

questions.question: Which epigenomic regulatory gene is mutated in most of the follicular lymphomas?
questions.explanation:
MLL2 is an epigenomic regulatory gene that is mutated in most follicular lymphomas. It results in histone methylation.

Epigenetics refers to factors other than the sequence of DNA that regulate gene expression. These factors involved in epigenetics are:

• Histone modifications

• DNA methylation

• Nucleosome positioning/ chromatin remodeling

questions.question: The loss of which of the following micro RNAs leads to upregulation of BCL-2?
questions.explanation:
The loss of miR-15 leads to upregulation of the anti-apoptotic protein BCL-2.

miR-15 and miR-16 are tumor-suppressive miRNAs involved in chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL).

Onco-miRNAs include:

• miR200 - promotes epithelial-mesenchymal transitions that promote tumor invasion and metastasis

• miR155 - involved in human B-cell lymphomas

chapters.chapter: Carcinogenesis, Paraneoplastic Syndromes And Tumor Markers

questions.question: Which of the following tumors is best suited to study the mechanism of multi-step carcinogenesis?
questions.explanation:
Multi-step carcinogenesis is best studied in colon carcinoma.

The molecular model for the evolution of colorectal cancers is described as Fearon-Vogelstein adenoma-carcinoma sequence.

questions.question: Which of the following procarcinogens does not require metabolic activation?
questions.explanation:
Cyclophosphamide is a directly-acting carcinogen that does not require metabolic activation.

Carcinogens can be direct-acting or indirect-acting based on their activation.

Direct-acting carcinogens require no metabolic conversion to become carcinogenic. Most are weak carcinogens, but some are important because they are cancer chemotherapeutic drugs (e.g., alkylating agents). The direct-acting carcinogens include:

• Alkylating Agents:

• β-Propiolactone

• Dimethyl sulfate

• Diepoxybutane

• Anticancer drugs (cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nitrosoureas, and others)

• Acylating Agents:

• 1-Acetyl-imidazole

• Dimethylcarbamyl chloride

Indirect-acting carcinogens (procarcinogens) are chemicals that require metabolic conversion to become active carcinogens. The carcinogenic product of metabolism is called an ultimate carcinogen. The indirect-acting carcinogens include:

• Polycyclic and heterocyclic aromatic hydrocarbons:

• Benz[a]anthracene

• Benzo[a]pyrene

• Dibenz[a,h]anthracene

• 3-Methylcholanthrene

• 7,12-Dimethylbenz[a]anthracene

• Aromatic amines, amides, azo dyes:

• 2-Naphthylamine (β-naphthylamine)

• Benzidine

• 2-Acetylaminofluorene

• Dimethylaminoazobenzene (butter yellow)

• Natural plant and microbial products:

• Aflatoxin B1

• Griseofulvin

• Cycasin

• Safrole

• Betel nuts

• Others

• Nitrosamine and amides

• Vinyl chloride, nickel, chromium

• Insecticides, fungicides

• Polychlorinated biphenyls

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with a hyperpigmented lesion on his face. He is a farmer by occupation and works for long hours with sun exposure. He is at increased risk for all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Seborrheic keratosis is not associated with exposure to ultraviolet (UV) rays from sun exposure.

UV rays derived from sun exposure are associated with the increased incidence of:

• Squamous cell carcinoma

• Basal cell carcinoma

• Melanoma of the skin

Actinic keratosis is a precancerous skin condition that can cause squamous cell cancer if untreated.

questions.question: Which form of radiation is responsible for cutaneous cancer?
questions.explanation:
UVB (ultraviolet B) causes cutaneous cancers due to the formation of pyrimidine dimers in DNA.

When DNA absorbs energy from UVB, there is a covalent crosslinking of pyrimidine bases and distortion of the DNA helix. This prevents proper pairing of the dimer with bases in the opposite DNA strand.

Normally, these defects are repaired by nucleotide excision repair pathway. Defects in nucleotide excision repair pathway result in xeroderma pigmentosum.

UV portion of the solar spectrum is divided into three wavelength ranges:

Spectrum
Wavelength

UVA
320-400 nm

UVB
280-320 nm

UVC
200-280 nm

Note: UVC is the most potent mutagen but is not considered significant as it is filtered out by the ozone layer.

questions.question: Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of which of the following malignancies?
questions.explanation:
Individuals with repeated exposure to ionizing radiation are at increased risk of myeloid leukemia.

Carcinogenic radiations include:

• Electromagnetic radiation -

• X-rays

• γ rays

• Particulate radiation -

• α particles

• β particles

• Protons

• Neutrons

Cancers due to ionizing radiation:

• Most frequent - myeloid leukemia and thyroid cancer

• Intermediate frequency - cancers of breast, lungs, and salivary glands

• Relatively resistant cancers - cancers of skin, bone, and gastrointestinal tract

questions.question: Which of the following tumors is not caused by microbes?
questions.explanation: Adenocarcinoma carcinoma of the lung is not associated with microbial etiopathogenesis. It is associated with smoking and genetic predispositions.

questions.question: Which of the following malignancies is caused by HTLV-1?
questions.explanation:
Human T-cell leukemia-lymphoma virus (HTLV-1) causes adult T-cell leukemia/lymphoma (ATLL).

HTLV-1 encodes the viral protein Tax, which leads to polyclonal expansion of T cells. It exhibits tropism for CD4+ T cells.

Human infection requires transmission of infected T cells through sexual intercourse, blood products or breast feeding. Leukemia develops only in 3-5% of infected individuals, typically after a long latent period of 40-60 years.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of HPV oncoproteins and target genes are correctly matched?
questions.explanation:
The target genes for viral oncoproteins of human papilloma virus (HPV) are as follows:

• E6 - p53

• E7 - RB

The image given below shows the functions of the E6 and E7 oncoproteins of HPV.

questions.question: A 13-year-old child presents to the OPD with fever, pharyngitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy. Peripheral smear showed a predominance of lymphocytes. The heterophile agglutination test is positive. The causative organism of this condition is not implicated in which of the following tumors?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario is suggestive of infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. This virus is not implicated in follicular lymphoma.

Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), a member of the herpesvirus family, has been implicated in:

• African form of Burkitt lymphoma

• B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed

• A subset of Hodgkin lymphoma

• Nasopharyngeal carcinoma

• Gastric carcinoma - most common EBV associated malignancy

• T-cell lymphoma and natural killer (NK) cell lymphoma

questions.question: Which of the following statements about Epstein-Barr virus is incorrect?
options: EBV infection always results in Burkitt lymphoma
It uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach and infect B cells
It is implicated in B-cell lymphomas in immunosuppressed people
It is a potent inducer of B-cell growth and transformation
questions.answer: A. EBV infection always results in Burkitt lymphoma
questions.explanation:
Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection does not always result in Burkitt lymphoma.

EBV infection is highly prevalent even in areas where Burkitt lymphoma is not found. It commonly causes infectious mononucleosis.

EBV uses the complement receptor CD21 to attach to and infect B cells. EBV genome triggers B-cell signaling pathways inducing B-cell growth and transformation.

The infection of B cells is latent as there is no viral replication and the cells are not killed. However, B cells latently infected with EBV express viral proteins that result in the ability to propagate indefinitely in vitro. In the absence of T-cell immunity, EBV-infected B cells can rapidly grow out as aggressive B-cell tumors.

questions.question: Which of the following pathogens is implicated in the causation of primary effusion lymphoma and Castleman disease?
questions.explanation:
Human herpesvirus 8 (HHV8) is a gamma-herpesvirus associated with Kaposi sarcoma, multicentric Castleman disease, and primary effusion lymphoma.

They are lymphoproliferative diseases that are most commonly observed in immunocompromised individuals. The viral genome expresses genes responsible for inhibition of apoptosis, cell cycle entry, and angiogenesis.

questions.question: Which of the following is an EBV oncogene behaving like a constitutively active CD40 receptor?
questions.explanation:
LMP-1 is an EBV oncogene that behaves like a constitutively active CD40 receptor.

The CD40 receptor-like activity stimulates B-cell growth. LMP-1 activates the NF-κB and JAK / STAT signaling pathways and promotes B-cell survival. It also prevents apoptosis by activating BCL2.

questions.question:
Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of development of which of the following conditions?

1. Peptic ulcer

2. Barrett's esophagus

3. Gastric adenocarcinoma

4. MALT lymphoma

5. Adenocarcinoma of esophagus
questions.explanation:
Helicobacter pylori is implicated in the following conditions:

• Peptic ulcer

• Gastric adenocarcinoma - preceded by chronic gastritis, gastric atrophy, intestinal metaplasia, and dysplasia

• MALT lymphoma of the stomach - through polyclonal B cell proliferation

Helicobacter pylori is protective for:

• Barrett's esophagus

• Adenocarcinoma of esophagus

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common endocrinopathy caused by tumors?
questions.explanation:
Cushing syndrome is the most common endocrinopathy caused by tumors.

Endocrinopathy refers to ectopic hormone production by non-endocrine tumors. Approximately, 50% of the individuals with Cushing syndrome as endocrinopathy have carcinoma of the lung, chiefly the small-cell type.

Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome. Cancer-associated hypercalcemia occurs due to:

• Osteolysis induced by cancer - due to primary or secondary involvement of the skeleton by tumor

• Production of calcemic humoral substances by extraosseous neoplasms - for example, parathyroid hormone-related protein. Only this mechanism is considered to be paraneoplastic.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following tumors present with pure red cell aplasia as a paraneoplastic manifestation?
questions.explanation:
Thymoma often presents with pure red cell aplasia as a paraneoplastic manifestation.

Thymomas are unusual neoplasms of thymic epithelial tissue, ranging from small indolent tumors to aggressive thymic carcinomas.

Pure red cell aplasia is a rare cause of anemia, caused by the absence of RBC precursors in the bone marrow. Causes of pure red cell aplasia include:

• Neoplasms - thymomas and large granular lymphocytic leukemia

• Drug exposure - phenytoin, azathioprine, and isoniazid

• Auto-immune disorders - neutralizing antibodies against erythropoietin

• Parvovirus infection

• Hereditary - Diamond Blackfan syndrome

questions.question: Which subtype of acute myeloid leukemia presents with disseminated intravascular coagulation as a paraneoplastic manifestation?
questions.explanation:
Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) as a paraneoplastic syndrome is most commonly associated with acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) and prostatic adenocarcinoma.

Major determinants of coagulopathy in APL are endogenous factors of the malignant leukemic cells and their interaction with host defense mechanisms.

Factors that cause coagulopathy include:

• Increased expression of procoagulant activity (PCA)

• Expression of fibrinolytic and proteolytic properties

• Secretion of pro-inflammatory cytokines - interleukin-1b (IL-1b) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient presents with loss of weight and appetite. On clinical examination, grade IV clubbing is evident. Imaging shows periosteal new bone formation and synovial effusion. Which of the following tumors is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history is suggestive of hypertrophic osteoarthropathy. It is commonly associated with bronchiogenic carcinoma.

Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy is characterised by the following:

• Periosteal new bone formation, primarily at the distal ends of long bones, metatarsals, metacarpals, and proximal phalanges

• Arthritis of the adjacent joints

• Clubbing of the digits

questions.question: A 55-year-old patient presents with generalized tiredness, malaise, muscle weakness, and bone pain. Laboratory investigations reveal serum calcium to be 13 mg/dL. Which of the following is lung cancers is implicated in this patient?
questions.answer: A. Squamous cell carcinoma of lung
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and laboratory investigations are suggestive of hypercalcemia. It is associated with squamous cell carcinoma of the lung.

Tumors associated with paraneoplastic hypercalcemia:

• Breast carcinoma

• Lung carcinoma

• Renal cell carcinoma

• Ovarian carcinoma

questions.question: Which of the following paraneoplastic manifestations is likely to occur in a patient with a phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor?
questions.explanation:
Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor presents with osteomalacia as a paraneoplastic manifestation.

Phosphaturic mesenchymal tumor is caused due to mutation of the FGF-23 gene.

questions.question: A 48-year-old obese female presents with skin changes in her axilla and neck as shown in the image. Which of the following tumors is not associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of acanthosis nigricans. It is not associated with thymoma.

Acanthosis nigricans is a disorder characterized by gray-black patches of thickened, hyperkeratotic skin with a velvety appearance. The causal mechanism is immunologic due to secretion of epidermal growth factor.

Acanthosis nigricans is commonly associated with:

• Gastric carcinoma

• Lung carcinoma

• Gynecological cancers

• Breast carcinoma

• Bladder carcinoma

• Gallbladder and bile-duct carcinoma

• Acromegaly and gigantism

• Dermatomyositis

• Diabetes

• Hashimoto thyroiditis

• Lupus erythematosus

• Phenylketonuria

• Polycystic ovary syndrome

• Systemic sclerosis

• Wilson syndrome

questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with headache, vertigo, tinnitus, and visual disturbance. On further evaluation, blood hemoglobin and hematocrit levels are found to be 18 g/dL and 62% respectively. Which of the following tumors does not present with these paraneoplastic manifestations?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and laboratory investigations are suggestive of polycythemia which is not seen in melanoma as a paraneoplastic manifestation.

Polycythemia, as a paraneoplastic syndrome, is mediated by erythropoietin (EPO). EPO is a glycoprotein that induces differentiation of erythrocyte colony-forming units in the bone marrow to promote red blood cell production.

Under normal physiological conditions, EPO is produced by peritubular renal interstitial cells in response to local tissue hypoxia. However, in tumors, EPO production occurs in the neoplastic cells themselves.

questions.question: Which of these paraneoplastic syndromes is associated with small-cell carcinoma lung?
questions.explanation: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) is associated with small cell carcinoma of lung.

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient notices spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules in different parts of the body. Which of the following malignancies is not associated with this clinical presentation?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical presentation is suggestive of migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and it is not associated with bladder carcinoma.

Trousseau syndrome may be encountered in association with deep-seated cancers, most often carcinomas of the pancreas or lung. It is caused by hypercoagulability leading to multiple repeated venous thromboembolism.

Malignant brain tumors, hematological malignancies, and adenocarcinomas of the pancreas, stomach, ovary, uterus, lungs, and kidneys are at the highest risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) development.

Advanced, metastatic cancer has been shown to be associated with an increased risk of VTE compared with localized tumors.

questions.question: A 24-year-old patient with paroxysmal hypertension is suspected to have malignant pheochromocytoma. Which of the following tumor markers will help you confirm your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The serum levels of catecholamines are elevated in malignant pheochromocytoma. Extra-adrenal location is the only criteria for malignancy in pheochromocytoma.

Pheochromocytoma is a rare catecholamine-secreting tumor that may precipitate life-threatening hypertension. It is classically associated with three syndromes:

• von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome

• Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN 2)

• Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1)

Catecholamines produced by pheochromocytomas are metabolized within chromaffin cells. Norepinephrine is metabolized to normetanephrine, and epinephrine is metabolized to metanephrine. Because this process occurs within the tumor, independent of catecholamine release, pheochromocytomas are best diagnosed by the measurement of these metabolites, rather than by measurement of the parent catecholamines.

questions.question:
Which of the following are oncofetal antigens?

1. α-fetoprotein

2. Carcinoembryonic antigen

3. Human chorionic gonadotropin

4. Placental alkaline phosphatase

5. Immunoglobulins
questions.explanation:
Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) are oncofetal antigens.

Alpha-fetoprotein is a valuable clinical aid in diagnosis, prognosis, and monitoring of the following tumors:

• Primary hepatocellular carcinoma

• Hepatoblastoma

• Non-seminomatous testicular germ cell tumors

• Embryonal carcinoma

• Teratomas

• Choriocarcinoma

• Yolk sac carcinoma

• Germ cell tumors of the ovary and extragonadal germ cell tumors

Regenerated hepatic tissue following liver damage due to viral hepatitis, chemically induced necrosis, and liver surgery are associated with moderately raised serum AFP levels.

Carcinoembryonic antigen is normally detected in glycocalyx of fetal epithelial cells. It is useful in detection, assessing recurrence, and prognosis of the following tumors:

• Adenocarcinoma of lung

• Colorectal carcinoma

CEA levels >5 ng/dL are noted in ascites fluid associated with malignancy. Canalicular pattern for polyclonal CEA more sensitive for hepatocellular carcinoma, metastases in pancreatic adenocarcinoma and not sensitive for metastasis in bile duct adenoma.

Elevated levels are also present in the following non-neoplastic conditions:

• Cirrhosis

• Biliary obstruction

• Hepatitis

• Inflammatory bowel disease

• Smokers

• Post-surgical bowel sequestration

• Mucocele

• Benign cysts may be positive for carcinoembryonic antigen

questions.question: A 42-year-old patient is diagnosed with breast cancer. Which of the following glycoproteins is expected to be elevated in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The level of cancer antigen 15-3 (CA 15-3) is elevated in patients with breast cancer.

The reference range of serum CA 15-3 is less than 30 U/mL. It is used to monitor response to breast cancer treatment and disease recurrence.

questions.question: A 51-year-old male patient who is a chronic smoker presents with dry persistent cough and progressive dyspnea. You are suspecting small cell carcinoma of lung. Which of the following tumor markers is likely to be elevated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of small cell carcinoma of the lung (SCLC) in which levels of neuron-specific enolase (NSE) are elevated.

NSE is also called gamma enolase or enolase 2 (ENO2) and is encoded by ENO2 gene. It is a phosphopyruvate hydratase that is produced by small-cell lung carcinomas, which are neuroendocrine in origin. Their levels have been implicated as a prognostic factor for patients with small-cell lung cancer.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a component of innate immunity?
questions.explanation:
B cell is not a component of innate immunity. It is a component of adaptive immunity.

Innate immunity refers to the body’s natural immunity. It is a built-in defence system that is present since birth. It differs from adaptive immunity in that it does not require any prior sensitization to an antigen.

The major components of innate immunity are as follows:

• Epithelial barriers that block the entry of microbes

• Phagocytic cells (neutrophils and macrophages)

• Natural killer (NK) cells

• Dendritic cell

• Cells that can sense and react to microbes - mast cells, epithelial and endothelial cells

• Plasma proteins - complement system factors, mannose-binding lectin, and C-reactive protein

• Innate lymphoid cells

• Lung surfactant

questions.question: What is the mechanism by which toll-like receptors stimulate immune response against bacterial products?
options: NFκB mediated transcription of nuclear factor
questions.answer: C. NFκB mediated transcription of nuclear factor
questions.explanation:
Toll-like receptors (TLRs) stimulate immune response by NFκB mediated transcription of nuclear factors.

TLRs are pattern recognition receptors which activate two sets of transcription factors:

• NF-κB - stimulates the synthesis and secretion of cytokines and the expression of adhesion molecules. Both are critical for the recruitment and activation of leukocytes

• Interferon regulatory factors - stimulate the production of the antiviral cytokines like type I interferons

The image given below shows a toll-like receptor.

The various classes of innate immune receptors are as follows:

 Receptors
Location
Function

Toll-like receptors
Plasma membrane and endosomal vesicles

Important TLRs and molecules recognised:

• TLR2 - peptidoglycan of gram + bacteria, lipopolysaccharide of Leptospira

• TLR3 - dsRNA viruses

• TLR4Q - Chlamydia and lipopolysaccharide

NOD-like receptors
Cytosol of immune cells and epithelial cells

• Recognise substances from necrotic cells and microbial products

• Signals via inflammasome which activates caspase and IL-1

C-type lectin receptors
Plasma membrane of macrophages and dendritic cells

• Detect fungal glycans and elicit inflammatory reactions to fungi

RIG-like receptors
Cytosol of most cell types

• Detect nucleic acids of viruses that replicate in the cytoplasm of infected cells

• Stimulate the production of antiviral cytokines

• Recognize short bacterial peptides containing N-formyl methionyl residues and stimulate chemotaxis

Mannose receptors
Plasma membrane of macrophages, immature dendritic cells, and liver sinusoidal endothelial cells

• Detect microbial sugars (which often contain terminal mannose residues) and induce phagocytosis of the microbes

Mannose receptor is a soluble pattern-recognition receptor. All the others are surface pattern-recognition receptors.

questions.question: Which of the following occurs due to gain-of-function mutations in NOD-Like receptors?
questions.explanation:
The gain of function mutations in NOD-Like receptors (NLRs) result in periodic fever syndromes called autoinflammatory syndromes.

They are a group of clinical conditions characterised by recurrent inflammatory episodes. This disorder is marked by abnormally increased inflammation, mediated predominantly by cells and molecules of the innate immune system, with a significant host predisposition.

NOD-like receptors are cytosolic receptors that signal via a cytosolic multiprotein complex called the inflammasome. This activates caspase-1 that generates biologically active form of interleukin-1 (IL-1). IL-1 is a mediator of inflammation that recruits leukocytes and induces fever. The autoinflammatory syndromes respond very well to treatment with IL-1 antagonists.

Note: Autoimmune diseases result from T and B-lymphocyte reactions against self-antigens.

questions.question: What is the normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio?
questions.explanation:
Normal CD4+: CD8+ T lymphocyte ratio is 2:1. Approximately 60% of mature T cells are CD4+ and about 30% are CD8+.

T-lymphocytes (thymus-derived cells) constitute 60–70% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. T-cell progenitors are derived from the bone marrow, but travel to the thymus, where they mature. T cells can be divided into three main subtypes:

Type of T cell

Function

Helper T cell (CD4+)

Helps B lymphocytes to make antibodies and activate other leukocytes to destroy microbes

Cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs or CD8+)

Kill infected cells

Regulatory T cells

Limit immune responses and prevent reactions against self-antigens.

They are located in the paracortical areas of lymph nodes and the periarteriolar sheaths of the spleen. They have an antigen-specific T-cell receptors (TCR) which have alpha/beta polypeptide chains components. Demonstration of TCR gene rearrangement by southern blot is a molecular marker of T-cell lineage.

The CD molecules present on T cells are CD1, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD7, CD8 and CD28. CD3 is involved in signal transduction and is also called a pan T-cell marker. CD40 ligand on the surface is required for B-cell activation and induction of immunoglobulin.

questions.question: Which of the following is not expressed in the B-cell receptor complex?
questions.explanation:
CD86 is a protein expressed on antigen-presenting cells, and not B-cell receptor complex. This protein provides costimulatory signals necessary for T-cell activation and survival.

B-cell receptor complex expresses the following:

• CD79a and CD79b - essential for signal transduction through the antigen receptor

• CD21 or CR2 - complement receptor (recognize complement products during innate immune response) and Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) receptor

• CD40 - receives signals from helper T cells

Other B cell-associated markers are CD10 (CALLA), CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23.

questions.question: Which of the following are the most important antigen-presenting cells?
questions.explanation:
Dendritic cells or interdigitating dendritic cells are the most important antigen-presenting cells. They initiate T-cell responses against protein antigens.

They are located in the epithelium and interstitium. They express many receptors for capturing and responding to microbes (and other antigens), including toll-like receptors (TLRs) and lectins. They also express high levels of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) for presenting antigens to and activating T cells.

In response to microbes, dendritic cells are recruited to the T-cell zones of lymphoid organs. Here, they present antigens to T cells with help of MHC.

Similar cells with dendritic morphology in the germinal centers of lymphoid follicles in the spleen and lymph nodes are follicular dendritic cells. They bear Fc receptors for IgG and receptors for C3b. Immature dendritic cells within the epidermis are called Langerhans cells.

Note:

• Aggretope - part of the antigen associated with the MHC molecule on the antigen-presenting cell

• Epitope - antigenic part of contact with the T-cell receptor

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about macrophages?
options: It acts as an antigen presenting cell
It plays a role in humoral immunity
It plays a role in cell-mediated immunity
It is a component of innate immunity only
questions.answer: D. It is a component of innate immunity only
questions.explanation:
Macrophages are components of both innate and acquired immunity.

They phagocytose microbes and protein antigens. They process the antigens and present the peptide fragments to T cells. Thus, macrophages function as antigen-presenting cells in T-cell activation.

They also participate in the effector phase of humoral immunity. Macrophages efficiently phagocytose and destroy microbes that are opsonized (coated) with IgG or C3b.

They are key effector cells in certain forms of cell-mediated immunity to eliminate intracellular microbes. In this type of response, T cells activate macrophages and enhance their ability to kill ingested microbes.

questions.question: Which of the following is false about natural killer cells?
options: CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules
They are involved in antibody-dependant cytotoxic killing
IL-12 stimulates the proliferation of NK cells
They activate macrophages by secreting IFN-γ
questions.answer: C. IL-12 stimulates the proliferation of NK cells
questions.explanation:
IL-2 and IL-15 stimulate the proliferation of NK cells. On the other hand, IL-12 activates the killing of target cells and secretion of IFN-γ.

NK cells are large granular lymphocytes, which constitutes 5% to 10% of peripheral blood lymphocytes. CD16 and CD56 are the surface molecules.

Functions of NK cells:

• Killing of a variety of virus-infected cells and tumor cells, without prior exposure to or activation by these microbes or tumors

• Secretion of interferon-γ (IFN-γ), which activates macrophages to destroy ingested microbes

• Antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) - NK cells express CD16 which is a receptor for IgG Fc tails. Hence, these cells have the ability to lyse IgG-coated target cells.

ADCC is also seen in immune responses involving neutrophils, eosinophils, macrophages, etc.

The image given below shows activating and inhibitory receptors of natural killer (NK) cells.

Note: A new group of T cells has been discovered called NK-T cells. These are T cells that contain markers of NK cells. These are important defence mechanisms against microorganisms like Listeria monocytogenes and Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

questions.question: Which of these is common to both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells?
options: They are MHC l restricted cells
Require antibodies to be present for action
questions.explanation:
Both cytotoxic T-cells and NK cells are effective against virus-infected cells.

The NK cells have different mechanisms of action while killing target cells.

NK cells can lyse IgG-coated target cells by binding to the Fc tail of IgG, through the CD16 receptor expressed on NK cells. This phenomenon is known as antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC).

NK cells secrete various cytokines such as interferon-γ (IFN-γ), which activate macrophages to destroy ingested microbes.

Target cell destruction by NK cells is also mediated through two others receptors - activating receptors and inhibitory receptors.

The activating receptors enable NK cells to recognize infected and stressed cells. The inhibitory receptors recognize self class-I MHC molecules, that are expressed on all healthy cells thereby preventing NK cells from killing normal cells. Virus infection / neoplastic transformation overexpresses the activating receptors and simultaneously reduces the expression of class-I MHC molecules. As a result, NK cells are activated and the infected cells are killed.

CD8+ cytotoxic T lymphocytes directly kill damaged cells.

The differences between NK cells and cytotoxic T-cells are:

Natural killer (NK) cell
Cytotoxic T-cells

Does not require priming - rapid response in hours
 require priming - takes days to respond

MHC unrestricted
MHC restricted

Antibody-mediated and non-antibody-mediated killing

Non-antibody mediated killing / direct cytotoxicity

Kills virus-infected and neoplastic cells by apoptosis

Kills virus-infected, neoplastic, and donor graft cells by apoptosis

Antigen non-specific
Antigen-specific

Memory is absent
Memory is present

questions.question: Which of the following markers on antigen-presenting cells function as costimulatory molecules for T cells?
questions.explanation:
CD80 (B7-1) and CD86 (B7-2) are the costimulatory molecules present on antigen-presenting cells (APCs). They bind to CD28 protein present on T cells. This promotes the expansion of antigen-stimulated T cells and their differentiation into effector and memory cells.

T-cell activation requires two signals that are delivered by APCs. They include:

1. Antigens displayed by APCs in the form of peptides bound to MHC molecules, that are recognised by T-cell receptors

2. Costimulatory signal (as it stimulates T cells in conjunction with antigen) provided by molecules on APCs that engage particular costimulatory receptors on T cells

In the absence of costimulation, T cells that recognize antigen either fail to respond and die or enter a state of unresponsiveness known as anergy. Thus, costimulation is a key determinant of the outcome of a T-cell encounter with an antigen.

questions.question: Which of the following cytokines induces T-helper type 2 cells?
questions.explanation:
IL-4 induces T helper 2 cells.

Mechanism of cell-mediated immunity:

• Antigen-presenting cells → recognized by naive CD4+ T cells → IL-2 secretion → T-cell proliferation and differentiation → activated CD4+ T helper cells

• Activated CD4+ T cells further differentiate into effector cells that secrete different sets of cytokines and perform different functions

questions.question: Production of which of the following antibodies is induced by polysaccharides and lipids?
questions.explanation:
Polysaccharides and lipids stimulate the secretion of mainly IgM antibodies.

B lymphocytes use their antigen receptors to recognize various types of antigens:

• Proteins (through CD40L and cytokine-mediated helper T-cell actions) - induce production of IgG, IgA, IgE

• Polysaccharides and lipids - induce production of IgM mainly

Helper T cells also help in antibodies by the mechanisms:

• Stimulate formation of germinal centers which consist of proliferating B cells

• Induce isotype switching through cytokines IFN-γ and IL-4

• Affinity maturation - stimulate the production of antigen-specific antibodies

Isotype switching and affinity maturation occur mainly in germinal centers.

questions.question: In which of the following cells is recirculation seen?
options: Both plasma cells and T lymphocytes
Both B lymphocytes and plasma cells
questions.explanation:
Lymphocyte recirculation is seen in T lymphocytes.

Migration of the lymphocytes between blood and lymphoid organs is called recirculation. Naive lymphocytes traverse the peripheral lymphoid organs, where immune responses are initiated. When antigen-presenting cells activate them, the effector lymphocytes migrate to sites of infection and inflammation.

In contrast, plasma cells remain in lymphoid organs and the bone marrow. They do not need to migrate to sites of infection because they secrete antibodies that are carried to distant tissues.

questions.question: Which of the following is not encoded by MHC class III genes?
questions.explanation:
β2 microglobulin associated cell surface molecules are encoded by MHC class I and not class III.

Class III MHC molecules include:

• Complement proteins (such as C2, C4, and B factor)

• Cytokines (such as TNF-α, LTA, and LTB)

• Properdin factor BQ of alternate pathway

• Enzyme tyrosine hydroxylase

• Heat-shock proteins

Class III molecules are encoded by genes located between those that encode class I and class II molecules.

questions.question: A child, upon disturbing a beehive, had several stings. After a few minutes, he developed shock, respiratory failure, and vascular collapse. What is the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of anaphylaxis following a bee sting. This is an example of IgE-mediated reaction or type 1 hypersensitivity.

Injurious immune reactions are called hypersensitivity reactions. There are four types of hypersensitivity reactions.

Immediate (Type 1) hypersensitivity is also called allergic reactions. They are induced by environmental antigens (allergens) that stimulate strong TH2 responses and IgE production in genetically susceptible individuals.

IgE coats mast cells by binding to Fcεg receptors. Reexposure to the allergen leads to cross-linking of the IgE and FcεRI, activation of mast cells, and release of mediators. The principal mediators are histamine, proteases, and other granule contents like prostaglandins and leukotrienes and cytokines.

It occurs in two phases: immediate phase and late phase. The mediators are responsible for the immediate vascular and smooth muscle reactions and the late-phase reaction (inflammation). The clinical manifestations may be local or systemic and range from mildly annoying rhinitis to fatal anaphylaxis.

The image given below shows the sequence of events in immediate hypersensitivity.

questions.question: Arthus reaction is caused by which of the following process?
questions.explanation:
Arthus reaction is characterized by a localized area of tissue necrosis due to immune-complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity reaction) vasculitis in the skin.

This reaction can be produced experimentally by intracutaneous injection of antigen in a previously immunised animal that contains circulating antibodies against the antigen. As the antigen diffuses into the vessel wall, it binds with the preformed antibody, and immune complexes are formed locally. These complexes precipitate in the vessel walls and cause fibrinoid necrosis.

questions.question: A 42-year-old female patient presents with ptosis, diplopia, and progressive muscular weakness towards the end of the day. She has improvements in symptoms after administering edrophonium. The given clinical condition is an example of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical condition is highly suggestive of myasthenia gravis. It is an example of a type II hypersensitivity reaction.

Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease that is usually associated with autoantibodies directed against acetylcholine receptors. In Type II hypersensitivity, antibodies react with antigens present on cell surfaces or in the extracellular matrix cause. These antibodies destroy cells, trigger inflammation, or interfering with normal functions.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child abruptly develops malaise, fever, nausea, oliguria, and smoky, cola-colored urine 2 weeks after recovery from a sore throat. He is found to have periorbital edema and mild hypertension. Urine examination shows dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts in the urine with mild proteinuria. Which type of hypersensitivity is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nephritic syndrome due to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. This is an example of a type III hypersensitivity reaction.

In type III hypersensitivity, immune complexes may deposit in tissues or blood vessels, and elicit an acute inflammatory reaction by activating complement. The pathogenesis of systemic immune complex disease can be divided into three phases:

• Formation of immune complexes

• Deposition of immune complexes

• Inflammation and tissue injury

This results in various manifestations like vasculitis, glomerulonephritis and arthritis.

Examples of type III hypersensitivity reactions:

• Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis

• Systemic lupus erythematosus

• Reactive arthritis

• Polyarteritis nodosa

• Serum sickness

• Arthus reaction

• Farmer’s lung

• Hypersensitivity pneumonitis

• Type II lepra reaction

• Henoch–Schonlein purpura

The image given below shows the mechanism of type III hypersensitivity reactions.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man with a fever and chronic cough is administered 0.1 mL of purified protein derivative intradermally over the forearm. After a few hours, the injection site appears as follows. Which of the following does this represent?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario shows a positive tuberculin test. It is a classical example of type IV or delayed or cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction.

Tuberculin test involves intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD, also called tuberculin), a protein-containing antigen of the tubercle bacillus. In a previously sensitized individual, reddening and induration of the site appear in 8 to 12 hours, reach a peak in 24 to 72 hours, and thereafter slowly subside.

Morphologically, delayed-type hypersensitivity is characterized by the accumulation of mononuclear cells, mainly CD4+ T cells and macrophages, around venules. The cell-mediated type of hypersensitivity is caused by inflammation resulting from cytokines produced by CD4+ T cells and cell killing by CD8+ T cells.

questions.question: Which of the following autoimmune diseases are not mediated by antibodies?
questions.explanation:
Rheumatoid arthritis is mediated by T cells, not antibodies.

Antibody-mediated diseases:

• Autoimmune hemolytic anemia

• Autoimmune thrombocytopenic purpura

• Pemphigus vulgaris

• Vasculitis caused by ANCA

• Goodpasture syndrome

• Myasthenia gravis

• Acute rheumatic fever

• Graves disease

• Pernicious anemia

• Insulin resistant diabetes

T cell-mediated diseases:

• Rheumatoid arthritis

• Multiple sclerosis

• Psoriasis

• Type 1 diabetes mellitus

• Inflammatory bowel disease

• Contact sensitivity

Note: In T cell mediated diseases, although the role of T cells have been demonstrated, antibodies may also be involved in tissue injury.

questions.question: Which gene is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity?
questions.explanation:
PTPN22 gene is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.

PTPN22, which encodes the protein tyrosine phosphatase, is associated with the following conditions:

• Rheumatoid arthritis

• Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)

• Type 1 diabetes

Because these disorders have a fairly high prevalence, PTPN22 is said to be the gene that is most frequently implicated in autoimmunity.

Option A: Mutations in FOXP3 cause a systemic autoimmune disease called IPEX (immune dysregulation, polyendocrinopathy, enteropathy, X-linked).

Option C: Polymorphisms in the gene encoding for NOD2 are associated with Crohn's disease.

Option D: AIRE mutation is associated with the autoimmune polyendocrinopathy syndrome type 1 (APS-1).

questions.question: Which of the following is responsible for autoimmunity in Epstein-Barr virus infection?
questions.explanation:
Autoimmunity in Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection is the result of polyclonal B cell activation.

Microbes may induce other abnormalities that promote autoimmune reactions. Some viruses, such as EBV and HIV, cause polyclonal B-cell activation, which may result in the production of autoantibodies.

The role of infections in autoimmunity is exemplified by the following:

1. Molecular mimicry of antigenic cross-reactivity: The structural similarity of the microbial antigens and self-antigens. Rheumatic heart disease is an example in which streptococcal proteins cross-react with myocardial proteins causing myocarditis.

2. Upregulation of co-stimulatory molecules by infectious organisms.

3. Polyclonal B cell activation: Caused by EBV and HIV, resulting in the production of autoantibodies.

4. Alteration of tissue antigens: Infections may alter tissue self-antigens so that they activate T cells and lose the property of self-tolerance.

questions.question: Homogeneous or diffuse nuclear staining pattern may reflect antibodies to all the following except:
questions.explanation:
Homogeneous or diffuse nuclear staining does not reflect antibodies to RNA. The nucleolar pattern of staining represents antibodies to RNA.

 Antinuclear antibodies (ANAs) are directed against antibodies to:

• DNA

• Histones

• Nonhistone proteins bound to RNA

• Nucleolar antigens

The most widely used method for detecting ANAs is indirect immunofluorescence. The pattern of nuclear fluorescence suggests the type of antibody present in the patient’s serum.

questions.question: What type of cell is the lupus erythematosus cell?
questions.explanation:
The lupus erythematosus (LE) cell is a phagocytic neutrophil or macrophage.

Nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous to produce LE bodies or hematoxylin bodies. Phagocytic neutrophils or macrophages engulf the denatured nucleus of an injured cell. Demonstration of LE cells in vitro was used in the past for the diagnosis of SLE.

The image below shows a lupus erythematosus (LE) cell.

questions.question: A 32-year-old lady presents with the following finding. On further investigations, anti-ds DNA and anti-Smith antibodies are found to be positive. Which of the following is not seen in the given clinical condition?
questions.answer: D. Lymphocytic infiltration in salivary gland
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). In this condition, lymphocytic infiltration in the salivary gland is not seen. However, this finding is seen in Sjogren's syndrome.

If cell nuclei are exposed to anti-nuclear antibodies (ANAs), they can bind to them. The nuclei of damaged cells react with ANAs, lose their chromatin pattern, and become homogeneous. They are called lupus erythematosus (LE) bodies or hematoxylin bodies.

An acute necrotizing vasculitis involving capillaries, small arteries, and arterioles with fibrinoid necrosis is seen in SLE. Central penicilliary arteries in the spleen may show concentric intimal and smooth muscle cell hyperplasia, producing so-called onion-skin lesions.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a part of the IgG4 spectrum?
questions.explanation:
Celiac disease is not an IgG4-Related disease.

IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a newly recognized constellation of disorders characterized by tissue infiltrates dominated by IgG4 antibody-producing plasma cells and lymphocytes, particularly T cells, storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and usually increased serum IgG4.

IgG4-RD spectrum includes:

• Mikulicz syndrome - enlargement and fibrosis of salivary and lacrimal glands

• Riedel thyroiditis

• Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis

• Autoimmune pancreatitis

• Inflammatory pseudotumors of the orbit, lungs, and kidney

questions.question: Leukocyte-adhesion deficiency type 2 is due to the absence of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Leukocyte-adhesion deficiency (LAD) type 2 is due to the absence of Sialyl-Lewis X.

Physiologically Sialyl-Lewis X has the necessary ligand for the selectins which bind to leukocytes.

Inherited defects in leukocyte adhesion:

• Type 1 - defect in the biosynthesis of the β2 chain shared by the LFA-1 and Mac-1 integrins

• Type 2 - absence of sialyl-Lewis X, the fucose containing ligand for E- and P-selectins. It is due to a defect in the fucosyltransferase, the enzyme that attaches fucose moieties to protein backbones.

The major clinical problem in both conditions is recurrent bacterial infections due to inadequate granulocyte function.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about Chédiak-Higashi syndrome?
options: It has an autosomal recessive inheritance
Granules are absent in white blood cells
questions.answer: D. Granules are absent in white blood cells
questions.explanation:
Leukocytes contain giant granules in Chédiak–Higashi syndrome as seen in peripheral blood smears. They are due to aberrant phagolysosome fusion.

The image shows giant granules in a neutrophil in Chédiak–Higashi syndrome.

Chédiak–Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive condition. The defective fusion of phagosomes and lysosomes results in defective phagocytes function and susceptibility to infections.

The abnormalities are neutropenia, defective degranulation, and delayed microbial killing, causing:

• Albinism - melanocytes

• Nerve defects - nervous system cells

• Bleeding disorders - platelets

The gene associated with this disorder encodes a large cytosolic protein called LYST, which is believed to regulate lysosomal trafficking.

questions.question: A 2-month-old baby was brought with complaints of fever and fast breathing for 5 days, and was diagnosed with pneumonia. Further history revealed baby had recurrent infections.
