The image given below shows the NESTROFT.

questions.question:
A couple with a family history of thalassemia comes for genetic counselling. Their HPLC reports are given below. What is the risk of their offspring having thalassemia major?

Patient
HbA2 levels

Husband
2.5%

Wife
4.9%
questions.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the risk of their offspring having thalassemia major is 0%.

From the given HPLC reports, the husband is normal (normal value of HbA2 is 2.5%±0.3%) and the wife has β thalassemia minor (HbA2 level 4.9%). This disease is transmitted with an autosomal recessive inheritance. Hence, the chance of their offspring having full blown thalassemia is zero.

In β thalassemia minor, the Hb A2 levels are increased to 4–8%. This is due to an elevated ratio of δ chain to β chain synthesis. Hb F levels are generally normal or slightly increased.

Note: Increased HbF (diagnostic) and normal HbA2 levels are features of thalassemia major.

questions.question: A 25-year old man presents with chronic anemia and gall stones. His family history is significant for a similar illness. His peripheral blood smear is given below. What is the mode of the inheritance of the given clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear showing spherocytes, along with the history, is suggestive of hereditary spherocytosis. Inheritance of this condition is mainly autosomal dominant.

Hereditary spherocytosis is a structural RBC disorder making the RBCs more spheroid. The RBCs are less deformable and more vulnerable to splenic sequestration and destruction. This decreases the lifespan of RBCs.

questions.question: What is the most common protein deficiency associated with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Ankyrin is the most common protein deficiency associated with hereditary spherocytosis (HS).

The chief protein component of the RBC membrane skeleton is spectrin. It consists of two polypeptide chains, alpha and beta. These dimers associate with actin oligomers. The spectrin–actin skeleton is then connected to the cell membrane by two distinct interactions.

• Ankyrin and band 4.2 binds spectrin to the transmembrane ion transporter, band 3

• Protein 4.1 binds the tail of spectrin to the transmembrane protein glycophorin A

Defect in any of the components of the red cell membrane skeleton results in hereditary spherocytosis. The image given below shows the pathogenesis of this condition.

Note: Few one-liners on membrane skeleton -

• Most abundant integral proteins - glycophorin, band 3

• Responsible for biconcave shape of RBC - spectrin

• Most severe deficiency - spectrin

• Hereditary elliptocytosis is due to deficiency of alpha spectrin

• Mushroom cells appearance due to deficiency of band 3

• Never involved in HS - glycophorin

questions.question: The peripheral smear of a patient with anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly shows pincer cells. Which protein deficiency is responsible for this finding?
questions.explanation: Pincer cell or mushroom cell is seen in hereditary spherocytosis associated with deficiency of cytoskeletal protein band 3.

questions.question: Which of the following features would you least expect to see in a patient with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation:
Hemoglobinuria is not seen in hereditary spherocytosis where extravascular hemolysis occurs. It is a feature of intravascular hemolysis. Pigment gallstones, pallor and splenomegaly can be seen in this condition.

Cinical features of extravascular hemolysis include:

• Anaemia

• Jaundice

• Splenomegaly

Causes of extravascular hemolysis:

• Hereditary spherocytosis

• Thalassemia

• Sickle cell anaemia

Note: G6PD deficiency and autoimmune hemolytic anaemia can cause both intravascular and extravascular hemolysis.

questions.question: What is the life span of affected red cells in patients with hereditary spherocytosis?
questions.explanation: The life span of affected red cells in hereditary spherocytosis is 10 to 20 days. The normal life span of RBC is 120 days.

questions.question: In a patient with hereditary spherocytosis, MCHC of 38 g/dL was noted. What could be the probable reason for this finding?
questions.explanation:
Increased MCHC in hereditary spherocytosis is due to dehydration caused by the loss of K+ and H2O.

MCHC (mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration) is given by the formula hemoglobin / PCV (g/dL). It indicates the amount of hemoglobin per unit volume.

Note:

• MCV (mean corpuscular volume) is given by the formula PCV / RBC (fL). It denotes the size of the RBCs.

• MCH (mean corpuscular hemoglobin) is given by the formula hemoglobin / RBC (pg). It quantifies the hemoglobin in the RBCs.

questions.question: In the following osmotic fragility curve, A occurs in _________.
questions.explanation:
Osmotic fragility curve shifts to the right in hereditary spherocytosis.

In hereditary spherocytosis, the cells are spherocytic in normal plasma (0.9% NaCl) and hemolyse readily at higher concentrations than normal discoid red cells do, hence shifting the curve to the right.

Osmotic fragility is the susceptibility of the RBC to rupture under osmotic stress. In hypotonic solutions, RBCs swell to become spherical and eventually hemolyse. In the graph, the x-axis represents the saline concentration while the y-axis represents the percentage of red cells that have undergone hemolysis. When osmotic fragility is normal, red cells begin to hemolyse at 0.5% saline, with 50% of hemolysis occuring at 0.40-0.42% saline and complete hemolysis occuring at 0.35% saline as represented in the curve.

In thalassemia and sickle cell anemia on the other hand, the cells are resistant to hemolysis and don’t hemolyse unless the concentration of saline is very low, shifting the graph to the left.

questions.question:
A 7-year-old girl presents with fever and jaundice for 5 days. On examination, splenomegaly is noted. Her lab reports are given below. What is the likely trigger to have caused this condition?

Hb - 5 g%

WBC - 1000 /mm3

Platelets - 45,000 /mm3

Peripheral smear shows spherocytes
questions.explanation:
The given hemogram showing pancytopenia and spherocytes in peripheral smear is suggestive of aplastic crisis in hereditary spherocytosis. It is usually triggered by parvovirus infection.

Parvovirus infects and kills the red cell precursors. This creates a transient arrest of erythropoiesis i.e. aplastic crisis as the life span of RBCs are shortened. The immune response clears the virus in 1-2 weeks.

Blood transfusions may be necessary during acute phases of the infection. This crisis can also occur in other hemolytic anaemias.

questions.question: Which amino acid lies at the sixth position of the beta chain of hemoglobin?
questions.explanation:
Glutamate lies at the 6th position of the beta chain of hemoglobin.

Sickle-cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the sixth codon of β-globin. This leads to the replacement of a glutamate residue with a valine residue.

questions.question: A blood sample is taken from a suspected case of sickle cell anaemia. Which of the following properties can be used to differentiate HbS from HbA?
questions.explanation:
Solubility can be used to differentiate as HbS is less soluble than HbA. The function, stability and affinity of HbS are similar to that of HbA.

In HbS, glutamic acid, which is a polar amino acid, is replaced by a non-polar amino acid valine at the 6th position. HbS molecules have the tendency to stack into polymers when deoxygenated. This process converts the red cell cytosol from a free-flowing liquid into a viscous gel. This causes a change in the solubility of the hemoglobin.

The major pathologic manifestations of decreased solubility and polymerisation of HbS are chronic hemolysis, microvascular occlusions, and tissue damage.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man was diagnosed to have heterozygous sickle cell trait. What will be the approximate percentage of HbS in this patient?
questions.explanation:
In heterozygotes with sickle-cell trait, about 40% of the hemoglobin is HbS. The rest of hemoglobin (60%) is HbA.

Sickle cell trait is a largely asymptomatic condition characterised by heterozygosity seen for HbS (sickle hemoglobin). As only a fraction of the Hb are HbS, polymerization leading to sickling only occurs in severe and prolonged hypoxia. Offsprings of 2 heterozygotes have a 1 in 4 chance of having sickle cell disease.

In HbSC heterozygotes, HbS is 50% and HbC is 50%.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following combinations of beta-globin chains tend to have a more severe sickle cell disease?
questions.explanation:
Among the given options, the heterozygous combination of HbS and HbC causes a more severe form of the disease. Overall severity is more in homozygous HbS.

Severity sequence is HbSS > HbSC > HbSA > HbSF.

In HbC, lysine is substituted for glutamate in the sixth amino acid residue of β-globin. The percentage of HbS is 50% in HbSC red cells and 40% in HbAS cells. Moreover, HbSC cells tend to lose salt and water and become dehydrated, which increases the intracellular concentration of HbS. Both of these factors increase the tendency for HbS to polymerize. As a result, individuals who are compound heterozygotes for HbS and HbC, have symptomatic sickling disorder (termed HbSC disease). However, it is milder than sickle cell disease (HbSS).

HbF inhibits the polymerization of HbS even more than HbA. Hence, infants do not become symptomatic until they reach 5 or 6 months of age when the level of HbF normally falls.

questions.question: In patients with sickle cell anaemia, which of the following factors promote sickling of RBC?
questions.explanation:
HbC promotes the sickling of RBC, whereas HbF opposes it.

Factors that promote sickling are:

• Increased MCHC

• Hb C

• Acidic pH

• Hypoxia

HbF has a high affinity for oxygen than other hemoglobins. Hence, high oxygen content prevents sickling. HbF inhibits the polymerization of HbS. So the infants do not become symptomatic until they reach 5 or 6 months of age when the level of HbF normally falls.

questions.question: Which of the following reagents is used for sickling test?
questions.explanation:
The reagent used for the sickling test is sodium metabisulfite. It is an oxygen-consuming reagent, which induces the sickling of red cells in the presence of HbS.

Sickling test with sodium metabisulfite is used as a screening test for sickle cell anaemia.

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl presents with fever and severe pain in her hands and feet. There is no history of trauma. Her lab reports reveal Hb to be 8.2 g/dL and peripheral smear as shown below. Which of the following parasitic infections is this condition protective against?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of sickle cell anaemia. HbS gives protection against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Hand-foot syndrome or dactylitis of bones of hands and feet is a severe acute inflammatory response seen in sickle cell anaemia. It is caused by vaso-occlusive episodes leading to ischemia and finally infarction of the distal portions of the extremities.

Sickle cells impair the formation of membrane knobs containing a protein made by P. falciparum called PfEMP-1. This decreases the adherence of infected red cells to the endothelium.

Individuals with sickle cell trait are significantly less likely to have severe disease or to die from malaria. It is because of the increased phagocytosis of sickled cells in the spleen, which keeps the parasite load down.

The image given below shows sickle cells seen on peripheral smear in sickle cell anemia.

questions.question: What happens to the severity of hemolytic anaemia in concurrent sickle cell anaemia and α-thalassemia?
questions.explanation:
The concurrence of sickle cell anaemia and α-thalassemia results in less severe hemolytic anaemia.

Sickle cell anaemia is caused by point mutations in β globin synthesis leading to defective HbS synthesis. When these RBCs release oxygen, the HbS polymerises leading to membrane distortion

Thalassemia is due to germline mutations causing decreased globin chain synthesis (α or β). Since these diseases have a different pathogenesis, they can occur concurrently.

In alpha-thalassemia, the concentration of hemoglobin is decreased. Therefore the concentration of HbS in sickle cell anaemia is also decreased. Since HbS molecules should be close to each other for polymerization to occur. Since there is a decreased concentration of HbS in alpha-thalassemia, the HbS molecules are far apart. So there is a decreased polymerization of HbS and therefore less severity of the disease.

questions.question: A 23-year-old patient with sickle cell anaemia presents with fever and malaise. IgM ELISA confirms a parvovirus B19 infection. Which of the following crises will you expect to see in this patient?
questions.explanation:
Aplastic crisis in sickle cell anaemia is caused by parvovirus B19. It is a transient arrest of erythropoiesis, usually triggered by an acute parvovirus infection. Parvovirus infects and kills red cell precursors. It occurs in sickle cell disease and other hemolytic anaemias.

Vaso-occlusive crises (pain crises) are episodes of hypoxic injury and infarction that cause severe pain in the affected region. The most commonly involved sites are the bones, lungs, liver, brain, spleen, and penis. Acute chest syndrome is a type of vaso-occlusive crisis involving the lungs. It typically presents with fever, cough, chest pain, and pulmonary infiltrates. Pulmonary inflammation may cause blood flow to become sluggish and “spleenlike,” leading to sickling and vaso-occlusion.

Sequestration crises occur in children with intact spleens. Massive entrapment of sickle red cells leads to rapid splenic enlargement, hypovolemia, and sometimes shock. Both sequestration crises and acute chest syndrome may be fatal and sometimes require prompt treatment with exchange transfusions.

questions.question: During USG examination in a patient with hemolytic anemia, the spleen was not visualized. There is no past history of trauma or surgery. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Non-visualisation of the spleen on routine USG is suggestive of autosplenectomy, which is seen in sickle cell anemia. Splenomegaly is seen in thalassemia and hereditary spherocytosis.

In children with sickle cell anaemia, there is moderate splenomegaly. This is due to red pulp congestion caused by the entrapment of sickled red cells. As age advances, chronic erythrostasis produces hypoxic damage and infarcts. By adulthood, the spleen is reduced to a band of fibrous tissue. This process is called autosplenectomy.

chapters.chapter: G6Pd Deficiency And Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemias

questions.question: A 29-year-old African American man receives primaquine chemoprophylaxis before traveling for a business trip. Four days later, he presents with jaundice and dark urine. Laboratory investigations show anemia, reticulocytosis, and unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. The peripheral blood smear shows the presence of Heinz bodies. What is the most likely mode of inheritance of the given clinical condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history suggestive of hemolysis after the antimalarial (primaquine) and Heinz bodies on PBF, points to a diagnosis of G6PD deficiency (Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency). It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait.

G6PD is an enzyme belonging to the hexose monophosphate shunt (HMP) pathway. Deficiency of enzymes of this pathway causes hemolysis as the protective ability of RBCs from oxidative stress is impaired.

The image given below shows the Heinz bodies seen on peripheral smear.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common trigger for hemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency?
questions.explanation:
The most common trigger for hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is infection. Viral hepatitis, pneumonia, and typhoid are the common infections that trigger hemolysis.

Episodic hemolysis (both intravascular and extravascular) is seen in G6PD deficiency. It is due to exposures that cause oxidative stress. The triggers include:

• Infections - oxygen-derived free radicals produced by activated leukocytes

• Drugs

• Antimalarials - primaquine and chloroquine

• Sulfonamides

• Nitrofurantoin

• Diet - fava bean

questions.question: Peripheral smear of a patient with viral hepatitis is given below. Which of the following statements is false about this finding?
options: These are seen in G6PD deficiency
They are due to denaturation of globin chains
They are plucked out by macrophages in the spleen
They do not cause intravascular hemolysis
questions.answer: D. They do not cause intravascular hemolysis
questions.explanation:
The given peripheral smear shows Heinz bodies which are dark stained inclusion bodies in red cells. They can cause intravascular as well as extravascular hemolysis.

In G6PD-deficiency, the RBCs are exposed to high levels of oxidants. This causes cross-linking of reactive sulfhydryl groups on globin chains. The globin chains become denatured and form membrane-bound precipitates known as Heinz bodies. These can be detected by supravital staining.

Heinz bodies can damage the membrane sufficiently to cause intravascular hemolysis.

As RBCs with Heinz bodies pass through the spleen, the macrophages pluck out the Heinz bodies. As a result, some of these partially devoured cells retain an abnormal shape i.e. as if a bite was taken out of them. Such cells are called bite cells. Bite cells are trapped in splenic cords and removed by phagocytes leading to extravascular hemolysis.

The images given below show Heinz bodies and bite cells seen in G6PD deficiency.

questions.question:
A patient with G6PD deficiency was suspected to have acute hemolytic episode. Which of the following features would you expect to see in this patient?

1. Anaemia

2. Splenomegaly

3. Hemoglobinemia

4. Cholelithiasis

5. Hemoglobinuria
questions.explanation:
Acute hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is intravascular. This is marked by anaemia, hemoglobinemia, and hemoglobinuria.

These episodes are self-limited and intermittent. Reticulocytosis occurs during the recovery phase. Hence, features related to chronic hemolysis (e.g., splenomegaly, cholelithiasis) are absent.

questions.question: A 23-year-old food blogger presents with complaints of icterus and abdominal fullness. She returned yesterday from a vacation in Egypt where she tried fava beans. Her peripheral smear is given below. This condition is protective against which of the following malarial parasites?
questions.explanation:
The peripheral smear shows RBCs with anisopoikilocytosis with polychromasia and many bite cells (arrows) suggestive of G6PD deficiency. This condition is protective against Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Malarial parasites preferentially invade RBCs which are rich in G6PD. G6PD deficiency causes oxidative stress and hemolysis, preferably in the older RBCs. Reticulocytes and young erythrocytes have much higher G6PD activities and are less susceptible to oxidant damage.

P. falciparum can invade erythrocytes of all ages. P. vivax, and P. ovale invade reticulocytes (immature erythrocytes) preferentially. Hence, a low G6PD level in older RBC is protective against P. falciparum malaria.

Episodic hemolysis in this condition can be triggered by fava beans which is a staple in Egyptian cuisine.

The images given below show Heinz bodies and bite cells seen in G6PD deficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about G6PD-deficiency anemia?
options: Hemolytic episodes occur both intravascularly and extravascularly
G6PD Mediterranean deficiency is the most severe form.
Older RBCs are more prone to hemolysis than younger ones
Hemolysis continues as long as there is exposure to oxidant drugs
questions.answer: D. Hemolysis continues as long as there is exposure to oxidant drugs
questions.explanation:
Hemolysis in G6PD-deficiency anemia does not continue for the entire period that the patient takes the offending drug. It stops after a few days.

Two variants of G6PD, designated as G6PD– and G6PD Mediterranean, cause most of the clinically significant hemolytic anemias. The half-life of G6PD- is moderately reduced, whereas that of G6PD Mediterranean is markedly reduced; hence, the severity of deficiency is greater with the Mediterranean variant. The most common normal variant is G6PD B.

The hemolysis in G6PD deficiency is both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis. The damaged red cells are sequestered in the spleen and killed by macrophages, causing extravascular hemolysis. The oxidative stresses can denature hemoglobin, resulting in intravascular hemolysis.

In individuals with G6PD deficiency, acute intravascular hemolysis begins 2 to 3 days after exposure to oxidants. Only older RBCs are at risk for lysis. The hemolytic episode is self-limited because hemolysis stops when only younger G6PD-replete red cells remain, even if the patient continues to take the offending drug.

questions.question: What class of antibodies are involved in the most common form of immunohemolytic anaemia?
questions.explanation:
Warm antibody type is the most common form of immunohemolytic anaemia. Most of the causative antibodies in this condition belong to the IgG class.

Immunohemolytic anaemia is caused by antibodies that cause premature destruction of the red cells. Based on the temperature at which the different types of antibodies bind to the RBCs stably, they are classified as:

• Warm antibody type - most common

• Cold agglutinin type

• Cold hemolysin type

questions.question:
Match the immunohemolytic anaemia with the type of hemolysis.

Type
Hemolysis

1. Warm antibody
A. Intravascular

2. Cold agglutinin
B. Extravascular and intravascular

3. Cold hemolysin
C. Extravascular
questions.explanation:
The type of hemolysis seen in the different immunohemolytic anemia are:

Type
Hemolysis

Warm antibody
Extravascular

Cold agglutinin
Extravascular and intravascular

Cold hemolysin
Intravascular

Autoimmune hemolytic anemias (AIHA) cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis.

In warm antibody type, hemolysis is extravascular. IgG-coated red cells are phagocytosed and destroyed in the spleen.

In cold agglutinin type, hemolysis is extravascular and intravascular. In the peripheral vascular bed (low temperature), IgM binds to the red cells. This causes agglutination and complement-fixing. They are unbound when they reach the general circulation. However, the IgM interaction causes deposition of sublytic quantities of C3b. It is an excellent opsonin, which leads to the removal of RBCs by phagocytes in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

Cold hemolysin type is a rare subtype of AIHA. Hemolysis is intravascular. IgG binds to the P blood group antigen on the red cells, which leads to complement-mediated lysis.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman was brought to the casualty with loss of consciousness. On examination, pallor, icterus and splenomegaly were noted. Her past history was significant for meningitis 2 weeks ago which was treated with iv antibiotics. Lab investigations showed anemia and increased osmotic fragility. Which of the following statements is false regarding the probable diagnosis?
options: Rh blood group complex are involved in the pathogenesis
Direct Coombs agglutination test is diagnostic
questions.answer: B. LDH levels are always normal
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of drug-induced warm antibody type of immunohemolytic anemia. In this condition, primarily extravascular hemolysis is present. LDH may be increased when there is hemolysis.

Two different mechanisms for drug-induced immune hemolytic anemias are:

Antigenic drugs:

• Anemia occurs 1-2 weeks after initiation of large IV dose of the offending drug

• These drugs bind to red cell membrane and are recognised by anti-drug antibodies

• They can cause both extravascular and intravascular hemolysis

• E.g. penicillin, cephalosporins, quinidine

Tolerance-breaking drugs:

• Antibodies are produced against red cell antigens, particularly Rh antigens

• E.g. alpha-methyl dopa

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria?
options: IgG class of antibodies are involved
Antibodies are directed against Rh antigen
It mostly occurs in children following a viral infection
questions.answer: B. Antibodies are directed against Rh antigen
questions.explanation:
In paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria (PCH), antibodies are directed against the P blood group antigen.

PCH is a cold hemolysin type of hemolysis caused by IgG autoantibodies classically. They are also called Donath Landsteiner antibodies and are produced often in response to a viral infection. This antibody is a biphasic hemolysin. i.e., the antibody binds to RBC at colder temperature but hemolysis occurs at core temperature 37°C.

This can cause substantial, sometimes fatal, intravascular hemolysis, and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children following viral infections and usually recover within 1 month.

Immuno-hemolytic anaemias are of 3 types:

Antibody type
Antigen on the RBC surface

IgG

Cold agglutinin

30°C, usually 0-10°C

Cold hemolysin
IgG

questions.question: In which of the following conditions is microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia most commonly seen?
questions.explanation:
Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia is most commonly seen with disseminated intravascular coagulation.

It occurs in the following conditions:

• Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)

• Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP)

• Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS)

• Malignant hypertension

• Systemic lupus erythematosus

• Disseminated cancer

A common pathogenic feature in these disorders is a microvascular lesion. Deposition of fibrin and platelets result in luminal narrowing. These vascular changes produce shear stresses. These changes mechanically injure the passing red cells producing schistocytes or helmet cells on the peripheral smear.

The image given below shows schistocytes or helmet cells.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most potent vasoconstrictor?
questions.explanation: The most potent vasoconstrictor is urotensin2 followed by endothelin and angiotensin.

questions.question: Which of the following is a component of δ granules of platelets?
questions.explanation:
Epinephrine is a component of δ granules of platelets.

The different components of platelet granules are:

• α granules

• Fibrinogen

• Fibronectin

• PF4

• Factor V, VIII

• PDGF

• TGF

• δ granules

• ADP

• Calcium

• Serotonin

• Histamine

• Epinephrine

questions.question: A 12-year-old girl with dengue hemorrhagic fever is being monitored by measuring platelet count. Spontaneous bleeding is associated with platelet values below _______ /µL.
questions.explanation:
Spontaneous bleeding (non-traumatic) is associated with platelet values below 20,000 platelets/µL.

It most often involves small vessels. The common sites for such hemorrhages are:

• Skin

• Mucosa of gastrointestinal and genitourinary tracts

• Intracranial bleeding - most feared site of bleeding

The production of the platelets is regulated by the hormone thrombopoietin produced in the liver. The platelet synthesis is also specifically increased by interleukin 6. The average lifespan of the platelets is 7–10 days. The normal platelet count is 1,50,000 - 4,00,000 /µL.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is true regarding functional platelet disorders?
options: Normal platelet count and normal bleeding time
Normal platelet count and increased bleeding time
Decreased platelet count and increased bleeding time
Decreased platelet count and decreased bleeding time
questions.answer: B. Normal platelet count and increased bleeding time
questions.explanation:
Functional platelet disorders have normal platelet count and increased bleeding time.

Classification of platelet functional disorders:

• Defect in platelet-vessel wall interaction (disorders of adhesion)

• Von Willebrand disease - deficiency or defect in plasma vWF

• Bernard–Soulier syndrome - deficiency or defect in GP Ib IX

• Defects in platelet-platelet interaction (disorders of aggregation)

• Congenital afibrinogenemia - deficiency of plasma fibrinogen

• Glanzmann thrombasthenia - deficiency or defect in GPIIb-IIIa

• Disorders of platelet secretion and signal transduction

• Storage pool deficiency - α-Granule deficiency and gamma-Granule deficiency

• Quebec platelet disorder

• Chediak–Higashi syndrome

• Gray platelet syndrome

• Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome

• Disorders of platelet coagulation-protein interaction

• Scott syndrome - defect in factor Va-Xa interaction on platelets

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about vonWillebrand factor?
options: Its deficiency can also cause factor VIII defect
Its deficiency may cause defective platelet adhesion
It serves as a carrier for factor VIII
questions.answer: A. It is synthesized by hepatocytes
questions.explanation:
Von Willebrand factor (vWF) is not synthesized by hepatocytes. They are produced by endothelial cells of liver and megakaryocytes. It is also found in:

• Platelet granules - lesser compared to endothelial cells

• Endothelial cells within cytoplasmic vesicles called Weibel-Palade bodies

• Subendothelium - binds to collagen

It mediates the adhesion of platelets to sites of vascular injury (subendothelium). It links the exposed collagen to platelets. It facilitates platelet to platelet interaction and also stabilizes the hemostatic plug against shear forces.

It is a carrier protein for factor VIII and also protects it from proteolytic degradation and stabilizes it. The half-life of factor VIII is about 2.4 hours when free and 12 hours when bound to vWF in the circulation.

Since vWF stabilizes factor VIII, a deficiency of vWF gives rise to a secondary decrease in factor VIII levels. This may be reflected by a prolongation of the partial thromboplastin time (PTT) in von Willebrand disease types 1 and 3.

questions.question:
A 24-year-old woman is found to have uncontrolled bleeding after a minor cut injury. Her lab investigations are given below. Which of the following statements are false about her condition?

Platelet count - 4,60,000 /μL

Bleeding time - increased

PT - normal

APTT - increased
options: Type 3 is inherited as autosomal dominant
questions.answer: C. Type 3 is inherited as autosomal dominant
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of von Willebrand disease (vWD). Type 3 vWD is inherited as an autosomal recessive disease.

The characteristics of different subtypes of vWD are:

Subtype

Description

Inheritance

Lab findings

Type 1

Quantitative deficiency of vWF

Autosomal dominant

Reduced vWF antigen, activity and Factor VIII

Type 2

Qualitative defect in vWF

Autosomal dominant

Reduced vWF activity to antigen ration<0.6

Type 3

Near-complete (quantitative) deficiency of Factor VIII

Autosomal recessive

Marked reduction or absence in Factor VIII levels

Type 1 is the most common subtype of vWD. In Type 2, vWF is expressed in normal amounts, but missense mutations are present that lead to defective multimer assembly. This type has several subtypes, of which type 2A is the most common.

Laboratory findings in vWD:

• Prolonged bleeding time

• Normal platelet count

• Hess test - positive tourniquet test due to defective platelet adhesion

• Ristocetin-induced aggregation - defective and diagnostic of this disease

• Platelet aggregation with ADP, collagen, and thrombin - normal

• Increased aPTT

Though the synthesis of factor VIII remains normal, the half-life of VIII in plasma decreases due to reduced vWF (carrier) levels. This leads to secondary VIIIC deficiency in plasma. So, the intrinsic pathway of coagulation is affected. Hence, aPTT is increased in these patients.

questions.question: Which of the following occurs due to a defect in δ granules of the platelets?
questions.explanation:
Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome occurs due to a defect in platelet δ granules.

Platelet granules disorders include:

• Gray platelet syndrome - involves α granules and characterized by thrombocytopenia with large platelets that appear pale on the peripheral smear (due to deficiency of the α granules)

• Quebec platelet syndrome - defect in α granules

• Hermansky–Pudlak syndrome - defect in δ granules and characterized by hypopigmentation and bleeding manifestation

• Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome - mutations in the WASp gene expressed in the X chromosome and characterized by microthrombocytopenia, eczema, recurrent infections

questions.question: A patient with large platelets on peripheral smear is diagnosed to have Bernard-Soulier disease. Deficiency of which of the following causes this condition?
questions.explanation:
Bernard–Soulier disease is due to deficiency of Gp Ib/ IX.

Bernard–Soulier syndrome is characterized by large platelets. Ristocetin aggregation is abnormal.

Deficiency

Defect

Disease

Gp Ib/IX

Adhesion of platelets

Bernard–Soulier syndrome

Gp IIb/IIIa

Aggregation of platelets

Glanzmann thrombasthenia

von Willebrand factor

Adhesion>Aggregation

Von Willebrand disease

Factor VIII deficiency causes hemophilia.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about Bernard-Soulier syndrome?
options: There is defective adhesion of platelets to sub-endothelial matrix
Deficiency of the platelet membrane glycoprotein complex Ib-IX is seen
Platelet aggregation by ristocetin is normal
It has an autosomal recessive inheritance
questions.answer: C. Platelet aggregation by ristocetin is normal
questions.explanation:
In Bernard–Soulier syndrome, platelet aggregation by ristocetin is abnormal.

The receptor for vWF i.e. Ib-IX is essential for normal platelet adhesion to the subendothelial extracellular matrix. In this condition, there is deficiency of Gp Ib/ IX. Clinical manifestations include epistaxis, ecchymoses, menorrhagia, gingival bleeding, and gastrointestinal bleeding.

Laboratory findings seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome:

• Prolonged bleeding time

• Moderate thrombocytopenia

• Platelet aggregation by ristocetin is deficient (but ADP, arachidonic acid, epinephrine, collagen - normal).

• Clot retraction - normal

• Abnormally large platelets

The image given below shows the abnormally large platelets on peripheral smear seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome.

questions.question:
A 4-year-old girl with a history of easy bruising was referred for further evaluation. Her previous lab reports showed that platelet count and morphology were normal. Platelet aggregations tests are given below. What is the likely diagnosis?

Agonist used
Aggregation

ADP
Absent

Epinephrine
Absent

Collagen
Absent

Ristocetin
Normal
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Glanzmann thrombasthenia.

It is an abnormality of platelet GPIIb-IIIa (fibrinogen receptor). Platelets are unable to adhere to each other and to the underlying tissue of the damaged blood vessels. It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. The symptoms include mucocutaneous bleeding in the neonatal period, menorrhagia, ecchymoses, epistaxis, and gingival hemorrhage.

Types of Glanzmann thrombasthenia include:

• Type 1: Absence of GPIIb-IIIa

• Type 2: Reduced surface expression of GPIIb-IIIa/ Essentialis athrombia - clot retraction is normal

• Type 3: Dysfunction of GPIIb-IIIa

Laboratory features of Glanzmann thrombasthenia:

• Normal platelet count and morphology

• Platelet aggregation occurs in response to ristocetin, but not to other agonists (such as ADP, thrombin, collagen or epinephrine)

• Clot retraction is absent

questions.question: A 1-year-old boy is brought with a history of recurrent impetigo. Physical examination findings are given below. Platelet counts are low and peripheral smear shows abnormally small-sized platelets. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome (WAS). The given image shows (A) multiple petechiae over face and hematoma under the right eye and (B) eczema of the foot.

This syndrome is an X-linked recessive, primary immunodeficiency disorder involving the WAS gene. It is characterised by the triad of:

• Severe eczema

• Thrombocytopenia

• Recurrent infections

Small platelets are seen in:

• Wiskott–Aldrich syndrome

• X-linked thrombocytopenia

Large platelets are seen in:

• Bernard-Soulier syndrome

• Myeloproliferative syndrome

• Myelodysplastic syndrome

• May–Hegglin anomaly

• Gray platelet syndrome

questions.question:
A 28-year-old woman presents with epistaxis, easy bruising and menorrhagia. There is no history of drug intake. Physical examination shows scattered petechiae and a normal-sized spleen. Her lab investigations are given below. Antibodies against which of the following can lead to this condition?

Platelet count - 37,000/μL

Bleeding time - 16 minutes

PT - 13 seconds

aPTT - 30 seconds

Peripheral blood smear - megathrombocytes
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP). Autoantibodies seen in ITP are most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX. It is a diagnosis of exclusion due to the following findings:

• Bleeding tendency - petechiae

• Low platelet count, elevated bleeding time

• Presence of megathrombocytes in the peripheral smear - a sign of accelerated thrombopoiesis

• Female preponderance

• Absence of splenomegaly

 Note: Prothrombin time (PT) is normal in ITP.

questions.question: Which class of antiplatelet antibodies are seen in patients with chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura?
questions.explanation:
Antiplatelet antibodies in chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) are mainly IgG class.

Autoantibodies most often directed against platelet membrane glycoproteins are IIb-IIIa or Ib-IX. It can be demonstrated in the plasma and bound to the platelet surface in about 80% of patients.

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is diagnosed to have idiopathic ITP. Which of the following features is least likely to be seen in her?
questions.explanation:
Lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly are uncommon in idiopathic (primary) ITP. They are seen in secondary ITP.

Chronic ITP occurs most commonly in adult women younger than 40 years of age. The female-to-male ratio is 3: 1. It is a type II hypersensitivity reaction. It is of 2 types:

• Primary or idiopathic - without any risk factors

• Secondary - presence of predisposing conditions like SLE, HIV, CLL

Signs of accelerated thrombopoiesis that are seen in this condition are:

• Megakaryocytes in bone marrow

• Megathrombocytes (abnormally large platelets) in peripheral blood

The image given below shows 2 megakaryocytes seen in bone marrow aspirate (Wrights stain).

Acute ITP is mainly a disease of childhood. It occurs with equal frequency in both sexes, mostly after a viral illness. It is self-limited condition, resolves within 6 months.

questions.question:
Patients with which of the following predisposing conditions are likely to develop chronic immune thrombocytopenic purpura?

1. Systemic lupus erythematosus

2. HIV infection

3. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

4. Rheumatoid arthritis

5. Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome
questions.explanation:
Systemic lupus erythematosus, HIV infection, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, antiphospholipid antibody syndrome can predispose to the development of secondary immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP).

The predisposing conditions of secondary chronic ITP include:

• Autoimmune conditions

• Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)

• Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome (APS)

• Immune thyroid disease

• Evans syndrome

• Lymphoproliferative diseases

• Chronic lymphocytic leukemia

• Large granular T-lymphocyte lymphocytic leukemia

• Chronic infection

• Helicobacter pylori

• Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

• Hepatitis C virus (HCV)

questions.question:
A 63-year-old man with moderate COVID pneumonia developed DVT. Therapeutic anticoagulation with heparin was started. His lab investigations are given below. Which of the following is false about this condition?

Timing
Platelet count

Before heparin therapy
3,50,000 /μL

Day 3 of therapy
3,20,000 /μL

Day 7 of therapy
53,000 /μL
options: Lesser incidence with use of LMWH
questions.answer: D. It is a self-resolving condition
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of type II heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT). It is not self-resolving.

Thrombocytopenia occurs in about 5% of persons receiving heparin and is of two types:

Feature
Type I
Type II

Incidence
More common
Less common

Occurrence
Rapidly after onset of therapy
5 to 14 days after therapy

Pathogenesis
Direct platelet-aggregating effect of heparin
Antibodies against heparin-platelet factor 4 complexes

Severity
Less severe
Often leads to life-threatening venous and arterial thrombosis

Treatment
Self-resolving

Immediate discontinuation of heparin

Alternate non-heparin anticoagulant to be used

questions.question: All of the following commonly cause drug-induced thrombocytopenia except _____
questions.explanation:
Terlipressin does not cause drug-induced thrombocytopenia.

Drug-induced thrombocytopenia can be caused by:

• Vancomycin

• Quinine

• Rifampin

They cause thrombocytopenia through direct effects on platelets or secondary to immunologically mediated platelet destructions. Quinine, quinidine, and vancomycin bind to platelet glycoprotein and create antigenic determinants that are recognized by antibodies.

questions.question: A post-operative patient was started on prophylactic unfractionated heparin for DVT. Which of the following is false regarding this drug?
options: It is an indirect thrombin-factor Xa inhibitor
It is safe in patients with renal impairment
On development of HIT, LMWH can be started alternately
questions.answer: D. On development of HIT, LMWH can be started alternately
questions.explanation:
The risk of severe heparin-induced thrombocytopenia is lowered with LMWH but not eliminated. Hence, once severe HIT develops even LMWH exacerbates the thrombotic tendency and must be avoided.

Management of HIT includes the immediate withdrawal of heparin therapy and instituting an alternative non-heparin anticoagulant.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following conditions is associated with ADAMTS13 deficiency?
questions.explanation:
ADAMTS13 deficiency is associated with thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP).

ADAMTS13 is also called vWF metalloprotease which degrades very high-molecular-weight multimers of von Willebrand factor (vWF). Its deficiency causes accumulation of these multimers in the plasma and promotes platelet activation and aggregation.

TTP is a part of a spectrum of clinical syndromes called thrombotic microangiopathy. They are caused by insults that lead to excessive activation of platelets, which deposit as thrombi in small blood vessels.

Features of TTP include:

• Fever

• Thrombocytopenia

• Microangiopathic hemolytic anaemia

• Transient neurologic deficits

• Renal failure

questions.question: A 7-year-old girl is brought with complaints of hematuria and melena for 10 days. Laboratory investigations reveal mild thrombocytopenia and normal coagulation tests. Peripheral smear is given below. Which organism is most frequently involved in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and peripheral smear showing helmet cells or schistocytes are suggestive of hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS). This condition is most commonly associated with enterohemorrhagic Escherichia coli strain O157: H7 worldwide.

This strain releases Shiga-like toxin. This toxin is absorbed from the inflamed gastrointestinal mucosa into the circulation and causes endothelial dysfunction. It leads to platelet activation and aggregation. Children and older adults are at the highest risk.

The image given below shows schistocytes or helmet cells seen in HUS.

questions.question: Deficiency of which of the following complement components is not associated with atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome is not associated with deficiency of CD59.

It is associated with deficiency of the following components:

• Complement factor H

• Membrane cofactor protein (CD46)

• Complement factor I

These three proteins prevent excessive activation of the alternative complement pathway.

Deficiencies of these proteins can be caused by inherited defects or acquired inhibitory autoantibodies. The disease may be associated with a remitting, relapsing course.

questions.question: Coombs test is found to be positive in a patient with thrombocytopenia. Which of the following conditions could be a likely cause?
questions.explanation:
Coombs test is positive in immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) as it is an immunogenic cause of thrombocytopenia.

Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS) and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) are nonimmunogenic causes. Hence, Coombs test is negative in these conditions.

questions.question: Which of the following is affected in patients with Weber-Osler-Rendu syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Weber–Osler–Rendu syndrome is a disorder of the blood vessels.

It is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations that modulate TGF-β signalling. It is also known as hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia.

This condition is characterized by dilated, tortuous blood vessels with thin walls that bleed readily. Bleeding is most common in the mucous membranes of the nose (epistaxis), tongue, mouth, and eyes, and throughout the gastrointestinal tract.

Platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) are normal.

Clinical conditions in which abnormalities of vessel wall cause bleeding include:

• Infections - meningococcemia, infective endocarditis, rickettsioses

• Collagen defects - Ehlers–Danlos syndrome, scurvy, and Cushing's syndrome

• Perivascular amyloidosis - most common with amyloid light-chain (AL) amyloidosis

• Henoch–Schönlein purpura

• Drug reactions

questions.question: What is the most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding?
questions.explanation:
The most common hereditary disease associated with life-threatening bleeding is hemophilia A. It is caused by mutations in factor VIII, an essential cofactor for factor IX in the coagulation cascade.

Note: von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder.

questions.question:
A 12-year-old boy presents with the following finding after a trivial fall. His lab investigations are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Platelet count - 4,00,000 /μL

Bleeding time - normal

PT - normal

aPTT - prolonged
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario showing hemarthrosis and elevated aPTT is suggestive of hemophilia.

Specific tests for measuring levels of factor VIII and factor IX can determine whether it is hemophilia A or hemophilia B respectively.

Clinical features of hemophilia:

• Hemarthroses - joint hemorrhages, later causing progressive deformities

• Recurrent bleeding

• Pseudotumour syndrome - fascial hemorrhages that occur as blood-filled cysts with calcification and proliferation of fibroblasts, giving the appearance of the tumor

It is associated with elevated aPTT and normal platelet count, bleeding time, and PT.

Option A: In ITP, the platelet count is low and bleeding time is prolonged.

Option B: In functional platelet disorders, like Bernard Soulier syndrome, the platelet count is normal and bleeding time is prolonged.

Option D: In vitamin K deficiency, both PT and aPTT are prolonged. PT is relatively more prolonged than is the aPTT.

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy was found to have excessive bleeding following tooth extraction. Lab investigations revealed prolonged aPTT, decreased serum factor VIII levels and normal VwF activity. What is the mode of inheritance of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Hemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency). It is inherited as an X-linked recessive trait. Hence, it affects mainly males and homozygous females.

Hemophilia B is also inherited as X-linked recessive trait.

Hemophilia C is inherited as an autosomal-recessive trait.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about hemophilia?
options: Hemophilia A in female may indicate unfavourable lyonization
Hemophilia A can occur without any family history
questions.answer: A. Hemophilia B never affects females
questions.explanation:
Hemophilia A and B mostly affect males, but rarely can affect females also.

Hemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder, affecting mainly males and homozygous females. Rarely, excessive bleeding occurs in heterozygous females. It is due to the inactivation of the X chromosome bearing the normal factor VIII allele by chance in most cells (unfavourable lyonization). About 30% of patients have no family history and the disorder is caused due to new mutations.

Hemophilia B is inherited as X-linked recessive trait. There is a deficiency of factor IX.

Hemophilia C is an autosomal-recessive condition and hence can occur in females. There is a deficiency of factor XI.

questions.question: A 10-year-old child with easy bruising was diagnosed to have moderate hemophilia A. What will be the percentage of normal factor VIII in her?
questions.explanation:
Patients with moderate hemophilia A have 2% - 5% of normal levels of factor VIII.

The clinical manifestations of Hemophilia A vary in severity, corresponding to the level of factor VIII present. They can be classified as:

Severity
Levels of factor VIII

Mild
6-50%

Moderate
2-5%

Severe
<1%

Patients with hemophilia A have:

• Normal prothrombin time (PT)

• Normal bleeding time

questions.question:
A newborn baby develops severe umbilical cord bleeding soon after birth. Lab investigations are given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Bleeding time - normal

Platelet count - normal

PT - normal

aPTT - normal

TT - normal

Urea lysis test - positive
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of factor XIII deficiency. A positive urea lysis test confirms the diagnosis.

Factor XIII is also known as clot-stabilizing factor that converts unstable fibrin clot into a stable clot. Its deficiency typically presents as excessive umbilical cord bleeding in the newborn.

Laboratory findings in this condition are:

• Normal levels of bleeding time (BT), platelet count, prothrombin time (PT), activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and thrombin time (TT)

• Positive urea lysis test - confirmatory test which demonstrates lysis of clot by hyperosmolar urea in affected individuals

questions.question:
A Hemogram of a 23-year-old patient with a bleeding disorder is given below. Which of the following would you use to differentiate between heparin-induced thrombocytopenia and afibrinogenemia in this patient?

Platelet count - 3,23,000 /μL

PT - elevated

aPTT - elevated

TT - elevated
questions.explanation:
Reptilase is a thrombin agonist which is used to differentiate heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and afibrinogenemia. It is resistant to the action of heparin.

The differential diagnosis for normal platelet count with elevated PT, aPTT and TT are HIT and afibrinogenemia. After adding reptilase, if the TT is corrected, it points to HIT. In afibrinogenemia, since there is an absence of fibrin, there is no change in the TT.

questions.question: A 1-year-old child was diagnosed to have Kasabach-Merritt syndrome. What is this condition associated with?
questions.explanation:
Kasabach–Merritt syndrome is associated with DIC (disseminated intravascular coagulation). This syndrome is characterised by the following features:

• Rapidly growing vascular tumour

• Thrombocytopenia

• Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia

• Consumptive coagulopathy

An unusual form of DIC occurs in association with giant hemangiomas. In this type, stasis and recurrent trauma to the fragile blood vessels cause thrombi to form within the neoplasm.

The image given below shows a reddish-blue lesion covering the lower part of the abdomen. It is a caverno-capillary haemangioma seen in Kasabach–Merritt syndrome.

questions.question: You are collecting a blood sample to send for prothrombin time in a patient in the ward. Which of the following is true about this investigation?
options: Test must be done within 2 hours of sample collection
questions.answer: C. Test must be done within 2 hours of sample collection
questions.explanation:
The test for prothrombin time is done within 2 hours.

The differences between PT and aPTT are:
