questions.question: At what temperature should you store the sample for antiphospholipid antibody factor assays?
questions.explanation:
The sample for antiphospholipid antibody assay must be stored at <4°.

Samples for coagulation studies should be stored always at room temperature (20 to 25 degrees).

questions.question: A 50-year-old male patient presents to the casualty with severe bleeding following a road traffic accident. He is a known cardiac disease patient on anticoagulant therapy. As an intern, you were asked to collect blood for coagulation studies. Which colour vacutainer will you pick?
questions.explanation:
The most commonly used vacutainer for coagulation studies is a blue vacutainer containing trisodium citrate.

The benefits of trisodium citrate are that the calcium ion is neutralized more rapidly in citrate.

Other anticoagulants are unacceptable for coagulation studies. The labile factors (factors V and VIII) are unstable in oxalate (grey), whereas heparin (green) and EDTA (lavender) directly inhibit the coagulation process and interfere with end-point determinations. Also, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) tests are more sensitive to the presence of heparin (green).

The image given below shows colour coding of vacutainers with the anticoagulant used and their practical uses.

Note: Heparin is used for blood sample collection for electrolyte estimation.

questions.question: Which of the following patients receiving blood transfusions are more prone to develop bacterial sepsis?
options: A young women with severe anaemia
questions.answer: B. A patient with severe thrombocytopenia
questions.explanation:
Patients with thrombocytopenia receiving blood transfusions (platelets) are more prone to develop bacterial sepsis.

Sepsis is mostly due to significant bacterial contamination of the blood products. Platelets have the maximum risk of causing this condition when compared to red cell preparations. Since patients with thrombocytopenia receive platelet transfusion, they are at an increased risk of infections.

Platelets (unlike red cells) must be stored at room temperature. This is a condition that is favourable for bacterial proliferation. Broad-spectrum antibiotics must be started while waiting for the culture reports.

The blood components that are preferred for the other conditions are:

• Anaemia - RBCs

• Hemophilia - FFP

• vonWillebrand disease - cryoprecipitate

questions.question: What is the most common reaction occurring in patients undergoing blood transfusions?
questions.explanation: The most common blood transfusion reaction is the febrile nonhemolytic reaction.

questions.question: Blood transfusion was started in a patient with severe anaemia. Within a few minutes she developed generalised pruritis, swelling of the tongue and stridor. Which antibody deficiency in the recipient most commonly causes this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of severe, potentially fatal, allergic reactions. These are most likely to occur in patients with IgA deficiency.

Such reactions may occur when blood products containing certain antigens are given to previously sensitized recipients. It is triggered by recipient IgG antibodies that recognize IgA in the infused blood product.

questions.question: Following blood transfusion in a post-operative patient, the following finding was noted. Which of the following is responsible for this reaction?
questions.answer: B. Ig E antibodies of recipient
questions.explanation:
The given image, showing a raised and erythematous lesion, is suggestive of urticaria. Such reactions may be triggered by the presence of an allergen in the donated blood product that is recognized by IgE antibodies in the recipient.

These are mild reactions occurring more commonly in 1% to 3% of transfusions.

questions.question:
A patient with thalassemia developed pallor and dizziness 1 week following blood transfusion. His lab reports are given below. Which of the following is seen in this condition?

LDH - increased

Haptoglobin - decreased
options: Direct coombs test negative, IgG mediated
Direct Coombs test positive, IgG mediated
Direct coombs test negative, IgM mediated
Direct coombs test positive, IgM mediated
questions.answer: B. Direct Coombs test positive, IgG mediated
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of delayed hemolytic reaction following blood transfusion. It is IgG mediated and gives a positive result in direct Coombs test.

These antibodies recognize foreign protein red cell antigens in a previously sensitized recipient (through a prior blood transfusion). They present with laboratory features of hemolysis like low haptoglobin level and elevated LDH.

Acute hemolytic reactions are usually caused by preformed IgM antibodies against donor red cells that fix complement. The direct Coombs test is usually positive.

questions.question: A patient who was admitted for blood transfusion developed transfusion-related acute lung injury. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
options: Pre-existing lung diseases are a risk factor
Incidence with platelet transfusion is more than that with whole blood
Symptoms develop after 2 days of transfusion
Subsequent transfusions from the same donor increases the incidence
questions.answer: C. Symptoms develop after 2 days of transfusion
questions.explanation:
Transfusion-related acute lung injury (TRALI) is sudden-onset respiratory failure that occurs during or soon after the transfusion. It occurs within 6 hours, and not after 2 days following transfusion.

TRALI is a severe fatal complication of blood transfusion. The incidence of TRALI is low (1 per 10,000 transfusions). However, it may occur more frequently in patients with preexisting lung disease.

The pathogenesis involves a two-hit hypothesis:

• Priming event - increased sequestration and sensitization of neutrophils in the microvasculature of the lung

• Second hit - the factor (most commonly MHC class I antigens) present in the transfused blood product activates the primed neutrophils

TRALI can occur in transfusions with all plasma-containing blood products. However, it is more likely to occur following the transfusion of fresh frozen plasma and platelets. This is because these products contain high levels of donor antibodies.

Note: TRALI is important to recognize because donor products that induce complications in one patient are much more likely to do so in a second. Indeed, recent measures to exclude multiparous women from plasma donation have resulted in reduced incidence of TRALI.

questions.question: A 33-year-old man is receiving massive blood transfusion following a fall from height. 4 hours after transfusion, he becomes breathless and oxygen saturation decreases. Chest X-ray shows diffuse bilateral lung infiltrates. Which of the following statements is false regarding this condition?
options: Treatment involves discontinuation of blood transfusion
It is mediated by macrophages in lung vasculature
questions.answer: D. It is mediated by macrophages in lung vasculature
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of TRALI (transfusion-related acute lung injury). It is mediated by neutrophils entrapped in the lung vasculature.

Features of TRALI are:

• Fever

• Hypotension

• Hypoxemia

• Bilateral pulmonary infiltrates - not responsive to diuretics

Treatment is mainly supportive and blood transfusions are discontinued. The mortality rate in this condition is 5-10%.

topics.topic: Leukemia, Lymphoma and White Cell Disorders

questions.question: Reed-Sternberg cells are characteristic of:
questions.explanation: Owl-eye binucleate cells, CD15/CD30 positive.

questions.question: Which is the most common subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Nodular sclerosis is the most common type of Hodgkin's lymphoma, while mixed cellularity is most common in India.

The incidence of nodular sclerosis is equal in men and women. It commonly involves the lower cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal lymph nodes. It commonly affects adolescents and young adults. It has an excellent prognosis.

Mixed-cellularity Hodgkin lymphoma is seen in patients older than 50 years of age. There is a male predominance.

The image given below shows the histology of nodular sclerosis showing a lacunar variant of Reed–Sternberg cells

questions.question: A lymph node biopsy specimen of a patient shows giant cells with an owl-eyed appearance. Which of the following statements is incorrect with respect to the diagnosis in this case?
options: Single axial group of lymph nodes is affected
Spleen is the first extranodal tissue to be involved
questions.answer: C. Mesenteric nodes are frequently involved
questions.explanation:
An owl-eyed appearance of giant cells in lymph nodes is characteristic of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). Mesenteric lymph nodes are infrequently involved in HL.

Hodgkin’s lymphoma is a group of lymphoid neoplasms arising in a single group of lymph nodes. Extranodal involvement is uncommon. However, if it spreads from the nodes, the first organ to be involved is the spleen, then the liver, and finally the bone marrow. This pattern of spread is known as the contiguous spread.

This predictable route of spread is important clinically as it aids in staging and prognosis as well as treatment of HL.

questions.question: Activation of which of the following is a common event in classical Hodgkin's lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Activation of the transcription factor NF-κB is a common event in classical Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL).

NF-κB may be activated by Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection. EBV+ tumor cells express latent membrane protein-1 (LMP-1) which upregulates NF-κB. Activation of NF-κB may occur in EBV tumors as a result of the acquired loss-of-function mutations in TNF alpha-induced protein 3 (TNFAIP3).

Activation of NF-κB by EBV rescues crippled germinal center B cells that cannot express Igs from apoptosis, eventually leading to the formation of Reed–Sternberg cells.

questions.question: Copy-number gains of which proto-oncogene on chromosome 2p are common in Hodgkin lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Copy-number gains in the REL proto-oncogene on chromosome 2p are particularly common in Hodgkin's lymphoma. It may also contribute to increased NF-Κβ activity.

Reed-Sternberg cells are aneuploid and possess diverse clonal chromosomal aberrations.

Note: the MYC gene, commonly associated with Burkitt lymphoma is present on chromosome 8.

questions.question:
In which of the following lesions can we see the Reed-Sternberg-like cells?

1. Hodgkin Lymphoma

2. Large-cell NHL

3. Infectious mononucleosis

4. Mantle cell lymphoma
questions.explanation:
Reed–Sternberg-like cells (RSLC) can be seen in the following:

• Infectious mononucleosis

• Large-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas (most common in immunoblastic NHL)

• Solid tissue cancers

While Reed-Sternberg cells (RS cells) are seen in Hodgkin’s lymphoma, there can be presence of Reed-Sternberg like cells which that may have morphologic features resembling RS cells.

Diagnostic Reed–Sternberg cells are large cells with multiple nuclei or a single nucleus with multiple nuclear lobes, each with a large inclusion-like nucleolus, about the size of a small lymphocyte with abundant cytoplasm (owl-eye appearance).

The image given below shows the classic Reed Sternberg cells.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a variant of the Reed-Sternberg cell?
questions.explanation:
Monomorphic is not a variant of RS cell.

Reed–Sternberg cell (RS cell) is the characteristic tumor giant cell of Hodgkin Lymphoma. It is derived from the germinal center B cell. It has a classic owl-eyed appearance due to the presence of a symmetric or mirror-image bilobed nucleus, with prominent nucleoli surrounded by a clear space. It has the following variants:

• Lacunar

• Classic

• L&H Popcorn cells

• Pleomorphic

• Mononuclear

RS cells should be present in a background of non-neoplastic inflammatory cells like lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils, to make a diagnosis of Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

The image given below shows the diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cell, with two nuclear lobes, large inclusion-like nucleoli, and abundant cytoplasm, surrounded by lymphocytes, macrophages, and an eosinophil.

The image below shows Reed-Sternberg cell, mononuclear variant.

The image below shows Reed-Sternberg cell, lacunar variant. This variant has a folded or multilobated nucleus and lies within an open space, which is an artefact created by disruption of the cytoplasm during tissue sectioning.

The image below shows the Reed-Sternberg cell, lymphohistiocytic variant. Several such variants with multiple infolded nuclear membranes, small nucleoli, fine chromatin, and abundant pale cytoplasm are present.

questions.question: A patient with generalized lymphadenopathy and Pel-Ebstein fever is diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. Which of the following is a characteristic finding seen in this condition?
options: Pain in nodes relieved by alcohol
Pain in nodes aggravated by alcohol
questions.answer: B. Pain in nodes aggravated by alcohol
questions.explanation:
In the case of Hodgkin's Lymphoma, the pain in the lymph nodes aggravates following the intake of alcohol.

Clinical features of HL:

• Painless enlargement of lymph nodes is the most common presenting symptom.

• Cyclical fever (Pel–Ebstein fever) - cyclical increase, which then decreases over an average period of one or two weeks and night sweats in disseminated disease. This cyclical fever may be due to the release of cytokines.

A unique paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma is the occurrence of pain in the affected lymph nodes during alcohol consumption. This has been attributed to the enlargement of the affected lymph nodes following alcohol consumption, which stretches the capsule of the lymph node and produces pain.

questions.question: A lymph node biopsy sample of a patient showed Reed-Sternberg cells that were CD15 & CD30 negative. Which of the variants of Hodgkin lymphoma is the patient most likely to have?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with biopsy findings of CD15 and CD30 negative Reed–Sternberg cell is suggestive of nodular lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma.

The Reed–Sternberg cells are positive for CD15 and CD30 for most subtypes, except in lymphocyte-predominant HL, in which the neoplastic cells stains for CD20 and BCL-6.

questions.question: Which subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma has an incidence as shown in the graph given below?
questions.explanation:
The given graph shows a disease with a biphasic incidence which is characteristically seen in mixed cellularity type of Hodgkin lymphoma.

It has a male predominance, biphasic incidence, peaking in young adults and again in adults older than 55 years. It has more systemic symptoms like night sweats and weight loss. There is diffuse involvement of the entire lymph node. It consists of a mixture of cells composed of T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, and benign macrophages mixed with Reed–Sternberg cells. The mononuclear variant and diagnostic Reed–Sternberg cells are seen in this type.

Reed–Sternberg cell is infected with Epstein–Barr virus in 70% of cases. It has very good prognosis.

Image given below shows mononuclear variant of RS cell.

questions.question: Which subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma is associated with older age, systemic symptoms, and advanced tumor stage?
questions.explanation:
Mixed-cellularity Hodgkin's lymphoma is associated with older age, systemic symptoms like night sweats and weight loss, and advanced tumor stage.

It has a biphasic incidence peaking in young adults and again in adults more than 55 years of age. It also has a strong association with HIV. It is more common in males than females.

Nonetheless, the overall prognosis is very good.

questions.question: The given histological findings were noted on a lymph node biopsy of a patient with lymphadenopathy. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows a lacunar variant of Reed–Sternberg cell. These are common in the nodular sclerosis subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma.

Subtypes of Hodgkin's lymphoma along with their characteristic types of RS cells is given below:

Hodgkin lymphoma (subtypes)
Diagnostic cells in histology
Immunophenotype

Nodular sclerosis
Lacunar variant
CD 15+, CD 30 +

Mixed cellularity

Mononuclear and Diagnostic RS cells (70% EBV +)

CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte Rich

Mononuclear and Diagnostic RS cells (40% EBV +)

CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte Depletion
Reticular variant; (most EBV+)
CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte predominance
Lymphocytic and histiocytic variant, popcorn cells (EBV -)

CD 20+, BCL6+

CD 15 -, CD 30 -

The image given below shows nodular sclerosis type of HL with lacunar cells.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding the nodular sclerosis variant of Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: Reed-Sternberg cells are positive for PAX 5
It is uncommonly associated with Epstein Barr Virus
Reed-Sternberg cells are positive for CD45
questions.answer: D. Reed-Sternberg cells are positive for CD45
questions.explanation:
Reed–Sternberg cells in nodular sclerosis variant of Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) are negative for CD45. It is the most common variant.

These are characterized by the presence of lacunar variant Reed–Sternberg cells and the deposition of collagen bands. These bands divide involved lymph nodes into circumscribed nodules.

The Reed-Sternberg cells are found in a polymorphous background of T cells, eosinophils, plasma cells, and macrophages. Diagnostic Reed-Sternberg cells are often uncommon.

The Reed–Sternberg cells are positive for PAX5 (a B-cell transcription factor), CD15, and CD30, and negative for other B-cell markers, T-cell markers, and CD45 (leukocyte common antigen). This subtype is uncommonly associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

Involvement of the spleen, liver, bone marrow and other organs and tissues can occur later in the disease.

The prognosis is excellent.

questions.question: Lymph node biopsy of which of the following variants of Hodgkin lymphoma will show the maximum area of necrosis?
questions.explanation:
The lymphocyte-depleted subtype of Hodgkin lymphoma is associated with maximum necrosis of the lymph nodes.

Lymphocyte-depleted is the least common type (<5%). It is seen in older and HIV-infected individuals and can present with systemic symptoms. There is a paucity of lymphocytes and a relative abundance of Reed–Sternberg (RS) cells or their pleomorphic variants. RS cells are CD15+ and CD30+ RS cells are infected with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) in 90% of the cases. It has a poor prognosis.

questions.question: Which subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma is most commonly associated with HIV?
questions.explanation:
The Mixed cellularity subtype of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is most commonly associated with HIV.

Note: Although both mixed cellularity and lymphocyte depletion are seen in patients with HIV, mixed cellularity is more commonly associated with HIV.

questions.question: A 15-year-old male patient came to the OPD with cervical lymph node enlargement. The biopsy was examined, which showed a variant of the Reed-Sternberg cell given in the image. Which of the following types of Hodgkin's lymphoma frequently has this cell in its histology?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the lymphohistiocytic variant (L&H) of Reed–Sternberg (RS) cell. It is seen frequently in lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma.

The cell has the following features:

• Polypoid nuclei

• Inconspicuous nucleoli

• Moderately abundant cytoplasm

As it resembles popcorn in its morphology it is also termed popcorn cell.

Note: A unique paraneoplastic syndrome associated with Hodgkin's lymphoma is the occurrence of pain in the affected lymph nodes during alcohol consumption. This has been attributed to the enlargement of the affected lymph nodes following alcohol consumption, which stretches the capsule of the lymph node and produces pain.

questions.question: In a patient with lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin lymphoma, cells are found to be positive for which of the following marker?
questions.explanation:
Nodular-lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin Lymphomas have Reed Sternberg cells(aka L&H CELL) that are BCL-6 positive & CD 20 positive and CD 15 & CD 30 negative.

Note:

• CD30 is the most sensitive marker of Reed–Sternberg cell.

• PAX5 is the most specific marker of Reed–Sternberg cell.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma?
options: It can progress to a tumor resembling DLBCL
The bone marrow involvement is rare
A strong association with EBV is seen
questions.answer: D. A strong association with EBV is seen
questions.explanation:
Lymphocyte-predominant Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL) is not associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection.

In 3% to 5% of cases, this type transforms into a tumor resembling diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

A majority of patients are males, usually younger than 35 years of age, who typically present with cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Mediastinal and bone marrow involvement is rare.

This form of HL is more likely to recur than the classical subtypes, but the prognosis is excellent.

questions.question: A 23-year-old man is diagnosed to have Stage II (A) Hodgkin's lymphoma. What staging system was most likely used to classify the tumor of this patient?
questions.explanation:
Clinical staging of both Hodgkin and Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is done by Ann-Arbor classification.

Option B: Masaoka staging is used for thymoma.

Option C: Modified Durie–Salmon staging is used for multiple myeloma.

questions.question: Who among the following patients is likely to have the best prognosis?
options: A patient with mononuclear variant of Reed-Sternberg cells on lymph node biopsy
A patient whose lymph node biopsy showed lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells
A patient with predominant reticular variant of Reed- Sternberg cells
A patient with Reed-Sternberg cells amid mixed variety of background cells
questions.answer: B. A patient whose lymph node biopsy showed lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells
questions.explanation:
The prognosis of the nodular sclerosis ( a subtype of classical Hodgkin lymphoma) is excellent compared to the other subtypes mentioned in the options. Lacunar Reed-Sternberg cells are seen in this condition.

The nodular sclerosis type occurs with equal frequency in males and females. It has a propensity to involve the lower cervical, supraclavicular, and mediastinal lymph nodes of adolescents or young adults.

Subtypes of Hodgkin's lymphoma along with their characteristic types of RS cells is given below:

Hodgkin lymphoma (subtypes)
Diagnostic cells in histology
Immunophenotype

Nodular sclerosis
Lacunar variant
CD 15+, CD 30 +

Mixed cellularity

Mononuclear and Diagnostic RS cells (70% EBV +)

CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte Rich

Mononuclear and Diagnostic RS cells (40% EBV -)

CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte Depletion
Reticular variant; (most EBV+)
CD 15+, CD 30 +

Lymphocyte predominance
Lymphocytic and histiocytic variant, popcorn cells (EBV -)

CD 20+, BCL6+

CD 15 -, CD 30 -

Nodular lymphocyte-predominant non-classical Hodgkin lymphoma also has an excellent prognosis.

questions.question: Which among the following is incorrect about Hodgkin's lymphoma?
options: Histologic type is the most important prognostic variable.
The cure rate of patients with stages I and IIA is close to 90%.
Long-term survivors treated with radiotherapy had a much higher incidence of secondary malignancies.
It most commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy.
questions.answer: A. Histologic type is the most important prognostic variable.
questions.explanation:
With current treatment protocols, the tumor stage is the most important prognostic variable, not histologic type.

Hodgkin's Lymphoma most commonly presents as painless lymphadenopathy.

The cure rate of patients with stages I and IIA are close to 90%.

Long-term survivors treated with radiotherapy had a much higher incidence of certain malignancies, such as lung cancer, melanoma, and breast cancer.

questions.question: Which of these parameters would be considered a poor prognostic factor in patients with Hodgkin's lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Absolute lymphocyte count <600 cells/cumm is a poor prognostic factor for Hodgkin lymphoma.

Poor prognostic factors for Hodgkin's lymphoma:

• Age >45 years

• Male gender

• Haemoglobin <10.5 g/dl

• Total WBC count >15000 cells/mm3

• Lymphocytopenia: absolute count <600/mm3 or lymphocytes <8% of leukocytes

• Serum albumin level: <4g/dl

• Stage IV

questions.question: Which of these is not a pre-leukemic condition?
questions.explanation:
Paroxysmal cold hemoglobinuria is not a preleukemic condition.

It is an autoimmune hemolytic anemia due to IgG autoantibodies that bind to the P blood group antigen and cause intravascular hemolysis and hemoglobinuria. Most cases are seen in children and show recovery within a month.

Option A: Few patients with paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) develop acute non-lymphocytic leukemia. This is thought to arise from the injured marrow as a secondary hematopoietic disorder.

Option B: Bone marrow aplasia preceding acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is a rare condition that usually affects children. It generally follows the recovery of normal blood counts and most commonly occurs within 6 months of the onset of aplasia.

Option C: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) occurs in 10% to 40% of individuals with myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS). It is usually accompanied by the appearance of additional cytogenetic abnormalities.

questions.question: Which of the following is true about the pathogenesis of acute leukemia?
options: Arrest in differentiation and increased apoptosis
Arrest in differentiation and decreased apoptosis
questions.answer: D. Arrest in differentiation and decreased apoptosis
questions.explanation:
In acute leukemia, there is an arrest in differentiation and decreased apoptosis.

Genomic aberrations create oncoproteins. They arrest normal maturation, turn on pro-growth signaling pathways, or protect cells from apoptotic death.

questions.question: As per WHO classification, what percentage of blast cells in bone marrow biopsy is required to diagnose a patient with acute leukemia?
questions.explanation:
As per WHO classification, 20% of blast cells must be present in the bone marrow and / peripheral smear for the diagnosis of acute leukemia.

In FAB criteria, the cut-off is more than 30%.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions does not increase the risk of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
questions.explanation:
Polycythemia vera increases the risk of developing AML, not ALL.

Inherited diseases that are associated with a higher risk of developing leukemias are:

• Bloom syndrome

• Fanconi anemia

• Ataxia–telangiectasia

• Down syndrome

• Type-1 neurofibromatosis

Other germline risk factors for the development of ALL:

• Li-Fraumeni syndrome

• Familial ALL syndrome

Note: AML has a higher incidence during the neonatal period than ALL among children with Fanconi anemia, Bloom syndrome, and Down syndrome.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common type of acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
questions.explanation: Precursor B-cell or pre B cell (previously classified as L1) type is the most common subtype of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL).

questions.question: Which of the following is not a primary T-cell marker?
questions.explanation:
CD10 is not a primary marker of T cells. It is a marker of pre-B cells and germinal-center B cells.

Note: Although CD10/ Common ALL antigen (CALLA) can be found in B-ALL and T-ALL, it is primarily expressed by pre-B cells and germinal centre B cells. Lymphoblasts of both B and T cell lineages, express CD10 that is lost upon progression to a mature phenotype. It is variably expressed by a few mature B cell tumours. However, the expression of CD10 by mature T cells has not been well established.

questions.question: Block-like positivity for PAS on immunohistochemistry of a bone marrow sample is seen. Which of the following cells show this finding?
questions.explanation:
Lymphoblasts in acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL) show block-like or dot-like PAS positivity.

Erythroblasts in acute myeloid leukemia-M6 (AML-M6) show diffuse periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) positivity.

The image given below shows dot-like positivity for periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) in lymphoblasts.

questions.question: Which of the following cells does not stain positively with Sudan black?
questions.explanation:
Lymphocytes do not stain positively with Sudan black dye. Although some positivity may be seen in azurophilic granules of lymphoblasts.

Sudan Black B (SBB) is a lipophilic dye that binds irreversibly to an undefined granule component in granulocytes, eosinophils, and some monocytes.

questions.question: What is the most commonly affected gene in patients with T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia?
questions.explanation:
The most commonly affected gene in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is NOTCH1.

B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia is associated with mutations of genes such as PAX5, E2A, and EBF. It may be associated with balanced t(12;21) involving the genes ETV6 and RUNX1.

questions.question: A patient with acute lymphoblastic leukemia is found to have t(9;22). What will be the size of BCR-ABL fusion protein produced?
questions.explanation:
The size of BCR-ABL protein in t(9;22) associated with acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) is 190 kDa.

BCR-ABL fusion transcript protein with t(9;22):

• Major BCR (M-BCR) 210 kDa size in chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) with weaker tyrosine kinase activity

• Minor BCR (m-BCR) 190 kDa size in acute lymphoblastic leukemia ( ALL) with stronger tyrosine kinase activity

• Micro BCR (μ-BCR) 230 kDa size in myeloproliferative neoplasm (MPN) with exuberant neutrophilia

questions.question: On immunophenotyping of a patient with early pre-B acute leukemia, which of the following marker will be negative?
questions.explanation: Cytoplasmic immunoglobulins and CD10 are negative in early pre-B acute leukemia but become positive in pre-B ALL.

questions.question: An adolescent male patient presents with fatigue. His total leucocyte count is 138 x 10^9 / L with 80% blasts on the peripheral smear. Chest X-ray shows a large mediastinal mass. The bone marrow aspirate is as shown below. What would the immunophenotyping of this patient’s blasts most likely demonstrate?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and bone marrow aspirate are suggestive of T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Thus, immunophenotyping of the blasts would demonstrate an immature T-cell phenotype (Tdt/CD34/CD7 positive).

The bone marrow aspirate shows lymphoblast with condensed nuclear chromatin, small inconspicuous nucleoli, and scanty cytoplasm lacking granules.

ALL is usually seen in adolescent boys with thymic involvement in 50% to 70%. It has an abrupt stormy onset, within days to a few weeks of the first symptoms.

Clinical features of ALL include:

• Bone marrow failure - anemia, fever, infections, bleeding

• Mass effects due to neoplastic infiltration - bone pain, generalized lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and testicular enlargement

• CNS manifestations - headache, vomiting, and nerve palsies

• B-ALL - Pancytopenia due to marrow involvement

• T-ALL - Mediastinal mass, compression of  large vessels and airways in the mediastinum, lymphadenopathy, splenomegaly

questions.question: In a patient with acute leukemia, the immunophenotype pattern of the blasts is positive for CD10, CD13, CD19, and CD33. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) based on immunophenotyping.

CD10 and CD19 are markers for B-cell lineage and this patient most probably have B-ALL. Although CD13 and CD33 are myeloid antigens, their expression does not exclude the diagnosis of B- ALL.

Option B: The diagnosis of mixed phenotypic acute leukemia (MPAL)/ acute leukemia of ambiguous lineage (ALAL) (previously known as biphenotypic leukemia) requires a demonstration of multiple lineages in blast cells. According to WHO's latest update (2022), the requirements for assigning more than one lineage to blast cells are :

 B cell lineage

• CD19 strong:

≥1 expressed CD10, CD22, CD79a

• CD 19 weak:

≥ 2 or more strongly expressed CD10, CD22, CD79a

T cell lineage
CD3 positive

Myeloid lineage

Myeloperoxidase (MPO)

OR

Monocyte differentiation (non-specific esterase, CD11c, CD14, CD64, lysozyme)

In the absence of MPO or evidence of monocytic differentiation, expression of CD13 and CD33 is not sufficient for a diagnosis of MPAL. Hence, biphenotypic leukemia is not the answer here.

questions.question: A patient with weight loss and fever is diagnosed with acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Which of the following is a good prognostic indicator of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The presence of t (12;21) indicates a good prognosis in acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It involves genes ETV6 and RUNX1.

Conversely, a translocation involving the MLL gene, t(9;22), and hypodiploidy are associated with a bad prognosis.

questions.question:
Bone marrow biopsy of a patient shows > 20% immature blasts with scanty cytoplasm, no granules, and inconspicuous nucleoli. They also stain positive with PAS. Which of the following are good prognostic markers of this condition?

1. Trisomy 7

2. Hyperdiploidy

3. t (8,14)

4. Pseudodiploidy

5. Age of 5 years
questions.explanation: The given bone marrow biopsy report is suggestive of acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). The good prognostic markers of ALL include trisomy 7, hyperdiploidy, and age of 5 years.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a myeloid marker?
questions.explanation:
CD3 is not a myeloid marker. It is a T-cell lymphoid marker.

Cell markers:

• B-cell: CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23, CD24, CD79b, CD103, Pax-5, kappa, lambda, CD200, cytoplasmic kappa, cytoplasmic lambda

• T- cell: CD1, CD2, CD3, CD4, CD5, CD6,CD7, CD8, TCR apha-beta, TCR gamma-delta, cytoplasmic CD3

• Myeloid: CD11b, CD13, CD14, CD15, CD33, CD64, CD 117, myeloperoxidase

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common type of acute myeloid leukemia?
questions.explanation:
The most common type of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is AML - M2 or AML with maturation.

The least common type of AML is AML M7 or megakaryocytic.

questions.question: What is the most common subtype of acute myeloid leukemia seen in patients with Down's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The most common subtype of AML seen in Down's syndrome is acute myeloid leukemia-M7 (AML - M7) or acute megakaryocytic leukemia.

Myeloid proliferations of Down's syndrome are usually megakaryoblastic. It includes:

• Transient abnormal myelopoiesis (TAM) - occurs at birth or within days of birth and resolves in 1 to 2 months

• Myeloid leukemia associated with Down syndrome - occurs later, but usually in the first 3 years of life.

Both are characterized by GATA1 mutations and mutations of the JAK-STAT pathway.

questions.question:
A 35-year-man presents with nosebleeds, bleeding gums, and multiple ecchymoses. Lab investigations show the following findings. The blasts are positive for CD33. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hb: 8.5 g/dL

Platelet count: 12,000/Cumm

TLC: 52,000/Cumm with 83% blasts
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

AML is a tumor of hematopoietic progenitors caused by acquired oncogenic mutations that impede differentiation, leading to the accumulation of immature myeloid blasts in the marrow. It occurs at all ages, but the incidence rises throughout life, peaking after 60 years of age.

The peripheral smear shows blasts with abundant cytoplasm, fine azurophilic granules, Auer rods, and delicate nuclear chromatin with 1-4 prominent nucleoli. The blasts are positive for CD33. Occasionally, blasts are entirely absent from the blood (aleukemic leukemia). Bone marrow examination is essential to exclude acute leukemia in pancytopenic patients.

questions.question: Peripheral smear of a patient with acute promyelocytic leukemia shows myeloblasts with the following finding. What are these made of?
questions.explanation:
The image shows Auer rods in myeloblasts. These are needle-shaped azurophilic intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies formed by the fusion of lysosomes.

Auer rods contain peroxidase and lysosomal enzymes. Myeloblasts with bundles of Auer rods are called faggot cells and are seen in acute promyelocytic leukemia.

questions.question:
In which of the following conditions are Auer rods seen?

1. Acute promyelocytic leukemia

2. Acute monocytic leukemia

3. Myelodysplasia

4. Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia

5. Acute lymphoblastic leukemia
questions.explanation:
Auer rods are seen in:

• Acute promyelocytic leukemia

• Myelodysplastic syndromes

• Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia

These are not seen in acute monocytic leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia.

questions.question: Increased levels of serum muramidase are seen in patients with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Serum muramidase or lysozyme levels are seen to be increased in patients with acute myelomonocytic leukemia (AML - M4).

It is also increased in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia and chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).

questions.question: Which type of AML is known as Di Guglielmo disease?
questions.explanation:
Acute myeloid leukemia-M6 (AML-M6) or acute erythroid leukemia is known as Di Guglielmo disease.

AML-M6 accounts for 1% of AML cases. It has two subtypes:

• Erythroid/myeloid leukemia (M6a, more common) - Dyserythropoiesis is prominent

• Pure erythroid leukemia/ erythemic myelosis/ Di Guglielmo disease (M6b, rare) - >80% erythroid precursors. Clinical findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, and variable neutropenia.

Positive stains for erythroid cells are glycophorin A, hemoglobin A, CD36, CD71, CD117, and PAS.

questions.question: In patients with which of the following conditions, a dry tap may be seen on bone marrow aspiration?
questions.explanation:
Acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AML M7) may yield a dry tap on marrow aspiration.

It may be associated with extensive bone marrow fibrosis as a result of the stimulation of the normal fibroblasts by the local secretion of platelet-derived growth factor (PDGF) by the leukemic cells.

questions.question: Bone marrow aspirate of a patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia shows the presence of faggot cells. What is the most likely subtype of acute myeloid leukemia, the patient is suffering from?
questions.explanation:
The presence of faggot cells is highly suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia - M3 (AML - M3) or acute promyelocytic leukemia.

A cluster of Auer rods is known as a faggot cell. It is characteristic of acute myeloid leukemia (AML) M3.

The image given below shows AML M3 with a cluster of Auer rods (faggot cell).

questions.question:
A patient diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia presents with a one-day history of bleeding gums, subconjunctival bleed, and purpuric rash. Investigations done are given below. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely to be detected?

Hb: 6.4 gm/dL

TLC: 26,500 cells/mm3

Platelet: 35,000 mm3

Prothrombin time: 20 sec with a control of 13 sec

Partial thromboplastin time: 50 sec

Fibrinogen: 10 mg/dL
questions.explanation:
The patient shows features of disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). It is most likely to be associated with acute myeloid leukemia - M3 or acute promyelocytic leukemia. The pathogenesis behind this is t(15,17) or PML-RARA fusion gene.

Option A: Inversion 16 is seen in acute myelomonocytic leukemia or AML - M4.

Option B: t(8;21) is seen in AML with differentiation or AML - M2.

Option C: Inversion 3 is seen in AML - M7 (megakaryoblastic) which shows normal or increased platelet count. It has a poor prognosis.

questions.question: Which type of acute myeloid leukemia is myeloperoxidase negative?
questions.explanation:
AML M0 is negative for myeloperoxidase (MPO). AML-M5 (monocytic), AML-M6 (erythroid), and AML-M7 (megakaryocytic) are also negative for MPO.

Myeloperoxidase (MPO) is located in the primary granules of neutrophils and their precursors, in eosinophil granules, and in the azurophilic granules of monocytes.

The most primitive myeloblasts are negative, with granular positivity appearing progressively as they mature toward the promyelocyte stage. Promyelocytes and myelocytes are the most strongly staining cells in the granulocyte series. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive.

AML-M4 shows both myelocytic and monocytic differentiation. Hence, it shows both MPO and non-specific esterase (marker for monocytes) positivity.

questions.question: A patient with fatigue and recurrent infections undergoes bone marrow evaluation. It shows > 20% myeloblasts, which stain positive for CD61. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with myeloblasts that stain positive for CD61 is suggestive of acute megakaryocytic leukemia (AML-M7).

AML M7 is the least common type of AML. Blasts of megakaryocytic lineage predominate and are associated with marrow fibrosis. There is also frequent budding of cytoplasmic margins.

They are CD41+ and CD61+. They stain negatively with Sudan black B (SBB) and myeloperoxidase (MPO). Blasts are reactive with PAS and acid phosphatase.

The prognosis for this type of acute leukemia is poor.

questions.question: A patient who developed the following lesions over the body was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia. Which subtype of AML does this patient most likely have?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows leukemia cutis. It is seen in acute myeloid leukemia - M4 and acute myeloid leukemia - M5. It refers to leukemic cells infiltrating the skin.

Signs and symptoms related to the involvement of tissues other than the marrow are usually less striking in AML than in acute lymphocytic leukemia (ALL). But tumors with monocytic differentiation (AML M4, M5) often infiltrate the skin (leukemia cutis) and the gingiva. This probably reflects the normal tendency of monocytes to extravasate into tissues.

questions.question:
A 38-year-old man presents with bleeding gums for 20 days. He has gingival hyperplasia, hepatosplenomegaly, and lymphadenopathy. Investigations done are given below. Bone marrow biopsy shows 100% cellularity with many blasts cells that are peroxidase negative and non-specific esterase positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Hb: 11 g/dL

Platelet count: 95,000 platelets/mm3

WBC count: 45000 cells/mm3.
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute myeloid leukemia-M5 (AML-M5) or acute monocytic leukemia.

The patients with AML - M5 develop organomegaly, lymphadenopathy, gingival hyperplasia, CNS involvement, and other tissue infiltration. The bone marrow aspirate shows 20% or more blasts. Monoblasts have folded or lobulated nuclei, lack Auer rods, and are nonspecific esterase positive.

Myeloperoxidase is present in the azurophilic granules of neutrophils and their precursors. It is positive in AML M1, M2, M3, M4 and negative in AML M0. Monoblasts and monocytes may be negative or positive. When positive, the granules are smaller than in neutrophils and diffusely scattered throughout the cytoplasm.

The image given below shows bone marrow aspirate in AML - M5.

questions.question: A child presents with bilateral proptosis. After evaluation, he is diagnosed with chloroma. Which of the following is not a marker for this condition?
questions.explanation:
CD61 is a marker of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia, not chloroma. Lysozyme, CD43, CD45, CD117, and MPO are positive markers of chloroma.

Chloroma, also called myeloid sarcoma, granulocytic sarcoma, or myeloblastoma is an extramedullary tumor that occurs in 2% to 14% of patients with AML. Frequent sites of involvement are:

• Skin

• Lymph nodes

• Gastrointestinal tract

• Bone

• Soft tissue, testis

• Peritoneum

Orbital involvement of myeloid sarcoma is rare without any evidence of systemic involvement. Proptosis is the most common presentation. Other symptoms include lacrimal swelling, conjunctival mass lesion, retinal hemorrhages, ptosis, dystopia. Decreased visual acuity and ocular movement restriction have also been reported.

questions.question: In which of the following conditions are Arbiskov cells seen?
questions.explanation:
Arbiskov cells are monocytes seen in myeloblastoma or chloroma.

Chloroma, also known as granulocytic sarcoma, is a hematopoietic stem cell tumor, where myeloblasts are located at extramedullary sites. Orbit is one of the most common sites of occurrences in pediatric population. It is seen in AML - M2 most commonly. Other conditions associated are myelodysplastic and myeloproliferative syndromes.

The image given below shows Arbiskov cells in chloroma.

questions.question: Which of the following cytogenetic changes suggest a favorable prognosis in patients with acute myeloid leukemia?
options: t (11q23;v) with diverse MLL fusion genes
questions.answer: B. Normal karyotyping with mutated NPM
questions.explanation: Normal karyotyping with mutated NPM indicates a favorable prognosis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

questions.question: Which among the following patients with acute myeloid leukemia has a good prognosis?
options: A 56-year-old patient who developed post-chemotherapy AML
An infant with AML having complex karyotype
A 60-year-old patient diagnosed with AML-M0 type
A patient with AML having Inversion 16
questions.answer: D. A patient with AML having Inversion 16
questions.explanation: Inversion 16 is associated with a good prognosis in acute myeloid leukemia (AML).

questions.question: Which of the areas in the histology of lymph nodes show small-unchallenged B cells surrounding pale-staining germinal centres?
questions.explanation:
The mantle zone of the lymph nodes shows small, unchallenged B cells surrounding pale-staining germinal centres.

Structures in a follicle:

1. Germinal centre - round/oval zone containing pale-staining cells surrounded by darker cells.

2. Mantle zone - small, unchallenged B cells surrounding pale-staining germinal centres.

3. Marginal zone - Light zone surrounding follicles; contains post-follicular memory B cells derived after stimulation of recirculating cells from T-cell-dependent antigen.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a B lymphocyte marker?
questions.explanation: CD13 is an antigen of monocyte/macrophage and not B-cell.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding Non-Hodgkin lymphoma?
options: It involves multiple peripheral lymph nodes
Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring are rarely involved
questions.answer: B. Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring are rarely involved
questions.explanation: Mesenteric nodes and Waldeyer ring are commonly involved in non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL).

questions.question: Which is the most common non-Hodgkin lymphoma in adults?
questions.explanation:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is the most common form of non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in adults and children over the age of 15 years, worldwide and in India.

Burkitt's lymphoma is the most common NHL in children under the age of 15 years.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a B-cell neoplasm?
questions.explanation: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma is a T-cell lymphoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common site for primary extranodal lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
The most common site for primary extranodal lymphoma is the stomach.

The term primary extranodal non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma (PE-NHL) refers to lymphomas that present with the disease at any organ or tissue other than lymph nodes or spleen.

Gastrointestinal lymphoma is the most common form of primary extranodal lymphoma, accounting for 30%–40% of cases. The most common site involved is the stomach (60%–75% of cases), followed by the small bowel, ileum, cecum, colon, and rectum.

Note: The most common site for extranodal non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) in AIDS is Primary CNS lymphoma.

questions.question: Which lymphoid neoplasm is associated with the human herpesvirus 8?
questions.explanation:
Primary effusion lymphoma is associated with human herpesvirus 8 (HHV-8).

It is a rare type of diffuse large B cell lymphoma with lymphomatous effusions in pleural, pericardial, and abdominal cavities, but no tumor mass.

Only one body cavity is typically involved. It is strongly associated with HHV8 and advanced HIV and usually EBV. It can also occurs in non-immunosuppressed patients, often the elderly.

questions.question:
Which of the following is correctly matched with its associated etiological factor?

1. Extranodal marginal cell lymphoma
a. HIV infection

2. Intestinal T-cell lymphomas
b. Breast implants

3. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma
c. H.pylori infection

4. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma
d. Gluten-sensitive enteropathy

5. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
e. Hepatitis C infection
questions.explanation:
The correctly matched neoplasms with their associated etiological factor:

1. Extranodal marginal cell lymphoma - H.pylori infection (c)

2. Intestinal T-cell lymphomas - Gluten-sensitive enteropathy (d)

3. Anaplastic large cell lymphoma - Breast implants (b)

4. Lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma - Hepatitis C infection (e)

5. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma - HIV infection (a)

questions.question: The peripheral smear finding of a patient with fever and lymphadenopathy is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The peripheral smear finding shows Downey cells or ballerina skirt cells. These are typically seen in infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV).

They are atypical lymphocytes with abundant basophilic cytoplasm containing clear vacuolations and prominent nucleoli. They become large as a result of antigen stimulation.

questions.question: Bruton tyrosine kinase is involved in which type of B-cell lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Bruton tyrosine kinase (BTK) is associated with B-cell chronic lymphocytic lymphoma/ small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL).

Tumour cells in CLL rely on signals generated by the B-cell receptor for growth and survival. These signals are transduced by a cascade of kinases that include BTK.

Note: BTK is also defective in patients with congenital X-linked agammaglobulinemia.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presents with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. On examination, he is found to have generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly. Investigations show a total WBC count of 1 lakh per microliter, with 80% lymphocytes. Peripheral smear is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation and peripheral smear findings point toward a diagnosis of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.

The peripheral smear shows smudge cells and increased lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm, round to slightly irregular nuclei containing clumped chromatin. This large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes is often described as a "convent-girl" appearance.

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) / Small lymphocytic lymphoma(SLL) is the most common leukemia among adults in the western world.

The differentiating point between CLL and SLL is that in CLL the absolute lymphocyte count is >5000 per mm³ and in SLL:<5000 per mm³.

It is usually asymptomatic at diagnosis but can present with easy fatigability, weight loss, and anorexia. Generalized lymphadenopathy and hepatosplenomegaly are usually seen.

• Total blood count:

• Total leukocyte count is highly variable; leukopenia is seen when the marrow is involved.

• Hypogammaglobulinemia is common and contributes to increased susceptibility to infections.

• 10% to 15% of patients develop hemolytic anemia or thrombocytopenia due to autoantibodies made by nonneoplastic B cells.

• Peripheral smear:

• Predominantly shows small lymphocytes with scant cytoplasm

• Smudge cells or basket cells or parachute cells - artifacts of the lymphocytes which are disrupted during the process of making smears.

• Contains a large number of monotonous, uniform-looking, mature lymphocytes, which is often described as a convent-girl appearance.

• Spherocytes (due to coexisting autoimmune hemolytic anemia) and nucleated RBCs (due to premature release of progenitors in face of severe anemia, marrow infiltration by the tumor, or both)

• Lymph node biopsy:

• Diffuse effacement composed of small lymphocytes admixed with variable numbers of larger activated lymphocytes that often gather in loose aggregates

• Referred to as proliferation centers, which contain mitotically active cells. Proliferation centers are pathognomonic for CLL / SLL.

The chromosomal defects:

• Deletion of 13q (commonest and has a good prognosis)

• Deletion of 11q

• Trisomy 12q

• Deletion of 17p (poor prognosis).

questions.question: The neoplastic cells in chronic lymphocytic leukemia/ small lymphocytic lymphoma originate from which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The cell of origin for chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL) is either a post-germinal center memory B cell or a naive B cell.

The cells of CLL show both unmutated Ig segments (those of naive B-cell origin) and somatic hypermutated Ig segments (those of post-germinal center memory B cell).

Tumours with unmutated Ig segments (those of naive B-cell origin) pursue a more aggressive course.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a genetic anomaly seen in patients with chronic lymphocytic lymphoma/ small lymphocytic lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Deletion of 17p is a genetic anomaly seen in chronic lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL)/ small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), not trisomy 17p.

The genetic anomalies seen in CLL/SLL are:

• Trisomy 12q

• Deletion of 13q

• Deletion of 17p (bad prognosis)

• Deletion of 11q (bad prognosis)

questions.question: A 70-year-old man presents with weakness and generalized lymphadenopathy. Lymph node biopsy shows difuse effacement with small lymphocytes and proliferation centers. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.answer: B. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/SLL).

Lymph node biopsy in CLL/SLL shows effacement of normal nodal architecture by sheets of predominantly small lymphocytes. They have round to slightly irregular nuclei, condensed chromatin, and scant cytoplasm.

Admixed are a variable number of larger activated lymphocytes that often gather in loose aggregates referred to as proliferation centers. These contain mitotically active cells. When present, proliferation centers are pathognomic for CLL/SLL (also known as a pseudofollicular pattern).

The image given below shows a lymph node biopsy of CLL in a low-power view. It shows loss of normal architecture and a large, pale-staining area in the center of the node (a proliferation center)

questions.question: A 58-year-old man with cervical lymphadenopathy is suspected to have chronic lymphocytic leukemia. What should be the absolute lymphocyte count/mm3 to diagnose this condition?
questions.explanation:
The diagnostic requirement for chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) is absolute lymphocyte count >5000 per cubic millimetre.

Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL) differ only in the degree of peripheral blood lymphocytosis:

• CLL - 5000/mm3

• SLL - <5000 cells/mm3

Note: CLL is the most common leukemia of adults in the western world.

questions.question: Flow cytometric analysis of four patients is given below. Who among the following is most likely suffering from chronic lymphocytic leukemia?
questions.explanation:
Small lymphocytes of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL)/ small lymphocytic leukemia (SLL) are CD23 and CD5 positive. Hence, the flow cytometry of patient 1 (CD23 and CD5 positive) correctly represents the phenotype of CLL.

The tumour cells also express the pan B-cell markers CD19 and CD20

Low-level expression of surface Ig (usually IgM or IgM and IgD) is also typical.

Given below is the explanation of how to interpret flow cytometry results:

Interpretation of results:

Quadrant 1- Cells marked in green: -VE for A antigen, +VE for B antigen

Quadrant 2- Cells marked in purple: -VE for both the antigens.

Quadrant 3- Cells marked in yellow: +VE for both the antigens

Quadrant 4- Cells marked in red: +VE for A antigen, -VE for B antigen

questions.question: A 73-year-old man came with complaints of malaise and low-grade fever. He had generalized lymphadenopathy. The histopathological examination of the lymph node is as shown below. These cells showed positivity for CD5, CD19, CD20, and CD23. Which of the following does not indicate a poor prognosis in this condition?
questions.answer: D. Absence of of NOTCH1 mutations
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and histopathological findings are suggestive of chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL). The presence of NOTCH1 mutation is associated with a poor prognosis in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

The histopathological image shows small, darker staining lymphocytes with prominent nucleoli which are typically seen in chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL).

Variables that correlate with a worse outcome include:

• The presence of deletions of 11q and 17p

• Lack of somatic hypermutation

• Expression of ZAP-70

• Presence of NOTCH 1 mutations

questions.question: A middle-aged woman presented with chronic fatigue and generalized lymphadenopathy. Investigations revealed overexpression of BCL2. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of follicular lymphoma. This condition is associated with overexpression of BCL2.

It usually presents in middle age as painless generalized lymphadenopathy. The involvement of extranodal sites is relatively uncommon. It has an indolent waxing and waning course.

In almost 50% of patients, this cancer gets transformed to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. The median survival rate is for 7-9 years.

The cell of origin for follicular lymphoma is germinal centre B cells. It shows (14;18) translocation.

Lymph node biopsy shows closely packed follicles. Centrocytes (small cells with the cleaved nucleus and scant cytoplasm) and centroblasts (large cells with open nuclear chromatin and multiple nucleoli) are seen.

Bone marrow is involved in 85% of the cases and shows para-trabecular lymphoid aggregates.

questions.question: Which of the following chromosomal abnormality is likely to be seen in patients with follicular lymphoma?
questions.explanation:
Follicular lymphoma shows t(14;18).

Its hallmark is a translocation that juxtaposes the IgH locus on chromosome 14 and the BCL2 locus on chromosome 18. It is seen in up to 90% of follicular lymphomas and leads to overexpression of BCL2.

BCL2 inhibits apoptosis and promotes the survival of follicular lymphoma cells.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with painless generalized lymphadenopathy and weakness. Lymph node biopsy shows the following picture. Which of the following is not true for this condition?
options: Possible transformation into diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
questions.explanation:
The lymph biopsy shows closely packed back-to-back follicles of variable areas and very less inter-follicular area. It is suggestive of follicular lymphoma.

Follicular lymphoma usually follows an indolent waxing and waning course, not an aggressive course.

Lymph node (LN) biopsy shows a nodular pattern with centrocytes and centroblasts as shown below.

Immunophenotyping:

• The cell of origin is germinal-center B cell, so it is positive for CD19, CD20, CD10, BCL6, and surface Ig.

• BCL2 expression is positive in over 90% of cases.

Histologic transformation to diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) occurs in 30 to 50% of cases.

Note: In contrast to follicular lymphoma, DLBCL has an aggressive course, shows a diffuse pattern of growth in lymph node biopsy and shows BCL-6 positivity.

questions.question: A patient with longstanding cervical lymphadenopathy was diagnosed with mantle cell lymphoma. What is the cell of origin for this condition?
questions.explanation:
Mantle-cell lymphoma arises from the mantle-zone B cells which are naive B cells as they lack somatic hypermutation IgH gene.

Mantle-cell lymphomas have an (11;14) translocation involving the IgH locus on chromosome 14 and overexpression of cyclin D1.

It is CD5 positive and CD23 negative.

Comparison between mantle-cell lymphoma and chronic lymphocytic leukemia/ small lymphocytic lymphoma (CLL/ SLL):
