Option C: Granulosa cell tumor usually presents as a slow-growing and non-functioning testicular mass. Gynecomastia is rare. They usualy secrete estrogen.

questions.question: What is the most common testicular neoplasms in men older than 60 years?
questions.explanation:
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is the most common testicular neoplasm in men older than 60 years.

The most common types of testicular lymphomas in decreasing order of frequecy:

• Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma

• Burkitt lymphoma

• Epstein–Barr virus - positive extranodal NK/T cell lymphoma.

Testicular lymphomas are aggressive tumors with a poor prognosis. They have a higher propensity for CNS involvement.

questions.question: In patients with testicular tumors, what lymph nodes are primarily involved?
questions.explanation:
Retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes are the first to be involved in the lymphatic spread of testicular tumors.

Testicular tumors have a characteristic mode of spread:

• Lymphatic spread is common to all forms of testicular tumors. Initially, it spreads to retroperitoneal para-aortic nodes, then spreads to the mediastinal and supraclavicular nodes.

• Hematogenous spread is primarily to the lungs, but the liver, brain, and bones may also be involved.

questions.question: Laboratory testing of a 30-year-old man diagnosed with a testicular mass showed increased levels of alpha-fetoprotein. All of the following can be included in the differential, except:
questions.explanation:
Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) level is raised in all the above conditions except pure choriocarcinoma and pure seminoma.

Choriocarcinomas have elevated levels of HCG, which can be readily demonstrated in the cytoplasm of syncytiotrophoblastic cells.

AFP is a marker of hepatocellular cancer and non-seminomatous germ cell tumors of testes, mainly yolk sac tumors.

questions.question: Which tumor responds best to radiation therapy?
questions.explanation:
Seminomas are extremely radiosensitive tumors.

The counterpart of seminoma, which arises in the ovary, is dysgerminoma.

questions.question: What is the most common malignant paratesticular tumor in children?
questions.explanation:
The most common malignant paratesticular tumor in children is rhabdomyosarcoma.

The paratesticular region is an extratesticular anatomical area, which includes the contents:

• Spermatic cord,

• Testicular tunics,

• Epididymis

• Vestigial remnants, such as the appendices epididymis and testis.

The most common malignant paratesticular tumor in adults is liposarcoma.

The most common benign paratesticular tumor is an adenomatoid tumor.

The most common paratesticular mesenchymal tumor is a lipoma.

questions.question: Which of the following is not used as a tumor marker for germ cell testicular tumors?
questions.explanation:
Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is not used as a tumor marker for germ-cell testicular tumors. It is an oncofetal antigen used as a tumor marker in adenocarcinoma of the colon, pancreas, lung, breast, and ovary.

Markers of germ cell testicular tumors include alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), human chorionic gonadotropin, placental alkaline phosphatase, placental lactogen, and lactate dehydrogenase (LDH).

questions.question: A 61-year-old male patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia is planned for transurethral resection of the prostate. Which of the following is removed during the procedure?
questions.explanation:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia originates almost exclusively in the transitional zone, hence it is surgically removed.

Nodular hyperplasia or benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is the most common benign prostatic disease in men above 50 years. It arises from the inner aspect of the prostate gland, i.e., the transitional zone. It is characterized by benign, hyperplastic proliferation of prostatic stroma and epithelial elements, which is driven by dihydrotestosterone. This growth progressively compresses the urethra resulting in urinary obstructive symptoms.

The normal prostate contains several distinct regions, including a central zone (CZ), peripheral zone (PZ), transitional zone (TZ), and periurethral zone, as shown in the image below.

Note: Most carcinomas arise from the peripheral zone and maybe palpable during the digital examination of the rectum.

questions.question: An elderly man presenting with the features of urinary retention was thoroughly investigated and diagnosed with prostate carcinoma. All of the following statements about the Gleason system used for prognosis/survival of the patient are true except:
options: Grade group 1 represents the most well-differentiated tumors.
Tumors with Gleason scores 8 to 10 tend to be advanced cancers.
Gleason system correlates with pathologic stage and prognosis.
Gleason Score is reported from 1 to 10.
questions.answer: D. Gleason Score is reported from 1 to 10.
questions.explanation:
The Gleason score is currently reported from 6-10.

WHO/ISUP modified Gleason score is the histopathological grading system, which corresponds with the clinical behavior of prostate cancer. It is one of the key methods used in confirmation of the diagnosis, prognostication, and staging of prostate cancer (adenocarcinoma).

The Gleason grading system is primarily based on analyzing the architecture of the tumor cells in the biopsy specimens obtained. The architecture, i.e., the Gleason Patterns are classified as:

• Pattern 3: Well-formed glands

• Pattern 4: Poorly formed/Fused/Cribriform glands/Glomeruloid glands

• Pattern 5: Sheets of the tumor, individual cells, cords, and solid nests of cells, Comedo necrosis

• Pattern 1 and 2 are no longer defined

Most tumor specimens contain more than one pattern. Therefore, a numeric grade is assigned to both the primary pattern and the next most frequent secondary pattern. The sum of the numeric grades provides the Gleason score.

• Scores 2–5 are no longer assigned.

• Scores of 6 - 7 are potentially treatable cancers

• Scores 8 - 10 are advanced cancers that are less likely to be cured.

Based on the gleason score, they are classified into the following grade groups:

• Grade group 1: score<=6

• Grade group 2: 3+4=7

• Grade group 3: 4+3=7

• Grade group 4: score 8

• Grade group 5: scores 9-10

questions.question: A 68-year-old man presented with hesitancy, incomplete voiding, and pelvic pain. On a digital rectal examination, an irregularly enlarged prostate with a nodular surface was felt. Transrectal biopsy revealed poorly formed glands arranged in a cribriform pattern. According to the modified Gleason score, how would you classify the pattern seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of prostate cancer and all cribriform patterns are now defined as Gleason pattern 4 according to the 2014 WHO/ISUP grading consensus conference.

The below image of prostate cancer with Gleason pattern 4 shows cribriform pattern

Highlights of 2014 WHO/ISUP modified Gleason score:

1) Gleason Pattern:

• Pattern 3- Well formed glands

• Pattern 4- Poorly formed/Fused/Cribriform glands/Glomeruloid glands

• Pattern 5- Sheets of the tumor, individual cells, cords and solid nests of cells, Comedo necrosis

• Pattern 1 and 2 are no longer defined

2) Gleason Score:

The current Gleason score ranges from 6–10. Scores 2–5 are no longer assigned.

3) Grade group:

• Grade group 1: score ≤6

• Grade group 2: 3+4=7

• Grade group 3: 4+3=7

• Grade group 4: score 8

• Grade group 5: scores 9–10

questions.question: What is the normal upper limit of prostate-specific antigen value for a 75-year-old man?
questions.explanation:
The upper-age-specific reference value of serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) in men of age 70–79 is 6.5 ng/mL.

PSA is a product of prostatic epithelium secreted in the semen. Measurement of serum PSA levels is widely used to assist the diagnosis, prognosis, and management of prostate cancer. Older men have a higher serum PSA level than younger men, so the normal range varies with age.

Age
Upper age-specific PSA(ng/mL)

40–49 yrs
2.5

50–59 yrs
3.5

60–69 yrs
4.5

70–79 yrs
6.5

The serum PSA levels as a screening test for prostatic cancer has poor sensitivity and specificity. This is because various other factors such as trauma, infections, BPH, instrumentation/digital exam of the prostate, and ejaculation can increase serum PSA levels. A value of ≥4 ng/mL usually warrants serial testing or further evaluation.

In an effort to improve the sensitivity and specificity of serum PSA levels, many novel indices are used:

• Age-specific PSA reference ranges

• PSA velocity: Rate of change of PSA values with time. It is considered that PSA velocity of 0.75 ng/mL per year measured at least 3 times over a period of 1.5 to 2 yrs is significant to diagnose Prostate cancer.

• PSA density: Serum PSA/volume of the prostate gland

• The ratio of free to bound serum PSA

questions.question: A 68-year-old patient was diagnosed with prostate cancer. Hematogenous spread of this cancer would occur predominantly to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Hematogenous spread of carcinoma prostrate occurs predominantly to the bones and are typically osteoblastic.

The commonly involved bones in decreasing order of frequency:

• Lumbar spine

• Proximal femur

• Pelvis

• Thoracic spine

• Ribs

questions.question: Which of the following lesions does not arise from the terminal duct lobular unit of the breast?
questions.explanation:
Periductal mastitis arises from the large lactiferous ducts.

It is also known as squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts, recurrent subareolar abscess, or Zuska disease.

The terminal duct lobular unit (TDLU) is the basic functional and histopathological unit of the breast. Successive branching of large ducts eventually leads to the TDLU. Sclerosing adenosis, blue dome cyst, and carcinoma breast arise from the TDLU.

questions.question:
Which of the following lesions arise from the large ducts of the breast?

1. Duct ectasia

2. Fibroadenoma

3. Paget's disease

4. Atypical hyperplasia

5. Phyllodes tumor
questions.explanation:
Duct ectasia and Paget's disease arise from the large ducts of the breast.

Normal anatomy of the breast includes ducts, lobules, and stroma. Successive branching of the large ducts eventually leads to the terminal duct lobular unit.

Atypical hyperplasia arises from the terminal ducts and lobules, whereas, fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumors arise from the intralobular stroma.

questions.question: A 28-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast. On examination, you notice her nipple is erythematous and tender with a purulent exudate. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute mastitis. The most common cause of acute mastitis is Staphylococcus aureus.

Acute bacterial mastitis typically occurs during the 1st month of breastfeeding (lactational breast abscess). It is caused by a local bacterial infection when the breast is most vulnerable due to cracks and fissures in the nipples.

Staphylococcal acute mastitis typically results in localized abscesses.

Option A: Breast abscess caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa is uncommon, only a few cases have been documented in immunocompromised patients.

Options B and C: Streptococcal infections tend to spread throughout the breast in the form of cellulitis.

questions.question: Which of the following diseases is most strongly associated with a history of smoking?
questions.explanation:
Periductal mastitis is strongly associated with a history of smoking. More than 90% of the affected individuals are smokers.

Periductal mastitis is also called recurrent subareolar abscess or squamous metaplasia of lactiferous ducts or Zuska disease. In this condition, a relative deficiency of vitamin A associated with smoking or toxic substances in tobacco smoke alters the differentiation of the ductal epithelium.

Histologically, there is keratinizing squamous metaplasia of the nipple ducts. Keratin shed from these cells is trapped and plugs (keratin plug) the ductal system, causing dilation and eventually rupture of the duct. This results in keratin spillage into the surrounding periductal tissue forming a chronic granulomatous inflammatory response.

It presents with a painful erythematous subareolar mass that clinically mimics bacterial abscess. It has a high recurrence rate.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a painless palpable lump in her left breast. She had sustained a traumatic blow to her left breast 1 month back. Mammography showed a radiolucent cystic lesion with rimmed calcification. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The typical history of a breast lump following trauma and mammography findings of a radiolucent cystic lesion with rimmed calcification suggests a diagnosis of fat necrosis.

About half the affected women with fat necrosis of the breast have a history of breast trauma or previous surgery. It can present as a painless palpable mass, skin thickening or retraction, or mammographic densities or calcifications.

Histologically, necrotic adipose tissue with foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and chronic inflammatory cells are seen often with hemosiderin deposits, fibrosis, and calcification.

The following image shows an area of fat necrosis within breast tissue.

Note: Calcifications are seen on mammography in the following conditions -

• Apo­crine cysts

• Hyalinized fibroadenomas

• Sclerosing adenosis

• Duct ectasia

• Breast carcinoma- shows irregular densities and small, numerous, clustered calcification (microcalcifications).

questions.question: Which of the following is a proliferative breast lesion?
questions.explanation:
Papillomas are classified under proliferative breast diseases without atypia.

Proliferative breast lesions without atypia are not clonal and usually have no genetic changes. Thus they are predictors of risk but are not true precursors of carcinoma.

Benign epithelial lesions are classified into three groups, according to the subsequent risk of developing breast cancer. These are:

• Non-proliferative breast changes

• Proliferative breast disease without atypia

• Atypical hyperplasia

Note: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) has recently been classified as a benign lesion with associated risk for developing carcinoma in the future but not as a malignancy capable of metastases.

questions.question: All of the following lesions are proliferative breast lesions without atypia except:
questions.explanation:
Duct ectasia is a non-proliferative breast change.

Radial scar, sclerosing adenosis, and florid hyperplasia belong to proliferative breast lesions without atypia.

Proliferative breast lesions without atypia are not clonal and are not commonly found to have genetic changes. Thus they are predictors of risk but unlikely to be true precursors of carcinoma.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical presentation seen in patients with duct papilloma?
questions.explanation:
The most common clinical presentation seen in patients with duct papilloma is nipple discharge. More than 80% of large duct papillomas produce a nipple discharge.

Papillomas grow within a dilated duct and are composed of multiple branching fibrovascular cores. It can be serous or bloody.

• Serous discharge - due to intermittent blockage and release of normal breast secretions or irritation of the duct by the papilloma

• Bloody discharge - due to torsion of the stalk, causing infarction

questions.question: A young man presents to your clinic with the following finding. Which of the following is not associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The image given depicts gynecomastia. Seminoma is not a cause of this condition.

Gynecomastia occurs due to increased estrogenic action. The most common causes of gynecomastia include:

• Cirrhosis of the liver

• Alcohol

• Marijuana, heroin

• Antiretroviral therapy

• Anabolic steroids

• Klinefelter syndrome (XXY karyotype)

• Functioning testicular neoplasms such as Leydig cell or Sertoli cell tumors

Microscopically, there is an increase in the dense collagenous connective tissue. It is associated with epithelial hyperplasia of the duct lining with characteristic tapering micro-papillae. Lobule formation is almost never observed.

questions.question: A biopsy was performed on a female patient who presented with a lump in her right breast. Presence of which of the following findings is not associated with an increased risk of cancer?
questions.explanation:
Apocrine change does not increase the risk of cancer as it is a non-proliferative change.

Moderate or florid hyperplasia, fibroadenoma with complex features, and sclerosing adenosis are classified under proliferative disease without atypia with a 1.5- to 2-fold increased risk of carcinoma.

Both breasts are at increased risk, although the risk to the ipsilateral breast may be slightly higher.

questions.question: While undergoing a routine mammogram, a 45-year-old woman was found to have clusters of microcalcification in her right breast. A needle biopsy was done and revealed the following. Which of the following markers can be used to rule out invasive disease?
questions.explanation:
The given image is suggestive of the comedo type of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS). Myoepithelial cell markers like p63 can differentiate DCIS from invasive carcinoma.

DCIS is a malignant clonal proliferation of epithelial cells limited to ducts and lobules by the intact basement membrane. It is rarely palpable and is almost always detected by mammography.

Myoepithelial cells (basal cell layer) are preserved in involved ducts or lobules in DCIS. Hence the myoepithelial cell markers like p63, basal cytokeratin (CK 5/6), calponin will be positive in DCIS whereas it will be absent in infiltrating ductal carcinoma. However, myoepithelial markers may be diminished in high-grade DCIS compared to surrounding normal ducts or lobules.

Once the tumor cells penetrate through the basement membrane and grow within the stroma, they are considered to be invasive carcinoma.

Note: Lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS) has recently been classified as a benign lesion with associated risk for developing carcinoma in the future but not as a malignancy capable of metastases.

questions.question: A 55-year-old woman presents with persistent soreness and itching in her right nipple. On examination, the following finding is noted. What would be the next best step in her management?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario showing a red eczematous rash over the areola of the breast is suggestive of Paget's disease of the nipple. The next best step in management is biopsy of the nipple.

Paget's disease can be mistaken for eczema, and hence, biopsy of the nipple should be the initial management of choice. Paget cells are readily detected by nipple biopsy.

questions.question: Histopathological examination of a middle-aged woman who presented with redness and itching over the nipple of her left breast is given below. Which of the following statements is incorrect about her condition?
options: Prognosis depends on the underlying carcinoma
The cells show overexpression of HER2
questions.answer: A. The cells are ER positive
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image showing Paget's cells (malignant cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and pleomorphic nuclei) are suggestive of Paget's disease of the nipple. These cells are ER-negative.

Paget's disease of the nipple is a rare form of ductal carcinoma in-situ (DCIS). The characteristic Paget's cells are scattered individually throughout the squamous epithelium. They do not breach the basement membrane but extend via the lactiferous sinuses into the nipple skin.

The following images show Paget's cells that do not breach the basement membrane.

It presents as a unilateral erythematous eruption with a scale crust. A palpable mass is seen in about half the patients with this disease.

The underlying carcinomas are usually poorly differentiated, ER-negative, and overexpress HER2. The prognosis of Paget's disease depends on the features of the underlying carcinoma.

Paget's disease may mimic the following conditions:

• Eczema (clinical appearance) - can be differentiated by the presence of malignant cells on biopsy

• Superficial spreading melanoma (histological appearance) - Paget's cells are PAS-positive and diastase resistant unlike melanoma cells

Note: Paget's disease of the bone is a distinct condition that results in abnormal bone metabolism due to osteoclastic overactivity.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a risk factor for breast cancer?
questions.explanation:
Early full-term pregnancy (younger than 20 years) is protective against breast cancer. It halves the risk of developing breast cancer compared to that of nulliparous women.

Women with very dense breasts on mammography have a four- to six-fold higher risk of both ER-positive and ER-negative breast cancer compared to women with low density.

Obese women under the age of 40 years have a decreased risk as a result of anovulatory cycles and lower progesterone levels. In contrast, postmenopausal obese women are at an increased risk, which is attributed to the synthesis of estrogens in fat depots.

Early menarche, late menopause, and nulliparity are risk factors of breast cancer due to hyperestrogenemia. Exercise and breastfeeding are protective against breast cancer.

questions.question: What is the most common site of carcinoma in the breast?
questions.explanation:
The upper outer quadrant is the most common site of carcinoma in the breast.

Approximately 50% of carcinomas are located in the upper outer quadrant, 10% in each of the remaining quadrants, and about 20% in the central or subareolar region.

A palpable mass is the most common clinical sign of invasive breast carcinoma.

Triple assessment is recommended for the diagnosis of any palpable breast lump. It includes:

• Clinical examination

• Radiological assessment (mammography/USG)

• Pathological assessment (FNAC/biopsy)

Techniques of palpation for breast examination are:

1. Vertical strip/lines pattern

2. Circular pattern

3. Wedges or radial spokes pattern

questions.question: On which of the following chromosomes is the BRCA2 gene located?
questions.explanation:
BRCA2 gene is located on the long arm of chromosome 13 (13q12.3).

Mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 are responsible for 80 to 90% of single gene familial breast cancers and about 3% of all breast cancers.

ER-positive, HER2-negative cancers (luminal type) is the most common subtype of breast cancer in individuals who inherit germline mutations in BRCA2. This gene is associated more frequently with male breast cancer.

Single gene mutations associated with familial breast cancer can be categorized into:

• High penetrance germline mutations (>4 fold increased risk) - BRCA1, BRCA2, TP53, PTEN, STK11, CDH I, PALPB2

• Moderate penetrance germline mutations (2-4 fold increased risk) - ATM, CHEK2

questions.question: Immunohistochemical testing was performed on a biopsy sample taken from a patient with breast cancer. It revealed lack of expression of ER, PR, and HER2. Which of the following genes is most commonly mutated in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of triple-negative breast cancer (ER-negative, PR-negative, and HER2-negative). TP53 is the most commonly mutated gene in triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC).

Common gene mutations in the 3 major molecular types of invasive breast carcinoma are:

Molecular Subtype
Common gene mutations

Luminal (ER+/HER2-)

Luminal A: PIK3CA (more common), TP53

Luminal B: PIK3CA (more common), TP53

HER2 Positive (HER 2+)
TP53 (more common), PIK3CA

TNBC (ER-/ HER2-)
TP53 (more common), PIK3CA

questions.question: A 44-year-old woman has been diagnosed with breast carcinoma. Immunohistochemistry staining of a tissue biopsy specimen of this patient is given below. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?
options: It is not associated with tP53 mutations
questions.explanation:
The given immunohistochemistry (IHC) staining shows positive ER, PR (brown nucleus), and negative Her-2 (no membrane-bound brown stain) expression, which is suggestive of luminal A molecular subtype. It shows a poor response to paclitaxel.

Hormone receptors (ER, PR) are present in the nucleus. Therefore ER, PR–positive breast cancer cells will stain dark in the nucleus on IHC. Her-2 receptors are membrane-bound receptors, and hence, cells having these receptors are darkly stained on the membranes.

Luminal A type is more commonly associated with BRCA2 mutations.

Hormone receptor-positive tumors are responsive to hormonal chemotherapeutic agents like tamoxifen and aromatase inhibitors. In Her-2 negative cases, trastuzumab is not effective as it is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody directed against HER-2.

The following image shows ER/ PR/ Her-2 positivity:

Note: At least 10% of luminal type A breast cancers express tp53 mutations. tP53 mutations are associated with triple-negative tumors as well.

questions.question: Immunohistochemistry test of a breast cancer patient was reported negative for ER and HER2. This molecular subtype includes all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
Carcinomas with immunohistochemistry ER and HER2/ν negative are all of the above except mucinous carcinomas. Mucinous carcinomas are usually ER-positive and HER2/neu negative (luminal A type)

ER-negative, HER2-negative (triple-negative) molecular subtype commonly includes the following histological subtypes:

• Medullary

• Adenoid cystic

• Secretory

• Metaplastic

• Spindle cell

• Squamous

• Matrix-producing

questions.question: Patients with all of the following conditions have ER-positive and HER2-negative tumors except:
questions.explanation:
ER-positive, HER2-negative status on immunohistochemistry is suggestive of the luminal type of breast carcinoma, which does not include secretory carcinoma.

The ER-positive, HER2-negative molecular subtype (luminal type) commonly includes the following histological subtypes:

• Well and poorly differentiated lobular carcinoma

• Tubular carcinoma

• Mucinous carcinoma

• Papillary carcinoma

Secretory carcinomas are usually ER-negative and Her2/neu negative (basal type).

questions.question: Which of the following breast cancers most commonly presents as an occult primary carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Lobular carcinoma is the most common type of breast carcinoma to present as an occult primary carcinoma.

Lobular carcinoma of the breast is seen bilaterally and with multicentricity. Loss of E-cadherin is the hallmark of lobular carcinoma. They also have characteristic patterns of metastatic spread, often involving the peritoneum and retroperitoneum, leptomeninges (carcinomatous meningitis), gastrointestinal tract, ovaries, and uterus.

The histological hallmark of lobular carcinoma is the presence of discohesive infiltrating tumor cells, often arranged in a single Indian file pattern or in loose clusters or sheets.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of lobular breast carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
There is no or very slight desmoplastic response seen in lobular carcinomas.

Desmoplasia refers to collagenous stromal proliferation induced by tumor cells which is essential for tumor growth and spread. It results in hard and stony tumors. However, this is not seen in lobular carcinoma. This is likely due to the loss of expression of CDH1, the gene that encodes e-cadherin (normally maintains intercellular adhesiveness). This also results in disaggregation of cells.

Lobular carcinomas are often bilateral and multicentric. It shows characteristic metastatic spread, often involving:

• Peritoneum and retro­ peritoneum

• Leptomeninges (carcinomatous meningitis)

• Gastrointestinal tract

• Ovaries

• Uterus

Histopathological image of invasive lobular carcinoma of breast showing discohesive cells with few signet ring cells.

Note: Individuals with heterozygous germline mutations in CDH1 (loss of E-cadherin) also have a greatly increased risk of gastric signet-ring cell carcinoma.

questions.question: A 53-year-old woman with breast cancer is found to have TNM staging of T4dN0M0. Which of the following statements is true regarding her condition?
options: There is loss of e-cadherin expression
It has a relatively favorable prognosis
There is obstruction of dermal lymphatics by neoplastic cells
History of trauma to the breast is usually present
questions.answer: C. There is obstruction of dermal lymphatics by neoplastic cells
questions.explanation:
T4d in the TNM staging of carcinoma breast points toward a diagnosis of inflammatory breast carcinoma. It shows extensive invasion and proliferation of tumor cells within the dermal lymphatics leading to obstruction.

Inflammatory breast cancer is the most aggressive subtype of breast cancer. The hallmark of this condition is the overexpression of e-cadherin. This results in increased tumor cohesion and the formation of tumoral clumps which can result in emboli. It has a particularly poor prognosis.

These tumors are usually of high grade but do not belong to any particular molecular subtype. More than half (60%) are ER-negative and 40% to 50% overexpress HER2. There is no association with trauma.

Due to lymphatic obstruction, it results in brawny induration, erythema with a raised edge, and edema called peau d’orange appearance. This may mimic non-neoplastic inflammatory lesions like mastitis. A breast lump may or may not be present.

The following image shows a peau d’orange appearance of the right breast.

questions.question: Immunohistochemistry for HER2 protein expression is performed in 3 patients with breast carcinoma, with the following results. Which of the following patients should be subjected to fluorescence in-situ hybridization?
questions.explanation:
The immunohistochemistry (IHC) pattern of patient C reveals moderately strong circumferential staining (faint brown color) in >10 % of cells, which is classified as 2+ or equivocal staining. Hence, she should be subjected to fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm HER2-positive gene amplification status.

The following are classified as HER2-positive tumors:

• Tumors that show 3+ staining on IHC (here FISH is not needed).

• Tumors with 2+ staining on IHC, followed by HER2-gene amplification confirmed by FISH

Once HER2-positive status is confirmed, targeted therapy against HER2 can be initiated with trastuzumab or lapatinib.

questions.question: A middle-aged woman is diagnosed with low-grade mucinous carcinoma of the breast. IHC showed HER2 overexpression and a low Ki67 index. Which of the following would be considered as a poor prognostic factor?
questions.explanation:
HER2 overexpression in a patient with carcinoma breast is associated with poor survival.

The main importance of HER2 status is as a predictor of response to agents that target this receptor.

Prognostic and predictive factors in breast carcinoma:

Good prognosis
Bad prognosis

Extent and spread

In situ carcinoma

Invasive carcinoma

Locally advanced disease

Lymphovascular invasion

Distant metastasis

Size
Size <1 cm
Size >2 cm

Histological subtype

Tubular carcinoma

Mucinous carcinoma

Lobular carcinoma

Papillary carcinoma

Adenoid cystic carcinoma

Metaplastic carcinoma

Micropapillary carcinoma

Histologic grade
Low grade
High grade

Molecular subtype
Luminal A subtype
Her2-enriched and basal subtype

Proliferation rate (Ki67 index & mitotic counts)
Low proliferation rate
High proliferation rate

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman on cyclosporin-A following renal transplantation developed multiple bilateral breast lumps that regressed after cessation of treatment. Her biopsy finding is shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing duct proliferation are suggestive of fibroadenomas. The use of cyclosporin-A after transplantation is associated with fibroadenomas that regress after cessation of the treatment.

Fibroadenomas are the most common benign tumor of the female breast. Nearly 2/3 cases are associated with mutations in the MED12 gene.

They are frequently multiple and bilateral and usually occur in women <30 years of age. They are solid, well-defined, highly mobile masses (also known as breast mice).

Fibroadenomas can be classified into 2 types:

• Without complex features - classified as a non-proliferative condition

• With complex features -

• Associated with cysts > 0.3 cm, sclerosing adenosis, epithelial calcifications, or papillary apocrine change

• Classified as proliferative changes without atypia

questions.question: A 58-year-old woman presented with a large, rapidly growing painless breast lump. On examination, a smooth, multinodular breast lump was noticed. Microscopic examination of the core biopsy sample is shown below. Which of the following is an incorrect statement regarding this condition?
options: Stromal cellularity is increased next to the epithelium
Absence of epithelial elements suggests malignancy
Both epithelial and stromal components can metastasize
questions.answer: D. Both epithelial and stromal components can metastasize
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image are suggestive of phyllodes tumor. Here, only the stromal component is involved in metastasis.

Phyllodes tumor is a fibroepithelial tumor arising from the intralobular stroma. It presents as a smooth, rapidly growing, multinodular, painless breast lump that is usually palpable. It most commonly presents in the 6th decade of life and is associated with:

• Gain in chromosome 1q

• HOXB13 overexpression

Phyllodes tumors show stromal cellularity next to the epithelium (subepithelial or periepithelial regions). This feature helps to differentiate it from intracanalicular fibroadenoma.

The prognosis of phyllodes tumors depends on their histological grade. Most phyllodes tumors are low grade, with limited stromal cellularity. They recur only occasionally and do not metastasize.

The features of malignant (intermediate and high grade) phyllodes tumors are:

• Markedly increased stromal cellularity

• Stromal overgrowth - absence of epithelial elements

• Nuclear atypia

• Increased mitosis (>10/ 10 hpf)

• Highly recurrent

Regardless of the grade, lymphatic spread is rare in phyllodes tumors. Hence, axillary lymph node dissection is contraindicated.

questions.question: What is the most common stromal malignancy in the breast?
questions.explanation:
Angiosarcoma is the most common stromal malignancy in the breast.

It arises in the interlobular stroma and accounts for < 0.05% of breast malig­nancies. It is a high-grade tumor with a poor prognosis. It can either be sporadic or occur in association with radiation therapy. The mean age of affected individuals is 35 years.

questions.question: BRCA-2 mutation does not predispose to the development of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
BRCA-2 mutation does not predispose to the development of renal cell carcinoma.

BRCA-2 mutation predisposes to the development of prostate and pancreatic cancer. It is also associated with an increased risk of male breast cancer.

questions.question:
A 50-year-old man who developed myocardial infarction 3 days ago now presents with jaundice. Lab investigations done are given below. Which region of the liver lobule is most likely affected here?

Bilirubin: 3 mg/dL

ALT: 1250 IU/L

AST: 1050 IU/L
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute hepatocellular injury due to ischemia. Zone 3 (centrilobular zone) of the liver is most susceptible for ischemia because this zone is the farthest from the blood supply.

On the basis of blood flow, liver parenchyma can be divided into three zones. Zone 1 is closest to the blood supply and zone 3 is the farthest. They are:

• Zone 1 - Periportal (around portal triad)

• Zone 2 - Midzonal parenchyma

• Zone 3 - Centrilobular (around hepatic vein)

A schematic diagram showing the hepatic lobule indicating the direction of blood flow and the zones of decreasing oxygenation is given below.

Note: Zone most susceptible to toxin damage is zone 1.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are least likely to develop centrilobular necrosis of liver?
questions.explanation:
Centrilobular necrosis is not seen in yellow fever. In yellow fever, swelling and necrosis of hepatocytes are seen in the midzone of the liver lobule.

Conditions causing tissue injury in the different zones of liver:

• Centrilobular (Zone 3)

• Chronic venous congestion (cardiac failure)

• Acetaminophen toxicity

• Budd Chiari syndrome

• Ischemia

• Alcoholic hepatitis

• Midzonal (Zone 2)

• Yellow fever

• Periportal (Zone 1)

• Viral hepatitis

A schematic diagram showing the hepatic lobule indicating the direction of blood flow and the zones of decreasing oxygenation is given below.

questions.question: A chronic alcoholic developed cirrhosis of the liver. Which is the principal cell type involved in scar deposition in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The principal cell type involved in scar deposition in cirrhosis of the liver is the hepatic stellate cell or Ito cell.

Hepatic stellate cells deposit primarily type I and type III collagen in the lobule and cause fibrosis. In their quiescent form, these cells store lipids and vitamin A.

questions.question: Histopathological examination of liver biopsy reveals steatosis. Which of the following conditions is least likely to cause this change?
questions.explanation:
Steatosis or fatty change of liver is not seen in hepatitis B infections.

Steatosis is the abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within a cell due to impaired lipid metabolism. In the liver, pathological steatosis is defined as fatty change involving >5% of hepatocytes. In the histologic sections, they appear as empty vacuoles within the hepatocyte cytoplasm.

Hepatitis C genotype 3 is reported to cause periportal steatosis. It is due to its association with metabolic syndrome and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

In Wilson's disease, there is focal hepatocyte necrosis and steatosis due to toxic injury by the excess copper.

In protein malnutrition, fatty liver results from the reduced synthesis of the carrier protein component of lipoproteins.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions causes macrovesicular steatosis of liver?
questions.explanation:
Macrovesicular fatty liver (steatosis) is seen in obesity.

Macrovesicular steatosis is characterized by a single, large vacuole of fat that fills up the hepatocyte and displaces the nucleus to the periphery. Causes include:

• Late alcoholic liver disease

• Obesity

• Protein-energy malnutrition

• Non-alcohlic steatohepatitis (NASH)

• Chronic hepatitis C

Microvesicular steatosis is characterized by small intracytoplasmic fat vacuoles, which accumulate in the cell. Causes include:

• Acute fatty liver of pregnancy

• Reye syndrome

• Early alcoholic liver disease

• Drugs and toxins

The image given below shows macrovesicular and microvesicular steatosis of liver:

questions.question: A 4-year-old girl, with a history of URTI, now presents with severe vomiting, lethargy, and altered mental status. You are suspecting Reye's syndrome. Which of the following liver biopsy findings will confirm your diagnosis?
options: Portal tract edema and perisinusoidal fibrosis
Cirrhosis and periportal eosinophilic inclusion bodies
questions.explanation:
The liver biopsy in Reye's syndrome will show marked microvesicular steatosis.

Reye's syndrome is an acute illness, encountered exclusively in children <15 years. Its onset usually follows upper respiratory tract infections. The actual cause is unknown, although viral agents and salicylates (aspirin) have been implicated.

Pathogenesis behind this condition is generalized mitochondrial dysfunction with structural and functional alterations of mitochondria in the liver, brain, and muscle. Liver is enlarged but jaundice is absent or minimum. It is characterized by clinical features such as:

• Vomiting

• Signs of progressive CNS damage

• Signs of hepatic injury

• Hypoglycemia

Extensive accumulation of fat droplets within hepatocytes (microvesicular steatosis) can be seen in histopathology. Extra-hepatic changes include fatty changes of renal tubular cells, cerebral edema, and neuronal degeneration of the brain.

The image given below shows microvesicular steatosis of liver.

Note: Aspirin is generally contraindicated in children, except in the treatment of Kawasaki disease and juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

questions.question: Histopathological examination of liver biopsy in a patient with jaundice shows the following finding. Which of the following conditions is least likely in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The marked structure in the image is Mallory hyaline body which is not seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis. In this condition, onion skin fibrosis is seen.

Mallory hyaline bodies (Mallory–Denk bodies) are usually present as clumped, amorphous, eosinophilic material in ballooned hepatocytes. They are made up of cytokeratin 8 and cytokeratin 18. They have a twisted rope-like appearance. On trichrome stain, they appear green/dark brown. They are seen in:

• Alcoholic liver disease

• Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

• Wilson's disease

• Hepatocellular carcinoma

• Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

• Primary biliary cholangitis (formerly called primary biliary cirrhosis)

• Indian childhood cirrhosis

The image given below shows Mallory hyaline bodies.

questions.question: Which of the following causes Laennec cirrhosis?
questions.explanation:
Laennec cirrhosis is the classic micronodular cirrhosis seen in end-stage alcoholic liver disease.

There are three distinctive, overlapping forms of alcoholic liver injury:

• Hepatic steatosis (fatty liver)

• Fatty change - completely reversible if there is abstention from further intake of alcohol

• Starts in centrilobular area

• Alcoholic (steato) hepatitis

• Ballooning degeneration and necrosis

• Mallory–Denk bodies

• Neutrophilic reaction

• Alcoholic steatofibrosis

• Perisinusoidal fibrosis and sclerosis of the central vein

• Diffuse nodularity of liver surface

• Micronodular/ Laennec cirrhosis

• Irreversible

questions.question: Which of the following histopathological findings will be seen in patients with chronic alcoholism?
questions.explanation:
Chicken-wire fence pattern of fibrosis is seen in the liver biopsy of patients with alcoholic steatohepatitis. This pattern is due to perisinusoidal fibrosis encircling small clusters of hepatocytes.

Trichrome staining of liver biopsy specimen showing perisinusoidal fibrosis (stained blue) in characteristic chicken-wire fence pattern is given below.

Note: Other conditions with chicken-wire pattern in histopathology:

• Chicken wire calcification - chondroblastoma

• Chicken wire vasculature - oligodendroglioma and myxoid liposarcoma

questions.question: Which of the following conditions does not result in micronodular cirrhosis?
questions.explanation:
Viral hepatitis is associated with macronodular cirrhosis.

Cirrhosis is comprised of regenerating parenchymal nodules surrounded by dense bands of the scar and variable degrees of vascular shunting. It is of two types:

Macronodular cirrhosis
Micronodular cirrhosis

Irregular nodules with variation in size >3 mm
Uniform nodules of size <3 mm

Causes:

• Chronic viral hepatitis

• Wilsons disease

• α1-antitrypsin deficiency

• Drugs and toxins

• Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia

• Cryptogenic cirrhosis

Causes:

• Alcoholic cirrhosis

• Primary biliary cirrhosis

• Hepatic vein obstruction

• Large bile duct obstruction

• Hemochromatosis

• Intestinal bypass

• Cystic fibrosis

• Indian childhood cirrhosis

The images given below show gross and histopathological micronodular alcoholic cirrhosis.

questions.question: In patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis, which of the following features is not seen on liver biopsy?
questions.explanation:
The presence of lymphoid follicles is not a feature on liver biopsy in patients with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH). It is a feature of chronic hepatitis C infection.

The histopathological features of NASH include:

• Ballooning degeneration of hepatocytes

• Steatosis

• Perisinusoidal inflammation and fibrosis

• Portal fibrosis

• Mallory-Denk bodies

• Mononuclear infiltrate

NASH and alcoholic liver disease (ALD) have almost similar histopathological features. They can be differentiated as follows:

Features
ALD
NASH

Mallory-Denk bodies
More prominent
Less prominent

Fibrosis
Perivenular and perisinusoidal>portal
Portal fibrosis is more prominent

Inflammation
More pronounced
Less pronounced

Inflammatory cells
Neutrophils>macrophages
Macrophages>neutrophils

questions.question: What is the most common hepatotoxin causing acute liver failure?
questions.explanation:
The most common hepatotoxin causing acute liver failure is acetaminophen.

Acetaminophen itself is not toxic. The toxic metabolite produced by the cytochrome P-450 system in zone 3 hepatocytes causes hepatocellular necrosis.

The most common hepatotoxin causing chronic liver failure is alcohol.

questions.question: Which of the following does not cause chronic infection?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis A does not cause chronic infection. It is usually a benign, self-limited disease.

Hepatitis B, C, and D can cause chronic infection. Hepatitis E causes chronic infection only in immunocompromised individuals, not in immunocompetent.

questions.question: There is an outbreak of hepatitis A infection in a college hostel. Which of the following is false about this infection?
options: It does not cause hepatocellular carcinoma
Liver failure is not a complication
questions.answer: C. Liver failure is not a complication
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis A virus (HAV) can cause acute hepatic failure in a few patients. However, it does not cause chronic hepatitis or a carrier state.

HAV is a usually benign, self-limited disease, with an incubation period of 15- 50 days (2 - 6 weeks).

HAV is spread by feco-oral route and is shed in the stool for 2 to 3 weeks before and 1 week after the onset of jaundice. It can also spread by sexual route. Diagnosis is by the detection of serum IgM anti HAV.

Since it does not progress to chronic infection, it does not cause hepatocellular carcinoma. The fatality rate associated with HAV is only about 0.1-0.3%.

questions.question: Which among the following is the most common cause of sporadic acute hepatitis in India?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis E virus (HEV) infection accounts for most of the cases of sporadic acute hepatitis in India. It exceeds the frequency of hepatitis A virus infection.

A feature of HEV infection is the high mortality rate among pregnant women, approaching 20%.

questions.question: A 53-year-old man who has a history of chronic hepatitis B is diagnosed to have hepatocellular carcinoma. Which of the following is involved in the pathogenesis of this condition?
questions.explanation:
HBx protein has been implicated in the pathogenesis of hepatocellular carcinoma in hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. HBx protein is involved in the intracellular regulation of virus replication, transcription, and signal transduction.

Option A: HBsAg (surface antigen) indicates current hepatitis B infection.

Option B: HBeAg (precore antigen) is an indicator of active viral replication. It is a qualitative marker of infectivity.

Option C: HBV DNA polymerase is an indicator of active viral replication. It is a quantitative marker of infectivity.

questions.question: Which of the following serological markers can be used to diagnose hepatitis B infection during the window period?
questions.explanation:
During the window period of hepatitis B, the serologic diagnosis can be made by the detection of IgM anti-HBc antibody.

The window period of hepatitis B refers to the time between the disappearance of the HBsAg antigen and appearance of Anti-HBs antibody.

The window period for a test designed to detect a specific disease is the time between the first infection and when the test can reliably detect that infection.

questions.question: In a patient who is both HBsAg and HBeAg positive, what does declining IgM anti-HBc and rising total anti-HBc indicate?
questions.explanation:
In patients who are both HBsAg and HBeAg positive, declining IgM anti-HBc and rising total anti-HBc are indicative of chronic infective hepatitis.

Anti-HBc IgM antibody signifies acute infection/window period, whereas, the presence of IgG anti-HBc indicates chronic infection. However, there is no test available to directly detect the IgG anti-HBC. Over a period of months, the IgM anti-HBc antibodies are replaced by the IgG anti-HBc antibodies. Thus a decline of IgM antibodies in the presence of rising total anti-HBC indicates that the IgM is being converted to IgG and thus the infection is chronic.

HBeAg, HBV-DNA, and DNA polymerase appear in serum soon after HBsAg, and all signify active viral replication.

Occasionally, mutated strains of HBV emerge that do not produce HBeAg but are replication-competent and express HBcAg.

questions.question: A patient with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse turns out to be HBsAg positive. Which of the following is the best predictor for development of chronic disease?
questions.explanation:
The age at the time of infection is the best predictor of chronicity. Younger the age at the time of hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection, higher the probability of chronicity.

Other predictors in the development of chronic disease:

• comorbid conditions (including exposure to other infectious agents)

• host immunity

Presentations of hepatitis B infection:

• Asymptomatic - 65%

• Non-specific symptoms - 25%

• Chronic disease - 5-10%

• Acute fulminant liver disease - 0.1-0.5%

questions.question: An IV drug abuser has been found to be seropositive for HBsAg, HBeAg, and anti-HBc IgM. Which of the following is least likely to be seen in the liver biopsy of such patients?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of acute hepatitis B infection. Ground-glass hepatocytes are not seen in the liver biopsy of such patients.

Histopathological findings in acute hepatits are:

• Ballooning degeneration - due to inflammation

• Portal or lobular inflammatory infiltration - lymphocytes, plasma cells, and eosinophils

• Necrosis

• Confluent necrosis - group of hepatocytes

• Panlobular or panacinar necrosis - entire lobule

• Bridging necrosis (in severe cases) - connecting vascular structures

Ground-glass appearance of hepatocytes is due to the endoplasmic reticulum which is swollen with HBsAg accumulation. It is a diagnostic hallmark of chronic hepatitis B infection.

The image given below shows ground glass hepatocytes in the liver biopsy.

questions.question: A man with a history of intranasal cocaine abuse is at most risk for which of the following infections?
questions.explanation:
Intranasal cocaine abuse is a risk factor for hepatitis C.

Contaminated implements (like straws used to inhale cocaine) inserted into the nasal cavity might come into contact with hepatitis C virus (HCV)-infected mucus or blood. This might then be transmitted to a susceptible individual while sharing the same implements.

Transmission of hepatitis C infection:

• Intravenous drug abuse (54%) - Most common

• Multiple sex partners

• Needle-stick injury

• Multiple contacts with a person with hepatitis C virus infection

• Employment in medical or dental fields

• Blood transfusion

• Perinatal - major route of infection in children

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common clinical course in patients diagnosed with hepatitis C infection?
questions.explanation:
The most common clinical course seen in hepatitis C infection is chronic carrier state.

Acute clinical illness is often asymptomatic/mild with a high rate of conversion to chronic hepatitis (~85%).

questions.question: Which genotype of hepatitis C virus is associated with metabolic syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Hepatitis C virus (HCV) genotype 3 is associated with metabolic syndrome.

HCV can give rise to insulin resistance and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD).

questions.question: A 40-year-old male patient with chronic hepatitis B infection comes for a follow-up visit. Which of the following is not a histopathological feature of the liver in such cases?
questions.explanation:
Ballooning degeneration is not associated with chronic hepatitis. It is seen in acute hepatitis.

Histopathological findings in chronic viral hepatitis are:

• Portal lymphocytic/ lymphoplasmacytic inflammation

• Interface activity - inflammatory cells cross the limiting plate and cause periportal hepatocyte injury

• Portal, periportal, and portoportal bridging fibrosis

Specific findings in viral hepatitis:

• Hepatitis B - ground glass hepatocytes

• Hepatitis C - lymphoid aggregates and steatosis

questions.question: In patients with liver failure, which of the following tests is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes?
questions.explanation:
Serum alkaline phosphatase is used to evaluate biliary excretory function. It is not used to evaluate the synthetic function of hepatocytes.

Serum ammonia, activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT), and serum albumin are used to evaluate hepatic synthetic function.

Prothrombin time (PT), aPTT and serum ammonia levels are increased in liver failure, whereas serum albumin level is decreased.

questions.question: Which of the following is not seen in the histopathological examination of the liver in patients with malaria?
questions.explanation:
Macronodular cirrhosis is not seen in the histopathological examination of patients with malaria.

Histopathological changes in the liver in cases of malaria include the following:

• Kupffer cell hyperplasia

• Hemozoin pigment deposition within Kupffer cells and macrophages

• Focal necrosis

• Mild mononuclear portal infiltrate

• Fatty change and periportal inflammation

questions.question: Identify the incorrect match.
questions.explanation:
Councilman bodies are apoptotic hepatocytes seen in acute hepatitis and yellow fever.

Option A: Mallory–Denk bodies are eosinophilic materials made of keratin intermediate filaments. They are seen in alcoholic liver disease, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, Wilson's disease, and chronic biliary tract diseases.

Option C: Ground-glass hepatocytes are liver cells that have eosinophilic granular, glassy cytoplasm seen on light microscopy. The appearance is due to the swelling of the endoplasmic reticulum by HBsAg and is a diagnostic hallmark of chronic hepatitis B.

Option D: Circumferential onion skin fibrosis around a degenerating bile-duct lumen is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

questions.question: A patient with ascites, melena, and splenomegaly is diagnosed with portal hypertension. Which of the following is not an intrahepatic cause of this condition?
questions.answer: D. Obstructive thrombosis of portal vein
questions.explanation:
Obstructive portal vein thrombosis is the prehepatic cause of portal hypertension.

Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, cirrhosis, and schistosomiasis are intrahepatic causes of portal hypertension. The most dominant cause is cirrhosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of liver histology in patients with non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis?
options: Thrombosis of the medium and small portal vein branches
questions.explanation:
Bridging fibrosis is not seen in non-cirrhotic portal fibrosis. In this condition, there is periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis. The fibrous septa end blindly in the lobule and do not bridge with other portal tracts, unlike those seen in cirrhosis.

Idiopathic non-cirrhotic portal hypertension (INCPH) is a rare disease characterized by intrahepatic portal hypertension in the absence of cirrhosis or other causes of liver disease and splanchnic venous thrombosis.

A liver biopsy is essential in making a diagnosis of INCPH. The features observed are as follows:

• Luminal narrowing or obliteration of portal vein branches

• Micronodular transformation

• Sinusoidal dilatation with formation of mega sinusoids

• Periportal and perisinusoidal fibrosis

questions.question: Match the histopathological sections of liver and the different conditions.
questions.answer: C. 1-Normal liver, 2-Alcoholic steatosis, 3- Micronodular cirrhosis, 4-Alcoholic hepatitis
questions.explanation:
In the given image, images marked 1 is normal liver, 2 is alcoholic steatosis, 3 is micronodular cirrhosis and 4 is alcoholic hepatitis.

Histopathological findings in the following conditions are:

• Alcoholic steatosis:

• A mix of small and large fat droplets

• Ethanol inhibits fatty acid metabolism, leading to lipolysis and increased triglyceride. These triglycerides accumulate and cause steatosis. Liver enzymes are normal at this stage.

• Micronodular cirrhosis:

• The average nodule size is 3 mm in this close-up view, which is typical of the micronodular cirrhosis of alcoholic liver disease

• Alcoholic hepatitis:

• Mallory-Denk bodies - clumped, amorphous, eosinophilic material in ballooned hepatocytes. These inclusions are characteristic, but not a specific feature of alcoholic liver disease.

questions.question:
Match the following:

Drugs
Liver findings

1. Valproate
A. Mallory-Denk bodies

2. Allopurinol
B. Microvesicular steatosis

3. Amiodarone
C. Noncaseating epitheloid granuloma

4. Isoniazid
D. Fibrin ring granuloma
questions.explanation:
The liver findings seen in the hepatotoxic drugs are:

Drugs
Liver findings

Valproate
Microvesicular steatosis

Allopurinol
Fibrin ring granuloma

Amiodarone
Mallory-Denk bodies

Isoniazid
Noncaseating epitheloid granulomas

questions.question: Mutation in which of the following genes causes Wilson's disease?
questions.explanation:
Wilson's disease is caused due to a loss-of-function mutation in the ATP7B gene. It an autosomal recessive condition.

The ATP7B gene is located on chromosome 13q. The gene encodes a copper transporting ATPase (ATP7B) which has 2 functions:

• Maintains copper in bound form by binding copper to apoceruloplasmin

• Helps excrete free copper in bile.

The resulting ATP7B deficiency leads to reduced bound copper and impaired free copper excretion. This causes excess deposition of free copper in the tissues, particularly in the liver, brain and eye.

Menkes disease is an X-linked recessive condition leading to impaired absorption of copper and subsequent copper deficiency. Here, the mutation is in the ATP7A gene.

questions.question: A 35-year-old man with tremors and chronic hepatitis is found to have the following ophthalmic finding. This patient is also likely to have which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows the Kayser-Fleischer ring. This,along with the background of hepatitis and neuropsychiatric features is characteristic of Wilson's disease. The patient is thus likely to have basal ganglia atrophy.

In the majority of cases, neuropsychiatric manifestations follow hepatic manifestations. It is due to the deposition of free copper in the basal ganglia and cortex. Free copper deposition in the basal ganglia leads to bilateral degeneration and atrophy.

questions.question: Which of the following would you use to screen an asymptomatic sibling of a patient with Wilson's disease?
questions.answer: B. Genetic testing for ATP7B gene
questions.explanation:
Genetic testing for the ATP7B gene is used to screen asymptomatic 1st and 2nd-degree relatives of patients with Wilson's disease. This helps to differentiate the heterozygous from the homozygous individuals. This can be useful in the early initiation of treatment before the onset of symptoms.

Low serum ceruloplasmin, raised 24 hr urinary copper and Kayser-Fleischer rings are diagnostically helpful.

Estimation of hepatic tissue copper is the gold standard for diagnosis. It is measured using neutron activation analysis / atomic absorption spectrometry.

questions.question: A 30-year-old male patient presented with personality changes and jaundice. Slit-lamp examination confirmed the diagnosis of Wilson's disease. Which of the following statements is true regarding the condition?
options: Ceruloplasmin in blood increases and urinary copper excretion decreases
Ceruloplasmin in blood decreases and urinary copper excretion decreases
Ceruloplasmin in blood increases and urinary copper excretion increases
Ceruloplasmin in blood decreases and urinary copper excretion increases
questions.answer: D. Ceruloplasmin in blood decreases and urinary copper excretion increases
questions.explanation:
The ceruloplasmin level in the blood decreases, and the copper content in urine increases in Wilson's disease.

Lab markers
Change in Wilson's disease
Reason

Serum ceruloplasmin
↓↓
ATP7B deficiency results in reduced bound copper

24h urinary copper
↑↑
Excess free copper excreted in urine

questions.question: Which of the following stains can be used to demonstrate excess copper deposition in Wilson's disease?
questions.explanation:
Excess copper deposition in Wilson's disease is demonstrated by rhodanine stain.

Microscopic findings in Wilson's disease include:

• Fatty infiltration (macrovesicular)

• Glycogen deposition in periportal hepatocytes

• Macronodular cirrhosis in decompensated stages.

Orcein stain is used to stain copper-associated proteins (eg: ceruloplasmin).

questions.question: A patient with hereditary hemochromatosis is found to have a mutation in the HFE gene. On which chromosome is it located?
questions.explanation:
HFE gene is located on the short arm of chromosome 6 (6p). It is the most commonly mutated gene in patients with hereditary hemochromatosis.

HFE encodes an HLA class I–like molecule that regulates the synthesis of hepcidin in hepatocytes. The most common HFE mutation is a cysteine-to-tyrosine substitution at amino acid 282 (C282Y).

questions.question: A 34-year-old man evaluated for chronic abdominal pain is found to have hepatomegaly and serum ferritin level of 1800 micro g/l. Which of the following complications is he at the greatest risk of developing?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hemochromatosis. A patient with hemochromatosis is at risk of developing hepatocellular carcinoma.

Hepatocellular carcinoma is a significant cause of death in hemochromatosis. The risk is much greater than in the general population.

The disease progression of hemochromatosis is as shown below:

questions.question:
Which of the following is true regarding hemochromatosis?

1. Neonatal hemochromatosis is not an inherited disease.

2. Adult hemochromatosis is generally a milder disease than juvenile form.

3. The skin pigmentation is due to excessive hemosiderin deposition.

4. Bantu siderosis is due to dietary iron overload.

5. Total iron accumulation in severe cases exceeds 25 gm.
questions.explanation:
Neonatal hemochromatosis is not an inherited disease. It is a disease of unknown origin manifested by severe liver disease and extrahepatic hemosiderin deposition. It might be related to maternal alloimmune injury to the fetal liver.

Adult hemochromatosis is generally a milder disease than the juvenile form. With treatment, life expectancy is normal.

Bantu siderosis or African iron overload is due to dietary iron overload. Consumption of beer prepared in iron pots or drums is the cause of dietary iron overload.

Skin pigmentation in hemochromatosis mostly results from increased melanin synthesis. This is due to iron deposition and not hemosiderin deposition.

In severe hemochromatosis, total iron accumulation may exceed 50 gm. More than one-third of this accumulates in the liver. In normal adults, it is in the range of 2 to 6 gms.

questions.question: Which of the following organs does not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis?
questions.explanation:
The testes do not show hemosiderin deposits in hemochromatosis.

Hypogonadism in hemochromatosis is not due to the deposition of iron in the testis. It is due to a derangement in the hypothalamic-pituitary axis. This results in decreased gonadotrophins and testosterone levels. The testis will appear small and atrophic.

Deposition of hemosiderin is seen in the following organs in the decreasing order of severity:

1. Liver

2. Pancreas

3. Myocardium

4. Pituitary gland

5. Adrenal gland

6. Thyroid

7. Parathyroid gland

8. Joints

9. Skin

questions.question: A 35-year-old male patient with emphysema was found to have elevated liver transaminases. His liver biopsy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
In the given clinical scenario, the most likely diagnosis is alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The liver biopsy image shows periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive and diastase-resistant round-to-oval cytoplasmic globular inclusions in hepatocytes. These are characteristic of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

It is an autosomal-recessive disorder of protein misfolding that results in impaired secretion of α1 antitrypsin into the serum. α1AT deficiency results in excessive degradation of alveoli by neutrophil elastase causing panacinar emphysema. It also causes liver disease as a consequence of an abnormal accumulation of the misfolded protein within hepatocytes. Cutaneous necrotizing panniculitis also occurs in a minor subset of patients. Hepatocellular carcinoma develops in 2% to 3% of cases.

The image given is a photomicrograph of a liver biopsy from a patient with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. The PAS with diastase stain shows the diastase-resistant pink globules that are characteristic of this disease.

questions.question: On which chromosome is the gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin present?
questions.explanation:
The gene for alpha-1 antitrypsin is located on the long arm of chromosome 14. Alpha-1 antitrypsin is a plasma glycoprotein synthesized predominantly by hepatocytes.

For α1-antitrypsin genes, the general notation is “Pi” for “protease inhibitor." An alphabetic letter is given for the position on the isoelectric gel.

This gene has different alleles that produce different amounts of alpha-1 antitrypsin (AAT).

• M allele - normal levels of the AAT protein

• S allele - moderately low levels

• Z allele - very low levels

The alleles are expressed in a codominant manner.

questions.question: What is the most common clinically significant mutation causing alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency?
questions.explanation:
The most common clinically significant mutation causing α1-antitrypsin deficiency is PiZ. Homozygous individuals, with PiZZ, have only 10% of normal circulating α1-antitrypsin. So, they are at high risk of developing clinical disease.

PiMM is the most common genotype seen in normal individuals, present in about 90% of individuals.

PiS variant is clinically asymptomatic.

Pi-null is a rare variant with no detectable serum alpha-1 antitrypsin.

questions.question: An 11-year-old girl with persistently elevated serum aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and alanine aminotransferase (ALT) has been diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis. Which of the following pathological features would you not expect in this patient?
questions.answer: D. Bile duct injury and granulomas
questions.explanation:
Bile duct injury and granulomas are uncommon in autoimmune hepatitis except in case of overlap with primary biliary cirrhosis.

Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is characterised by extensive inflammation, fibrosis and ultimately cirrhosis. The pathologic features include:

• Emperipolesis - Lymphocytes and plasma cells within the cytoplasm of hepatocytes.

• Interface hepatitis or piecemeal necrosis.

• Rosette formation due to necrosis of groups of hepatocytes and resultant regeneration.

The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis with lymphoplasmacytic interface hepatitis.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false with regard to autoimmune hepatitis?
options: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows antinuclear antibodies (ANA).
It can progress to liver failure.
Inflammatory infiltrate is predominantly composed of plasma cells.
questions.answer: A. Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows antinuclear antibodies (ANA).
questions.explanation:
Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-liver kidney microsomal autoantibodies (anti-LKM1) and anti–liver cytosol-1 (ACL-1) antibodies not ANA.

Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis shows anti-nuclear (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibodies (ASMA) and anti–soluble liver antigen / liver pancreas antigen (anti-SLA/LP) antibodies. It less commonly shows anti-mitochondrial (AMA) antibodies.

Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic disorder characterized by continuing hepatocellular necrosis and inflammation. It can progress to cirrhosis and liver failure.

Histocompatibility haplotypes such as HLA-B1, HLA-B8, HLA-DR3, and HLA-DR4 are common in patients with autoimmune hepatitis.

Histopathological features include:

• Plasma cell predominance in inflammatory infiltrates

• Extensive interface hepatitis (piecemeal necrosis)

• Hepatocyte rosettes

The image given below shows autoimmune hepatitis showing characteristic lymphoplasmacytic infiltrate and interface hepatitis.

questions.question: Which of the following antibodies would you not expect to see in a patient with autoimmune hepatitis?
questions.explanation: Anti-TIF1γ antibodies are not associated with autoimmune hepatitis. Anti-TIF1γ antibodies are found in patients with dermatomyositis.

questions.question: Identify the incorrect match.
questions.explanation: Chronic hepatitis D is associated with anti-LKM 3 antibodies.

questions.question: The histopathological findings obtained after a liver biopsy is given below. What would be the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Onion-skin fibrosis is seen in primary sclerosing cholangitis.

The smaller ducts in primary sclerosing cholangitis show a striking circumferential “onion skin” fibrosis around an increasingly atrophic duct lumen. This eventually leads to the obliteration by a “tombstone” scar.

The image shows primary sclerosing cholangitis. There is a degenerating bile duct that is entrapped in the dense concentric onion-skin fibrosis.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a feature of primary sclerosing cholangitis?
questions.explanation:
Primary sclerosing cholangitis is characterized by inflammation and obliterative fibrosis of intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. There is dilation of preserved segments.

On histopathologic examination, large ducts show acute neutrophilic inflammation of the epithelium. The inflamed areas develop strictures. Small ducts show onion-skin fibrosis around the atrophic duct lumen. There is an obliteration of ducts by a tombstone scar.

questions.question: Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Primary biliary cholangitis is most commonly associated with Sjogren's syndrome. Other associated conditions are:

• Thyroiditis

• Scleroderma

• Rheumatoid arthritis

• Raynaud phenomenon

• Celiac disease

PBC is an autoimmune disease. It is characterized by nonsuppurative, inflammatory destruction of small and medium-sized intrahepatic bile ducts. Large intrahepatic ducts and the extrahepatic biliary tree are not involved. It is a disease of middle-aged women, with a female predominance of 9:1. Antimitochondrial antibodies are the most characteristic laboratory finding in PBC.

Histopathologic examination shows diagnostic florid duct lesions. These are lymphoplasmacytic infiltrates with or without granulomas centred around the bile duct. They also show Mallory–Denk bodies.

The image given below shows primary biliary cholangitis.

chapters.chapter: Neoplasms Of Liver And Biliary Tract

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common benign tumor of the liver?
questions.explanation:
Cavernous hemangioma is the most common benign tumor of the liver.

It appears as a red-blue, soft nodule, usually < 2 cm in diameter. It may be mistaken radiographically or intraoperatively for a metastatic tumor.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a history of abdominal pain. She has been taking oral contraceptives for the past 7 years. CECT reveals an isodense lesion in the liver with homogenous enhancement in the arterial phase and washout in the portal venous phase. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: It can be associated with MODY-3
Serum amyloid A may be upregulated
β-catenin-activated adenoma has no risk of malignant transformation
questions.answer: D. β-catenin-activated adenoma has no risk of malignant transformation
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of hepatic adenoma. β-catenin-activated adenomas have a high risk of malignant transformation.

Hepatic adenomas are benign tumors of hepatocytes. Spontaneous rupture of the hepatic adenoma may cause intraabdominal bleeding, which is a surgical emergency.

Hepatic adenomas are classified into 3 subtypes:

• HNF1-α-inactivated adenomas -

• No risk of malignant transformation

• Often associated with oral contraceptive pill use (OCP) and MODY-3

• β-catenin-activated adenoma -

• High risk of malignant transformation

• Associated with oral contraceptive pills (OCP) and anabolic steroids usage

• Inflammatory adenomas -

• Associated with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)

• Upregulation of C-reactive protein (CRP) and serum amyloid A

• 10% may have concomitant β-catenin activating mutations

• Moderate risk of malignant transformation

The gross specimen of hepatic adenoma is shown below.

questions.question: Patients with cirrhosis of the liver are at a higher risk of developing which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Dysplastic nodules are associated with liver cirrhosis.

High grade dysplastic nodules may eventually develop into hepatocellular carcinoma in viral hepatitis and alcoholic liver disease.

questions.question: A 2-year-old boy is brought with abdominal swelling. On examination, a mass is palpable in the right upper quadrant. Laboratory evaluation shows serum alpha-fetoprotein level of 1,50,000 ng/mL. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and elevated serum alpha-fetoprotein level are suggestive of hepatoblastoma.

Hepatoblastoma is the most common malignant liver tumor of early childhood, usually < 3 years. Serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is the most important clinical marker for hepatoblastoma. It remains the key clinical marker of malignant change, response to the treatment, and relapse.

Histological section of hepatoblastoma showing proliferating hepatoblasts consisting of round epithelial type cells is given below.

questions.question: Patients with all of the following are at a higher risk of developing hepatoblastoma except:
options: A 6-year-old child diagnosed with new-onset hypertension
A premature infant with low birth weight
A 5-year-old child diagnosed with Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome
A 9-year-old child with a family history of familial adenatomatous polyposis
questions.answer: A. A 6-year-old child diagnosed with new-onset hypertension
questions.explanation:
Hypertension is not a risk factor for hepatoblastoma.

Risk factors for hepatoblastoma include:

• Prematurity and low birth weight (LBW)

• Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome

• Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

questions.question: Which of the following parameters indicates a good prognosis in hepatoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Pure fetal histology hepatoblastoma is associated with a very good prognosis. They may be cured by surgical resection without adjuvant chemotherapy.

Prognostic factors in hepatoblastoma include:

Good prognosis
Bad prognosis

Low tumor stage

Pure fetal histology

High tumor stage

Low AFP levels

Small cell undifferentiated histology

Rhabdoid features

Vascular invasion

Prematurity and low-birth weight (LBW) are associated with hepatoblastoma but do not affect its outcome.

questions.question: Which one of the following syndromes is associated with a higher incidence of hepatoblastoma?
questions.explanation:
Gardner syndrome, a variant of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) syndrome is associated with hepatoblastoma.

Activation of WNT signaling plays a major role in hepatoblastomas. This occurs by a variety of mechanisms including mutations in APC gene. Hence, patients with FAP syndromes frequently develop hepatoblastomas.

The following syndromes are associated with hepatocellular carcinoma:

• Hereditary tyrosinemia

• Alpha-1 antitrypsin defeciency

• Familial hemochromatosis

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of hepatocellular carcinoma is chronic hepatitis B virus infection. More than 85% of cases of hepatocellular carcinoma occur in countries with high rates of chronic hepatitis B virus infection.

Risk factors for hepatocellular carcinoma are:

• Hepatitis B virus

• Hepatitis C virus

• Alcohol

• Aflatoxin

• Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency

• Hemochromatosis

• Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis

• Tyrosinemia

• Smoking

Activation of β-catenin and inactivation of p53 are the two most common early mutational events seen in hepatocellular carcinoma.

questions.question:
Which of the following are the precursor lesions for hepatocellular carcinoma?

1. Hepatocellular adenoma

2. Small cell change

3. Nodular regenerative hyperplasia

4. Large cell change

5. Focal nodular hyperplasia
questions.explanation:
Focal nodular hyperplasia and nodular regenerative hyperplasia are not precursors for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

The precursors of HCC inlcude:

• Hepatocellular adenoma - especially those with β-catenin-activating mutations

• Small cell and large cell change - cellular dysplasias

• Dysplastic nodules - low-grade and high-grade

questions.question: A 25-year-old woman presents with chronic abdominal discomfort. Imaging reveals a solitary well-encapsulated hepatic mass with a central fibrous scar and stellate calcification. Further investigations reveal elevated neurotensin levels and negative hepatitis B serology. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: Histology reveals oncocytic hepatocytes separated by collagen bundles
It is associated with a relatively good prognosis
Majority of these tumors are resectable
It is associated with liver cirrhosis
questions.answer: D. It is associated with liver cirrhosis
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of fibrolamellar carcinoma. It is usually not associated with liver cirrhosis.

Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a distinctive and rare variant of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). It usually occurs < 35 years of age. There is no gender predilection and no identifiable predisposing conditions. It has a good prognosis compared to the classical HCC. Majority (50-75%) of these tumors are resectable.
