It usually presents as a single large, hard scirrhous tumor with fibrous bands coursing through it. Microscopically, it is composed of oncocytes growing in nests or cords separated by parallel lamellae of dense collagen bundles.

The histological section of fibrolamellar carcinoma is given below. It shows malignant-appearing, oncocytic hepatocytes separated by dense bundles of collagen.

questions.question: Which of the following agents is not associated with the development of hepatic angiosarcoma?
questions.explanation:
Hepatic angiosarcoma is associated with exposure to arsenic, thorotrast and vinyl chloride.

Angiosarcoma is a malignant endothelial neoplasm. There is equal gender predilection. The tumor may occur at any site, but most often involves skin, soft tissue, breast and liver.

Various hepatic tumors and associated etiological agents are given below:

Tumor

Etiological agents

Hepatocellular adenoma

Oral contraceptives, anabolic steroids

Hepatocellular carcinoma

Alcohol, thorotrast

Cholangiocarcinoma

Thorotrast

Angiosarcoma

Thorotrast, vinyl chloride, arsenic

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common tumor of the liver?
questions.explanation:
The most common tumors of the liver are metastatic tumors.

The common primary sources of liver metastasis are:

• Colon carcinoma

• Breast carcinoma

• Lung carcinoma

• Pancreatic carcinoma

questions.question: A 53-year-old patient with anorexia and weight loss is found to have non-tender hepatomegaly on physical examination. CT scan of the abdomen shows multiple nodules in the liver and investigations reveal elevated ALP and AST levels, with no elevations in AFP. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a metastatic liver tumor.

Metastases are the most common malignant neoplasms of the liver. The most common primary sources are the colon, breast, lung, and pancreas, although any cancer at any site of the body may spread to the liver.

Patients with metastases typically have multiple nodules replacing the normal liver parenchyma. There may be no clinical or laboratory evidence of hepatic insufficiency. Often, the only telltale sign of secondaries in the liver will be hepatomegaly.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk for cholangiocarcinoma?
questions.explanation:
Typhoid carriers are not at risk of developing cholangiocarcinoma.

Cholangiocarcinoma is the second most common primary malignant tumor of the liver after hepatocellular carcinoma. It is a malignancy of the biliary tree, arising from bile ducts within and outside of the liver.

The risk factors for cholangiocarcinoma include the following:

• Infestation by liver flukes (particularly Opisthorchis and Clonorchis )

• Primary sclerosing cholangitis, and other chronic inflammatory diseases of the large bile ducts

• Chronic hepatitis B and C infections

• Cirrhosis

• Inflammatory bowel disease

• Diabetes mellitus, obesity, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)

• Alcohol and tobacco

• Precursor lesions -

• Biliary intraepithelial neoplasias

• Mucinous cystic neoplasms

• Intraductal papillary biliary neoplasia

questions.question: What does Klatskin tumor refer to?
questions.explanation:
Klatskin tumors are extrahepatic cholangiocarcinomas located in the perihilar region.

These tumors are located at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. Distal tumors arise in the common bile duct posterior to the duodenum. Regardless of the site, the prognosis is poor.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding gallbladder carcinoma?
options: Gallstones are the most important risk factor
Her2 overexpression is seen in about 2/3 of the cases
It usually has a good prognosis
questions.answer: D. It usually has a good prognosis
questions.explanation:
Gallbladder carcinoma carries a poor prognosis because it is typically detected late due to non-specific symptoms.

Carcinoma of the gallbladder is the most common malignancy of the extrahepatic biliary tract. Most carcinomas of the gall bladder are adenocarcinomas.

Gallbladder cancer is at least twice as common in women than in men. The most important risk factor for gallbladder cancer (besides gender and ethnicity) is gallstones, which are present in 95% of cases. Her-2/neu is overexpressed in around 2/3 of the cases, and therefore, they can be targeted for therapy.

questions.question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder?
questions.explanation:
The most common congenital anomaly of the gallbladder is the Phrygian cap. It refers to an inward folding of the fundus of the gallbladder. It is named for its resemblance to a conical hat.

The other common congenital anomalies of the gallbladder are:

• Agenesis - absence of all or any portion of the hepatic or common bile ducts

• Biliary atresia - hypoplastic narrowing of biliary channels

• Choledochal cysts - congenital dilations of the intra and/or extrahepatic biliary system

questions.question: A 24-year-old man presented with severe right upper quadrant pain for 8 hours associated with nausea and vomiting. A diagnosis of acute cholecystitis was made and he underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The specimen is shown below. This finding is associated with all the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
The given image shows pigmented gallstones, which are not associated with hyperlipidemia syndromes.

Pigmented gallstones are made of bilirubin and calcium salts. They can occur in:

• Chronic hemolytic syndromes

• Ileal resection

• Biliary infection

• Cystic fibrosis with pancreatic insufficiency

Cholesterol stones are made of crystalline cholesterol monohydrates. Dyslipidemia is a risk factor for the development of cholesterol gallstones.

The following image shows cholesterol gallstones:

questions.question: A 52-year-old man was rushed to the ER with right upper quadrant pain for the last 6 hours. He had been diagnosed with gallstones 10 years ago but had not undergone any treatment. Imaging revealed gallbladder wall thickening. He underwent a cholecystectomy which revealed a shrunken and nodular gallbladder with a thick wall. The following was noted on microscopy. This condition is associated with:
options: Dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario of chronic cholecystitis and image showing lipid-laden xanthoma cells are suggestive of xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis. This condition results due to the rupture of Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses.

Rokitansky–Aschoff sinuses are bile-filled outpouchings of the gallbladder mucosa through the gallbladder wall. They develop in reaction to chronic inflammation of the gallbladder. Eventually, they may rupture into the wall of the gallbladder. This results in the accumulation of macrophages that have ingested biliary phospholipids, which are called xanthoma cells.

Chronic cholecystitis may have other sequelae:

• Porcelain gallbladder - dystrophic calcification of the gallbladder wall

• Hyalinizing cholecystitis - replacement of the gallbladder wall by dense fibrosis, with or without calcification (leads to higher incidence of gallbladder carcinoma)

• Hydrops of the gallbladder - atrophic, obstructed, dilated gallbladder containing clear fluid

Acute cholecystitis includes the following variants:

• Emphysematous cholecystitis - acute infection of the gallbladder by gas-forming organisms

• Acalculous cholecystitis - due to gallbladder stasis and ischemia

questions.question: What is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas?
questions.explanation:
Pancreas divisum is the most common congenital anomaly of the pancreas.

The pancreas develops by fusion of the larger dorsal and smaller ventral pancreatic buds. The dorsal duct is the dominant duct during development and it drains into the minor papilla. The ventral duct drains into the major papilla. After fusion, the following ducts are formed:

• Main pancreatic duct (of Wirsung) - formed by fusion of ducts of dorsal and ventral buds, drains into the major papilla

• Accessory pancreatic duct (of Santorini) - formed by the proximal portion of the dorsal duct, drains into the minor papilla

In pancreas divisum, the ventral and dorsal ducts fail to fuse. Hence, the majority of the pancreas continues to drain through the dominant dorsal duct that enters the duodenum at the minor papilla while the ventral duct, along with the bile duct, drains into the major papilla. These patients are more prone to pancreatitis.

The other congenital anomalies of the pancreas are:

• Annular pancreas - band-like ring of normal pancreatic tissue encircling 2nd part of duodenum, may cause obstruction

• Ectopic pancreas - common in stomach, duodenum, and jejunum (found in about 2% of postmortem exams)

• Agenesis - rarely seen, associated with mutations of PDX1 (homeobox gene)

questions.question: A 19-year-old boy presented with severe abdominal pain for the last 24 hours with radiation to the upper back. He has had multiple similar episodes since his childhood. Family history revealed similar episodes in the father. Investigations revealed elevated serum levels of amylase and lipase. Which of the following statements is not true about the given condition?
options: It is commonly associated with mutations in the PRSS1 gene
This boy has a 40 % lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer
It may be associated with mutations in the CFTR gene
Hypocalcemia is an important triggering factor this condition
questions.answer: D. Hypocalcemia is an important triggering factor this condition
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario in a young patient with positive family history of similar episodes is suggestive of hereditary pancreatitis. Acute episodes of pancreatitis can be precipitated by hypercalcemia, not hypocalcemia.

The following genes are implicated in hereditary pancreatitis:

• Gain-of-function mutation in trypsinogen gene (PRSS1) - most common

• Loss-of-function mutation in trypsin inhibitor gene (SPINK1)

• Loss of CFTR - abnormal secretions that promote protein plugging, duct obstruction, leading to pancreatitis

Hereditary pancreatitis is associated with a 40% lifetime risk of developing pancreatic cancer.

questions.question: A 65-year-old man presented with vague abdominal pain, anorexia, weight loss for the last 6 months. He also reported spontaneously appearing and disappearing painful, linearly arranged nodules at different locations on his body. On examination, thrombophlebitis and epigastric tenderness were noted. Investigations revealed elevated serum CEA and CA 19-9. Which of the following genetic mutations is most frequently associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The presence of the above clinical symptoms with migratory thrombophlebitis (Trousseau syndrome) and elevated serum levels of CEA and CA 19-9 in an elderly man point to a diagnosis of pancreatic cancer. The most frequently associated mutation with this condition is K-RAS.

It is attributed to the production of platelet-aggregating factors and procoagulants from the tumor or its necrotic products. Both venous and arterial thrombi can occur. Venous thrombi can embolize to the lungs.

Molecular alterations involved in pancreatic carcinogenesis are:

Tumor suppressor gene

Tumor suppressor gene

Following genes are associated with an inherited predisposition to pancreatic cancer:

• BRCA2 mutation - pancreatic cancer, breast cancer, prostate cancer, and ovarian cancers

• PRSS1 mutation - pancreatic carcinoma secondary to hereditary pancreatitis

questions.question: A pathologist was studying a biopsy specimen from a patient with pancreatic cancer. He observed that it resembled ovarian stroma. What is it likely to be?
questions.explanation:
Mucinous cystic neoplasms of the pancreas have dense stroma, similar to the ovarian stroma.

These tumors have large cystic cavities filled with thick, tenacious mucin. They are lined by columnar, mucin-producing epithelium with dense stroma. This results in similarity to ovarian stroma.

They usually arise in the tail of the pancreas and can be precursors to invasive carcinomas. They are associated with mutations in the KRAS oncogene, and the tumor-suppressor genes TP53 and RNF43.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following have the highest risk of pancreatic cancer?
questions.explanation:
Patients with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome have the highest risk of pancreatic cancer.

Hereditary syndromes and their associated risk of pancreatic cancer:

questions.question: What is the most common site of fistulization in GIT?
questions.explanation:
The esophagus is the most common site of fistulization in the gastrointestinal tract (GIT).

A tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF) is an abnormal fistula communication between the esophagus and trachea. The fistula is usually present near the tracheal bifurcation, with or without esophageal atresia. A blind proximal pouch with a distal tracheo­oesophageal fistula is the most common type of tracheoesophageal fistula (Type C).

10% of the patients have associated VACTERL anomalies (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheal, esophageal, renal, and limb).

questions.question: What is the most frequent site of ectopic gastric mucosa?
questions.explanation:
The most frequent site of the ectopic gastric mucosa is the upper third of the esophagus, where it is referred to as an inlet patch.

It is congenital and mostly asymptomatic. Occasionally, it can release acid, which can result in dysphagia, esophagitis, Barrett esophagus, or, rarely, adenocarcinoma.

questions.question: A 57-year-old man came with complaints of difficulty in swallowing and a persistent feeling of something stuck in his throat. He also reports bad breath and regurgitation of food particles. Barium swallow revealed the following. This condition occurs due to a defect in which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and barium swallow image are diagnostic of Zenker’s diverticulum. It occurs due to a defect in the Killian's triangle (Killian's dehiscence).

Killian's triangle is an anatomical triangular area bordered superiorly by the firm oblique fibers of the thyropharyngeus muscle and inferiorly by the horizontal fibers of the cricopharyngeus muscle. It is located immediately above the upper esophageal sphincter.

Although the Killian-Jamieson diverticulum is an anterolateral defect, it is rarely symptomatic.

questions.question: All of the following may be seen in patients with Plummer-Vinson syndrome except:
questions.explanation:
Paterson–Brown–Kelly or Plummer–Vinson syndrome is associated with non-progressive dysphagia, especially with incompletely chewed food.

This syndrome is common in women aged >40 years. The other components of this syndrome are:

• Post-cricoid webs in the upper esophagus

• Iron-deficiency anemia

• Glossitis

• Cheilosis

Esophageal webs are idiopathic, semi-circumferential lesions composed of fibrovascular connective tissue and overlying epithelium. They are usually limited to the proximal esophagus and may cause obstruction. They are associated with:

• Plummer–Vinson syndrome

• Gastroesophageal reflux disease

• Chronic graft-versus-host disease

• Blistering skin diseases

 The images below show endoscopic and barium swallow appearances of esophageal webs.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presented with complaints of difficulty in swallowing solid foods. An upper GI endoscopy revealed the following finding just above the gastroesophageal junction. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows an esophageal ring. Rings located above the gastroesophageal junction are classified as type A esophageal rings.

Esophageal rings are circumferential and thick. They include mucosa, submucosa, and occasionally, hypertrophic muscularis propria. There are 3 types:

Type A rings
Type B or Schatzki rings
Type C rings

Caused by normal physiologic smooth muscle contractions

Most common type

Associated with hiatus hernia

Rare findings

Indentations on radiographic studies due to diaphragmatic crural pressure

Seen above the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) in the distal esophagus

Covered by squamous mucosa

Located at the squamocolumnar junction

Covered by gastric cardia-type mucosa

Found in the most distal portion of the esophagus

Steakhouse syndrome refers to intermittent food impaction causing complete obstruction due to the presence of Schatzki rings.

questions.question: A 52-year-old woman is being evaluated for dysphagia and chest pain. She traveled to Brazil on a business trip 5 months ago. Barium swallow reveals the following finding. Which of the following could have caused this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and barium swallow showing the bird-beak appearance are suggestive of achalasia cardia. With respect to this patient's travel history, Chagas' disease due to infection with Trypanosoma cruzi must be suspected.

The infection destroys the myenteric plexus which results in failure of peristalsis and esophageal dilatation. Duodenal, colonic, and ureteric myenteric plexuses can also be affected by Chagas' disease.

questions.question: A mother brought her 8-year-old son to the OPD with complaints of refusal to eat and poor weight gain. The child complained that food often gets stuck in his throat. Endoscopy revealed the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image showing multiple stacked esophageal rings are characteristic of eosinophilic esophagitis.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect about eosinophilic esophagitis?
options: Majority of patients have associated atopic conditions
Feline esophagus is an endoscopic finding
Treatment of choice is systemic steroids
May be associated with food products like cow’s milk and soy products
questions.answer: C. Treatment of choice is systemic steroids
questions.explanation:
Treatment of choice are proton pump inhibitors, which when started as primary therapy is effective in 30 - 50 % of affected individuals.
Additionally, elimination of allergenic proteins from diet as it is is associated with atopy and exposure to food allergens like cow’s milk and soy products.
Swallowed topical steroids are used as well.

Immunocompromised patients are treated with acyclovir, famciclovir or valacyclovir.

questions.question: A 47-year-old woman comes to you with progressive heartburn and difficulty in swallowing. She also describes episodes of painful blanching and bluish discoloration of her fingers and toes on exposure to cold. The following findings are noted on examination. Antibodies to which of the following are most likely to be seen in this patient?
questions.explanation:
The symptoms of the patient in the above case scenario and the image showing calcinosis are the characteristic findings of the CREST syndrome or limited scleroderma. Patients with this condition characteristically have antibodies directed against centromeric proteins (anti-centromere antibodies).

CREST syndrome is characterized by the following:

• Calcinosis

• Raynaud phenomenon

• Esophageal dysmotility

• Sclerodactyly

• Telangiectasia

In the esophagus, progressive atrophy and fibrous replacement of the muscularis propria leads to hypomotility and dysphagia. The lower 2/3 of the esophagus develops a rubber-hose–like inflexibility. The associated dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter gives rise to gastroesophageal reflux, Barrett metaplasia, and stricture.

questions.question: A 50-year-old man presented with blood in his vomitus. He gives a history of binge drinking followed by multiple episodes of vomiting the prior night. He is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?
options: It is due to longitudinal mucosal tears
The gastroesophageal musculature fails to relax
The tears cross the gastroesophageal junction
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a Mallory–Weiss tear. They require only conservative management and healing tends to be rapid and complete.

They are longitudinal mucosal tears that may cross the gastroesophageal junction (GEJ). Forceful retching or vomiting along with failure of reflex relaxation of the gastroesophageal musculature results in tears involving the mucosa and submucosa. It usually occurs secondary to conditions like acute alcohol intoxication or hyperemesis gravidarum.

Boerhaave syndrome is a much more serious disorder characterized by transmural rupture of the distal esophagus. This results in acute mediastinitis with severe chest pain, tachypnea, and shock. Such patients generally require urgent surgical intervention.

questions.question: What is the most frequent cause of esophagitis?
questions.explanation:
The most frequent cause of esophagitis is reflux of gastric acid into the lower esophagus.

The most common cause of gastroesophageal reflux is transient lower esophageal sphincter relaxation. Reflux esophagitis leads to chronic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). This can cause Barrett's esophagus and eventually can cause adenocarcinoma.

questions.question: Which organism can cause esophageal infections in healthy individuals?
questions.explanation:
Esophagitis in healthy individuals can be caused by the Herpes simplex virus. However, it is relatively uncommon.

In immunosuppressed individuals, infections can be caused by:

• Herpes simplex virus

• Cytomegalovirus

• Candida

questions.question: A 28-year-old patient with haematemesis is found to have the following finding on upper GI endoscopy. He has traveled to Zambia several times over the past 3 years. What could be the likely cause of this condition?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing bleeding esophageal varices are suggestive of hepatic schistosomiasis. It is the second most common cause of varices worldwide.

Liver cirrhosis, mostly in association with alcoholic liver disease, is the most common cause of varices.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man with chronic dyspepsia underwent upper GI endoscopy. The biopsy findings are shown below. What is the special stain that has been used?
questions.explanation:
The given image is of Barrett's esophagus showing intestinal metaplasia. The special stain used here is Alcian blue, which stains the acid mucin present in the goblet cells.
