questions.question: A 60-year-old man presented with dyspnea and cough. Chest X-ray revealed irregular linear densities, particularly in both lower lobes. Histopathological examination of lung biopsy is shown below. This patient has a higher risk of developing:
questions.explanation:
The image shows golden-brown, beaded rods with a translucent center called asbestos bodies which are seen in asbestosis. These patients are at risk of developing both lung carcinoma and mesothelioma.

Asbestosis is marked by diffuse pulmonary interstitial fibrosis and the presence of multiple asbestos bodies.

Option A: Centrilobular emphysema may develop in simple coal workers' pneumoconiosis.

Option B: Increased susceptibility to tuberculosis is seen in silicosis.

Option C: Occupational asthma may be triggered by fumes (epoxy resins, plastics), organic and chemical dust (wood, cotton, platinum), gases (toluene), or other chemicals (formaldehyde, penicillin products).

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with complaints of low-grade fever, dry cough, and progressive dyspnea. Examination reveals the following painless skin lesion. Chest X-ray shows bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. Lung biopsy shows non-caseating granulomas. Which of the following is not a feature of this condition?
options: Anergy to common skin test antigens
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and image showing the lesion of lupus pernio point towards sarcoidosis. It is a multisystemic disease characterized by polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia.

Lupus pernio is seen in cutaneous sarcoidosis and presents as infiltrated erythematoviolaceous plaques involving the nose, cheeks, ears, lips, forehead, and fingers. On the cheeks, telangiectasia is characteristic. It is usually painless. As it does not ulcerate, it is not as mutilating as lupus vulgaris.

Immunological abnormalities include:

• Polyclonal hyperglobulinemia

• A CD4/CD8 ratio > 3.5

• T- cell expansion and macrophage activation

• Impaired dendritic cell function

• Anergy to common skin tests.

The hallmarks of sarcoidosis include:

• B/L hilar lymphadenopathy

• Non-caseating granulomas

• Lupus pernio

• Erythema nodosum (acute sarcoidosis)

Syndromes associated with sarcoidosis are:

• Mikulicz syndrome - sarcoidosis combined with uveoparotid involvement

• Lofgren's syndrome - acute presentation of sarcoidosis, consisting of arthritis, erythema nodosum, and bilateral hilar adenopathy

The image below shows the characteristic non-caseating sarcoid granuloma.

The image below shows stellate inclusions known as asteroid bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.

The image below shows laminated concretions composed of calcium and proteins known as Schaumann bodies that are found within giant cells in approximately 60% of the granulomas.

questions.question: What is the most common gene mutation associated with pulmonary hypertension?
questions.explanation:
Bone morphogenetic protein receptor 2 (BMPR2) is the most common gene mutation in pulmonary hypertension. Inactivating mutations in this gene are found in 75% of the familial cases of pulmonary hypertension, and 25% of sporadic cases.

The BMPR2 receptor is a cell surface protein belonging to the TGF-β receptor superfamily. It is involved in the regulation of growth, differentiation, and apoptosis of pulmonary artery endothelial and smooth muscle cells.

Due to the mutation, there is enhanced proliferation and reduced apoptosis of vascular endothelial and smooth muscle cells leading to pulmonary hypertension.

questions.question: A 57-year-old man presented with a persistent dry cough and progressive dyspnea. HRCT showed a crazy-paving pattern. Microscopy of BAL aspirate is shown below. Antibodies against which of the following are seen in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario and microscopy showing alveoli filled with a dense, amorphous, protein-lipid granular precipitate are suggestive of autoimmune pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP). It is caused by circulating neutralizing antibodies specific for granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF).

PAP is a condition characterized by the accumulation of surfactants in alveoli and terminal airways. It can be due to impaired clearance or abnormal production of surfactants.

PAP can be of three forms:

• Primary (most common): There is impaired GM-CSF-dependent surfactant clearance by the alveolar macrophages. It can be due to:

• Autoantibodies against GM-CSF (acquired/idiopathic/autoimmune PAP)

• Mutation in GM-CSF receptors (hereditary PAP)

• Secondary: There is a reduction in the number or ability of alveolar macrophages that causes impaired surfactant clearance. It can be due to:

• Silicosis

• Immunodeficiency disorders

• Hematopoietic disorders and malignancies

• Congenital: It affects neonates and children. There is abnormal surfactant production due to mutation in the genes coding for:

• Surfactant protein B

• Surfactant protein C

• ATP binding cassette protein member 3

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?
options: The most common cancer worldwide is lung cancer
The most common malignant tumors of the lung are metastases
The most common cause of cancer mortality worldwide is lung cancer
The lung is the most common site of metastatic neoplasms
questions.answer: A. The most common cancer worldwide is lung cancer
questions.explanation:
According to Globocan 2020, the most common cancer worldwide is breast cancer. However, lung cancer remains the leading overall cause of cancer mortality.

Lung cancers:

• The most common malignant tumors of the lung are metastases/ secondaries.

• The most common primary malignant tumor of the lung is bronchogenic cancer.

• The most common histology is adenocarcinoma (43.8%), followed by squamous cell (26.2%).

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common symptom seen in patients with lung cancer?
questions.explanation:
The major presenting complaints of lung cancer patients are cough (75%), weight loss (40%), chest pain (40%), and dyspnea (20%).

Paraneoplastic syndromes associated with lung cancer:

Paraneoplastic syndrome

Type of cancer

SIADH
Inappropriate ADH secretion
Small-cell carcinoma

Cushing syndrome

Small-cell carcinoma

Carcinoid syndrome
Serotonin and Bradykinin
Small-cell carcinoma

Hypercalcemia
Parathyroid hormone-related peptide
Squamous cell carcinoma

Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome
Auto-antibodies directed to the neuronal calcium channel (possibly elicited by tumor ionic channels)
Small-cell carcinoma (rarely in other lung cancers)

Acanthosis nigricans

secretion of epidermal growth factor

Lung carcinoma

Hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy
Unknown
Lung carcinoma

SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion

ADH: Antidiuretic hormone

ACTH: Adrenocorticotropic hormone

questions.question: Histopathological findings of a lung tumor biopsy are shown below. Which of the following is the most sensitive and specific marker of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows keratin pearls and islands of large polygonal malignant cells. These as seen in squamous cell carcinoma of the lungs. P40 is the most sensitive and specific marker for squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lungs.

Other markers include cytokeratin 5/6 and P63.

TTF-1 and napsin-A are the markers for adenocarcinoma.

Chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56 are the markers for small cell lung carcinoma.

Note: The 2015 World Health Organization Classification of Lung Tumors has made a recommendation that at least one antibody each for squamous (P40 or P63) and glandular (e.g. TTF-1) differentiation should be used for an initial workup. Thus a simple panel of TTF-1 and p40 may be able to classify most non-small cell carcinoma-not otherwise specified cases.

questions.question: Which is the most aggressive type of lung cancer?
questions.explanation:
Small-cell carcinoma of the lung is the most aggressive type of lung cancer.

This tumor originates from neuroendocrine progenitor cells (Kulchitsky cells), which are present in the lining bronchial epithelium.

Histopathological examination of small cell lung carcinoma shows:

• Clusters of small cells with scant cytoplasm

• Ill-defined cell borders

• Finely granular nuclear chromatin (salt and pepper pattern)

• Absent or inconspicuous nucleoli

The cells are round, oval, or spindle-shaped, and nuclear molding is prominent.

The image below shows the histopathological findings of small cell lung carcinoma.

questions.question: A 53-year-old man who is a chronic smoker is diagnosed with lung carcinoma. Histopathology of the lung tissue is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features and the histopathology showing the Azzopardi effect are suggestive of a small cell carcinoma of the lung.

Azzopardi effect is described as basophilic staining of vascular walls due to encrustation by DNA from necrotic tumor cells.

questions.question: Non-smoker patients with lung carcinoma are most likely to have a mutation in which of the following genes?
questions.explanation:
Non-smoker patients with lung carcinoma are most likely to have a mutation in the EGFR gene.

Molecular genetics of lung cancer:

Histological type
Mutated genes

Adenocarcinoma

Tyrosine kinase genes (EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, RET)

or

KRAS gene

Squamous cell carcinoma

TP53

CDKN2A/p16

FGFR1 gene amplification

Loss of RB gene

Small cell carcinoma

TP53

Loss of RB gene

3p deletion

MYC amplification

questions.question: A woman presents to the OPD with complaints of bloody cough, dyspnea, and weight loss. During the evaluation, a CT-guided lung biopsy reveals the following picture. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of adenocarcinoma lung.

It is the most common form of lung cancer. It is an invasive malignant epithelial tumor with glandular differentiation. The tumor cells produce mucin. It is usually located peripherally (it arises from the terminal bronchiole).

Molecular genetics show frequent mutations in EGFR, ALK, ROS, MET, and RET (Receptor tyrosine kinase genes) or KRAS mutations.

Histologically, lepidic growth patterns are seen. It refers to the pattern of spread of the tumor in which the tumor cells “crawl” along normal-appearing alveolar septae and resembles butterflies resting on a fence.

Adenocarcinomas grow in various patterns, including acinar, lepidic, papillary, micropapillary, and solid with mucin formation. Tumor cells are positive for mucin and thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1)

Tumors 3 cm or less in diameter characterized by lepidic growth pattern without stromal invasion are now called adenocarcinoma in situ (formerly called bronchoalveolar carcinoma).

The image below shows histopathological findings of adenocarcinoma of the lung.

questions.question: Which of the following immunohistochemical markers would be positive in a patient with adenocarcinoma lung?
questions.explanation:
Thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), mucin, and napsin-A are positive in adenocarcinoma lung.

TTF-1 is required for normal lung development. It can be used to distinguish primary adenocarcinoma of the lungs (TTF-1 positive) from other histological types of lung cancers, metastatic adenocarcinoma, and mesothelioma (TTF-1 negative).

P40 and P63 are the markers for squamous cell carcinoma.

Chromogranin, synaptophysin, and CD56 are the markers for small cell lung carcinoma.

questions.question: A 75-year-old man presents with a cough and shortness of breath. He has been working in a shipping factory for 30 years. On x-ray, a mass is seen in the right apical region of the lung. A biopsy sample is taken from the mass. Which of the following tumor markers is likely to be positive in this tumor?
questions.explanation:
Calretinin is most likely to be positive in this tumour as the given clinical scenario points to the diagnosis of malignant mesothelioma.

Malignant mesothelioma is a rare malignant tumour of the pleura, associated with heavy asbestos exposure (shipping factory). The lifetime risk of developing mesothelioma in heavily exposed individuals is as high as 7% to 10%.

It has strong male predilection (3:1). There is a long latent period of 25 to 45 years for the development of asbestos-related mesothelioma.

The image below shows a lung autopsy sample with mesothelioma.

Grossly, it appears as a diffuse lesion arising either from the visceral or parietal pleura. The affected lung becomes ensheathed by a thick layer of soft, gelatinous, grayish pink tumor tissue.

Microscopically, they are of three types: epithelioid (60%), sarcomatoid (20%), and mixed (20%).

Electron microscopy in mesothelioma will show numerous long, slender microvilli and abundant monofilaments but absent microvillous rootlets and lamellar bodies.

The image below shows the epithelioid type of mesothelioma showing cuboidal, columnar, or flattened cells forming tubular or papillary structures resembling adenocarcinoma. Inset shows strong positivity for Calretinin immunostain.

questions.question: A 59-year old man presented with persistent wheezing, episodes of hemoptysis, and dry cough. Bronchoscopy revealed a mass occluding the left bronchus. Biopsy of the specimen revealed polygonal cells with fine stippled chromatin and eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in nests. The tumor was positive for CD 56, synaptophysin, and chromogranin. What is the cell of origin of this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of bronchial carcinoid. Bronchial neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) arise from Kulchitsky cells.

WHO divides neuroendocrine neoplasms into four categories:

• Typical carcinoid

• Atypical carcinoid

• Large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma

• Small-cell carcinoma

Carcinoid tumors are low-grade malignant epithelial neoplasms that represent 1% to 5% of all lung tumors. It is not related to smoking. Carcinoids may occur in patients with multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1.

On gross examination, these tumors grow as fingerlike or spherical polypoid masses that project into the lumen of the bronchus or as collar button lesions, penetrating the bronchial wall to fan out in the peribronchial tissue.

Histologically, the tumor is composed of organoid, trabecular, palisading, ribbon, or rosette-like arrangements of cells separated by a delicate fibrovascular stroma. On electron microscopy, the cells exhibit the dense-core neurosecretory granules.

Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for serotonin, neuron-specific enolase, bombesin, calcitonin, or other peptides.

10% of the cases may produce carcinoid syndrome.

Most carcinoids follow a relatively benign course and have good prognosis.

questions.question: What percentage of patients with bronchial carcinoids present with carcinoid syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Approximately, 10% of bronchial carcinoids give rise to the carcinoid syndrome.

Most bronchial carcinoids follow a relatively benign course, do not have secretory activity and do not metastasize to distant sites.

Classic carcinoid syndrome is characterized by intermittent attacks of diarrhea, flushing, bronchospasm and cyanosis.

Carcinoid syndrome is due to excessive production of serotonin, a specialised product of tryptophan metabolism by argentaffin cells (cells in the carcinoid tumor). It is then metabolised and excreted in urine.

If urinary levels of 5- HIAA exceed 25 mg/day, a diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome can be made.

questions.question: A solitary coin lesion was seen on a routine X-ray of a patient. After evaluation, he was diagnosed with lung hamartoma. Which of the following is the most common tissue seen in these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Cartilage is the most common connective tissue in lung hamartoma.

Pulmonary hamartoma consists of nodules of connective tissue intersected by epithelial clefts. There are islands of cartilage, fat, smooth muscle, and entrapped respiratory epithelium in pulmonary hamartoma.

It is a benign clonal neoplasm associated with chromosomal aberrations involving either 6p21 or 12q14-q15.

Lung hamartoma is usually discovered as an incidental coin lesion on a routine chest radiograph.

The given below is an image of lung hamartoma.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman is being evaluated for chronic headaches, infertility, and galactorrhea. MRI of the brain shows the following finding. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and brain MRI showing a pituitary adenoma are suggestive of a lactotroph adenoma (prolactinoma).

Pituitary adenomas are usually found in adults. The most common genetic alterations in this condition are mutations in G ­proteins (particularly GNAS).

Depending on their size, they are classified as:

• Microadenomas - diameter < 1 cm

• Macroadenomas - diameter > 1 cm

They may be functioning or non-functioning. The most common type of functioning pituitary adenomas are prolactinomas.

The clinical features of prolactinoma include:

• Due to mass effect -

• Features of raised intracranial tension

• Visual field disturbances (bitemporal hemianopia) - due to compression of optic chiasm

• Hypopituitarism - due to compressed hypophyseal stalk

• Due to hyperprolactinemia -

• Galactorrhoea

• Amenorrhoea or oligomenorrhoea

• Infertility

• Loss of libido

• Gynecomastia

Serum prolactin concentrations tend to correlate with the size of the adenoma. The normal range of serum prolactin is 5-20 μg/L. The diagnosis of prolactinoma is most likely to be associated with a prolactin level >200 μg/L.

questions.question: Presence of which of the following features is required to diagnose a patient with pituitary carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
The following features are required for the diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma:

• A pituitary tumor that has metastasized to distant sites, either craniospinal or systemic sites (and/or)

• Presence of a pituitary tumor that is not contiguous with the primary sellar tumour

Pituitary carcinoma is extremely rare (< 1% of total tumors). They are associated with activating mutations of the HRAS oncogene.

The diagnosis of pituitary carcinoma cannot be made based on histologic appearance alone. Though pituitary adenomas normally show cellular monomorphism and the absence of a reticulin network, they can have some overlapping features with malignant tumors such as:

• Atypical adenomas - show pleomorphism and atypical mitosis

• Invasive adenomas -

• Non-encapsulated

• Show local invasion into cavernous and sphenoid sinuses, dura, brain

• However, they remain confined to the primary tumor site

questions.question: Which of the following cells secrete parathyroid hormone?
questions.explanation:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH) is secreted by the chief cells of the parathyroid glands.

The function of the parathyroids is to regulate calcium homeostasis. This gland is composed of two cell types:

• Chief cells -

• Polygonal cells with uniform nuclei and pink cytoplasm

• Water-clear appearance - due to presence of large amounts of cytoplasmic glycogen

• Secretory granules containing PTH

• Oxyphil cells - Slightly larger cells with acidophilic cytoplasm with no known function.

The following image shows the normal histology of the parathyroid gland:

C-cells or parafollicular cells are present in the thyroid. They secrete calcitonin.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of asymptomatic hypercalcemia (isolated hypercalcemia without signs or symptoms) is primary hyperparathyroidism. It is also the most common cause of hypercalcemia overall.

Primary hyperparathyroidism results in autonomous overproduction of parathyroid hormone (PTH), resulting in elevated levels. It usually results from an adenoma or hyperplasia of parathyroid tissue.

The most common cause of symptomatic hypercalcemia is malignancy. The most common mechanism through which osteolytic tumors induce hypercalcemia is the secretion of the PTH-related peptide (PTHrP).

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presented with bone pain and abdominal cramps for the past 1 week. She has had multiple prior hospital admissions for management of recurrent renal calculi. Investigations revealed elevated serum calcium and PTH levels with reduced phosphate levels. Which of the following is the most common pathological change responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is highly suggestive of primary hyperparathyroidism. The most common cause is a sporadic, solitary parathyroid adenoma.

Parathyroid tumors may be associated with cyclin D1 gene inversions and MEN1 mutations. Hyperparathyroidism refers to elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH). It is classified into:

• Primary - autonomous overproduction of PTH

• Secondary - compensatory hypersecretion of PTH in response to prolonged hypocalcemia

• Tertiary - persistent hypersecretion of PTH even after correction of prolonged hypocalcemia. (e.g. after renal transplant)

The classical symptoms and signs of primary hyperparathyroidism are due to hypercalcemia as well as increased parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. The features of hypercalcemia are as follows:

System
Clinical features

Musculoskeletal

• Bone pain

• Skeletal deformities

• Pathological fractures

• Myalgia and arthralgia

Renal

• Renal stones(Calcium oxalate > calcium phosphate)

• Nephrocalcinosis

• Polyuria and dehydration

• Renal failure

GIT

• Constipation

• Nausea, vomiting, anorexia

• Abdominal pain

• Peptic ulcer disease

• Acute pancreatitis

Neuropsychiatric

• Anxiety, depression

• Cognitive dysfunction

• Irritability

• Hallucinations

Cardiac

• Short QT interval

• Bradycardia

• Hypertension

Ectopic calcification

• Cornea: Band keratopathy

• Extravascular tissues: calcinosis

• Small arteries: calciphylaxis

The features of elevated PTH levels are as follows:

• Osteitis fibrosa cystica

• Osteopenia/osteoporosis

• Hyperuricemia and gout

• Pseudogout

• Increased production of calcitriol

• Nephrolithiasis

• Hypophosphatemia

• Anemia

The clinical signs associated with primary hyperparathyroidism can be remembered with the mnemonic - “bones, stones, groans, moans with fatigue overtones”

questions.question:
A 47-year-old woman was evaluated for chronic backache and abdominal pain. Investigations revealed the following. What is the most likely bone finding seen in this condition?

Serum calcium - 15.1 mg/dL

Parathormone (PTH) level - 2105 pg/mL

USG Abdomen - multiple renal calculi
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and lab findings point towards a diagnosis of hyperparathyroidism. The bone finding associated with this condition is osteitis fibrosa cystica.

This condition is also called brown tumor or von Recklinghausen disease of bone.

In hyperparathyroidism, high levels of PTH result in increased osteoclast activity. This results in bone loss which predisposes to microfractures and secondary hemorrhages. This results in the following changes:

• An influx of macrophages that form giant cells

• Mass of reparative fibrous tissue

• Increased vascularity, hemorrhage, and hemosiderin deposition - results in brown color

The image given below is showing a brown tumor with numerous giant cells with interstitial hemorrhage, hemosiderin.

Option A: Osteoporosis circumscripta is a large, well-defined lytic lesion seen in the skull of patients with Paget's disease.

Option B: Fraying and cupping of the metaphysis of the bones are classically seen in patients suffering from rickets.

Option D: Punched out lytic lesions of the bone are seen in patients with multiple myeloma.

questions.question: A 46-year-old woman is referred with recurrent episodes of hypoglycemia. During the evaluation, she is found to have high serum levels of insulin. Measurement of which of the following can help in reaching the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinemia. As C-peptide is a marker of endogenous insulin secretion, its levels would help in identifying the source of insulin:

• High C-peptide - excess insulin production (insulinoma)

• Normal/ low C-peptide - exogenous insulin administration (factitious disorder)

The precursor molecule of insulin is pre-proinsulin, which gets cleaved to form proinsulin. This proinsulin gets cleaved to form insulin and C-peptide (by-product). Hence, both are secreted in equimolar quantities during insulin secretion. Hence, the level of C-peptide corresponds to the level of endogenous insulin.

The levels of C-peptide decrease with the loss of β-cell mass in type 1 diabetes.

questions.question: Patients with which of the following chromosomal anomalies are least likely to develop diabetes mellitus?
questions.explanation:
Edward's syndrome or trisomy 18 is not associated with diabetes mellitus.

Genetic syndromes associated with diabetes mellitus include:

• Down's syndrome (trisomy 21)

• Klinefelter's syndrome (XXY karyotype)

• Turner's syndrome (XO karyotype)

• Prader–Willi syndrome (deletion of paternal chromosome 15)

Other causes of diabetes mellitus include:

• Genetic defects in insulin action -

• Type A insulin resistance

• Lipoatrophic diabetes

• Exocrine pancreatic defects -

• Chronic pancreatitis

• Pancreatectomy/trauma

• Neoplasia

• Cystic fibrosis

• Hemochromatosis

• Fibrocalculous pancreatopathy

• Endocrinopathies -

• Acromegaly

• Cushing syndrome

• Hyperthyroidism

• Pheochromocytoma

• Glucagonoma

• Infections -

• Cytomegalovirus

• Coxsackie B virus

• Congenital rubella

questions.question: A pathologist is studying a Congo red-stained slide of pancreatic tissue. He observes it under polarized light and notes the following finding. This finding is commonly associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
The image shows a Congo red-stained biopsy specimen with apple-green birefringence under polarized microscopy. It is indicative of amyloid accumulation within the pancreatic islets. This is commonly associated with type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Amyloid deposition begins in and around capillaries and between cells. In advanced stages, the islets may be virtually obliterated and fibrosis may also be observed.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a detrimental effect of advanced glycation end-products in patients suffering from diabetes mellitus?
options: Deposition of excess basement membrane material due to TGF-β release
Generation of reactive oxygen species in endothelial cells
Increased anticoagulant effect on endothelial cells and macrophages
Increase in vascular smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix
questions.answer: C. Increased anticoagulant effect on endothelial cells and macrophages
questions.explanation:
Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) result in increased procoagulant effects on endothelial cells and macrophages, not anticoagulant effects.

AGEs are formed by nonenzymatic reactions between intracellular glucose-derived dicarbonyl precursors with the amino groups of proteins. They bind to a specific receptor (RAGE) that is expressed on inflammatory cells (macrophages and T cells), endothelium, and vascular smooth muscle.

The detrimental effects of the AGE-RAGE signalling axis within the vascular compartment include:

• Release of cytokines and growth factors, including TGF-β - leads to deposition of excess basement membrane material

• Generation of reactive oxygen species in endothelial cells.

• Increased procoagulant activity on endothelial cells and macrophages.

• Enhanced proliferation of vascular smooth muscle cells and synthesis of extracellular matrix

These effects are responsible for the microvascular and macrovascular complications in diabetes mellitus.

questions.question: What is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm?
questions.explanation:
Insulinoma (β­-cell tumors) is the most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm. It produces sufficient insulin to induce clinically significant hypoglycemia.

The three most common and distinctive clinical syndromes associated with functional pancreatic endocrine neoplasms are as follows:

• Hyperinsulinism

• Zollinger–Ellison syndrome (hypergastrinemia)

• Multiple endocrine neoplasias (MEN)

questions.question: A 39-year-old man was referred to a higher center for further evaluation of peptic ulcer disease refractory to high doses of proton pump inhibitors. There is a history of pituitary and parathyroid tumors in his family members. Serum gastrin level was found to be 1690 pg/ml (normal < 100) and a neuroendocrine tumor is suspected. Which of the following is false about this condition?
options: It is associated with intractable jejunal ulcers
This patient likely has a solitary tumor
Tumors usually originate in Passaro's triangle
questions.answer: B. This patient likely has a solitary tumor
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of a gastrin-producing tumor or gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome). The family history of pituitary and parathyroid tumors is suggestive of MEN1 syndrome. This syndrome is associated with multifocal gastrinomas.

On the other hand, sporadic gastrinomas are usually single.

Gastrinomas usually arise in the duodenum, peripancreatic soft tissues, pancreas. The site of origin is the duodenum when ZES is associated with MEN1. Most tumors are locally invasive and metastasize early.

Hypergastrinemia gives rise to extreme gastric acid secretion and peptic ulceration, that is refractory to proton pump inhibitors. It results in multiple ulcers in duodenum, stomach, and uncommon areas like jejunum.

questions.question: A patient with longstanding diabetes mellitus came with complaints of bulky stools. Ultrasound abdomen showed the presence of multiple gallstones. Hypersecretion of which of the following leads to this presentation?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of a δ-cell tumor or somatostatinoma. It results in hypersecretion of somatostatin.

Somatostatin inhibits pancreatic and biliary secretions. Patients with somatostatinoma usually present with vague abdominal pain along with the triad of:

• Gallstones - due to bile stasis

• Diabetes mellitus - due to inhibition of insulin secretion

• Steatorrhea - due to inhibition of pancreatic exocrine secretion and bile secretion

questions.question: A patient presented with profuse watery diarrhoea and muscle cramps for the past few weeks. The diarrhoea was intractable to antibiotics and stool culture was negative for organisms. He also complained of indigestion and frequent bloating. On investigation, he was found to have microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Serum potassium was 2.4 mmol/L. Upper GI endoscopy was normal. Excess of which of the following hormones leads to this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given scenario is suggestive of WDHA syndrome. It is due to hypersecretion of VIP (vasoactive-intestinal peptide).

WDHA syndrome includes the following features:

• Watery diarrhea

• Hypokalemia (Serum K+< 3.5 mmol/L)

• Achlorhydria (bloating, indigestion, iron deficiency)

Neural crest tumors, such as neuroblastomas, ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuromas, and pheochromocytomas can also be associated with VIPoma syndrome.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism?
questions.explanation:
Graves' disease is the most common cause of endogenous hyperthyroidism.

It is an autoimmune disorder due to the production of TSH-receptor stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI) which cause hyperthyroidism.

It is characterized by the triad of:

• Thyrotoxicosis

• Infiltrative ophthalmopathy (exophthalmos)

• Dermopathy (pretibial myxedema)

Glycosaminoglycan deposition, lymphoid infiltrates, and fatty infiltrates are responsible for ophthalmopathy and dermopathy.

Grossly, there is a diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland and a beefy deep red parenchyma. Histology shows tall crowded follicular cells with scalloped margins and lymphoid infiltrates. Laboratory features include elevations in free T3 and T4 and decreased TSH.

questions.question:
A 32-year-old lady presents with loss of weight, tremors of the hand, and irritability for the past 4-5 months. Examination findings and investigations are given below. All of the following contribute to these eye findings except:

 Parameter
 Values
 Normal values

TSH
 0.2 mIU/L
0.4-4.0 mIU/L

fT4
5.6 ng/dL
 0.7 to 1.9 ng/dL

fT3
 17.4 pmol/l
 4.6 to 9.7 pmol/L
options: Lymphocytic infiltration in the retroorbital space
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the given image showing exophthalmos is suggestive of Graves' ophthalmopathy. Sympathetic overactivity of Muller's muscle results in a wide, staring gaze and lid lag, but not exophthalmos.

Exophthalmos is characterized by abnormal protrusion of the eyeball. It is due to increased volume of the retroorbital connective tissues and extraocular muscles because of:

• Marked lymphocytic infiltration of the retro-orbital space

• Inflammation with edema and swelling of extraocular muscles

• Accumulation of hydrophilic glycosaminoglycans such as hyaluronic acid and chondroitin sulfate

• Increased numbers of adipocytes (fatty infiltration)

questions.question: Which of the following disorders does not lead to hyperthyroidism?
questions.explanation:
Hashimoto thyroiditis is not associated with hyperthyroidism. It is associated with transient thyrotoxicosis, followed by chronic hypothyroidism.

Thyrotoxicosis is a hypermetabolic state caused by elevated circulating levels of free T3 and T4. On the other hand, hyperfunctioning of the thyroid gland itself is referred to as hyperthyroidism.

questions.question: What is the finding seen in the following histopathological examination of a biopsy specimen from a patient with an enlarged thyroid?
options: Dense lymphoid infiltrate with germinal centre
questions.answer: D. Follicular hyperplasia with scalloping colloid
questions.explanation:
The given image shows follicular hyperplasia with a scalloping colloid. The clinical scenario along with the image is suggestive of Graves' disease.

In Graves' disease, the thyroid is diffusely hyperplastic. The follicles are lined by tall columnar epithelial cells that project into lumina. The cells actively resorb the colloid in the center of the follicle which results in a scalloped appearance of the edges of the colloid.

questions.question: A 50-year-old woman presented with diffuse thyroid swelling for the past 6 months. She says that it has increased in size over the last 1 month. Investigations reveal elevated TSH levels. Histopathological examination is done, as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture and image showing Hurthle cells are suggestive of Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

In this condition, the following microscopic features are seen:

• Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well developed germinal centers

• Atrophied thyroid follicles

• The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm (oncocytes)

• This is called oncocytic metaplasia

• These cells are called Hurthle cells

• Ultrastructurally, these cells have numerous mitochondria

Hashimoto's thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease, characterized by the gradual destruction of the thyroid gland leading to thyroid failure. It is commonly seen in women between 45 to 65 years of age. It is caused by the presence of circulating autoantibodies against thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase.

Morphologically, there is a diffuse enlargement of the thyroid gland, with an intact capsule. It is well demarcated from the adjacent structures.

Note: Oncocytes can arise in various tissues and are referred to as follows:

• Hurthle cells/ Ashkenazy cells - thyroid gland

• Oxyphilic cells - parotid gland

• Apocrine metaplasia - breast

questions.question: Which of the following findings will you not observe in a thyroid gland biopsy taken from a patient suffering from Hashimoto thyroiditis?
questions.explanation:
Orphan-Annie eye nuclei are a feature of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, not Hashimoto's thyroiditis.

Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that results in the destruction of the thyroid gland and gradual and progressive thyroid failure.
It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in areas of the world where iodine levels are sufficient.

The thyroid gland is often diffusely enlarged, painless, with some degree of hypothyroidism. This may be preceded by transient thyrotoxicosis (Hashitoxicosis). It is associated with an increased risk of:

• Other autoimmune conditions

• Extranodal marginal zone B-cell lymphomas

• Papillary carcinoma

Histologically, the following findings are seen:

• Intense lymphocytic infiltrate containing small lymphocytes, plasma cells, and well developed germinal centers

• Atrophied thyroid follicles

• The epithelial cells lining the follicles contain eosinophilic granular cytoplasm

• This is called oncocytic metaplasia

• These cells are called Hurthle cells

questions.question: What is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world?
questions.explanation:
Autoimmune hypothyroidism is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient areas of the world.

The thyroid gland is typically enlarged. The circulating autoantibodies found in this disorder are:

• Antimicrosomal antibodies

• Antithyroid peroxidase antibodies

• Antithyroglobulin antibodies

Note: Wolff-Chaikoff effect refers to iodine-induced hypothyroidism.

questions.question: A 48-year-old woman presented with fever, malaise, and painful enlargement of the thyroid gland after a few days following viral fever. On investigation, thyroid antibodies were normal and serum T4 was slightly raised. Which of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical condition is suggestive of subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

It is the most common cause of a painful thyroid. It is also known as painful subacute thyroiditis, de Quervain thyroiditis, or migratory thyroiditis (this is because the pain can shift to different locations in the thyroid).

Option A: Subacute lymphocytic thyroiditis (postpartum thyroiditis) is typically painless. It often occurs after pregnancy and is characterized by lymphocytic inflammation in the thyroid.

Option B: Riedel's thyroiditis is a rare disorder characterized by a painless, rapidly growing thyroid mass with extensive fibrosis involving the thyroid and contiguous neck structures.

Option C: Hashimoto thyroiditis is an autoimmune disease that presents as painless enlargement of the thyroid associated with some degree of hypothyroidism in middle-aged women.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about solitary thyroid nodule is incorrect?
options: They are more common in women
Solitary nodules are more likely to be malignant than are multiple nodules
Nodules in younger patients are less likely to be malignant
questions.answer: D. Nodules in younger patients are less likely to be malignant
questions.explanation:
Nodules in younger patients are more likely to be malignant than those in older patients.

The solitary thyroid nodule is a palpably discrete swelling within an otherwise apparently normal thyroid gland. A higher incidence is seen in areas with endemic iodine deficiency. They are more common in women than in men.

Malignant transformation is more common in:

• Solitary nodules > Multinodular goiter

• Solitary nodules in males > females

• Cold nodules > Hot nodules

However, benign neoplasms are more common than thyroid carcinomas by a ratio of nearly 10:1.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common thyroid cancer?
questions.explanation:
The most common thyroid cancer is papillary carcinoma.
Major subtypes of thyroid carcinoma and their relative frequencies are as follows:

• Papillary carcinoma - most common

• Follicular carcinoma

• Medullary carcinoma

• Anaplastic carcinoma - least common

Thyroid carcinomas are derived from the thyroid follicular epithelium, except medullary carcinoma which is derived from parafollicular C cells.

questions.question: A patient with a long-standing history of thyroglossal cyst develops a neck swelling. The biopsy of the lesion is given below. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given image shows psammoma bodies, which are seen in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. This type of carcinoma is associated with a history of long-standing unresected thyroglossal cyst.

Psammoma bodies are concentrically calcified structures often present within the cores of papillae in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. These structures are almost never found in follicular and medullary carcinomas. They arise from:

• Infarction and dystrophic calcification of papillae tips

• Calcification of intra-lymphatic tumor thrombi.

Psammoma bodies are seen in:

• Papillary carcinoma (thyroid, kidney, endometrium, lungs)

• Prolactinoma

• Meningioma

• Papillary serous cystadenocarcinoma of the ovary

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presented with a solitary, non-tender, firm nodule on the left side of her neck. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits. A fine-needle biopsy revealed malignant cells. The tumor was excised and examined under light microscopy as shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The presence of empty appearing nuclei, also called Orphan Annie eye nuclei as seen in the above image is diagnostic of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid.

Microscopic features of papillary thyroid carcinoma include:

• Branching papillae with fibrovascular stalk

• Covering epithelium is simple or stratified cuboidal

• Orphan Annie eye nuclei -

• Empty-appearing nuclei due to dispersed chromatin

• They are diagnostic, regardless of papillary architecture

• Psammoma bodies - concentric calcified structures

• Foci of lymphatic invasion

Note: Orphan Annie refers to a comic book character with empty appearing eyes, as shown below.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect?
options: It is the most common form of thyroid carcinoma
Diagnosis can be made based on nuclear features, even in the absence of typical architecture
It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation
questions.explanation:
Hematogenous spread is rare in papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Metastases to lymph nodes are more commonly associated with this condition.

It is associated with previous exposure to ionizing radiation. The presence of nuclear features such as Orphan Annie eye nuclei (empty-appearing nuclei) are diagnostic, regardless of papillary architecture.

questions.question: A pathologist is studying the following FNAC from a patient's thyroid nodule. Which is the most common site of metastasis for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The FNAC image is suggestive of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid. Among the given options, the most common site of metastasis is the lungs.

The histological features of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid are:

• Papillary architecture

• Nuclear findings (enough to diagnose the condition even in the absence of papillary architecture)

• Nuclear overlapping, grooving, crowding

• Ground-glass appearance (Orphan Annie eye nuclei)

• Dusty and pale chromatin

• Intranuclear inclusion bodies

The most common mode of spread overall is through the lymphatic route, with lymph node metastases being common at initial presentation.

questions.question:
In patients with papillary carcinoma of the thyroid, which of the following genes may be involved?

1. NTRK1

2. BRAF

3. RET

4. TP53

5. RAS
questions.explanation:
Papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is associated with gain-of-function mutations in the following genes:

• NTRK1 (receptor tyrosine kinase)

• RET (receptor tyrosine kinase)

• BRAF (serine/threonine kinase)

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common variant of papillary thyroid cancer?
questions.explanation:
The most common variant of papillary carcinoma of the thyroid is the follicular variant.

It has the following features:

• Characteristic nuclear features of papillary carcinoma

• Almost entirely follicular architecture

• Can be either -

• Encapsulated - favorable prognosis (or)

• Poorly circumscribed and infiltrative - requires aggressive treatment

The variants of papillary carcinoma include:

Variant

Description

Tall-cell variant

50% of cells with height 2 times the width

Seen in older individuals

Have higher frequencies of vascular invasion

Extrathyroidal extension, and cervical and distant metastases

Diffuse sclerosing variant

In younger individuals, including children

Diffuse fibrosis throughout the gland

Lymph node metastases are present in almost all cases.

Lacks BRAF mutations

Cribriform variant

Associated with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)

Beta-catenin mutation

Columnar-cell variant

Elongated nuclei with pseudostratification of the nuclei

Poor prognosis

Solid variant

More common in children

Associated with Chernobyl nuclear accident

Note: According to the latest WHO classification of thyroid tumors, the non-invasive encapsulated follicular variant of papillary thyroid carcinoma (FVPTC) has been renamed as non-invasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features (NIFTP) to better reflect the indolent course of this tumor. This was done to prevent potential overtreatment and reduce the burden to patients of a cancer diagnosis.

questions.question: Which of the following patients is likely to have the best prognosis?
options: A 30-year-old man with papillary carcinoma thyroid
A 45-year-old woman with follicular carcinoma thyroid
A 78-year-old man with anaplastic carcinoma thyroid
A young man with MEN- II syndrome having medullary carcinoma thyroid
questions.answer: A. A 30-year-old man with papillary carcinoma thyroid
questions.explanation:
Papillary thyroid cancers have the best prognosis, with a 10-year survival rate seen in more than 95% of the patients.

The prognosis of papillary thyroid cancers is dependent on several factors, including age (being less favorable among patients older than 40 years), the presence of extrathyroidal extension, and presence of distant metastases.

The thyroid cancer with the worst prognosis is anaplastic carcinoma.

questions.question: A 56-year-old woman coming from a hilly area presents with a hard swelling in the neck which moves up with deglutition and does not move with protrusion of the tongue. The biopsy of the frozen section is given below. What is your diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario along with the given histopathological image showing uniform sheets of cells with capsular invasion by tumor cells is suggestive of follicular carcinoma thyroid.

The following images show follicular carcinoma of the thyroid.

Option A: In follicular adenoma, there is no capsular invasion.

Option C: Anaplastic carcinoma is associated with rapidly progressive swelling with obstructive features and undifferentiated cells on histopathology.

Option D: In medullary carcinoma, amyloid stroma is seen on histopathology.

questions.question: Which of the following mutations may be found in patients with follicular carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
RAS mutations are associated with follicular carcinoma.

It is also associated with acquired muta­tions in the PIK3CA gene (PI­3K/AKT arm of the receptor tyrosine kinase signaling pathway) and the PAX8-PPARG fusion gene.

questions.question: A middle-aged woman presents with thyroid swelling. The histology of the swelling is as shown below. Investigations reveal elevated calcitonin levels. Which of the following is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario and histological appearance showing amyloid stroma are suggestive of medullary carcinoma of the thyroid. This condition can occur in the setting of MEN2A (Sipple syndrome) or MEN2B.

Medullary carcinomas of the thyroid are neuroendocrine neoplasms derived from the parafollicular cells or C cells of the thyroid. They may be:

• Sporadic (70%)

• Familial or associated with MEN2 syndromes (30%) -

• More aggressive and metastasize more frequently than sporadic

• Usually bilateral and multicentric

Both forms can be associated with RET mutations.

These tumors may present with:

• Mass in the neck

• Dysphagia

• Hoarseness

• Diarrhea due to the secretion of VIP

• Cushing's syndrome due to ACTH secretion

Histopathology shows polygonal to spindle-shaped cells, which may form nests, trabeculae, and even follicles. Acellular amyloid deposits derived from calcitonin polypeptides are present in the stroma. These lesions secrete calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents to the OPD with rapid weight gain and easy bruisability over the past 1 month. She was started on oral prednisolone for dermatomyositis 2 months ago. On examination, moon facies and abdominal striae are noted. Her BP is 160/110 mm Hg. Which of the following pathological changes is seen in this condition?
options: Corticotroph cells with homogenous and pale cytoplasm
Accumulation of keratin filaments in adrenal cells
Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells
Basophilic nuclear inclusion bodies in corticotroph cells
questions.answer: A. Corticotroph cells with homogenous and pale cytoplasm
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome. In this condition, the normal basophilic cytoplasm of the corticotrophs of anterior pituitary becomes homogeneous and pale. This is termed the Crooke hyaline change and is due to the accumulation of intermediate keratin filaments in the cytoplasm.

This change occurs due to high levels of circulating glucocorticoids in Cushing's syndrome.

Based on the cause of Cushing's syndrome, the following pathological changes are seen in the adrenals:

• Iatrogenic - atrophy of zona fasciculata and zona reticularis (as zona glomerulosa functions independently of ACTH)

• ACTH-dependent - diffuse hyperplasia (due to high ACTH levels)

• ACTH-independent - nodular hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma

Note: Eosinophilic inclusion bodies in adrenal cells are called spironolactone bodies. They are seen in Conn's syndrome.

questions.question: What is the most common clinical feature of Cushing syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Obesity is the most common clinical feature of Cushing's syndrome.

Clinical features of Cushing’s syndrome are attributed to the glucocorticoid, mineralocorticoid, and sex steroid actions of cortisol. They include:

System
Clinical features

Body fat

• Central or truncal obesity (most common)

• Buffalo hump (fat deposition behind the neck)

• Moon facies

Skin

• Purple striae (over abdomen & flanks)

• Acne and Hirsutism

• Easy bruising

• Facial plethora

• Hyperpigmentation

Musculoskeletal

• Proximal myopathy

• Osteoporosis

Metabolic

• Poorly controlled hyperglycemia

• Dyslipidemia

Reproductive

• Oligomenorrhea

• Amenorrhea

Renal

• Hypokalemic alkalosis

CVS

• Atherosclerosis

• Diastolic Hypertension

• Edema

Hematologic

• Hypercoagulable state

• Lymphopenia

• Neutrophilia

• Eosinopenia

CNS

• Depression

• Psychosis

• Anxiety

questions.question: A 27-year-old woman is brought to the casualty with severe abdominal pain, diarrhea, and dizziness for the past 3 days. On examination, the following findings are noted. Blood pressure is 80/50 mm Hg and blood glucose is 48 mg/dl. Which of the following would you expect in this patient?
options: High ACTH and low renin levels
High ACTH and high renin levels
Low ACTH and normal renin levels
Low ACTH and low renin levels
questions.answer: B. High ACTH and high renin levels
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and the image showing hyperpigmentation of palmar creases and oral mucosa are suggestive of primary adrenal insufficiency. It presents with low aldosterone, high renin, and high ACTH levels.

In primary adrenal insufficiency, lack of aldosterone production results in compensatory rise in ACTH and renin levels. The high ACTH results in hyperpigmentation. The most common causes are autoimmune in developed countries and tuberculosis in developing countries.

In secondary adrenal insufficiency, there is pituitary dysfunction leading to low ACTH levels. Renin and aldosterone levels are normal, as they function independently of ACTH.

questions.question: A 6-year-old boy was referred with fever, altered sensorium, and non-blanching rash for the past 2 days. He developed rapidly progressive shock and DIC. Despite resuscitation measures, he died. The following appearance of his adrenals was noted on autopsy. All of the following can cause this condition except:
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing bilateral adrenal hemorrhage are suggestive of Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Neisseria gonorrhoeae is not a cause of this condition.

It is caused by highly virulent organisms such as:

• Neisseria meningitidis or meningococci (classically)

• Streptococcus pneumoniae or pneumococci

• Pseudomonas aeruginosa

• Haemophilus influenzae

• Staphylococcus species

This condition is more common in children. Overwhelming bacterial infection leads to bilateral adrenal hemorrhage, thereby causing acute adrenal insufficiency. This is likely a result of direct bacterial seeding of small vessels and endothelial dysfunction caused by microbial products and inflammatory mediators.

It usually presents with rapidly progressive hypotension and shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) with widespread purpura. Without prompt recognition and treatment, death occurs within hours to a few days.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism?
questions.explanation:
Bilateral nodular hyperplasia of the adrenal glands is the most common cause of primary hyperaldosteronism.

Adrenal adenoma is the second most common cause. It is usually solitary, but multiple adenomas may occur occasionally. Other rare causes include:

• Ectopic aldosterone-producing tumors

• Familial idiopathic hyperaldosteronism - due to germline mutations of KCNJ5 (encodes a potassium channel)

questions.question: What is the underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome?
questions.explanation:
The underlying pathology in patients with Conn's syndrome is adrenal adenoma.

Hyperaldosteronism may be primary or secondary.

Primary hyperaldosteronism is due to autonomous overproduction of aldosterone with resultant suppression of RAAS. It can occur due to adrenal hyperplasia, adenoma, or carcinoma. It presents with the following features:

• Hypertension (most common)

• Hypokalemia

• Metabolic alkalosis

• Polyuria (due to ANP)

• Polydipsia (due to polyuria)

• Muscle weakness

It is confirmed by elevated ratios of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity (PAC / PRA).

When primary hyperaldosteronism is due to an aldosterone-secreting adenoma, it is called Conn syndrome. Patients are usually treated with spironolactone followed by surgical removal of adenoma. In patients treated with spironolactone, the adenomas contain eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions called spironolactone bodies.

In secondary hyperaldosteronism, aldosterone release occurs in response to the activation of the renin-angiotensin system (RAAS).

questions.question: Patients with which of the following conditions are not at risk of developing adrenocortical carcinoma?
questions.explanation:
MEN2B syndrome is associated with pheochromocytoma and medullary carcinoma of thyroid, not adrenocortical carcinoma.

Adrenocortical carcinoma is associated with the following hereditary cancer syndromes:

• Li–Fraumeni syndrome - due to germline TP53 mutations

• Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome - a disorder of epigenetic imprinting

• MEN1 syndrome - due to mutations of MEN1 gene

questions.question: A 7-year-old boy is brought for the evaluation of recurrent seizures over the last 3 months. Past history is significant for chronic oral candidiasis for 2 years. On examination, nail dystrophy is noted. Further investigation reveals serum calcium of 6.9 mg/dl and prolonged QT interval. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of autoimmune polyendocrinopathy (APS) type 1. It is also called APECED (autoimmune polyendocrinopathy, candidiasis, and ectodermal dystrophy).

It is caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene. This gene usually increases tolerance of central T-cells to peripheral tissue antigens. When this function is lost, the T-cells become more prone to mount immune reactions against tissue antigens, promoting autoimmunity. These patients develop autoantibodies against IL-17 and IL-22, which are crucial for defense against fungal infections.

It presents in childhood with the following features:

• Chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis

• Ectodermal dystrophy (abnormalities of the skin, dental enamel, and nails)

• Organ-specific autoimmune disorders such as -

• Autoimmune adrenalitis

• Autoimmune hypoparathyroidism

• Idiopathic hypogonadism

• Pernicious anemia

Autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome (APS) type 2 usually presents in early adulthood as a combination of the following:

• Adrenal insufficiency

• Autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes

questions.question: A 24-year-old woman presented with recurrent episodes of palpitations, headaches, and sweating. Her BP was 155/95 mm Hg and HR was 135/min. Investigations revealed elevated 24-hour urinary metanephrines and a right adrenal mass on CT abdomen. She should be examined for the presence of all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of pheochromocytoma. This patient does not need to be examined for a shagreen patch. It is a feature of tuberous sclerosis syndrome, which is not associated with pheochromocytoma.

Familial syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma are:

Syndrome
Clinical manifestations

Neurofibromatosis

Café-au-lait spots

Axillary and inguinal freckling

Optic nerve glioma

Lisch nodules

von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome

Hemangioblastomas

Renal cell carcinoma

Pancreatic endocrine neoplasms

MEN2A syndrome

Medullary thyroid carcinoma

Parathyroid hyperplasia

MEN 2B syndrome

Medullary thyroid carcinoma

Marfanoid habitus

Mucocutaneous ganglioneuromatosis

Even patients with no family history must be evaluated for findings of these genetic syndromes, as they may occur sporadically in some cases.

questions.question: Which of the following is most commonly involved in Wermer syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common manifestation of Wermer’s syndrome or MEN-1 syndrome.

MEN1 syndrome is due to germline mutations in the MEN1 tumor-suppressor gene, which encodes a protein called menin. The most commonly secreted products are pancreatic polypeptides.

questions.question: Which of the following is an indicator of malignant transformation in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.explanation:
The definitive diagnosis of malignancy in pheochromocytomas is based exclusively on the presence of metastases to regional lymph nodes as well as distant sites like liver, lung, and bone.

Capsular and vascular invasion may be encountered even in benign lesions. Malignant pheochromocytomas are histologically and biochemically the same as benign ones. Hence, typical histological criteria like cellular atypia, mitotic spindles, and vascular invasion are insufficient to confirm malignancy in pheochromocytomas.

questions.question: A pathologist is studying the following slide from the biopsy of a patient with an abdominal mass. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given histopathology slide shows nests of cells arranged in an organoid pattern, with fibrovascular septae, and finely granular cytoplasm. This is called the zellballen pattern. It is typically seen in paragangliomas and pheochromocytomas.

Paragangliomas are benign neuroendocrine tumors arising from paraganglia in the neck or abdomen. They are composed of chief and sustentacular cells arranged in an organoid pattern.

questions.question: A 38-year-old woman was being evaluated for persistent hypertension. Workup revealed a tumor located near the bifurcation of the aorta. Surgical excision was done and HPE examination revealed a zellballen pattern of cells. Where did this tumor likely originate from?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of a paraganglioma (ectopic pheochromocytoma) located in the abdomen. They commonly arise from the organ of Zuckerkandl, located at the bifurcation of the aorta. It is part of the vertebral paraganglia (clusters of chromaffin cells along the autonomic nerve chains).

Other sites of origin of paragangliomas include:

• Urinary bladder - rarely

• Carotid and aortic bodies

• Ganglion nodosum of the vagus nerve

• Jugulotympanic ganglia

questions.question: What mutation is likely to be seen in patients with familial paraganglioma syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Familial paraganglioma is most likely associated with mutations in the SDH (succinate dehydrogenase) gene.

The SDH complex is involved in mitochondrial electron transport and oxygen sensing. It is believed that SDH mutations also lead to the upregulation of HIF-1α, which is a key oncogenic driver in this type of tumor.

questions.question: A 21-year-old young man presents with a neck mass. Past history is significant for surgical removal of a pheochromocytoma 6 months ago. On examination, a marfanoid habitus is noted along with the following finding. Which of the following should the patient be screened for?
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario and image showing mucosal neuromas are suggestive of MEN2B syndrome. This condition is associated with medullary carcinoma of the thyroid.

The MEN syndromes are a group of inherited diseases of multiple endocrine organs. Tumors occur at a younger age than sporadic tumors, either synchronously (at the same time) or metachronously (at different times).

MEN2 syndrome occurs due to abnormal activation of the RET gene. Medullary carcinoma is seen in both MEN 2A and 2B syndromes. However, it tends to be more aggressive and metastasizes more frequently in MEN2B syndrome.

Note: RET gene is deactivated in Hirschsprung disease.

questions.question: What gene is mutated in polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Polycythemia paraganglioma syndrome occurs due to germline mutations in the EPAS1 gene. This syndrome presents with neuroendocrine tumors and early-onset polycythemia.

RET gene mutation is seen in MEN2A and MEN2B syndromes.

SDHD and SDHB mutations are seen in hereditary paraganglioma 1 and hereditary paraganglioma 4 syndromes respectively.

topics.topic: Bone, Joint, Soft Tissue and Skin

chapters.chapter: Developmental Disorders,Infections And Tumors Of Bone

questions.question: What are the specialized multinucleated macrophages in bone called?
questions.explanation:
Osteoclasts are specialized multinucleated macrophages derived from circulating monocytes that are responsible for bone resorption.

Osteocytes are formed when osteoblasts are embedded in the matrix within lacunae and canaliculi. They control calcium and phosphate levels in the microenvironment.

Osteoblasts are mesenchymal cells that rim the bony spicule, responsible for bone synthesis and mineralization.

Chondrocytes are specialized cells that produce and maintain the extracellular matrix of cartilage.

The image given below shows different cells present in a bone.

questions.question: Which of the following is not a marker of bone resorption?
questions.explanation:
Osteocalcin is not a bone resorption marker.

It is a protein secreted only by osteoblasts. Thus, it is a bone formation marker (osteoblastic marker).

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common benign bone tumor?
questions.explanation:
Osteochondroma, also known as exostosis, is the most common benign bone tumor.

It is a benign cartilage-capped tumor. 85% of osteochondromas are solitary. The remainder is seen as part of the multiple hereditary exostosis syndromes, an autosomal-dominant hereditary disease.

Lesions arise from the metaphysis near the growth plate of long tubular bones, especially near the knee. They are either sessile or pedunculated and range in size from 1 to 20 cm. Histologically, the cap is composed of benign hyaline cartilage varying in thickness and is covered peripherally by perichondrium.

Osteochondromas can progress to chondrosarcoma.

The image below shows the histopathological specimen of osteochondroma, displaying a cartilage cap lined by perichondrium contiguous with mature bone.

questions.question: A woman delivered a child who died a few minutes after birth. The infant was found to have blue sclera and fractures of the right humerus, ulna, and femur at birth. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteogenesis imperfecta type II.

The type II variant of osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is uniformly fatal in utero or during the perinatal period. Type II OI is characterized by extraordinary bone fragility with multiple intrauterine fractures.

Osteogenesis imperfecta (brittle bone disease) is caused by deficiencies in the synthesis of type I collagen. It can be separated into four major clinical subtypes that vary widely in severity. The severity of the disease is based on the location of the mutation within the protein.

Individuals with type I OI have a normal life span, but experience childhood fractures that decrease in frequency following puberty.

questions.question: A 29-year-old woman gives birth to an infant with less than 5th percentile length. The head and torso are of normal size but extremities are short. The head circumference is at the 95th percentile, and frontal bossing is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This given clinical scenario is suggestive of achondroplasia.

Achondroplasia is the most common skeletal dysplasia and a major cause of dwarfism. It has autosomal dominant inheritance.

It occurs due to the gain of mutation in fibroblast growth factor receptor (FGFR3). This leads to abnormal cartilage proliferation at growth plates and affects endochondral bone growth. Infants present with:

• Short stature

• Rhizomelic shortening of limbs

• Frontal bossing

• Midface deficiency

The condition is not associated with changes in longevity, intelligence, or reproductive status.

The image below shows a baby affected with achondroplasia. Note the prominent forehead, triangular face, and body asymmetry in the image (a); a low nasal bridge in the image (b); trident hands in the image (c); and scoliosis in the image (d).

questions.question: Which of the following is also called marble bone disease?
questions.explanation:
Albers-Schönberg disease or osteopetrosis is also known as marble bone disease.

The term osteopetrosis reflects the stone-like quality of the bones. The bones are abnormally brittle and fracture easily, like a piece of chalk. It occurs due to reduced bone resorption and diffuse symmetric skeletal sclerosis because of impaired formation or function of osteoclasts.

Note: Osteogenesis imperfecta is also called brittle bone disease. Paget's disease is also called osteitis deformans; it presents with mosaic pattern of lamellar bone.

questions.question: An infant is being evaluated for multiple fractures over the last 3 months. On examination, hydrocephaly, cranial nerve defects, and hepatosplenomegaly are noted. Imaging reveals generalized sclerosis and a bone-in-bone appearance. Which of the following is the most likely enzyme to be deficient in this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteopetrosis. It occurs due to autosomal recessive defects in the gene for the enzyme carbonic anhydrase II.

Carbonic anhydrase II is required by osteoclasts and renal tubular cells to generate protons from carbon dioxide and water (acidification). The absence of carbonic anhydrase II prevents osteoclasts from acidifying the resorption pit and dissolution of calcium hydroxyapatite within the bone matrix. It also blocks the acidification of urine by the renal tubular cells. This leads to reduced bone resorption and diffuse symmetric skeletal sclerosis.

Due to deficient osteoclast activity, bones involved by osteopetrosis lack a medullary canal giving it a bone-in-bone appearance. The ends of long bones are bulbous (Erlenmeyer flask deformity) and misshapen. The neural foramina are small and compress the exiting nerves, leading to cranial nerve palsies.

Extensive extramedullary hematopoiesis leads to leukopenia and prominent hepatosplenomegaly. As carbonic anhydrase II is widely expressed, mutations of this gene result in a condition called marble brain disease or Guibaud-Vainsel syndrome.

questions.question: A 60-year-old postmenopausal woman presents with sudden severe back pain. There is no history of trauma. X-ray findings are given below. MRI shows thinning of trabecular plates of the vertebrae and vertebral collapse. Levels of which of the following will be increased in her condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteoporosis. Cytokines stimulate osteoclast recruitment and activity in osteoporosis by increasing the levels of RANKL.

RANKL helps in diminishing the expression of osteoprotegerin (OPG), increasing osteoclast proliferation, and preventing osteoclast apoptosis.

Decreased estrogen levels after menopause actually increase both bone resorption and formation. However, the latter does not keep up with the former, leading to a high turnover. Decreased estrogen appears to increase the secretion of inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-1.

questions.question: In patients with which of the following conditions will you see a histologically normal bone?
questions.explanation:
Histologically normal bone with decreased density is the hallmark feature of osteoporosis.

In advanced osteoporosis, both the trabecular bone of the medulla and the cortical bone are markedly thinned leading to progressive microfractures.

Option A: Inadequate mineralization in osteomalacia leads to a thickened osteoid matrix.

Option C: Paget's disease presents with a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone.

Option D: Dissecting osteitis cystica is seen in severe hyperparathyroidism.

questions.question: A patient presents with back pain, recurrent headaches, and increasing head size. On evaluation, raised alkaline phosphatase and a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone is seen. Which of the following statements is false about this condition?
options: It occurs due to mutations in the SQSTM1 gene
It is polyostotic in about 15% of cases
Sarcoma occurs in less than 1% of all individuals
questions.answer: C. It is polyostotic in about 15% of cases
questions.explanation:
Paget disease is monostotic in about 15% of cases and polyostotic in the rest of them.

Paget disease (osteitis deformans) is a disorder of increased, but disordered and structurally unsound, bone mass. The onset is in late adulthood (average age at diagnosis, 70 years).

It occurs due to mutations in the SQSTM1 gene. This increases the activity of NF-κB, which then increases osteoclast activity.

Three sequential phases exist:

• Initial osteolytic stage

• Mixed osteoclastic-osteoblastic stage

• Final burned-out quiescent osteosclerotic stage

The axial skeleton or proximal femur is involved in up to 80% of the cases. The typical x-ray findings are as follows:

• Enlargement of the craniofacial skeleton: leontiasis ossea or lion face

• Invagination of the skull base (platybasia)

• Chalk stick-type fractures in the long bones of the lower extremities

The pathological hallmark is a mosaic pattern of lamellar bone, seen in the sclerotic phase as shown below. It shows a jigsaw-like pattern produced by unusually prominent cement lines, which join haphazardly oriented units of lamellar bone.

Laboratory findings show elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and urinary hydroxyproline (normal serum calcium and phosphorus).

Following tumors can develop in the affected bones in Paget's disease:

• Benign tumors -

• Giant cell tumors

• Giant cell reparative granuloma

• Extra-osseous masses of hematopoietic tissue

• Sarcoma (osteosarcoma or fibrosarcoma) - most dreaded complication. Occurs in < 1 % of all individuals with Paget disease, and in 5% to 10% of those with the severe polyostotic disease.

questions.question: In patients with hyperparathyroidism, which of the following is least expected?
questions.explanation:
Osteopetrosis does not belong to the clinical spectrum of hyperparathyroidism.

The features of hyperparathyroidism are as follows:

• Osteitis fibrosa cystica

• Osteopenia/osteoporosis

• Hyperuricemia and gout

• Pseudogout

• Increased production of calcitriol

• Dissecting osteitis and brown tumors

• Nephrolithiasis

• Hypophosphatemia

• Anemia

Hyperparathyroidism leads to significant skeletal changes related to unabated osteoclast activity. Increased osteoclast activity is most prominent in cortical bone, but the medullary bone is not spared. Osteoclasts may tunnel into and dissect centrally along the length of the trabeculae, creating the appearance of railroad tracks, diagnostic of dissecting osteitis. Generalised osteoporosis may be seen in the phalanges, vertebrae, and proximal femur.

Brown tumor presents with bone loss leading to microfractures and secondary hemorrhages which causes influx of macrophages and ingrowth of reparative fibrous tissue. Generalized osteitis presents with increased bone cell activity, peri-trabecular fibrosis, and cystic brown tumors.

questions.question: A 7-year-old child presented with fever, pain, and swelling around the knee joint for 3 days. Lab investigations showed a WBC count of 23,500/mm3. An MRI was done, which demonstrated an intramedullary abscess of the proximal tibia. Which of the following is the most common causative organism of this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical picture is suggestive of acute pyogenic osteomyelitis. Staphylococcus aureus is the most common cause of culture-positive pyogenic osteomyelitis.

Osteomyelitis denotes inflammation of bone and marrow, almost always secondary to infection. Organisms may reach the bone by

1. Hematogenous spread

2. Extension from a contiguous site

3. Direct implantation

The common causative organisms include:

• Staphylococcus aureus - the most common cause overall

• Pseudomonas aeruginosa - most common cause in IV drug abusers

• Salmonella - common in patients of sickle cell anemia

• Haemophilus influenzae - was a common causative organism in children, less common now due to vaccination

• Streptococcus pyogenes - most common in neonates

• Escherichia coli, Klebsiella- most common cause in patients with genitourinary tract infections

questions.question: Patients with sickle cell disease are particularly susceptible to osteomyelitis caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Salmonella enteritidis is commonly implicated in osteomyelitis in patients with sickle cell anemia.

The common causative organisms include:

• Staphylococcus aureus - the most common cause overall

• Pseudomonas aeruginosa - most common cause in IV drug abusers

• Salmonella - most common in patients of sickle cell anemia

• Haemophilus influenzae - was a common causative organism in children, less common now due to vaccination

• Streptococcus pyogenes - neonates

• Escherichia coli, Klebsiella- most common cause in patients with genitourinary tract infections

questions.question: A patient who is a known case of TB presents to the orthopedic OPD with a 4-month history of progressively worsening back pain. He also complains of fatigue and irregular fever for 2 weeks. X-ray reveals lytic destruction of the anterior portion of the vertebral body and increased anterior wedging. All of the following are the complications of his condition except
questions.explanation:
The patient is most likely suffering from TB osteomyelitis. Brodie's abscess is not a complication of this condition.

In tuberculous osteomyelitis, weight-bearing joints - spine (Pott's disease), hips, and knees, are most commonly affected.

Complications of tuberculous osteomyelitis include:

• Scoliosis or kyphosis (gibbus)

• Neurologic deficits secondary to spinal cord and nerve compression leading to paraplegia -

• Tuberculous arthritis

• Sinus tract formation

• Psoas abscess - may be due to paravertebral “cold” abscess

• AA amyloidosis

questions.question: A 25-year-old man presents with back pain that is unresponsive to aspirin. Radiographs show a well-demarcated lesion in the posterior spine. A biopsy is done and the histopathological finding is given below. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteoblastoma.

Histopathology shows well-circumscribed lesions composed of randomly interconnecting trabeculae of woven bone that are prominently rimmed by a single layer of osteoblasts. Stroma surrounding the neoplastic bone consists of loose connective tissue that contains many dilated and congested capillaries.

The image below shows the histopathological findings in osteoblastoma.

Osteoid osteoma and osteoblastoma are benign bone-producing tumors that have identical histologic features. The differentiating features between them are given below:

Osteoid osteoma
Osteoblastoma

Less than 2 cm in diameter
Larger than 2 cm in diameter

Predilection for the appendicular skeleton

involves the posterior spine (laminae and pedicles)

Thick rind of reactive cortical bone is seen on radiography

Usually, no marked bony reaction is seen on radiography

Pain that is relieved by aspirin and other non-steroidal anti-inflammatory agents

Pain which is unresponsive to aspirin

questions.question: A 17-year-old man presents with progressive swelling of the upper end of the humerus. He also complains of arm pain and weight loss for 3 months. X-ray findings are given below. Which of the following is associated with a higher risk of developing this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given history and classic sunburst appearance on the X-ray are highly suggestive of osteosarcoma. Mutation of p53 (Li-Fraumeni syndrome) is associated with a greater risk of sarcomas, particularly osteosarcoma.

The image given below shows sunburst pattern seen in osteosarcoma.

Option A: Translocation (X;18) is characteristic of synovial sarcoma.

Option B: Translocation (12;16) is characteristic of myxoid liposarcoma.

Option D: 1p rearrangements are characteristic of conventional chondrosarcoma.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false about osteosarcoma?
options: It usually arises in the diaphyseal region of long bones
It has a bimodal age distribution
Codman triangle is characteristic of the tumor
Most common subtype is osteoblastic and high grade
