questions.answer: A. It usually arises in the diaphyseal region of long bones
questions.explanation:
Osteosarcomas usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the long bones of the extremities. It commonly occurs in the knee (i.e., distal femur or proximal tibia).

The most common subtype is primary, intramedullary, osteoblastic, and high grade. It is a malignant tumor in which the cancerous cells produce an osteoid matrix or mineralized bone. It occurs in all age groups but has a bimodal age distribution.

The formation of fine lace-like neoplastic bone by the tumor cells is diagnostic histopathologically of osteosarcoma as shown below.

Radiography shows a large destructive, mixed lytic and blastic mass with infiltrative margins, which breaks through the cortex and lifts the periosteum, resulting in reactive periosteal bone formation. The triangular shadow between the cortex and raised ends of the periosteum, known radiographically as the Codman triangle, is characteristic of osteosarcoma. This is shown in the radiograph below.

questions.question: Which of the following bone tumors is characteristically seen in patients with Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome?
questions.explanation:
Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are nonhereditary disorders characterized by multiple enchondromas. Maffucci syndrome is, in addition, distinguished by the presence of spindle-cell hemangiomas.

Enchondromas are benign tumors of hyaline cartilage that usually occur in bones of enchondral origin. They are usually diagnosed in individuals 20 to 50 years of age. They present as solitary metaphyseal lesions of tubular bones of the hands and feet.

The radiographic features consist of circumscribed lucencies with central irregular calcifications, a sclerotic rim, and an intact cortex. They are usually smaller than 3 cm. They are gray-blue and translucent, composed of well-circumscribed nodules of hyaline cartilage containing cytomorphologically benign chondrocytes.

The enchondromas in Ollier disease and Maffucci syndrome are sometimes more cellular than sporadic enchondromas and exhibit cytologic atypia, making them more difficult to distinguish from chondrosarcomas.

The image below displays the histopathological picture of an enchondroma showing lobules of hyaline cartilage encased by bone and covered by perichondrium (fibrous tissue).

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about chondrosarcoma?
options: Conventional central tumors constitute about 90% of chondrosarcomas.
Clear cell and the mesenchymal variants occur in older patients.
Chondrosarcomas commonly arise in the axial skeleton.
In multiple hereditary exostosis, osteochondromas progress to chondrosarcoma.
questions.answer: B. Clear cell and the mesenchymal variants occur in older patients.
questions.explanation:
The clear cell and the mesenchymal variants of chondrosarcoma occur in younger patients (teens or 20s).

Chondrosarcomas are malignant tumors that produce cartilage. They commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs.

They are subclassified histologically as following variants:

• Conventional (hyaline cartilage producing) - 90% cases

• Clear cell

• Dedifferentiated

• Mesenchymal

In multiple hereditary exostosis, osteochondromas can progress to chondrosarcoma. Increased thickness of the cartilage cap has been reported as an indicator of potential malignancy. The average age of secondary chondrosarcoma is younger than patients with primary tumors.

questions.question:
Which of the following can progress to become chondrosarcoma?

1. Osteochondroma

2. Multiple enchondromas

3. Synovial chondromatosis

4. Chondromyxoid fibroma

5. Solitary chondroma
questions.explanation:
Osteochondromas, multiple enchondromas, and synovial chondromatosis can progress to become chondrosarcoma.

The average age of patients with secondary chondrosarcoma is 35 years (less than that of those with primary tumors). These tumors most commonly affect the pelvic bones. The increased thickness of the cartilage cap (normally 1–3 mm) is considered an indicator of potential malignancy.

Multiple enchondromas in the setting of Ollier’s disease or Maffucci's syndrome carry a significantly higher risk of transformation to secondary chondrosarcoma than solitary enchondromas. Histological findings of abundant myxoid change, cyst formation, and permeation of existing trabeculae suggest malignancy.

Secondary malignancy in synovial chondromatosis has been reported, but it is rare.

questions.question: A plain radiograph of a patient shows a destructive lytic tumor that extends into the surrounding soft tissues with a characteristic onion-skin appearance. A biopsy image is shown below. Which of the following is not true about the tumor?
options: It is the second most common group of bone sarcomas in children
It arises in the epiphysis of long tubular bones
Most of these tumours contain a (11;22) (q24;q12) translocation
The amount of chemotherapy-induced necrosis is an important prognostic finding
questions.answer: B. It arises in the epiphysis of long tubular bones
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Ewing sarcoma. It arises in the diaphysis of long bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis.

Ewing sarcoma follows osteosarcoma as the second most common group of bone sarcomas in children. It generally affects patients < 20 years. Boys are affected slightly more frequently than girls. Usually, the tumor arises in the diaphysis of long tubular bones, especially the femur and the flat bones of the pelvis.

Fever, elevated sedimentation rate, anemia, and leukocytosis may be seen. Plain radiographs show a destructive lytic tumor with permeative margins that extend into the surrounding soft tissues. The characteristic periosteal reaction produces layers of reactive bone deposited in an onion-skin fashion. It arises in the medullary cavity and usually invades the cortex, periosteum, and soft tissue.

On microscopy, sheets of uniform, small, round cells with scant cytoplasm are seen, which may appear clear because they are rich in glycogen. The presence of Homer–Wright rosettes indicates a greater degree of neuroectodermal differentiation.

The image given below shows the histopathological findings in Ewing sarcoma.

Most Ewing sarcoma family tumors contain an (11;22) (q24;q12) translocation. Variant translocations fuse the EWS to other members of the ETS transcription factor family. CD99(MIC2), FLI1, and NSE would be positive in ES/PNET.

questions.question: A 30-year-old woman presents with a 1-month history of pain in the left knee, which is tender on palpation. X-ray shows a 5 cm mass in the distal femoral epiphysis, with a soap bubble appearance. Microscopy is as seen below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of osteoclastoma/ giant-cell tumor (GCT) of bone.

GCT is a relatively uncommon benign, but locally aggressive, neoplasm that usually arises in individuals in their 20s to 40s. The neoplastic cells express high levels of RANKL. It promotes the proliferation of osteoclast precursors and their differentiation into mature osteoclasts via RANK expressed by these cells.

GCTs arise in the epiphysis but may extend into the metaphysis. The majority arise around the knee (distal femur and proximal tibia). Most are solitary, multicentric tumors in the distal extremities. The tumors destroy the overlying cortex, producing a bulging soft tissue mass delineated by a thin shell of reactive tissue.

Histopathologically, sheets of uniform oval mononuclear cells and numerous osteoclast-type giant cells are seen with 100 or more nuclei. Necrosis and mitotic activity may be prominent.

The image given below shows the histopathological findings seen in osteoclastoma.

Typically, they are treated with curettage, but 40% to 60% recur locally.

Up to 4% of tumors metastasize to the lungs, but these sometimes spontaneously regress and they are rarely fatal. The RANKL inhibitor, denosumab, has shown promise as adjuvant therapy in GCT.

 Note: The E mnemonic for GCT:

• Epiphyseal

• Eccentric

• Egg-shell crackling

• Expansile

questions.question: A 19-year old man presents with back pain for 2 months. MRI of the spine reveals a bony cystic mass at the L1 vertebra. Biopsy shows multiple, blood-filled cystic spaces separated by septae, composed of multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells and reactive woven bone. There is no cartilage or necrosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of an aneurysmal bone cyst.

It affects all age groups, but generally occurs during the first 2 decades of life and has no sex predilection. It usually occurs in the metaphysis of long bones and the posterior elements of vertebral bodies.

This is a tumor characterized by multiloculated blood-filled cystic spaces separated by septae, composed of multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells and reactive woven bone. Radiographically, an aneurysmal bone cyst is seen as an eccentric, expansile, lesion with well-defined margins. Most lesions are completely lytic and often contain a thin shell of reactive bone at the periphery.

The spindle cells of aneurysmal bone cyst frequently demonstrate rearrangements of chromosome 17p13, leading to USP6 overexpression.

The majority of secondary aneurysmal bone cysts arise in association with:

• Benign neoplasms

• Giant-cell tumor of the bone (most common)

• Chondroblastoma

• Osteoblastoma

• Fibrous dysplasia

• Osteosarcoma

questions.question: A 60-year-old patient complains of severe back pain for 2 months, which worsens at night. An MRI shows multiple osteoblastic secondaries on the vertebrae. Which of the following tumors could be the primary source of these lesions?
questions.explanation:
Prostatic adenocarcinoma is associated with predominantly osteoblastic secondaries to the bones (vertebral column).

The radiographic appearance of bone metastases may be purely lytic (bone destroying), purely blastic (bone-forming), or mixed lytic and blastic. Most cancers are associated with predominantly one pattern or the other.

Parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) and transforming growth factor-β (TGF-β) are implicated in osteolytic secondaries, while proteins such as endothelin-1 and morphogenetic proteins are implicated in osteoblastic lesions.

questions.question: A 77-year-old woman presents with pain and limited movement of the left hip and knee for 10 years. The pain has increased in severity in the past 1 year. The x-ray of the hip is given below. Laboratory tests do not show RF or ANA in her serum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The x-ray image of the hip shows narrowing of the joint space and subchondral sclerosis which is diagnostic of osteoarthritis (OA), also called degenerative joint disease.

OA is the most common type of joint disease, which is characterized by the degeneration of joint cartilage. This results in structural and functional failure of synovial joints. Osteoarthritis can be classified into 2 types:

• Primary OA: Insidious onset, without apparent initiating cause, as an aging phenomenon

• Secondary OA: Predisposing conditions such as joint deformity, a previous joint injury, or an underlying systemic disease such as diabetes, ochronosis, hemochromatosis, or marked obesity.

The knees and hands are more commonly affected in women and the hips in men. OA lesions occur due to the degeneration of the articular cartilage and its disordered repair. Inflammatory cells are sparse, but cytokines and diffusible factors, particularly TGF-β (which induces matrix metalloproteinases), TNF, prostaglandins, and nitric oxide, have been implicated in OA.

questions.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with complaints of joint pain and progressive loss of joint motion. On examination, symmetric joint swelling of the hands is seen. A subcutaneous nodule is seen over her right forearm. Microscopy of the excised nodule shows the findings given in the image below. Which of the following lab findings will be seen in this patient?
options: Uric acid crystals in joint aspirate
Calcium pyrophosphate crystals in joint aspirate
questions.answer: C. Serum positive for rheumatoid factor
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of rheumatoid arthritis. The patient's serum will test positive for rheumatoid factor.

Microscopy of the excised nodule shows a necrotizing granuloma with a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded by a prominent rim of activated macrophages and numerous lymphocytes and plasma cells.

Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disorder of autoimmune origin that principally attacks the joints, producing nonsuppurative, proliferative, and inflammatory synovitis. The inflammation progresses to the destruction of the articular cartilage and ankylosis of the joints.

In RA, the synovium contains germinal centers with secondary follicles and abundant plasma cells, which produce antibodies, some are autoantibodies. Many of the autoantibodies produced in the lymphoid organs are specific for citrullinated peptides (CCPs). 80% of patients have serum IgM or IgA autoantibodies that bind to the Fc portions of their own IgG. These autoantibodies are called rheumatoid factor and may also deposit in joints as immune complexes

The characteristic histologic features of RA include:

• Synovial cell hyperplasia and proliferation

• Dense inflammatory infiltrates

• Increased vascularity due to angiogenesis

• Fibrinopurulent exudate on the synovial and joint surfaces

• Osteoclastic activity in underlying bone

• Subcutaneous nodule: necrotizing granulomas with a central zone of fibrinoid necrosis surrounded activated macrophages, lymphocytes, and plasma cells

This altogether leads to a mass of edematous synovium called pannus, which grows over the articular cartilage and causes its erosion.

questions.question: An obese 35-year-old man with renal failure presents with excruciating joint pain in the right knee. It is associated with localized hyperemia. Joint aspiration is done which shows dense neutrophilic infiltrate and the following finding under polarised light. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is gout. Aspirate from the joint shows dense neutrophilic infiltrate and crystals that are long, slender, needle-shaped, and negatively birefringent.

Gout is marked by transient attacks of acute arthritis initiated by crystallization of monosodium urate (MSU) within and around joints. This results in the production of cytokines that recruit leukocytes. Macrophages phagocytose the MSU and the inflammasome activates caspase-1, which is involved in the production of some biologically active cytokines.

The distinctive morphologic changes in gout are acute arthritis, chronic tophaceous arthritis, tophi in various sites, and gouty nephropathy. Tophi are the pathognomonic hallmark of gout. These are large aggregations of urate crystals surrounded by an intense inflammatory reaction of foreign body giant cells which may appear in the articular cartilage, ligaments, tendons, bursae, earlobes, fingertips, or kidneys.

Gouty nephropathy refers to the renal complications caused by MSU crystals or tophi in the renal medullary interstitium or tubules. Complications include uric acid nephrolithiasis and pyelonephritis.

questions.question: A 3-year-old child with knee pain is found to have uric acid crystal deposition in his joints. On examination, excessive nail-biting is seen as shown below. Congenital deficiency of which of the following enzyme is responsible for this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome. In this condition, there is a deficiency of the enzyme hypoxanthine-guanine phosphoribosyltransferase (HGPRT).

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is charecterised by neurological and behavioral abnormalities such as lip and finger biting and head banging.

It also causes the overproduction of uric acid, leading to gouty arthritis and impaired kidney function. It is classified as secondary gout.

questions.question: A 50-year-old patient presents with left knee pain, redness, and swelling for 3 days. Joint aspiration is performed and microscopic findings under polarised light are given in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition disease (CPPD), also known as pseudo-gout and chondrocalcinosis.

The image shows aspirated crystals which are rhomboid, 0.5 to 5 μm in the greatest dimension, and positively birefringent (yellow).

It usually occurs in individuals older than 50 years of age and becomes more common with old age.

CPPD is classified into sporadic (idiopathic), hereditary, and secondary types. It is caused by germline mutations in the pyrophosphate transport channel. The secondary form is associated with

• Previous joint damage

• Hyperparathyroidism

• Hemochromatosis

• Hypomagnesemia

• Hypothyroidism

• Ochronosis

• Diabetes

Inflammation is usually milder than in gout. CPPD may produce acute, subacute, or chronic arthritis that can be confused with osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis. The joint involvement may be monoarticular or polyarticular; the knees, followed by the wrists, elbows, shoulders, and ankles, are most commonly affected.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about liposarcoma?
options: Amplification of 12q13-q15 is characteristic of well differentiated liposarcoma.
The key gene in the amplified region of chromosome 12q is MDM2.
The pleomorphic variant is usually indolent and rarely metastasizes.
Myxoid liposarcoma shows delicate 'chicken-wire' or 'crow’s feet' vasculature.
questions.answer: C. The pleomorphic variant is usually indolent and rarely metastasizes.
questions.explanation:
The pleomorphic variant of liposarcoma is usually aggressive and frequently metastasizes.

Liposarcoma is one of the most common sarcomas of adulthood seen mainly in people in their 50s to 60s in the deep soft tissues of the proximal extremities and in the retroperitoneum.

Amplification of 12q13-q15 and t(12;16) are characteristic of well-differentiated and myxoid liposarcomas, respectively. One of the key genes in the amplified region of chromosome 12q is MDM2, which is a potent inhibitor of p53.

Well-differentiated liposarcoma contains adipocytes with scattered atypical spindle cells. Myxoid liposarcoma contains an abundant basophilic extracellular matrix, arborizing capillaries (“chicken-wire” or “crow’s feet” vasculature), and primitive cells reminiscent of fetal fat.

The well-differentiated variant is relatively indolent, while the myxoid/round cell type is intermediate in its malignant behavior.

questions.question: A 30-year-old man presented with a 2-cm, rapidly growing, painful, subcutaneous mass on his left arm. Microscopy revealed immature proliferation of fibroblasts and myofibroblasts with abundant mitotic figures. Immunohistochemistry was positive for vimentin and muscle-specific actin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of nodular fasciitis.

Nodular fasciitis is a self-limited fibroblastic and myofibroblastic proliferation that typically occurs in young adults in the upper extremity. Etiology is unclear but a history of trauma is present in approximately 25% of cases. The tumors grow rapidly over a period of several weeks, typically no larger than 3 cm. It typically regresses spontaneously and if excised, rarely recurs.

Microscopically, it is richly cellular and contains plump, immature-appearing fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, arranged randomly or in short fascicles reminiscent of tissue culture fibroblasts. A gradient of maturation from cellular, loose, and myxoid to organized and fibrous is typical. The cells vary in size and shape (spindle to stellate) and have conspicuous nucleoli; mitotic figures are abundant.

Immunohistochemistry shows positivity for vimentin, smooth muscle actin, and muscle-specific actin.

Desmoid tumours are firm and poorly demarcated masses which infiltrate the surrounding muscle, nerve and fat. Histologically, fibroblasts are arranged in long parallel fascicles amid dense collagen. (Option 2)

The image below shows the histopathological findings of nodular fasciitis.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man presented with a swelling in the floor of his mouth for 6 months. Intraoral examination revealed a soft, painless, non-tender mass in the left floor of the mouth, extending posteriorly into the supraglottic region. On histopathological examination, spider cells were seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of rhabdomyomas.

Rhabdomyoma is a benign neoplasm of skeletal muscle that mainly occurs in the head and neck region. Although the mass is usually asymptomatic, it may compress or displace the tongue or may cause partial obstruction of the pharynx.

Rhabdomyomas can be classified into cardiac (most common) or extracardiac.

Spider cells are seen in this condition. These are large, rounded, polygonal cells with glycogen vacuoles separated by strands of cytoplasm extending between the cell membrane and nucleus.

The image given below shows spider cells.

questions.question: A 17-month-old girl presented with abnormal vaginal bleeding. A gynecological examination showed abnormal vaginal tissue protruding through the introitus. Histopathological analysis showed sheets of spindled cells in a myxoid stroma, which stained positive for desmin and Myo-D1. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of sarcoma botryoids, which is a variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma. It is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with skeletal muscle differentiation.

Rhabdomyosarcomas are the common soft tissue sarcomas of childhood and adolescence, classified into four subtypes: alveolar, embryonal, pleomorphic, and spindle-shaped/ sclerosing.

• Embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma: It contains sheets of both primitive round and spindled cells in a myxoid stroma. Sarcoma botryoids is a variant that occurs in the walls of hollow, mucosal-lined structures, such as the nasopharynx, common bile duct, bladder, and vagina.

• Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma: consists of the network of fibrous septae that divide the cells into clusters or aggregates, creating a crude resemblance to pulmonary alveoli.

• Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma - consists of large, sometimes multinucleated, bizarre eosinophilic tumor cells.

• Spindle cell/sclerosing rhabdomyosarcoma - Consists of fusiform cells with vesicular chromatin arranged in long fascicles or in a storiform pattern.

On immunohistochemistry, they are positive for desmin, myoglobin, myogenin, MyoD1, and vimentin. Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma is seen predominantly in adults.

The botryoid variant of embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma has the best prognosis, while the pleomorphic subtype is often fatal.

questions.question: A 26-year-old man presents with left knee pain for 6 months. MRI shows a well-circumscribed 4-cm mass superior to the patella within soft tissue. Biopsy shows a biphasic pattern of spindle cells and epithelial cells forming gland-like structures. Karyotype shows t(X,18) translocation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of synovial sarcoma.

It can be present in locations (chest wall, head, and neck) that lack synovium. Most lesions occur in people in their 20s to 40s. Patients usually present with a deep-seated mass that has been present for several years.

Most synovial sarcomas show a characteristic chromosomal translocation t(x;18)(p11;q11) producing SS18-SSX1, SS18-SSX2, or SS18-SSX4 fusion genes.

They are morphologically classified into monophasic or biphasic:

• Monophasic synovial sarcoma consists of uniform spindle cells with scant cytoplasm and dense chromatin growing, in short, tightly packed fascicles.

• Biphasic type consists of a spindle cell component with gland-like structures composed of cuboidal to columnar epithelioid cells. Tumor cells, especially in the biphasic type, are positive for epithelial markers (e.g., keratins), differentiating them from most of the other sarcomas.

questions.question: A 13-year-old boy presents with fever, pain, and swelling in the left mid-thigh region. X-ray shows lamellated periosteal reaction resembling an onion skin. A biopsy from the lesion is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Ewing's sarcoma.

It is a malignant bone tumor that occurs primarily in children and young adults, in the age group of 10-20 years. It usually affects the long bones, such as the femur, tibia, or humerus. Occasionally, the tumor may begin in the muscles or soft tissues (extraosseous Ewing's sarcoma).

Microscopically, solid sheets of small uniform round cells with PAS-positive magenta pink colored cytoplasm are characteristic of Ewing’s Sarcoma/PNET. The cells show PAS positivity due to the presence of large amounts of cytoplasmic glycogen. This is an important feature for the differential diagnosis of Ewing's with other small round cell tumors.

questions.question: A 36-year-old man with a history of blunt trauma to the left upper arm presents with swelling and redness 3 weeks later. There is a 4-cm mass in the outer aspect of the upper left arm in the soft tissue. Radiographs show a radiolucent center and surrounding irregular bone formation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myositis ossificans (MO).

It is a pseudo-inflammatory tumor that originates from skeletal muscle and corresponds to a heterotopic, metaplastic, nonmalignant bone tumor.

It is a highly inflammatory, rapidly growing, and painful muscular mass, which is seen following muscular trauma. The late stage is characterized by a typical zonal pattern (zonal phenomenon). It consists of three zones:

• Innermost zone: made of proliferating fibroblasts and myofibroblasts with areas of hemorrhage and necrosis

• Intermediate zone: contains osteoblasts with the immature osteoid formation

• Peripheral zone: the mature bone

questions.question: An 18-months-old child is brought to you with complaints of fever with chills and right knee pain for 3 days. On examination, his knee is warm and swollen with localized erythema. Joint aspiration showed 60,000 /mm3 WBCs. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause of his condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of septic arthritis. The most common organism implicated in this condition in children < 2 years is Staphylococcus aureus.

Since the advent of the Haemophilus influenzae vaccine, the predominant causes of septic arthritis among children <5 years of age have been S. aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus), and (in some centers) Kingella kingae.

Causative organism of bacterial arthritis:

Age group /Condition
Most common Organism

Overall
S. aureus

Gram-negative bacteria in young children
Kingella kingae

Adolescents
Neisseria gonococcus

After surgical procedure
Staphylococcus aureus

Prosthetic joints
Coagulase-negative Staphylococci

Sickle-cell disease
Salmonella sp

Complement deficiency
Neisseria gonococcus

Note: H. influenza arthritis predominates in children younger than 2 years of age, particularly in areas with low Hib immunization rates, but it is not the most common organism.

questions.question: A child was brought with complaints of an eczematous lesion on the scalp. A biopsy from the lesion was taken. The cells stained positively for CD1a and CD207. What are these cells?
questions.explanation:
The above scenario is suggestive of Langerhans cell histiocytosis. The image shows Langerhans cells with abundant, often vacuolated cytoplasm and vesicular nuclei containing linear grooves or folds and surrounding eosinophils. They stain positive for CD1a and S-100. They are intraepidermal dendritic cells.

The image below shows Langerhans cells.

Clonal proliferation of Langerhans cells leads to Langerhans cell histiocytosis, a histiocytic and dendritic cell neoplasm.

These cells secrete factors that augment innate immune responses, and also the antigen-presenting cell of the skin, thereby stimulating the adaptive immune system.

questions.question: An elderly man presented with a rapidly growing lesion as shown below. A biopsy from this lesion showed malignant cells. The immunohistochemical staining was positive for CK-20. The tumor cells in this condition originated from which of the following cells?
questions.explanation:
The above scenario is suggestive of Merkel cell carcinoma. It arises from Merkel cells.

These cells are located in epithelial basal cell layer and have neuroendocrine and mechanoreceptor functions.

Merkel cell carcinoma is a rare and aggressive neuroendocrine tumor of the skin, most commonly found in white men and diagnosed at a mean age of 70 years. A rapidly growing, flesh-colored papule or plaque characterizes the disease. About 80% of the cases are seen associated with Merkel cell polyomavirus.

Regional lymph nodes are involved in 30% of the patients and 50% will develop systemic disease. CK-20 is a specific marker for Merkel cell carcinoma. Wide local excision is usually necessary.

The image below shows Merkel cell carcinoma composed of uniform small round cells having granular chromatin and scant cytoplasm.

questions.question: A histopathological examination of melanocytic nevus in a patient showed nests of large round pigmented cells superficially. At the deeper extent of the lesion, it showed fascicles of non-pigmented cells resembling neural tissue. What does this signify?
options: Risk of malignant transformation into melanoma
questions.explanation:
Nevus cells often become non-pigmented and resemble neural tissue as they grow deep into the dermis. This change is called neurotization and suggests the benign nature of the nevus.

This morphological change in nevus cells occurs due to progressive loss of tyrosinase activity and acquisition of cholinesterase activity in deeper “nervelike” nevus cells.

Melanocytic nevi (moles) are common benign neoplasms caused by acquired activating mutations in components of the RAS signaling pathway.

Based on the location, it may be junctional nevi, intradermal nevi, or compound nevi.

Melanocytic nevi are thought to progress through a series of morphologic changes over time. Superficial nevus cells are larger, tend to produce melanin, and grow in nests. Deeper nevus cells are smaller, produce little or no pigment, and appear as cords and single cells. At the deepest extent of the lesions, these cells often acquire fusiform contours and grow in fascicles resembling neural tissue (neurotization).

Melanocytic nevi with neurotization indicate normal maturation change and help in differentiating benign nevi from melanomas (which lacks such features).

questions.question: Which of the following driver mutations is not associated with given skin malignancy?
options: Mutations in receptor tyrosine kinase signalling pathway
questions.answer: D. Mutations in hedgehog signalling pathway
questions.explanation:
The above image is suggestive of melanoma. Mutations in the hedgehog signaling pathway are associated with basal cell carcinoma.

All other mutations are associated with melanoma.

Melanoma is a highly aggressive malignancy linked to UV exposure.

Most sporadic melanomas are associated with mutations in cell cycle regulators (p16/INK4a, CDK4), proteins in receptor tyrosine kinase signaling pathway (KIT, RAS, BRAF), and telomerase (TERT mutation).

Dysplastic nevus syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition with inherited CDKN2A mutation that can lead to familial melanoma.

questions.question: What is the most common type of melanoma?
questions.explanation:
The superficial spreading type of melanoma is the most common type of melanoma.

The progression of melanoma may be described as:

• Radial growth phase: the horizontal spread of melanoma within the epidermis and superficial dermis

• Acral lentiginous - unrelated to sun exposure

• Lentigo maligna (Hutchinson freckle) - sun-exposed regions

• Superficial spreading (most common)

• Vertical growth phase: the tumor cells invade downward into the deeper dermal layers as an expansile mass (nodular)

The image below shows melanoma in the radial growth phase. It shows the irregular nested and single-cell growth of melanoma cells within the epidermis and an underlying inflammatory response within the dermis.

The image below shows melanoma cells that have large nuclei with irregular contours. The chromatin is characteristically clumped at the periphery of the nuclear membrane with prominent red (eosinophilic) nucleoli.

questions.question: An elderly European man presented with a slowly progressing lesion on his scalp for 2 years. Immunohistochemistry revealed tumor cells that were positive for the S-100 marker. All are favorable prognostic factors for his condition except:
questions.explanation:
The above image is suggestive of melanoma. The absence of regression is a favorable prognostic factor in melanomas.

Immunohistochemistry markers for melanoma are:

• S-100

• HMB (Human Melanoma Black)-45

• LDH

• MELAN-A

Regression is defined as partial or complete disappearance of a previously documented tumor in the absence of therapeutic interventions or physical trauma. Microscopically, it is characterized by the replacement of melanoma cells by dense inflammtory cell infiltrate or dermal fibrosis.

This phenomenon explains some apparent discrepancies between expected and observed prognosis based on tumor thickness and also the cases of metastatic melanoma with occult primary.

Determinants of a more favorable prognosis in melanoma include:

• Thinner tumor depth

• No or very few mitoses (< 1 per mm2)

• A brisk tumor infiltrating lymphocyte response

• The absence of regression

• Lack of ulceration

• Absence of metastases in the sentinel lymph node

questions.question: Which of the following conditions is not associated with FGFR3 mutations?
questions.explanation:
Mutations in the FGFR3 gene are not described in melanomas.

Fibroblast growth factor receptor-3 (FGFR3) is a receptor tyrosine kinase.

Defects in the FGFR3 gene have been associated with several conditions:

• Hypochondroplasia

• Thanatophoric dwarfism

• Seborrheic keratosis

• Acanthosis nigricans

• Bladder cancer

• Craniosynostosis

• Severe achondroplasia with developmental delay and acanthosis nigricans (SADDAN)

questions.question: A patient presented with multiple, small, pink nodular growths on the temples. A biopsy from the lesion showed the following. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows a jigsaw puzzle appearance which is seen in cylindroma (turban tumor/Spiegler’s tumor).

Cylindroma is a familial autosomal dominant disorder. It is due to the loss of the cylindromatosis gene, CYLD on chromosome 16q12-13. It has also been reported to follow radiotherapy epilation of the scalp.

The lesions are frequently multiple, smooth, firm, pink to red, and somewhat pedunculated. They are mostly seen on the scalp. Histologically, it contains mosaic‐like masses - a jigsaw appearance. Malignant transformation is very rare.

Surgery is the treatment of choice.

Note: Genetic syndromes associated with adnexal tumors:

• Germline mutations in CYLD - familial cylindromatosis, familial trichoepithelioma

• Brooke–Spiegler syndrome - associated with trichoepithelioma, cylindroma, spiradenoma

• Muir–Torre syndrome - sebaceous adenomas

• Cowden syndrome - multiple trichilemmomas

questions.question: Histopathological examination of a biopsy taken from a rough, scaly macular lesion from a patient's forearm showed neoplastic dyskeratosis. What is the probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Neoplastic dyskeratosis is seen in actinic keratosis.

Dyskeratosis is premature keratinization of individual keratinocytes. These cells usually have pink or reddish cytoplasm. It can be benign or malignant:

• Benign dyskeratosis - seen in Darier’s disease, warty dyskeratoma, and familial benign pemphigus

• Neoplastic dyskeratosis - seen in Bowen’s disease, squamous cell carcinoma, and actinic keratosis

Actinic keratoses usually occur in sun-damaged skin and are considered precursor lesions of squamous cell carcinoma. Some lesions produce so much keratin that a cutaneous horn develops.

The image below shows the histology of actinic keratosis. It shows atypical basal cells, dyskeratotic cells, and parakeratosis in the stratum corneum (cells with a retained nucleus).

questions.question: A biopsy from a chronic oropharyngeal lesion of a patient showed the following. Which of the following is not a risk factor for developing this condition?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows keratinous pearls and atypical tumor cells suggestive of squamous cell carcinoma. Human papillomavirus (HPV) subtypes 5 and 8 may predispose to squamous cell carcinoma, but not Epstein–Barr virus (EBV).

Risk factors for squamous cell carcinoma:

• Exposure to UV light

• HPV subtypes 5 and 8

• Epidermodysplasia verruciformis

• Industrial carcinogens (tars and oils)

• Chronic ulcers and draining osteomyelitis

• Old burn scars (Marjolin ulcers)

• Ingestion of arsenicals

• Ionizing radiation

• Tobacco and betel nut chewing (in the oral cavity)

• Precursor lesions:

• Actinic keratosis

• Xeroderma pigmentosum

The image below shows an SCC lesion in the oral cavity.

questions.question: A 60-year-old man presents with a pearly papule over the face containing prominent dilated subepidermal blood vessels and surface ulceration. A histological picture of the tumor is shown below. All are true about the tumor except:
options: Incidence is increased in xeroderma pigmentosum
Presence of multiple such tumors is seen in Gorlin syndrome
questions.explanation:
The clinical presentation and histology are suggestive of basal cell carcinoma (BCC). It is a locally aggressive cutaneous tumor, and metastasis is very rare.

It occurs in sun-exposed areas with increased incidence in the setting of immunosuppression and in disorders of DNA repair, such as xeroderma pigmentosum.

BCCs usually present as pearly papules and locally invasive ulcers (rodent ulcers). Histologically, the tumor cells resemble those in the normal basal cell layer of the epidermis with peripheral palisading and retraction cleft.

It is associated with mutations that activate the hedgehog pathway signaling.

Gorlin syndrome is an autosomal-dominant disorder with multiple basal cell carcinomas, medulloblastomas, ovarian fibromas, and odontogenic keratocysts, pits of the palms, and soles.

The image below shows the histopathology of BCC.

questions.question: The clinical picture and a biopsy from the skin lesion of a patient are shown below. This condition is associated with which of the following?
questions.explanation:
The clinical image shows diffuse erythema and scaling of the entire body surface (erythroderma) and histopathology shows the presence of lymphocytes in the epidermal cell layer (epidermotropism). This is suggestive of Sézary syndrome which is a disseminated and severe form of mycosis fungoides (cutaneous T-cell lymphoma).

Mycosis fungoides is a cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (CD4+ T-cells) that presents in the skin. It remains localized to the skin for many years, but it may eventually evolve into a systemic lymphoma.

The image of mycosis fungoides showing hallmark features - Sezary Lutzner cells showing epidermal infiltration (epidermotropism),

questions.question: A child was brought with urticarial lesions on the forearm. On examination, Darier's sign was positive. The cells responsible for this condition can be stained with all of the following except:
questions.explanation:
The above scenario is suggestive of urticaria pigmentosa caused by cutaneous mastocytosis. The Masson-Fontana stain is used to demonstrate melanin in nevus and malignant melanoma.

Darier's sign is seen in urticaria pigmentosa. It refers to the development of urticaria and erythema around the lesions after mild trauma, including scratching or rubbing of the lesion.

Mast cells may be difficult to differentiate from lymphocytes in routine, hematoxylin, and eosin (H&E)–stained sections. Special metachromatic stains (toluidine blue or Giemsa) are used to visualize their granules.

Stains for mast cells:

• Toluidine blue

• Giemsa

• Tryptase

• Leder stain (Chloracetate esterase)

• CD 117

The image below shows mast cells stained with toluidine blue.

questions.question: A 40-year-old woman presents with oral ulcers and bullae over the mucosa and skin. On examination, the bullae are flaccid and filled with clear fluid. Histopathology of the lesion shows the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows the suprabasal splitting of the epidermis (acantholysis) giving rise to the row of tombstones appearance. This is suggestive of pemphigus vulgaris.

Pemphigus vulgaris is the most common type of pemphigus. It involves the mucosa and skin. Autoantibodies against desmoglein 1 and 3 are present.

Pemphigus is a blistering disorder caused by autoantibodies that result in the dissolution of intercellular attachments within the epidermis and mucosal epithelium.

Variants of pemphigus:

• Pemphigus vulgaris

• Pemphigus vegetans

• Pemphigus foliaceus - autoantibodies are against Dsg1 alone, leading to superficial, subcorneal blisters.

• Pemphigus erythematosus

• Paraneoplastic pemphigus - in association with various malignancies, most commonly non-Hodgkin lymphoma

questions.question: A 70-year-old woman presents with multiple tense itchy blisters on the trunk and thigh region. Histopathology demonstrates subepidermal, non-acantholytic blisters. Direct immunofluorescence for IgG and C3 shows the following. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image showing linear IgG and C3 deposits on direct immunofluorescence (DIF) microscopy is characteristic of bullous pemphigoid.

Bullous pemphigoid is characterized by tense itchy bulla in the flexor areas and trunk which do not rupture easily. In bullous pemphigoid, the antibodies are formed against bullous pemphigoid antigens (BPAGs)- BP 180 and BP 230, which are components of hemidesmosomes.

The separation of bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus is based on the identification of subepidermal, nonacantholytic blisters that are Nikolsky negative.

Nikolsky's sign is elicited by applying firm tangential sliding pressure with a finger on lesional or perilesional skin. If the lesion is opened (i.e., skin sloughed off), then the Nikolsky's sign is present/positive.

questions.question: A 28-year-old man with gluten sensitivity presents with severely itchy papulovesicular lesions on extremities, knees, elbows, and buttocks for one year. Direct immunofluorescence staining of the lesions showed IgA deposition as follows. What is the most probable diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image showing granular deposits of IgA on direct immunofluorescence is suggestive of dermatitis herpetiformis or Duhring's disease. These deposits localize in the tips of dermal papillae.

Dermatitis herpetiformis presents as grouped vesicles and papules. These lesions are commonly located over the extensor aspects of knees, elbows, buttocks, back, scalp which are associated with intense pruritus.

It is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy or celiac disease. It is also associated with HLA DQ2/DQ8/B8. Deposition of IgA antitransglutaminase antibodies in the dermal papillae results in true subepidermal blisters and vesicles.

The characteristic microscopic feature is subepidermal blisters with papillary tip microabscesses containing neutrophils.

The initial treatment of choice for dermatitis herpetiformis is a gluten-free diet.

The image below shows subepidermal vesicles, with papillary neutrophil microabscesses, with neutrophil, eosinophil and lymphocytes infiltrates in the superficial dermis in case of dermatitis herpetiformis.

The image below shows vesicular lesions of dermatitis herpetiformis.

questions.question: A pathology resident notes the following cells while examining a histopathological section. It may be seen in all of the following conditions except:
questions.explanation:
The image above shows Touton giant cells having a central ring of nuclei while the peripheral cytoplasm is clear due to accumulated lipid. These cells are formed by the fusion of lipid-containing macrophages. They are not seen in sarcoidosis.

These cells are seen in:

• Fat necrosis

• Xanthoma

• Xanthogranulomas

• Dermatofibroma

The cardinal histopathologic feature of sarcoidosis is the non-caseating epithelioid granuloma with occasional other microscopic features:

• Schaumann bodies - laminated concretions composed of calcium and proteins

• Asteroid bodies - stellate inclusions enclosed within giant cells

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presented with a single hypoaesthetic and a hypopigmented patch on the lateral aspect of the forearm. Microscopy of a biopsy sample from the lesion revealed granulomatous inflammation but acid-fast bacilli were not identified. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is tuberculoid leprosy.

On microscopic examination, tuberculoid leprosy has granulomatous lesions closely resembling those found in tuberculosis. Because of the strong host defense, bacilli are almost never found, hence the name paucibacillary leprosy.

Leprosy or Hansen disease is a slowly progressive infection caused by Mycobacterium leprae, mainly affecting the skin and peripheral nerves.

questions.question: A 25-year-old man from the eastern part of India presents with a shallow and slowly expanding ulcer with heaped-up borders over the face. Biopsy reveals granulomas and the following finding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The image shows many histiocytes containing Leishman–Donovan bodies and surrounding chronic inflammatory cells classically seen in cutaneous leishmaniasis.

Cutaneous leishmaniasis presents with a shallow and slowly expanding ulcer, often with heaped-up borders.

On microscopic examination, the lesion shows granulomatous inflammation, usually with many giant cells and few parasites.

Diffuse cutaneous leishmaniasis is characterized by a single skin nodule, which continues spreading until the entire body is covered by nodular lesions. Microscopically, they contain aggregates of foamy macrophages stuffed with leishmania.

questions.question: Max Joseph’s space is a histopathological feature of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Max Joseph’s space is a histopathological feature of lichen planus.

Histological features of lichen planus:

• Orthokeratosis, parakeratosis, thickening of the stratum granulosum.

• Acanthosis with the formation of colloid bodies (also known as Civatte bodies/Sabouraud bodies)

• Liquefactive degeneration of the stratum basale, with separation from the underlying lamina propria, as a result of desmosome loss, creating small spaces (Max Joseph spaces)

• Infiltration of T cells in a band-like pattern into the dermis “hugging” the basal layer (interface dermatitis)

questions.question: A 35-year-old man presents with the following lesions. Which of the following finding is likely to be seen in histopathology?
questions.explanation:
The image shows silvery-white scaly lesions on the extensor aspect of the knees suggestive of psoriasis. Munro microabscesses are seen in psoriasis.

Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory dermatosis that appears to have an autoimmune basis. The lesions are pink to salmon-colored plaque covered by loosely adherent silver-white scales. Auspitz sign and Koebner phenomenon can be demonstrated. Nail changes include pitting, dimpling, separation of the nail plate, onycholysis, thickening, and crumbling.

Microscopy shows thinning of stratum granulosum, supra papillary plates, and neutrophils forming small aggregates within the superficial epidermis (spongiform pustules) and within the stratum corneum (Munro microabscesses).

Some types of microabscesses and their examples are given below:

Predominant cell

Name of microabscess

Disease

Neutrophilic microabscess

Papillary tip microabscess

Munro microabscess (superficial)

Spongiform pustules of Kogoj (deep)

Dermatitis herpetiformis

Psoriasis

Psoriasis

Lymphocytic microabscess
Pautrier's microabscess
Mycosis fungoides

Eosinophillic microabscess

Pemphigus vegetans

questions.question: Which cells constitute the resident monocyte-lineage population of the CNS and accumulate in response to injury?
questions.explanation:
Microglia are mesoderm-derived phagocytic cells that serve as the resident monocyte-lineage population of the CNS and accumulate in response to injury.

They respond to injury by:

• Activation and proliferating

• Developing elongated nuclei (rod cells), as in neurosyphilis

• Forming aggregates around small foci of tissue necrosis (microglial nodules)

• Congregating around cell bodies of dying neurons (neuronophagia)

questions.question: Which of these are the earliest morphologic markers of neuronal cell death?
questions.explanation:
Red neurons are the earliest morphologic markers of neuronal cell death.

Acute neuronal injury refers to a spectrum of changes that accompany acute CNS hypoxia / ischemia or other acute insults and reflect the earliest morphologic markers of neuronal cell death. They are evident by about 12 to 24 hours after an irreversible insult.

Morphologic features consist of:

• Shrinkage of the cell body

• Pyknosis of the nucleus

• Disappearance of the nucleolus

• Loss of Nissl substance

• Intense eosinophilia of the cytoplasm.

Stages of neuronal injury and their pathological features are given below:

Stages
Time
Features

Early change
12–24 hr
Red neuron

Subacute change
24 hr–2 weeks
Necrosis, macrophages, vascular proliferation, gliosis

Repair
2 weeks +
Removal of necrosis, gliosis completed, loss of CNS architecture

questions.question: A 45-year-old male who is a known diabetic and hypertensive suffers a stroke. During this episode, which of the following cells are the least susceptible to injury, considering the stroke was transient and not severe?
questions.explanation:
Astrocytes are more resistant to focal cerebral ischemia than neurons, and die by delayed necrosis.

 The cells most susceptible to ischemia are:

• Pyramidal cell layer cells of the hippocampus (espe­cially area CA1, also referred to as Sommer sector)

• Purkinje cells of the cerebellum

• Pyramidal neurons of the cerebral cortex(the watershed zones)

questions.question:
A 50 year old man died of an unknown condition. On autopsy, a sample of the brain was taken as a specimen, and the following fibres were seen on microscopic examination.
These fibres are not seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
The image shows the presence of rosenthal fibres. Rosenthal fibres are not seen in Pick's disease.

Rosenthal fibers are thick, elongated, brightly eosinophilic, irregular structures that occur within astrocytic processes. They contain two heat­shock proteins (αB ­crystallin and HSP27) as well as ubiquitin.They are typically found in regions of longstanding gliosis and are characteristic of a type of glial tumor—pilocytic astrocytoma.

Alexander disease is a leukodystrophy associated with mutations in the gene encoding GFAP. In this condition, abundant rosenthal fibers are found in periventricular, perivascular, and subpial locations.

questions.question: Hemorrhage of which of the following areas of the brain are called ganglionic hemorrhages?
questions.explanation: Hemorrhages in the basal ganglia and thalamus are commonly designated ganglionic hemorrhages. Those that occur in the lobes of the cerebral hemispheres are called lobar hemorrhages.

questions.question: A patient is rushed into the ER with complaints of sudden excruciating headache and projectile vomiting. CT angiography shows the presence of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms. These are caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation: Charcot–Bouchard microaneurysms are caused by chronic hypertension. They are most commonly seen within the basal ganglia.

questions.question: A 66-year-old man with chronic hypertension presents to the ER with altered mental status and elevated blood pressure of 210/110 mm Hg. You suspect intracranial hemorrhage. What is the most common site of hemorrhage seen in such cases?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical condition is suggestive of hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage. The most common site (50-60%) of hypertensive hemorrhage in the brain is the putamen.

Hypertension is the most common cause of intracerebral hemorrhage.

questions.question: A patient with a known history of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, presents to the ER with a sudden, severe headache, photophobia and nausea. What type of aneurysm would you suspect in this patient?
questions.explanation:
In a patient with a known history of autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, the most common type of intracranial aneurysm is saccular aneurysm.

Although the majority occur sporadically, genetic factors may be important in their pathogenesis of saccular aneurysms. There is an increased incidence of saccular aneurysm in individuals with certain Mendelian disorders like autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease, Ehlers–Danlos syndrome type IV, neurofibromatosis type 1 [NF1], and Marfan syndrome, fibromuscular dysplasia of extracranial arteries, and coarctation of the aorta. Other predisposing factors include cigarette smoking and hypertension.

The most frequent cause of clinically significant subarachnoid hemorrhage is rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm in a cerebral artery.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is not true about CADASIL?
options: It is characterized by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene.
Recurrent strokes and dementia are seen.
questions.answer: A. It shows autosomal recessive inheritance.
questions.explanation:
Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL) is an autosomal-dominant disorder caused by mutations in the NOTCH3 gene.

This leads to the misfolding of the extracellular domain of the NOTCH3 receptor that is preferentially expressed in vascular smooth muscle. It is clinically characterized by recurrent strokes (usually ischemic, less often hemorrhages) and dementia.

Arteries in the CNS and in other tissues such as skin show concentric thickening of the media and adventitia, loss of smooth muscle cells, and the presence of basophilic, periodic acid Schiff (PAS)-positive deposits. Deposits contain the misfolded NOTCH3 protein. These appear as osmiophilic compact granular material on electron microscopy and are consistently detected in the walls of affected vessels.

questions.question:
A patient presented to the emergency department with high fever, photophobia and neck stiffness. A lumbar puncture was performed and findings are given below. Which of the following is the most common cause of this condition?

CSF Parameters
 Observation

Cell count
1500 (predominantly lymphocytes)

Protein
100 mg/dl

Glucose
40 mg/dl

Gram stain
Negative
questions.explanation: The above clinical scenario is suggestive of aseptic meningitis. Enterovirus is the most common cause, accounting for around 90% of the cases.

questions.question: A 34-year-old man is admitted with a history of altered sensorium and abnormal behavior. The patient subsequently died and on autopsy, the following findings are seen in the Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. What are these called?
questions.explanation:
The image shows characteristic Negri bodies found in the Purkinje cell of the cerebellum. These are the pathognomonic microscopic finding in rabies. This patient's clinical features of altered sensorium and abnormal behavior are suggestive of rabies.

Negri bodies are cytoplasmic, round to oval, eosinophilic inclusions that can be found in the pyramidal neurons of the hippocampus and Purkinje cells of the cerebellum. The rabies virus can be detected within Negri bodies by ultrastructural and immunohistochemical methods.

questions.question: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy is caused by which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is an encephalitis caused by the JC polyomavirus.

The disease occurs almost exclusively in immunosuppressed individuals, most commonly among patients with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS). The most prominent symptoms are clumsiness, progressive weakness, and visual, speech, and personality changes.

Since the virus preferentially infects oligodendrocytes, demyelin­ation is its principal pathologic effect. It affects the subcortical white matter, particularly that of the parietal and occipital lobes. On microscopic examination, enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei containing glassy amphophilic viral inclusions are seen.

The image below shows a brain biopsy of a progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy patient, showing oligodendrocytes with nuclear enlargement and glassy chromatin.

questions.question: A 35-year-old immunocompromised patient presented with fever, headache, and neurological deficits. MRI showed multiple enhancing lesions and a stereotactic biopsy of the lesion was done. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The above image shows lymphocytes, macrophages and eosinophils surrounding the toxoplasma bradyzoites encased in cysts. Along with the case scenario, the most likely diagnosis is cerebral toxoplasmosis.

Cerebral toxoplasmosis is an opportunistic infection commonly found in the setting of HIV-associated immunosuppression. Toxoplasmosis of the CNS produces brain abscesses, which are found most often in the cerebral cortex (near the grey-white junction) and deep gray nuclei.

Lesions of acute cerebral toxoplasmosis exhibit central necrosis, petechial haemorrhages surrounded by acute and chronic inflammation, macrophage infiltration, and vascular proliferation. Both free tachyzoites and encysted bradyzoites may be found at the periphery of the necrotic foci. Chronic lesions consist of small cystic spaces containing scattered lipid and hemosiderin-laden macrophages that are surrounded by gliotic brain.

Option A: In cerebral malaria caused by P. falciparum, brain vessels are plugged with parasitized red cells. Around the vessels, ring hemorrhages and small focal inflammatory reactions (called malarial or Dürck granulomata) are seen.

Option C: Herpes simplex encephalitis is necrotizing and often hemorrhagic. Cowdry type A intranuclear viral inclusion bodies may be found in both neurons and glia.

Option D: Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) is an encephalitis caused by the JC polyomavirus. The disease occurs almost exclusively in immunosuppressed individuals. The virus preferentially infects oligodendrocytes and hence demyelin­ation is its principal pathologic effect. The enlarged oligodendrocyte nuclei contain glassy amphophilic viral inclusions.

questions.question: A 40-year-old man with bronchiectasis presents with progressive focal neurologic deficits and symptoms related to increased intracranial pressure. On lumbar puncture, the CSF is found to have a high white cell count and an increased protein concentration, but the glucose content is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Brain abscess is the most likely diagnosis in the above patient with progressive focal neurologic deficits and increased intracranial pressure.

Predisposing conditions for brain abcess:

• Acute bacterial endocarditis, which may give rise to multiple brain abscesses.

• Congenital heart diseases with right to left shunt.

• Chronic pulmonary disease, as in bronchiectasis.

• Systemic disease with immunosuppression.

Organisms involved are:

• Streptococcus spp. and Staphylococcus spp. (most common aerobic organisms)

• Bacteroides fragilis and Peptostreptococcus spp.(most common anaerobic organisms).

Foci of organisms in brain abscess:

• Direct implantation of organisms

• Local extension from adjacent foci (mastoiditis, paranasal sinusitis)

• Hematogenous spread (from primary foci of heart, lungs, bones of extremities, dental extraction)

CSF analysis in brain abscess:

Parameters
Observation

WBC
Increased

Proteins
Increased

Glucose
Decreased (but it will be normal in a significant proportion of individuals)

Note: In Robbins and Cotran's Pathology of Diseases- edition 9 page no.1273, it is given that in a typical brain abscess patient, the glucose in the CSF will be normal.

questions.question: Which of the following is incorrect regarding the common locations of CNS infections?
options: Tuberculosis - basal part of the brain
questions.answer: C. HIV - frontal and parietal lobes
questions.explanation:
HIV encephalopathy is seen in subcortical regions of the brain and not in frontal and parietal lobes. It is characterized by defects in short-term memory and executive function. It is also known as subcortical dementia.

CNS manifestations seen in AIDS:

• Aseptic meningitis

• HIV-associated neurocognitive disorder (HAND)

• HIV encephalopathy

• AIDS dementia complex

• Myelopathy

• Pure sensory ataxia

• Paresthesia/dysesthesia

• Myopathy

• Peripheral neuropathy

• Acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre syndrome)

• Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP)

• Mononeuritis multiplex

• Distal symmetric polyneuropathy

questions.question: Which of the following statements is false regarding prion diseases?
options: Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease is most commonly sporadic
Spongiform neurons are seen in fatal familial insomnia
Startle myoclonus is seen in Creutzfeldt Jakob Disease
The disease causing isoform of prion protein is PrPC
questions.answer: D. The disease causing isoform of prion protein is PrPC
questions.explanation:
The disease causing isoform of prion protein is PrPSc.

Prions are the proteinaceous infectious particle that lacks nucleic acid, composed entirely of alternatively folded proteins that undergo self-propagation. They bind to the normal, cellular isoform of the prion protein (PrPC) which is rich in α-helix, and stimulate conversion of PrPC into the disease-causing isoform PrPSc which contain less α-helix and a high amount of β-structure. β structured proteins are resistant to digestion by human cellular enzymes. Transmission of prion disease may be sporadic, familial or iatrogenic.

This group of diseases include:

• Creutzfeldt­ Jakob disease

• Gerstmann­ Sträussler­ Scheinke syndrome

• Fatal Familial Insomnia

• Kuru disease

• Scrapie in sheep and goats

• Bovine spongiform en­cephalopathy in cows

Most common prion disease in humans is CJD, which is most commonly sporadic. CJD is characterized by a constellation of dementia, myoclonus, and periodic electrical bursts in EEG.

Autoclaving at 134 degree Celsius for 5 hours or treatment with 2 N NaOH for several hours is recommended for sterilization against prions (tip: 1234-5 for prions).

questions.question: A 15 year old boy is brought to the ER with complaints of seizures, spasticity of limbs and cognitive decline since two weeks. He has no history of recent illness, but mentions suffering from a high fever with a rash 5 years ago. What condition had he likely suffered from?
questions.explanation:
The patient is most likely suffering from subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE), a delayed late complication of measles.

Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE) is a rare, progressive clinical syndrome characterized by cognitive decline, spasticity of limbs, seizures and psychosis. It occurs in children or young adults, months or years after an initial, early­-age acute infection with measles.

The pathogenesis of SSPE is not well understood but may involve persistent infection with a genetic variant of measles virus within the central nervous system.

questions.question: During the autopsy of a 78-year-old man who had progressive memory loss for 2 years, the following histologic finding was noted in the brain tissue. Which of the following mechanisms is most likely responsible for this condition?
options: Conformational change in the prion protein
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario and the images showing amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary tangles are diagnostic of Alzheimer's disease (AD), complicated by cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA). The formation and aggregation of Aβ peptides are responsible for AD.

Amyloid precursor protein (APP) is neurotrophic and neuroprotective. It is present in astrocytes and neuroglia. This protein is cleaved at 3 sites by secretase enzymes (α, β, and γ), and the products are known as Aβ peptides.

In Alzheimer's disease, Aβ peptides get aggregated in the form of amyloid plaques, which stain positive for Congo red. These get deposited within the neural tissue (Aβ42) and the cerebral arterioles (Aβ40 protein, causing CAA), which causes neuronal dysfunction, and is the first sign of AD.

Normally, tau proteins within the neurons stabilize microtubules, however, in AD, these get hyperphosphorylated and lose their function. Hyperphosphorylated tau proteins combine with cytoplasmic fibrils, to form neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) and get abnormally accumulated around the neuronal nucleus.

questions.question: With respect to Alzheimer's disease, which of the following pairs is incorrectly matched?
questions.explanation:
In Alzheimer's disease, presenilin-2 (PS2) is present on chromosome 1, not chromosome 9.

The following gene loci are seen in Alzheimer's disease:

Gene locus
Chromosome
Significance

Amyloid precursor protein
21
Down syndrome region

Presenilin-1
14
Early-onset familial AD

Presenilin-2

questions.question: Patients with which of the following diseases develop features of androgen insensitivity?
questions.explanation:
Spinal bulbar muscular atrophy results in androgen insensitivity.

It is an X-linked lower motor neuron disorder caused by CAG repeats in the gene encoding the polyglutamine tracts of the androgen receptor. It presents with progressive weakness and wasting of limb and bulbar muscles and features of androgen insensitivity like gynecomastia and reduced fertility.

questions.question:
In which of the following conditions can neurofibrillary tangles be found?

1. Normal aging

2. Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

3. Multiple system atrophy

4. REM behavioral disorder

5. Alzheimer's disease
questions.explanation:
Neurofibrillary tangles (NFTs) are found in:

• Normal aging

• Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis

• Alzheimer's disease

NFTs are aggregates of hyperphosphorylated tau proteins (microtubule-associated proteins) found in numerous diseases known as tauopathies. NFTs can also be seen in relatively lower numbers in elderly people without dementia.

questions.question: A 43-year-old man who presented with tremors, bradykinesia, lack of coordination, and progressive declining cognitive functions was diagnosed with punch drunk syndrome. This condition is likely due to the deposition of which of the following in his brain?
questions.explanation:
Punch drunk syndrome is due to accumulation of tau proteins in the brain.

This condition is also called dementia pugilistica or chronic traumatic encephalopathy. It is a dementing illness that develops following repeated head trauma in boxers and other athletes. Affected brains are typically atrophic, with enlarged ventricles. They show accumulation of tau-­containing neurofibrillary tangles in a characteristic pattern involv­ing the superficial frontal and temporal lobe cortex.

questions.question: A 62-year-old man is brought with tremors of his hands at rest. His son says that he has difficulty initiating movements and seems to be moving very slowly. On examination, shuffling gait, pill-rolling tremors, and rigidity on passive arm movement are noted. Which of the following is not seen in this condition?
questions.answer: A. Pick cells and Pick bodies
questions.explanation:
This clinical scenario is suggestive of Parkinson's disease. This condition is not associated with Pick cells and Pick bodies. They are seen in Pick’s disease or frontotemporal dementia.

In Parkinson's disease, there is loss of the substantia nigra neurons projecting to the striatum. This leads to pallor of the substantia nigra as well as a decrease or absence of dopamine in the striatum. This leads to slowing of movements and tremors.

Lewy Bodies are seen within the neurons of affected patients. They are filamentous projections of the protein α‐synuclein or ubiquitin. They are present in surviving neurons and can be found in the cortex.

questions.question: LRRK2 mutation is associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Mutations in the gene encoding LRRK2 (leucine ­rich repeat kinase 2) are a common cause of autosomal dominant Parkinson's disease. They are also found in some sporadic cases of the disease.

questions.question: A wife brings her 52-year-old husband to the OPD with complaints of involuntary, sudden, jerky movements of his hands. She also tells that he has been occasionally forgetting the route to his office. His older brother also developed similar complaints last year. MRI revealed the following findings. Which of the following is incorrect about this condition?
options: It has an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance
The phenomenon of anticipation is seen
Severity is related to the length of the CAG repeats
There is degeneration of GABAergic neurons
questions.answer: A. It has an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance
questions.explanation:
The MRI shows bilateral atrophy of caudate nuclei with compensatory dilatation of lateral ventricles, also known as boxcar ventricles. Along with the clinical features, it is suggestive of Huntington's disease (HD). It has an autosomal dominant mode of inheritance.

It is commonly seen in the 4th and 5th decades of life. It is a degenerative disease of the caudate and putamen (striate neurons) caused by trinucleotide (CAG) repeats in the huntingtin gene on chromosome 4. The severity of the disease depends on the number of repeats. With more repeats, the disease becomes more severe. The disease also manifests at an earlier age, a phenomenon called anticipation.

The caudate nucleus is dramatically atrophied, with accompanying atrophy of the putamen, cortex, and hydrocephalus ex vacuo of the 3rd ventricle. The medium-sized GABAergic neurons are especially affected.

It causes chorea and dementia. Motor problems like chorea typically precede dementia.

questions.question: In patients with Huntington's disease, the mutated gene is located on which chromosome?
questions.explanation:
In Huntington's disease, the affected HTT gene is located on chromosome 4.

The coding region has a trinucleotide repeat (CAG/ glutamine). The severity and age of onset of the disease depend on the number of repeats increases. This phenomenon is called anticipation.

questions.question: A 10-year-old boy was brought to the OPD with difficulty in climbing stairs and walking long distances. His parents say that he has received complaints at school due to progressively worsening handwriting. On examination, pes cavus is noted. Investigations revealed scoliosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Which of the following is incorrect regarding this condition?
options: Expansion of a GAA trinucleotide repeat
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Friedrich's ataxia. It is associated with mutations of genes on chromosome 9q13.

It is an autosomal recessive disease caused by the expansion of a GAA trinucleotide repeat in the gene encoding frataxin. The clinical features are given by the mnemonic FRIEDRICHS:

• F - Frequent falls (ataxia), foot deformity (pes cavus or overarched foot)

• R - Recessive

• I - Iron accumulation in mitochondria

• E - Eye movements (nystagmus)

• D - Dorsal column (loss of fine touch, vibration, position)

• R - Reflexes (deep tendon) lost, with extensor plantar reflex

• I - Incoordination

• C - Cerebellar involvement

• H - Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM)

• S - Scoliosis (with kyphosis), staggering gait

questions.question: While studying a spinal cord section, a pathology resident noted that the nuclei of the Schwann cells of the dorsal root ganglia were enlarged nearly 5 times the normal size. This finding is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
In ataxia-telangiectasia, the nuclei of the Schwann cells of the dorsal root ganglia are enlarged to nearly 2-5 times the normal size. This finding is seen in the Schwann cells of dorsal root ganglia, peripheral nerves, endothelial cells, and pituicytes. These cells are called amphicytes.

Ataxia-telangiectasia is due to mutations of the ATM gene, located on chromosome 11q. It predominantly affects the cerebellum with the loss of Purkinje and granule cells. There is also degeneration of the dorsal columns, spinocerebellar tract, anterior horn cells, and peripheral neuropathy.

Telangiectatic lesions are found in the CNS as well as in the conjunctiva and skin of the face, neck, and arms. The lymph nodes, thymus, and gonads are hypoplastic.
