questions.question: Bergmann gliosis is due to the loss of which of the following?
questions.explanation:
Bergmann gliosis is due to the loss of Purkinje cells.

It occurs in advanced cases of chronic alcoholism. There is a loss of Purkinje cells and proliferation of the adjacent astrocytes between the depleted granular cell layer and the molecular layer of the cerebellum.

questions.question: A 5-month-old baby was brought to the OPD with complaints of irritability, stiffness, and weakness of limbs. On examination, there was hypertonia of limbs. After a few months, the baby died due to the rapid progression of the disease. A brain autopsy was done and the following cells were seen. What are these cells?
questions.explanation:
The clinical scenario showing motor symptoms and rapid progression to death, an autopsy of the brain showing globoid cells is highly suggestive of Krabbe's disease. The globoid cells are macrophages.

Krabbe's disease or globoid cell leukodystrophy is a neurodegenerative disorder with severe myelin destruction due to a deficiency of galactocerebroside β-galactosidase.

The onset of symptoms is between 3 to 6 months of age, dominated by motor signs such as stiffness and weakness. Survival beyond the age of 2 years is uncommon. The brain shows loss of myelin and oligodendrocytes with a similar process affecting the peripheral nerves.

questions.question:
A 35-year-old man presented with frequent falls and tingling in his extremities. On examination, an unsteady gait with a positive Romberg sign was noted. Additionally, there was loss of proprioception and vibration sense and deep tendon reflexes in the lower limbs. Blood investigations revealed the following. Deficiency of which of the following vitamins is the likely cause of this condition?

Hemoglobin: 8 mg/dl

Peripheral smear: Macrocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario with involvement of the dorsal column and investigations showing macrocytic anemia is suggestive of subacute combined degeneration (SACD) of the spinal cord. It is due to a deficiency of vitamin B12 which is involved in myelin synthesis.

The most severely affected regions are the posterior columns at the cervical and upper thoracic levels.

The clinical features include:

• Peripheral nerve and spinal cord involvement

• Paresthesias in the hands or feet

• Weakness and unsteadiness of gait

• Loss of vibration or joint position sense in the legs

• Mental slowing, depression, confusion, delusions, and hallucinations

MRI spine shows diffuse myelopathy and areas of demyelination. Treatment involves a replacement regimen of vitamin B12 intramuscular daily injections of 1000 μg for the first week followed by weekly 1000 μg injections for 1 month. Monthly injections are given thereafter.

While vitamin E deficiency can also cause SACD, it is rare and is associated with hemolytic anemia.

questions.question: Korsakoff syndrome is caused by the deficiency of which vitamin?
questions.explanation:
Korsakoff syndrome is caused by the deficiency of thiamine.

This syndrome is characterized by pronounced anterograde and retrograde amnesia along with impairment in visuospatial, abstract, and other types of learning. It is usually completely or partially permanent in about half the patients.

Wernicke's encephalopathy refers to the acute form of thiamine deficiency. It is characterized by nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia, mental status changes, and unsteadiness of stance and gait. It is a medical emergency and IV or IM thiamine should be initiated immediately.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common primary malignant brain tumor in children?
questions.explanation: Most common primary malignant brain tumor in children is medulloblastoma.

questions.question: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaints of unsteadiness and gait disturbance. On neurological examination, nystagmus, areflexia, and hypotonia are noted. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain shows enhancing nodule within the wall of a cystic mass. The mass is resected and histology shows the given finding. Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding this tumor?
options: BRAF mutation is seen in this tumor
It belongs to WHO grade II tumors
questions.answer: D. It belongs to WHO grade II tumors
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the image showing Rosenthal fibers is diagnostic of pilocytic astrocytoma. It belongs to WHO grade I tumors.

Pilocytic astrocytoma typi­cally occurs in children and young adults and is usually located in the cerebellum. It is usually a slow-growing tumor and if it occurs in the cerebellum, it can be resected. If it extends into the hypothalamic region from the optic tract, it can have a more ominous clinical course because of its location.

It is often cystic, if solid, it may be well circumscribed. It is often biphasic with both loose microcystic and fibrillary areas.

The tumor is composed of bipolar cells with long, thin hair-like processes that are GFAP-positive and form dense fibrillary meshworks. Rosenthal fibers and eosinophilic granular bodies are characteristic findings under microscopy. BRAF mutation is seen in this tumor.

questions.question: A 65-year-old patient presents with headache, seizures, and focal neurological deficit. Imaging shows a tumor in the right frontal lobe which crosses the midline and the histological section of the resected tumor is shown below. Which of the following molecular subtypes does this tumor belong to?
questions.explanation:
The clinical history and histological image are suggestive of primary glioblastoma, IDH - wild type.

The given histological image shows foci of necrosis with pseudo-palisading of malignant nuclei and endothelial cell proliferation, which are characteristic of glioblastoma (previously called glioblastoma multiforme).

According to the WHO classification of CNS diseases 2016, glioblastomas are classified as follows:

1. Glioblastoma, IDH - wild type:

• About 90% of the cases

• Primary or de novo glioblastoma

• Over 55 years of age

2. Glioblastoma, IDH - mutant type:

• About 10% of the cases

• Secondary glioblastoma, with a history of prior lower-grade diffuse glioma

• Arises in younger patients

3. Glioblastoma, NOS, where full IDH evaluation cannot be performed.

questions.question: A 40-year-old patient presents to the OPD with recurrent seizures, headache, and projectile vomiting. MRI brain reveals cortical-based heterogeneous tumor with calcification in the frontal lobe. The histological section of the resected tumor shows perineuronal satellitosis. Which of the following is the most common genetic alteration noted in this tumor?
options: Mutation of the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes
Deletion of portions of chromosomes 1p and 19q
questions.answer: A. Mutation of the isocitrate dehydrogenase genes
questions.explanation:
The clinical picture is suggestive of oligodendroglioma and the most common genetic alterations in oligodendroglioma are mutations of the isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH1 and IDH2) genes.

IDH1 and IDH2 gene mutations are seen in upto 90% of oligodendroglioma and they are associated with a better prognosis. Deletions of portions of chromosomes 1p and 19q are seen in up to 80% of the cases.

questions.question: The histological section of an intracranial space-occupying lesion resected from a patient is given below. Which of the following tumors shows this pattern?
questions.explanation:
The histological image shows fried egg appearance of cells and is seen in oligodendroglioma.

Oligodendroglioma is an infiltrating glioma comprised of cells that resemble oligodendrocytes. It commonly occurs in the fourth and fifth decades. The lesion is found mostly in the cerebral hemispheres, with a pre­dilection for white matter.

The tumor is composed of sheets of regular cells with spherical nuclei containing finely granular chromatin (similar to normal oligodendrocytes) surrounded by a clear halo of vacuolated cytoplasm giving a fried egg appearance. Tumor cells infiltrating the cerebral cortex often collect around the neurons (perineuronal satellitosis).

Fried eggs in pathology:

• Oligodendroglioma on histopathology

• Hairy cell leukemia on bone marrow biopsy

• Seminoma / Dysgerminoma on light microscopy

• Mycoplasma pneumonia fried egg colonies on Eaton agar

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding oligodendroglioma?
options: It shows perinuclear halos and perineuronal satellitosis
Tumor showing IDH1 and IDH2 mutation carries good prognosis
It commonly involves the white matter of the cerebral hemispheres
Tumor showing co-deletion of 9p and 10q is chemosensitive
questions.answer: D. Tumor showing co-deletion of 9p and 10q is chemosensitive
questions.explanation:
Oligodendroglioma showing co-deletion of 9p and 10q is chemoresistant.

Mutations in oligodendroglioma and their responsiveness to chemotherapy:

Mutations

CDKN2A mutation

questions.question: The spinal MRI of a 30-year-old patient with neurofibromatosis type 2 shows an ependymoma. Which of the following is true regarding this tumor?
options: Ependymoma is predominantly a spinal tumor
Ependymoma in children commonly arises from the roof of the fourth ventricle
CSF seeding of metastasis is commonly seen
Posterior fossa ependymoma mostly presents with ataxia
questions.answer: A. Ependymoma is predominantly a spinal tumor
questions.explanation:
Ependymoma is predominantly a spinal tumor in adults and is commonly associated with neurofibromatosis type 2.

Tumor site

Adults

Posterior fossa

Rare

Children

(floor of the fourth ventricle)

Frequent

CSF dis­semination is uncommon despite the relationship of the ependymoma with the ventricular system.

Posterior fossa ependymoma often manifests with hydrocephalus secondary to progressive obstruction of the fourth ventricle.

questions.question: The fluorescence in situ hybridization done in a patient with supratentorial ependymoma shows positivity for RELA fusion protein. What is the prognosis of this molecular subtype?
questions.explanation:
RELA fusion protein positive ependymoma carries the worst prognosis.

This highlights the importance of immunohistochemistry in the role of prognosis of ependymoma.

questions.question: An obese patient is being evaluated for recurrent low back pain radiating to both the lower limbs. Imaging shows a myxopapillary ependymoma located in the spinal cord. Which of the following statements regarding this tumor is incorrect?
options: It belongs to WHO grade 2 tumors
It commonly arises from the filum terminale
It consists of mucopolysaccharides and a papillary core consisting of blood vessels microscopically
It follows an aggressive clinical course
questions.answer: D. It follows an aggressive clinical course
questions.explanation:
Myxopapillary ependymoma is a slow-growing tumor and do not follow an aggressive clinical course.

Myxopapillary ependymoma belongs to WHO grade 2 tumors histologically as of the 2021 WHO clasiffication of central nervous system tumors. It occurs commonly in the filum terminale of the spinal cord and contains papillary elements in a myxoid (acidic and neutral mucopolysaccharides) background, admixed with ependymoma-like cells microscopically.

questions.question: A 12-year-old boy presents with complaints of headache, projectile vomiting, and blurring of vision. CT scan shows a mass lesion in the posterior cranial fossa. His medical records are unremarkable, except for a family history of colon cancer in three of his relatives. What is the most probable syndrome that this patient has?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical features and the family history of colon cancer point to the diagnosis of Turcot syndrome.

Turcot syndrome is a rare hereditary disorder clinically characterized by the occurrence of primary tumors of the colon and the central nervous system.

Two types of tumors are seen in Turcot syndrome. The first is characterized by childhood cerebellar medulloblastoma caused by mutations in the APC gene. The second type is characterized by gliomas, particularly glioblastoma multiforme, arising in both children and adults and is related to mismatch repair gene mutations.

Familial carcinoma syndromes and the common malignancies associated with them:

• Gorlin syndrome: Medulloblastoma and multiple early-onset basal cell carcinomas

• Lynch syndrome: Gastrointestinal and genito-urinary tumors and rarely gliomas in the brain

• Neurofibromatosis: Schwannoma

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding medulloblastoma is incorrect?
options: It belongs to WHO Grade II tumors
Drop metastases is a common complication
It is an extremely radiosensitive tumor
questions.answer: A. It belongs to WHO Grade II tumors
questions.explanation:
Medulloblastoma belongs to WHO grade IV tumors.

Medulloblastoma accounts for 20% of brain tumors in children. It occurs predominantly in children and exclusively in the cerebellum. Drop metastasis through CSF dissemination is a common complication. It is an extremely radiosensitive tumor.

questions.question: A 40-year-old smoker diagnosed with small cell carcinoma of the lung 1 year back now develops seizures, short-term memory loss, and psychiatric symptoms. Which of the following paraneoplastic conditions can be attributed to this presentation?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history is suggestive of limbic encephalitis.

Limbic encephalitis is characterized by subacute dementia. Histologically, it is characterised by perivascular inflammatory cuffs, micro­glial nodules, neuronal loss, and gliosis evident in the anterior and medial portions of the tem­poral lobe.

Some of these patients have a circulating ANNA­1 antibody (anti­Hu) that is most commonly associ­ated with small cell carcinoma of the lung. Another group of these patients have a circulating antibody that recognizes the NMDA receptor and cross­-reacts with hippocampal neurons.

questions.question: A 28-year-old pregnant woman is diagnosed with a meningioma. which of the following growth patterns does the tumor exhibit in the subsequent trimesters of her pregnancy?
options: The tumor grows rapidly throughout her pregnancy
The tumor shrinks throughout her pregnancy
The tumor grows rapidly in first trimester and shrinks thereafter
The size of the tumor exhibits no change throughout her pregnancy
questions.answer: A. The tumor grows rapidly throughout her pregnancy
questions.explanation:
Meningiomas express progesterone receptors and grow more rapidly during pregnancy.

Meningiomas are usually slow ­growing tumors. They show a moderate female predominance.

The common sites of involvement of meningiomas are:

• The parasagittal aspect of the brain convexity

• Dura over the lateral convexity

• Wings of the sphenoid

• Olfactory groove

• Sella turcica

• Foramen magnum.

The histological section of meningioma showing psammoma bodies is given below:

questions.question: The MRI of a woman presenting with recurrent headaches is given below. Microscopy of the resected tumor shows psammoma bodies and the tumor cells express progesterone receptors. Which of the following is the most common cytogenetic abnormality noted in this tumor?
questions.explanation:
The given MRI showing homogeneously enhancing extra - axial, dural based tumor and the microscopic findings are highly suggestive of meningioma. The most common cytogenetic abnormality in meningioma is 22q deletion.

Meningioma is predominantly a benign tumors of adults, usually attached to the dura. It arises from the meningothelial cells of the arachnoid. 50% - 60% of the sporadic meningioma harbors mutations in the NF2 gene (in chromosome 22q12) resulting in the absence of functional merlin protein. In meningioma without NF2 mutations, the most common mutations occur in TNF­ receptor - associated factor 7 (TRAF7).

questions.question: Which of the following tumors is most commonly associated with meningeal carcinomatosis?
questions.explanation:
Breast carcinoma is commonly associated with meningeal carcinomatosis.

Meningeal carcinomatosis presents as tumor nodules studding the surface of the brain, spinal cord, and intradural nerve roots.

questions.question: Which of the following types of herniation is characterised by duret hemorrhages?
questions.explanation:
Duret hemorrhages are characteristic of transtentorial herniation.

Transtentorial (uncinate, mesial temporal) herniation occurs when the medial aspect of the temporal lobe is compressed against the free margin of the tentorium. Progression of transtentorial herniation is often accompanied by secondary hemorrhagic lesions in the midbrain and pons, termed Duret hemorrhages. These linear or flame - shaped lesions usually occur in the midline and paramedian regions and are believed to be due to the distortion or tearing of penetrating veins and arteries supplying the upper brainstem.

With increasing displacement of the temporal lobe, the third cranial nerve is compromised, resulting in pupillary dilation and impairment of ocular movements on the side of the lesion. The posterior cerebral artery may also be compressed, resulting in ischemic injury to the territory supplied by that vessel, including the primary visual cortex.

When the extent of herniation is large enough, the contralateral cerebral peduncle may be compressed, resulting in hemiparesis ipsilateral to the side of the herniation. The compression in the peduncle in this setting is known as the Kernohan notch.

questions.question: Which of the following structures is involved in tonsillar herniation?
questions.explanation:
Cerebellum is involved in tonsillar herniation.

Tonsillar herniation refers to the displacement of the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum. This pattern of herniation is life-­threatening because it causes brainstem compression and compromises vital respiratory and cardiac centers in the medulla.

questions.question: Which of the following is the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppressed patients?
questions.explanation:
Primary central nervous system lymphoma is the most common CNS neoplasm in immunosuppressed individuals, including those with AIDS and immunosuppression after transplantation.

The vast majority of primary central nervous system lymphomas are of B-cell origin. Overall, primary central nervous system lymphomas are aggressive and have worst outcome. The Epstein-Barr virus plays an important role in the pathogenesis of HIV-related primary central nervous system lymphoma.

questions.question: CSF spread can occur in patients with all of the following tumors, except:
questions.explanation:
Most of the meningiomas are benign tumors and very rarely metastasize to CSF.

The primary intracerebral malignancies that may cause metastases to the subarachnoid space are:

• Glioblastoma (GBM)

• Anaplastic astrocytoma

• Medulloblastoma

• Ependymoma

• Pineoblastomas

• Oligodendroglioma

Leptomeningeal metastases, also known as carcinomatous meningitis, refer to the spread of malignant cells through the CSF space. These cells can originate both in primary CNS tumors (e.g. drop-metastases), as well as from distant tumors that have metastasized (hematogenous spread).

The most common secondary tumors that spread to CSF are breast cancer > lung cancer > melanoma > GI malignancies.

Contrast MRI is the investigation of choice and shows leptomeningeal enhancement and tumor scattered over the brain in a ‘sugar-coated’ manner.

questions.question: What is the most common cause of peripheral neuropathy?
questions.explanation:
The most common cause of peripheral neuropathy is diabetes mellitus.

The most common pattern of diabetic neuropathy is an ascending, distal symmetric, sensorimotor polyneuropathy (glove and stocking type).

The most common type of hereditary neuropathy is Charcot-Marie-Tooth (CMT) disease.

questions.question: A 20-year-old man presents with distal leg weakness with no complaints of tingling or numbness. On examination, you note reduced muscle stretch reflexes below the knee along with the following findings. This condition is associated with which chromosome?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Charcot–Marie–Tooth (CMT) disease. It is most commonly associated with chromosome 17.

It is the most common type of hereditary neuropathy. The most common variant of this condition is CMT1A. It is caused by a duplication of a region on chromosome 17 that includes the peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) gene.

It usually presents in the first to third decade of life with distal leg weakness, e.g., foot drop with no numbness or tingling. There is reduced sensation to all modalities with reduced muscle stretch reflexes. Atrophy of the muscles below the knee leads to inverted champagne bottle legs.

questions.question: A 32-year-old woman comes with complaints of double vision that gets worse after she reads a book or watches television. She also has drooping of the eyelids that gets better after a nap. Serology is positive for anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies. Which of the following is more commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of myasthenia gravis. It is most commonly associated with thymic hyperplasia (65% of cases).

Thymoma is seen in around 10% of patients with myasthenia gravis.

Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular disorder that is characterized by weakness and the fatigability of skeletal muscles. It is due to the autoantibody-mediated destruction of the acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) at the neuromuscular junction. This consequentially leads to a decreased transmission at the neuromuscular (myoneural) junction.

There is a characteristic pattern of muscle involvement. Lid and extraocular muscles (diplopia and ptosis) are involved early in the disease course. The facial muscles weakness can produce a snarling expression, weakness in chewing, and nasal timbre to the voice. Weakness increases with repeated use of the muscles and improves with rest. The reflexes are normal in this condition.

questions.question: A 52-year-old man presents with mild ptosis and proximal lower limb weakness. Nerve conduction studies show incremental response following brief exercise. Further investigations reveal antibodies against presynaptic P/Q voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following malignancies is associated with this condition?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical scenario is suggestive of Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (LEMS). It is associated with small-cell lung carcinoma.

It is an autoimmune disorder caused by antibodies that block acetylcholine release by inhibiting a presynaptic calcium channel. In contrast to myasthenia gravis, rapid, repetitive stimulation (muscle activity) results in an increase in muscle response and strength.

Patients typically present with weakness of their extremities. In about half the cases, there is an underlying malignancy; most often, neuroendocrine carcinoma of the lung (Small cell lung carcinoma). The stimulus for autoantibody formation in paraneoplastic cases may be the expression of the same calcium channel in the neoplastic cells.

Patients without cancer often have other autoimmune diseases, such as vitiligo or thyroid disease. Treatment consists of drugs that increase acetylcholine release by depolarizing synaptic membranes (pyridostigmine), plasmapheresis, and immunosuppressive agents, similar to myasthenia gravis.

questions.question: What is the most common inflammatory myopathy in children?
questions.explanation:
Dermatomyositis is the most common inflammatory myopathy in children.

Two types of dermatomyositis are known—juvenile and adult.

Juvenile dermatomyositis
Adult dermatomyositis

7 years

questions.question: A 51-year-old woman presents with complaints of weakness for 2 months. She reports that she has difficulty rising from a chair and combing her hair every morning. Physical exam reveals decreased strength in the shoulders and hip. Muscle biopsy findings are shown below. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The muscle biopsy shows myofiber atrophy accentuated at the edges of the fascicles (perifascicular atrophy). The biopsy along with the history is suggestive of dermatomyositis. It is associated with perimysial CD4+ cellular infiltrates.

Dermatomyositis is an immunologic disease in which damage to small blood vessels contributes to muscle injury.

Note: Viral myositis occurs 1-7 days after a viral infection (HIV-1, coxsackievirus). Muscle weakness and tenderness are seen. There are raised CK levels, muscle necrosis without inflammation, and positive urine myoglobin.

questions.question: A patient with gastric carcinoma develops proximal muscle weakness. Biopsy findings are suggestive of dermatomyositis. Which of the following antibodies are most likely to be present in this patient?
questions.explanation:
This patient has developed paraneoplastic dermatomyositis. Anti-P155/P140 antibodies (directed against several transcriptional regulators) are associated with paraneoplastic dermatomyositis and juvenile dermatomyositis.

It presents as gradual, symmetric muscle weakness and myalgias, typically affecting the proximal muscles first. Fine movements controlled by distal muscles are affected late in the disease. Myopathic changes and elevation in serum creatine kinase levels suggest muscle damage.

questions.question: A patient with muscle weakness is found positive for antibodies against cN1A. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Antibodies to cN1A are seen in inclusion-body myositis.

It is the most common inflammatory myopathy in patients >65 years.

Patients present with slowly progressive muscle weakness that tends to be most severe in the quadriceps and the distal upper extremity muscles. Dysphagia from esophageal and pharyngeal muscle involvement can also occur.

Laboratory studies usually show modestly elevated creatine kinase levels. Most myositis-associated autoantibodies are absent but are positive for antibodies to cN1A.

questions.question: An 8-year-old boy was brought with progressive muscle weakness and walking difficulties. The following finding was noted on examination. Genetic testing revealed a dystrophin gene mutation. On which chromosome is the affected gene located?
questions.explanation:
The given clinical history and the image showing pseudohypertrophy of calf muscles are highly suggestive of Duchenne's muscular dystrophy. It is an X-linked recessive condition.

Duchenne's and Becker's muscular dystrophy are caused by loss-of-function mutations in the dystrophin gene on the X chromosome. It is one of the largest human genes. Dystrophin provides mechanical stability to the myofiber during muscle contraction. Defects in the complex may lead to small membrane tears that permit the influx of calcium, triggering events that result in myofiber degeneration.

Duchenne's muscular dystrophy is associated with deletions or frame-shift mutations that result in the total absence of dystrophin. Immunohistochemical studies for dystrophin show the absence of the normal sarcolemmal staining pattern.

In contrast, the mutations in Becker's muscular dystrophy typically permit the synthesis of a truncated version of dystrophin, which retains some function. Immunohistochemical studies for dystrophin show reduced staining.

questions.question:
Which of the following are mitochondrial disorders?

1. Myotonic dystrophy

2. Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers

3. Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

4. Rett's syndrome

5. Kearns-Sayre syndrome
questions.explanation:
The following conditions are mitochondrial disorders:

• Myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibers

• Leber hereditary optic neuropathy

• Kearns-Sayre syndrome

The proteins and tRNAs in the mitochondria may be encoded by 2 sets of genes:

• Nuclear genome - Mendelian inheritance patterns

• Mitochondrial genome (mtDNA) - maternally inherited, as the oocyte contributes all the mitochondria in the embryo

Mitochondrial disorders are caused by mutations in the mitochondrial genome.

The most consistent pathologic change in skeletal muscle is abnormal aggregates of mitochondria. These are seen preferentially in the subsarcolemmal area of affected myofibers, producing a ragged red fibers appearance, as shown below.

questions.question: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is most commonly caused by the mutation of genes encoding which of the following ion channels?
questions.explanation:
Hypokalemic periodic paralysis is most commonly caused by the mutation of the genes encoding calcium channels (CALCL1A3).

It is an autosomal dominant ion channel myopathy with an onset in adolescence. Males are usually affected more than females. It presents as proximal muscle weakness. Ocular and bulbar muscles are less likely to be involved.

The diagnosis is established by a low serum potassium level during an attack, after excluding secondary causes.

questions.question: In a child diagnosed with myotonia congenita, which of the following ion channel is likely to be mutated?
questions.explanation:
Mutations affecting the chloride channel CLC1 cause myotonia congenita. The resulting deficiency of CLC1 is responsible for the characteristic myotonia in myotonic dystrophy.

questions.question: Glial hamartia is a feature of which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Glial hamartia are seen in neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF 2). These are microscopic nodular collections of glial cells at abnormal locations, often in the superficial and deep layers of the cerebral cortex.

NF2 is associated with the following:

• Bilateral eighth-nerve schwannomas

• Multiple meningiomas

• Gliomas - typically ependymomas of the spinal cord

• Nonneoplastic lesions - schwannosis, meningioangiomatosis, and glial hamartia

Option A: NF 1 is associated with neurofibromas of all types, malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors, gliomas of the optic nerve, other glial tumors, hamartomatous lesions, and pheochromocytomas.

Option C: Tuberous sclerosis is associated with hamartomas within the CNS in the form of cortical tubers and subependymal nodules. Other lesions include subependymal giant-cell astrocytoma, renal angiomyolipomas, retinal glial hamartomas, pulmonary lymphangioleiomyomatosis, cardiac rhab­domyomas, and cysts in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas.

Option D: Von Hippel–Lindau disease is associated with hemangioblastomas of the CNS and cysts involving the pancreas, liver, and kidneys, and have a propensity to develop renal cell carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

NOTE: A hamartia is not considered to be a tumor and is distinct from a hamartoma. A hamartoma is a benign neoplasm characterized by tissue misarrangement similar to a hamartia.

questions.question: A pathologist is examining a histopathological slide showing pseudo-Meissner corpuscles. This finding is seen in which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation:
Focal collections of pseudo-Meissner corpuscles or tactile-like bodies (cells mimicking the appearance of Meissner corpuscles) is a feature of diffuse neurofibroma.

Note: Meissner corpuscles consist of a cutaneous nerve ending responsible for transmitting the sensations of fine, discriminative touch and vibration.
